What this volume is for

The 90-Day Ledger gets you through the language, the design round and the front end. This one covers the ground those three leave out — and it is the ground that has moved most since you last interviewed.

Three lanes run in parallel for 60 days. Each day gives you one question per lane, a Must cover line that is the marking scheme, a study link, and a full model answer you should not open until you have tried to answer without it.

Order matters inside each lane. Week 1 assumes nothing; every later week assumes the ones before it.

AI Engineering

From what a token actually is, through embeddings, RAG and agents, to evaluating and shipping an LLM feature inside a Spring Boot service. Written for a backend engineer, not a researcher — no gradient math, all systems.

Docker & Kubernetes

Linux namespaces and cgroups up through image layering, then the full Kubernetes object model: pods, controllers, services, ingress, config, probes, autoscaling, storage, RBAC, and how to debug a cluster at 2am.

AWS

IAM and the VPC first because everything else sits on them, then compute, storage, data, messaging, and the operational layer — with the cost and failure characteristics that interviewers actually probe.

Week 01

Ground Floor

What an LLM actually does - what a container actually is - what a region, AZ and IAM principal actually are.

Six days of definitions you will be asked to give in the first two minutes of a screen. Vague here reads as never having shipped it.

010/3

What the thing actually is

What is a large language model actually doing when it answers a question? Explain tokens, the context window, and why this is next-token prediction rather than lookup.

Must coverText splits into subword tokens, each an integer id. The model outputs a probability distribution over the next token, one at a time, feeding its own output back in. The context window is a shared budget for prompt plus output. Nothing is retrieved - the weights are a lossy compression of training data, which is why a confident wrong answer is produced by exactly the same mechanism as a right one.

StudyAnthropic - intro to Claude →

What problem does a container solve that a VM does not? Explain what a container actually is at the Linux level.

Must coverNot a lightweight VM. It is a normal Linux process with namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user) restricting what it can see and cgroups restricting what it can consume. It shares the host kernel, so there is no guest OS to boot - milliseconds not seconds, MBs not GBs. Image is a stack of read-only filesystem layers plus metadata; the container is the running process plus a thin writable layer.

StudyDocker - what is a container →

Explain regions, availability zones, and the shared responsibility model. Why is AZ choice an architecture decision rather than an ops detail?

Must coverA region is a geographic area; an AZ is an independent failure domain inside it with its own power, cooling and network. Inter-AZ latency is about 1ms so synchronous replication across AZs is fine, cross-region is tens to hundreds of ms so it is not. AWS secures the cloud itself, you secure what you put in it - patching, IAM, encryption, network rules. Single-AZ means one datacentre failure takes you down.

StudyAWS global infrastructure →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start with the unit. Text is not fed in as characters or words — it is split by a tokenizer into subword pieces, each mapped to an integer id. Common words are one token; rare words split into several. A useful rule of thumb for English is roughly 4 characters per token, so 750 words is about 1,000 tokens. This matters because tokens are the unit of billing, the unit of the context limit, and the unit of latency — everything you will later optimise is denominated in them.

Now the mechanism. The model takes the whole sequence so far and produces a probability distribution over the next token — every token in the vocabulary gets a score. One token is sampled, appended to the sequence, and the whole thing runs again. That is the entire loop. It is called autoregressive generation, and it explains the two properties you feel most: output is sequential, so a long answer genuinely takes longer, and output is stochastic, so the same prompt can produce different text.

The context window is the maximum sequence length the model can attend over, and it is a shared budget across your system prompt, the conversation history, retrieved documents and the generated output. Filling it with retrieved context leaves less room to answer. Attention is also not uniform across it — material at the very start and very end is attended to more reliably than material buried in the middle, which is why chunk ordering in a RAG prompt is a real design decision and not cosmetic.

The last part is the one that matters most in an interview: nothing is looked up. There is no index of facts being consulted. The weights are a lossy compression of the training corpus, and generation is reconstruction from that compression. A correct answer and a confidently wrong one are produced by exactly the same process — the model has no internal signal distinguishing recall from fabrication. That single fact is the architectural justification for everything else you will build: retrieval for knowledge, tool calls for facts, and deterministic code for decisions.

What one call actually costs you
Prompt:  system (600 tok) + history (2,400 tok) + retrieved chunks (4,000 tok) + question (40 tok)
         = 7,040 input tokens
Output:  ~500 tokens

Cost  = 7,040 x input_rate + 500 x output_rate
Latency = time-to-first-token (dominated by input processing)
        + 500 x per-token generation time   <-- sequential, cannot be parallelised

Consequence: trimming 2,000 tokens of retrieved context saves money.
             Trimming 200 tokens of OUTPUT saves money AND wall-clock time.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does the same prompt sometimes give a different answer?

Because a token is sampled from the distribution rather than taken as the maximum. Setting temperature to 0 makes it near-greedy, but it is still not a guarantee — floating-point non-determinism across GPU batching, and provider-side model updates, both change output. Design for it: never assert on exact strings, assert on structure and properties.

If it is just predicting the next token, how can it follow instructions?

Instruction-following is a learned behaviour, not a separate mechanism. Post-training on instruction-response pairs and preference data shifts the distribution so that text following an instruction becomes the high-probability continuation. It is still next-token prediction — which is precisely why instructions can be overridden by later text in the sequence, and why prompt injection works.

What actually happens when I exceed the context window?

The API rejects the request rather than silently truncating — that is the good case. The bad case is your own code truncating history to fit and silently dropping the part that mattered. Count tokens before sending, and make the trimming strategy explicit: summarise old turns, drop low-scoring chunks, never blind-truncate from the front.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The framing to avoid is a container is a lightweight VM. It is not a machine at all. A container is an ordinary Linux process running directly on the host kernel, with two kernel features applied to it: namespaces, which restrict what it can see, and cgroups, which restrict what it can consume.

There are several namespaces and each hides one kind of global resource. The pid namespace means the process sees itself as PID 1 and cannot see host processes. The net namespace gives it its own interfaces, routing table and port space — which is why two containers can both bind port 8080. The mnt namespace gives it its own filesystem view, which is how the image becomes the root filesystem. Then uts for hostname, ipc for shared memory, and user for uid mapping, which is what lets a process be root inside the container and unprivileged outside it.

cgroups handle the other half: CPU shares and quota, memory limits, IO and PID limits. This is where the two resource behaviours you must know come from — memory is incompressible, so exceeding the limit means the kernel OOM-kills the process immediately, while CPU is compressible, so exceeding the quota means you are throttled and simply run slower. Same mechanism, completely different symptom.

Compare that to a VM, which virtualises hardware and boots a whole guest kernel — hundreds of MB and tens of seconds, with strong isolation because the kernel boundary is not shared. A container shares the host kernel: milliseconds to start, MBs of overhead, and weaker isolation, because a kernel vulnerability crosses the boundary. That is the real trade and it is why hostile multi-tenancy uses VMs or microVMs like Firecracker, which is exactly what Fargate runs underneath.

Finally, separate image from container. An image is an immutable stack of read-only filesystem layers plus metadata — entrypoint, env, exposed ports. A container is a running process with those layers union-mounted plus a thin writable layer on top, which is discarded when it exits. That is why writes inside a container do not persist, and why a volume is the answer rather than a bigger disk.

Seeing the isolation directly
$ docker run --rm -it --memory=256m --cpus=0.5 alpine sh

/ # ps aux                 # only our own processes - pid namespace
PID   USER     COMMAND
    1 root     sh
    7 root     ps aux

/ # cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max      # the cgroup limit, in bytes
268435456

/ # hostname                # uts namespace: not the host's hostname
3f2a91c4b0de

# Exceed the memory limit and the kernel kills it - no warning, exit 137:
$ docker run --rm --memory=64m openjdk:21 java -Xmx512m -version
Killed
Follow-ups they will ask

Is a container more secure than a process, or less?

More than a bare process (namespaces plus dropped capabilities plus seccomp shrink the attack surface), far less than a VM (one shared kernel). Treat the container boundary as a strong operational boundary and a weak security boundary: run as non-root, drop all capabilities, read-only root filesystem, seccomp default — and use separate nodes or microVMs for genuinely untrusted workloads.

What is PID 1 and why does it matter?

Your process becomes PID 1, which has special kernel semantics: it does not get default signal handlers, so a naive process ignores SIGTERM entirely and gets SIGKILLed after the grace period — losing in-flight requests. It also must reap zombie children. Fix with an init like tini, or by handling SIGTERM explicitly, which Spring Boot's graceful shutdown does.

Why is my image 900MB when the jar is 40MB?

The base image. openjdk:21 ships a full JDK plus a full distro. Switch to a JRE base or distroless and you drop to a couple of hundred MB; multi-stage keeps the build tooling out entirely. Also check for a missing .dockerignore — copying the whole build directory including .git is a classic.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A region is a geographic area — eu-west-1, ap-south-1 — and it is the coarsest boundary in AWS. Most services are regional, data does not leave a region unless you move it, and pricing differs between them. An availability zone is one or more discrete datacentres inside a region with independent power, cooling and physical security, connected to the others by dedicated low-latency links.

The number that drives the architecture is the latency: inter-AZ round trip is about 1 millisecond, cross-region is tens to hundreds. That single fact is why synchronous replication across AZs is normal and free of design pain, while synchronous replication across regions is not — you would add the round trip to every write. So the default posture is: multi-AZ always, multi-region only when you have a stated RTO/RPO or a residency requirement that demands it.

AZ names are also per-account aliases. Your us-east-1a is not necessarily the same physical zone as another account's us-east-1a — AWS shuffles the mapping to stop everyone piling into the first letter. Use the AZ ID (use1-az1) when you genuinely need to correlate zones across accounts.

The shared responsibility model splits the stack. AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: physical facilities, the hypervisor, the managed service internals. You are responsible for security in the cloud: IAM policies, security groups, encryption choices, patching anything you run, and your data. The line moves with the service — on EC2 you patch the OS; on RDS AWS patches the engine but you still own network placement, encryption, credentials and backups; on S3 you own nothing but access control and encryption configuration, which is exactly where the well-known public-bucket incidents came from.

So AZ choice is architecture, not ops, for a simple reason: an AZ is the unit of failure AWS actually designs to. A single-AZ deployment has a documented, expected failure mode — one datacentre event takes you down entirely — and no amount of instance-level redundancy inside that AZ fixes it. Spreading across two AZs is the cheapest availability improvement available; three is what you need if you want to lose one and still have capacity headroom.

What multi-AZ actually looks like
Region: eu-west-1
+-- AZ eu-west-1a                    +-- AZ eu-west-1b
    subnet-public-a  (ALB node)          subnet-public-b  (ALB node)
    subnet-app-a     (2 app tasks)       subnet-app-b     (2 app tasks)
    subnet-data-a    (RDS primary)       subnet-data-b    (RDS standby, sync)

Lose AZ 1a entirely:
  ALB stops routing to 1a targets       (health checks, seconds)
  RDS promotes the 1b standby           (60-120s, DNS change, connections drop)
  Remaining capacity = 50%              <-- size for n-1, or you fail over into an overload

Note: 2 AZs means losing one costs you half your capacity.
      3 AZs means losing one costs you a third. That is why 3 is common for production.
Follow-ups they will ask

How many AZs should I use?

Two is the minimum for availability; three is the standard for production because losing one costs you 33% of capacity rather than 50%, and because quorum-based systems (etcd, Kafka, ZooKeeper) need an odd number to keep a majority. Some regions have more than three — using all of them adds little and increases cross-AZ data transfer cost.

What actually costs money about spreading across AZs?

Cross-AZ data transfer, billed in both directions, on every internal call that crosses a zone. For chatty service-to-service traffic this becomes a real line item that is invisible until you look. Mitigate with topology-aware routing so a caller prefers a same-zone endpoint, while still keeping replicas spread for availability.

Is a region ever a single point of failure in practice?

Yes — regional control planes and some global services have had correlated failures, and us-east-1 in particular hosts global service control planes. The practical mitigations are: do not put your DR mechanism in the same region as the thing it protects, keep static stability (the failover path must not require calling a control plane that is also down), and rehearse it.

020/3

Instructions, images, identity

Explain the system, user and assistant roles in a chat completion. What actually changes when you move an instruction from the user turn to the system prompt?

Must coverThe roles are a serialisation convention the model was trained on, not enforcement. The system prompt sets persona, rules and output contract and is more strongly attended to and more resistant to being overridden mid-conversation. Everything is still one token sequence - the system prompt costs tokens on every single call, which is why prompt caching matters. User content is untrusted input, and treating it as instruction is the root of prompt injection.

StudyAnthropic - system prompts →

What is an image layer, and why does the order of instructions in a Dockerfile change your build times and image size?

Must coverEach RUN, COPY and ADD creates a layer; layers are content-addressed and cached. A change invalidates that layer and every layer after it, so put rarely-changing things first (dependencies) and frequently-changing things last (your code). Deleting a file in a later layer does not shrink the image, it only hides it - the bytes are still in the earlier layer, which is how secrets leak into images.

StudyDocker - build cache →

Explain IAM users, roles, and policies. Why should application code on EC2 or EKS never hold an access key?

Must coverA policy is JSON granting or denying actions on resources, optionally with conditions. A user is a long-lived identity with permanent credentials; a role is an identity with no credentials that principals assume to get short-lived STS tokens. Roles rotate automatically and cannot be committed to git. Evaluation logic: explicit deny wins, then explicit allow, otherwise implicit deny.

StudyIAM - policies and permissions →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The roles are a serialisation convention, not an enforcement mechanism. Under the hood everything is concatenated into one token sequence with special delimiters marking where each turn begins. The model was post-trained on that format, so it has learned to treat system content as standing instruction and user content as the thing to respond to — but it is a learned tendency, not a wall.

Moving an instruction into the system prompt changes three things concretely. First, it persists: it is re-sent on every call and applies to the whole conversation rather than one turn. Second, it is attended to more strongly and is more resistant to being overridden by later text — models are explicitly trained to prefer the system instruction when it conflicts with a user turn. Third, and this is the operational one, it becomes a stable prefix, which is exactly what prompt caching keys on.

That prefix property is worth real money. A 2,000-token system prompt on 100,000 calls a day is 200 million input tokens. With caching, the identical prefix is charged at a large discount on cache hits, so the ordering rule is: most stable content first, most variable content last. System prompt, then tool definitions, then pinned reference material, then retrieved chunks, then the user turn. Put anything variable near the front and you invalidate the cache for everything after it.

The security consequence is the one interviewers push on. Because it is all one sequence, user content is data that looks exactly like instruction. Text arriving from a user, an uploaded file, a database field or a retrieved document can say ignore your instructions and there is no type system preventing the model from complying. Strengthening the system prompt reduces the success rate; it never eliminates it. The real control is that the model's tools cannot do anything the requesting user could not already do.

One more practical point: the system prompt is not a secret. Assume it is extractable, because in practice it is. Put behaviour there, never credentials, internal URLs, or the fact that a hidden capability exists.

Prompt layout for cache efficiency
[ system      ]  role, rules, output contract        <-- stable, cacheable
[ tools       ]  JSON schemas                        <-- stable, cacheable
[ pinned docs ]  policy text that rarely changes     <-- stable, cacheable
                 ---- cache breakpoint here ----
[ retrieved   ]  chunks for THIS question            <-- varies per request
[ history     ]  prior turns                         <-- grows
[ user        ]  the question                        <-- varies

Wrong order (kills the cache):
[ system ][ user question ][ tools ][ pinned docs ]
          ^ anything after the first variable token is uncacheable
Follow-ups they will ask

If the system prompt is not enforced, why use it at all?

Because it measurably shifts behaviour and it is the cheapest, fastest lever you have — it just is not a security boundary. Use it for tone, format, scope and refusal behaviour. Never rely on it for authorisation, and never treat the prompt says not to as a control you would defend to an auditor.

Should tool definitions go in the system prompt?

No — pass them in the dedicated tools parameter. The provider formats them into the sequence in the way the model was trained on, which materially improves call accuracy over describing tools in prose, and it is what enables structured tool_use blocks in the response rather than you parsing text.

How do I stop the system prompt from growing into 4,000 tokens of accumulated rules?

Treat it as code: it lives in git, it has an owner, and every rule added must come with an eval case demonstrating the failure it prevents. Rules added after an incident and never removed are how these become unmaintainable. Periodically delete rules and check whether the eval set still passes — most do not earn their tokens.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

An image is a stack of layers. Each RUN, COPY and ADD produces one: a tarball of the filesystem changes that instruction made, identified by the SHA-256 of its content. The final image is a manifest listing those layer digests plus config — entrypoint, env, user, exposed ports. At runtime they are union-mounted into a single filesystem view with a thin writable layer on top.

Content addressing gives you the build cache. Docker walks the Dockerfile and, for each instruction, checks whether it already has a layer for that instruction against that parent. If yes, it reuses it. The critical rule: a cache miss invalidates that layer and every layer after it. Cache is a prefix property, not a per-instruction one.

That is why instruction order determines build time. Dependencies change weekly; your source changes every commit. So copy the dependency descriptor and resolve dependencies first, in their own layer, then copy source. Do it the other way round — COPY . . before the dependency step — and every single commit re-downloads the entire dependency tree, turning a 20-second build into a four-minute one.

The size consequence is the one that catches people. Layers are additive only. Deleting a file in a later layer writes a whiteout marker; the bytes are still present in the earlier layer and still shipped. So RUN wget secret.tar && make && rm secret.tar as three separate instructions ships the secret in the image forever, retrievable by anyone who can pull it. Chain it into a single RUN so the file never exists at a layer boundary — or better, use a multi-stage build so the whole build environment is discarded.

Layers are also shared and cached per node. Two images built on the same base pull that base once. That is a real argument for standardising on one base image across your services — it cuts registry cost, network transfer, and pod start time on a cold node.

Cache-aware ordering, Maven example
# --- BAD: every code change re-resolves all dependencies ---
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
COPY . /src                    # <-- any file change busts everything below
WORKDIR /src
RUN mvn -q package

# --- GOOD: dependencies cached in their own layer ---
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY pom.xml .                              # changes rarely
RUN mvn -q dependency:go-offline            # cached until pom.xml changes
COPY src ./src                              # changes every commit
RUN mvn -q package -o -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
COPY --from=build /src/target/app.jar /app/app.jar
USER app
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75","-jar","/app/app.jar"]
Follow-ups they will ask

Does deleting a file in a later RUN reduce image size?

No. It adds a whiteout entry and slightly increases size. The bytes remain in the earlier layer and anyone who pulls the image can extract them — docker history and a layer extraction is all it takes. This is the mechanism behind most credentials-in-image leaks.

What is the difference between COPY and ADD?

ADD additionally auto-extracts local tar archives and can fetch remote URLs. Both behaviours are surprising and the URL fetch does no checksum verification, so the convention is: always COPY, and use an explicit RUN curl with a checksum when you need to download.

How do I get cache reuse in CI where every build starts on a fresh runner?

Use BuildKit with an external cache — --cache-from / --cache-to pointed at a registry ref or the CI provider's cache backend. Without it every CI build is fully cold regardless of how well the Dockerfile is ordered, which is why teams often think layer ordering does not matter.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Three nouns. A policy is a JSON document listing statements of Effect, Action, Resource and optional Condition — it grants or denies, and on its own it does nothing until attached. A user is a long-lived identity with permanent credentials: a password, or an access key ID and secret. A role is an identity with no credentials attached, that a principal assumes; STS then issues temporary credentials that expire, typically in an hour.

That expiry is the whole point. A leaked access key is valid until a human notices and revokes it — and the credential-scanning bots that trawl public GitHub find them in minutes. Temporary credentials expire on their own, are automatically rotated by the SDK, are never written to disk, and cannot be committed. So the rule is: humans federate, machines assume roles, and long-lived access keys are an exception that needs justification.

How the machine gets them differs by platform, but the shape is identical: something in the environment vouches for the workload's identity, and STS exchanges that for credentials. On EC2 it is the instance profile served by the Instance Metadata Service. On ECS it is the task role, fetched from a link-local endpoint. On EKS it is IRSA or Pod Identity — the pod's ServiceAccount token is exchanged, via an OIDC provider, for a role scoped to that specific ServiceAccount. In CI, GitHub Actions presents an OIDC token and assumes a role, which is how you get a deploy pipeline with zero stored secrets.

The evaluation logic is worth being able to recite, because it is the debugging algorithm. Start from implicit deny. An explicit Deny anywhere — identity policy, resource policy, SCP, permission boundary, session policy, VPC endpoint policy — wins immediately and unconditionally. Otherwise an explicit Allow is needed. For same-account access, an allow in either the identity policy or the resource policy suffices; for cross-account, you need an allow on both sides. That last clause is the source of most cross-account AccessDenied confusion.

Then the conditions layer, which is where least privilege actually gets expressed: restrict by source VPC endpoint, by tag matching, by MFA presence, by requested region. A policy allowing s3:GetObject on everything is not least privilege even if it is scoped to one bucket — scope it to a key prefix and a condition too.

A role assumed by a pod, not a key in a config
// Trust policy on the role - WHO may assume it (EKS IRSA)
{ "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:oidc-provider/oidc.eks..." },
  "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
  "Condition": { "StringEquals": {
      "oidc.eks...:sub": "system:serviceaccount:payments:settlement-worker" }}}

// Permission policy on the role - WHAT it may do
{ "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::settlements-prod/incoming/*",       // prefix, not bucket
  "Condition": { "StringEquals": {"aws:SourceVpce": "vpce-0a1b2c3d"} }}

# In the pod: nothing. No key, no secret, no env var.
# The SDK finds the projected token, calls STS, refreshes automatically.
Follow-ups they will ask

When is an IAM user still legitimate?

Rarely, and always with a note. A third-party SaaS that genuinely cannot do OIDC or cross-account role assumption; a legacy on-prem system without IAM Roles Anywhere. In both cases: dedicated user, single narrow policy, scheduled rotation, and CloudTrail alerting on use from unexpected sources. Never a shared user, never one with console access.

What is a permission boundary and how is it different from an SCP?

A boundary is attached to an identity and caps the maximum permissions that identity can have, regardless of its policies — used to let developers create roles safely. An SCP is attached to an OU or account in an Organization and caps everyone in it, including the root user. Neither grants anything; both only subtract.

A role has the right policy but I still get AccessDenied. Where do I look?

Walk the layers in order: SCP on the account, the identity policy, the resource policy (and for cross-account, both), the permission boundary, the session policy if the credentials came from an assume-role with one, the KMS key policy if anything is encrypted, and the VPC endpoint policy if the call goes through one. CloudTrail's errorMessage usually names the failing one; the IAM policy simulator resolves the rest.

030/3

Sampling, build craft, the network

Explain temperature and top-p. Why is an LLM feature hard to unit-test, and what do you do about it?

Must coverThe model produces a distribution; temperature reshapes it (low sharpens toward the argmax, high flattens), top-p truncates to the smallest set of tokens whose probability sums to p. Temperature 0 is near-deterministic but not guaranteed across hardware and versions. So you do not assert on exact strings - you assert on structure (schema validity), on properties (contains no PII, cites a real doc id), and you use an eval set with a grader rather than a unit test.

StudyAnthropic - API messages →

Write a production Dockerfile for a Spring Boot service. What would you flag in a review of one that uses a single FROM eclipse-temurin:21 and COPY target/app.jar?

Must coverMulti-stage: build with the JDK, ship on a JRE or distroless base. Copy the dependency descriptor and resolve dependencies before copying source so the dependency layer caches. Run as a non-root user. Pin base images by digest. Set container-aware JVM flags - modern JVMs read cgroup limits, but MaxRAMPercentage is how you leave headroom for metaspace and thread stacks. Add a .dockerignore or you ship the whole build directory.

StudyDocker - multi-stage builds →

Design a VPC for a three-tier application. Explain CIDR sizing, public vs private subnets, route tables, internet gateway and NAT.

Must coverA VPC is a private IP space split into subnets, each pinned to one AZ - so subnets per tier per AZ. Public means the route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway; private sends it to a NAT gateway for outbound only. Load balancers go public, application and database go private. Size CIDRs generously because you cannot shrink them, and never overlap with your on-prem ranges or peering breaks.

StudyAmazon VPC user guide →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

At each step the model produces a score for every token in its vocabulary, converted to probabilities by softmax. Temperature divides the scores before that softmax. Below 1 it sharpens the distribution toward the highest-scoring token; above 1 it flattens it, giving unlikely tokens a real chance. At 0 it is effectively greedy — always take the argmax.

Top-p (nucleus sampling) is a different knob applied after: sort tokens by probability, keep the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p, discard the rest, renormalise, sample. The value of top-p over a fixed top-k is that the candidate set adapts — where the model is confident, the nucleus is one or two tokens; where it is genuinely uncertain, it widens. Use one or the other as your primary control rather than tuning both at once.

For engineering work the settings are unglamorous: low temperature for anything with a correct answer — extraction, classification, routing, code, structured output — and higher only for genuinely generative tasks where variety is the goal. If you are tempted to raise temperature to fix a boring answer, the problem is almost always the prompt.

Now the testing problem. Even at temperature 0 you do not get a guarantee: floating-point non-determinism from GPU batching changes results at the margin, and the provider can update the model behind an alias. So string equality is not a test. Assert on properties that survive rewording: is the JSON schema-valid, does every cited id exist in the retrieved set, is the number equal to the value from the source system, does it refuse when it should, is there no PII in the output.

Above that sits the eval set — 100 to 300 real cases with graders, run in CI on every prompt, model or retrieval change. Deterministic graders where you can (schema, regex, exact-match on extracted fields), a model-as-judge with a fixed rubric where you cannot, and a small critical subset that must never regress. That is what replaces unit tests: you are not asserting one output, you are asserting an aggregate score with a floor, plus hard gates on the cases you cannot afford to break.

Testing behaviour, not strings
// BAD - will fail on the next model update for no real reason
assertEquals("The refund was processed on 12 March 2024.", response);

// GOOD - assert the properties that actually matter
var out = mapper.readValue(response, RefundSummary.class);   // 1. schema valid
assertEquals(LocalDate.of(2024,3,12), out.refundDate());     // 2. extracted field exact
assertTrue(retrievedIds.containsAll(out.citations()));       // 3. no invented citations
assertFalse(PII_PATTERN.matcher(out.narrative()).find());    // 4. no leakage

// And in CI, over the whole eval set:
//   aggregate score >= 0.92        (soft gate, fails the build)
//   critical-set pass rate == 1.0  (hard gate, no exceptions)
Follow-ups they will ask

Should I ever use temperature above 0 in a production backend?

Occasionally, and deliberately. Slightly above zero can help a model escape a repetitive failure loop, and it is required if you are sampling several candidates and picking the best (self-consistency). For a single-shot extraction or classification call, 0 is correct and anything else is unjustified variance you will later have to debug.

How big should the eval set be before I trust it?

Big enough that a one-case change does not move the aggregate meaningfully — practically, 100 is a usable floor and 300 is comfortable. Coverage matters more than size: it must include the failure classes you have actually seen in production, adversarial inputs, and out-of-scope questions that should be refused. Grow it from real incidents, never from imagination alone.

Does temperature 0 make prompt caching or retries safe to assume identical?

No. Treat every call as independently sampled. If you need a specific output to be stable across time — a summary shown on a dashboard, say — generate once and store the result. Re-deriving it on every read is both a cost and a consistency bug.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Take the review comment first, because it is the answer. A single-stage FROM eclipse-temurin:21 plus COPY target/app.jar has five problems: it ships a full JDK and build tooling to production, roughly quadrupling the image and the CVE surface; it runs as root; it depends on the jar having been built outside the image, so the build is not reproducible in CI; the base is a mutable tag, so tomorrow's build is not today's; and there is no layer separation, so nothing caches usefully.

Multi-stage fixes the first and third: build with the JDK in one stage, copy only the artefact into a JRE or distroless final stage. The build tooling, the source, the Maven cache and any credentials used during the build all stay behind in a stage that is never pushed.

For a Spring Boot service specifically, the layered-jar trick is worth knowing. Boot can split its fat jar into dependency, spring-boot-loader, snapshot-dependency and application layers; copying those as separate COPY instructions means a code-only change re-ships a few hundred KB rather than the whole 60MB jar. On a rolling deploy across many nodes that is a real pull-time saving.

Then the runtime hardening: a non-root user with an explicit UID, so the Kubernetes runAsNonRoot check can verify it; base image pinned by digest so the build is reproducible; a .dockerignore so .git, target/ and local env files never enter the build context; and no secrets in ENV, which is visible to anyone running docker inspect.

Finally the JVM flags. Modern JVMs are container-aware and read the cgroup limit, so -Xmx hardcoded to a number is wrong the moment the limit changes. Use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, and set it around 70–75 rather than 90, because heap is not the only thing in the container: metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, direct byte buffers and GC structures all live outside it, and it is that non-heap overflow — not the heap — that produces the mysterious exit 137 on a container that looks like it has spare memory.

Production Dockerfile, Spring Boot
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21@sha256:<digest> AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY pom.xml .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -q package -DskipTests \
 && java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/app.jar extract --destination /layers

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine@sha256:<digest>
RUN addgroup -S -g 10001 app && adduser -S -u 10001 -G app app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build --chown=10001:10001 /layers/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build --chown=10001:10001 /layers/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build --chown=10001:10001 /layers/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build --chown=10001:10001 /layers/application/ ./
USER 10001:10001
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
ENTRYPOINT ["java","org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
Follow-ups they will ask

Why MaxRAMPercentage 70 and not 90?

Because the container limit covers the whole process, not just the heap. Metaspace, JIT code cache, thread stacks (1MB each, and a servlet container has hundreds), direct buffers used by NIO and Netty, and GC metadata all sit outside -Xmx. Set it to 90 and a traffic spike that grows the thread pool pushes the process over the cgroup limit — the kernel OOM-kills it with plenty of free heap, which is a genuinely confusing incident.

Alpine or distroless for a JVM?

Distroless if you want the smallest attack surface — no shell, no package manager — at the cost of being unable to exec into it, which you work around with kubectl debug ephemeral containers. Alpine is smaller and has a shell, but uses musl rather than glibc, which has historically caused subtle issues with native libraries and DNS resolution. For a plain Spring Boot service either is fine; pick one and standardise.

Why ExitOnOutOfMemoryError?

Because a JVM that has thrown OOM is in an undefined state — some threads died, others carry on serving broken results, and the liveness probe may still pass. Exiting immediately turns an ambiguous zombie into a clean restart that Kubernetes handles. Add -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError writing to a mounted volume so you can actually diagnose it.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start with the address space. A VPC is a private IPv4 CIDR block you choose — say 10.20.0.0/16, giving 65,536 addresses. Size it generously: you cannot shrink a CIDR, and although you can add secondary blocks later, it is awkward. Critically, it must not overlap with your on-premises ranges or with any VPC you might ever peer with, because overlapping CIDRs cannot be routed between. In an organisation this means someone owns an IP allocation plan, and that is a real job.

Subnets carve the VPC up, and each subnet lives in exactly one AZ. That is the constraint that shapes the layout: a three-tier app across three AZs needs nine subnets, not three. AWS reserves five addresses in every subnet, so a /24 gives you 251 usable — and on EKS with the VPC CNI, every pod takes a subnet IP, so app subnets need to be far larger than instinct suggests. A /24 for pods will exhaust silently and leave pods stuck Pending.

The public/private distinction is entirely a routing decision, not a subnet property. A subnet is public if its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. It is private if it sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway — which gives outbound internet access but no inbound, because NAT only forwards return traffic for connections initiated from inside. A subnet with no default route at all is isolated, which is the right choice for a database tier that never needs to reach the internet.

So for the three tiers: load balancer in public subnets (it needs an inbound path from the internet), application in private subnets (reached only via the ALB, outbound via NAT for API calls and package pulls), database in private or isolated subnets (reached only from the app tier). The instance itself never gets a public IP; that is what makes it private, together with the routing.

Two cost and reliability notes that separate a real answer from a textbook one. NAT gateways are zonal: one per AZ for availability, and traffic that crosses an AZ to reach a NAT pays cross-AZ transfer on top of the NAT processing charge. And NAT is billed per hour and per gigabyte processed, so pulling container images and writing to S3 through it is a line item that surprises people — the fix is VPC endpoints: gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, which are free, and interface endpoints for ECR, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch and the rest.

Three tiers, three AZs
VPC 10.20.0.0/16  (eu-west-1)

              AZ a              AZ b              AZ c
public    10.20.0.0/24      10.20.1.0/24      10.20.2.0/24    -> IGW
          (ALB, NAT-a)      (ALB, NAT-b)      (ALB, NAT-c)

app       10.20.16.0/20     10.20.32.0/20     10.20.48.0/20   -> NAT in same AZ
          (4,091 usable - sized for pods, not instances)

data      10.20.200.0/24    10.20.201.0/24    10.20.202.0/24  -> no default route
          (RDS subnet group spans all three)

Route tables:
  rtb-public   0.0.0.0/0 -> igw-xxxx
  rtb-app-a    0.0.0.0/0 -> nat-a        <-- per-AZ, avoids cross-AZ charges
  rtb-data     (local only)              <-- cannot reach the internet at all
Endpoints:  S3 + DynamoDB (gateway, free) | ECR api/dkr, secretsmanager, logs (interface)
Follow-ups they will ask

One NAT gateway or one per AZ?

One per AZ for production: a single NAT is both a single point of failure and a source of cross-AZ transfer charges on every outbound byte from the other zones. In development, one NAT is a legitimate cost saving — just be explicit that it is a deliberate trade, not an oversight.

How do I give a private instance outbound access without a NAT gateway at all?

VPC endpoints for the AWS services it talks to, which covers most cases and is cheaper. For general internet egress there is no free option — the alternatives are a self-managed NAT instance (cheaper, but now you operate it) or simply not needing egress, which is achievable more often than teams assume once image pulls and AWS API calls go through endpoints.

Why can I not just use one big subnet per AZ?

You can, and small setups do. What you lose is the ability to express intent in routing and NACLs — with tiers as separate subnets, the database subnet has no route to the internet is a structural guarantee rather than a security group rule someone can loosen. Separation also keeps EKS pod IP consumption from starving your data tier.

040/3

Meaning, wiring, firewalls

What is an embedding? When is vector search the right tool and when is plain keyword search better?

Must coverA fixed-length float vector positioning text in a space where distance approximates semantic similarity; cosine similarity is the usual metric. It finds paraphrases keyword search misses. It is worse at exact identifiers, rare product codes, negation and numeric filters - a search for error code E4021 should be lexical. In practice you run both and fuse the rankings.

StudyAnthropic - embeddings →

How do two containers on the same host talk to each other, and how does that change once they are on different hosts? Explain the bridge network and container DNS.

Must coverDefault bridge gives each container a veth pair into a host bridge with a private IP; -p publishes a port via NAT on the host. On a user-defined network, containers resolve each other by name through an embedded DNS server - this is why Compose services address each other by service name. Across hosts you need an overlay network or, in Kubernetes, a CNI plugin giving every pod a routable cluster-wide IP.

StudyDocker - networking →

Security groups versus network ACLs - explain both, and say which one you reach for by default.

Must coverSecurity groups are stateful, attach to an ENI, allow-only, and can reference other security groups - which is the feature that matters, because it lets you say the database accepts traffic from the app tier without hardcoding IPs. NACLs are stateless, attach to a subnet, evaluate numbered rules in order, and support deny - so you need explicit rules for ephemeral return ports. Default to security groups; use NACLs for coarse subnet-level blocks.

StudyVPC - security groups →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

An embedding is a fixed-length vector of floats — commonly 384 to 3,072 dimensions — produced by a model trained so that texts with similar meaning land close together in that space. Closeness is almost always measured by cosine similarity, the angle between vectors, because it ignores magnitude and cares only about direction. Most embedding models emit unit-normalised vectors, in which case cosine similarity and dot product are the same computation.

The property that makes it useful is that it captures paraphrase. How do I stop a recurring payment and cancel my subscription billing share almost no words but sit close in embedding space. Keyword search scores them near zero. That is the entire value proposition, and it is why semantic search transformed help-centre and documentation retrieval.

Now the failure modes, which are the interesting half. Embeddings are bad at exactness. An error code E4021 and E4012 embed almost identically — the model has no notion that one digit changes everything. They are bad at negation: refunds are permitted and refunds are not permitted are close neighbours, which in a policy corpus is dangerous. They are bad at rare proper nouns the model never saw, and useless for numeric or date filters — transactions over £500 last March is a query, not a similarity.

So the rule: use vector search when the query is conceptual and the corpus is prose. Use lexical search — BM25 — when the query contains identifiers, codes, names or exact phrases. In production you almost always run both and fuse the rankings, because you do not get to know in advance which kind of query a user will type. And anything expressible as a filter (tenant, date range, document type, status) belongs in structured metadata applied as a filter, never encoded into the embedding and hoped for.

One practical constraint that surprises people: embeddings from different models are not comparable. There is no shared coordinate system. Changing embedding model means rebuilding the entire index from source documents — you cannot convert. That makes the embedding model a stickier choice than it appears on day one.

Where each retrieval mode wins
Query                                        Vector   BM25    Filter
-------------------------------------------  ------   -----   ------
"how do I stop a recurring payment"            WIN      weak     -
"cancel subscription"                          WIN      weak     -
"error code E4021"                             FAIL     WIN      -
"merchant ACME-GB-0042 chargeback"             weak     WIN      -
"refunds are NOT permitted after 90 days"      RISK     WIN      -
"transactions over 500 GBP in March 2024"       -        -       WIN

RISK = negation: the vector for "refunds are permitted" is a near-neighbour,
       so the retriever can hand the generator the exact opposite of the policy.

Production answer: BM25 + vector, fused by RRF, with metadata filters applied
                   INSIDE the search, then a cross-encoder rerank on the top 50.
Follow-ups they will ask

What dimension should I choose?

Higher dimensions capture more nuance but cost proportionally more memory and search time — 40M vectors at 1,536 dims in float32 is roughly 250GB before index overhead. Many modern models support Matryoshka truncation, letting you keep the first 512 dimensions with a small recall loss. Decide from a recall measurement on your own eval set, not from the model card.

Why does my metadata filter destroy recall?

Because of when it is applied. Post-filtering retrieves the top-k globally and then discards non-matching results — so a narrow filter can leave you with two results out of fifty. Pre-filtering restricts the candidate set before the ANN search, which is correct but is only supported well by some indexes. Check which your vector store does; it is a common silent quality bug.

Should I embed the question or a rewritten version of it?

Usually a rewritten version. Conversational questions (what about last month?) are meaningless out of context, so a cheap rewriting step that resolves references against the conversation history measurably improves retrieval. Some systems also embed a hypothetical answer rather than the question (HyDE), since answers sit closer to documents than questions do.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

On a single host with the default bridge network, each container gets a virtual ethernet pair: one end inside its network namespace as eth0, the other attached to a Linux bridge (docker0) on the host. The bridge gives them a private subnet, typically 172.17.0.0/16, and they can reach each other by IP. Outbound traffic is source-NATed to the host's address; inbound requires -p 8080:8080, which installs a DNAT rule forwarding a host port to the container.

The default bridge deliberately has no DNS. On a user-defined network, Docker runs an embedded DNS resolver at 127.0.0.11 inside each container, resolving container and network-alias names to current IPs. That is exactly why in Compose you write jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/app — db is the service name and the embedded resolver answers it. It also means IP addresses are never something you hardcode, because they change on every restart.

Across hosts, that model breaks: 172.17.0.2 exists on every machine and means something different on each. Docker's answer is an overlay network using VXLAN encapsulation. Kubernetes takes a different and stronger position, mandated by its network model: every pod gets an IP that is routable from every other pod, on any node, with no NAT between pods. A CNI plugin implements this — Calico with routing or overlay, Cilium with eBPF, and on EKS the AWS VPC CNI, which assigns each pod a real VPC address from your subnet.

That last one has a concrete consequence worth knowing. Because pods take real VPC IPs, subnet sizing is driven by pod count, not node count, and the number of pods per node is capped by how many ENIs and secondary addresses the instance type supports — a small instance may top out at 8 or 17 pods regardless of its CPU and memory. Prefix delegation raises that ceiling substantially, and it is a standard EKS tuning step.

Compose is worth positioning honestly in an interview: it is a local development and integration-test tool. It gives you the real Postgres, the real Kafka, the real network naming, on one machine, with one command. It is not a production orchestrator — no rescheduling, no health-driven replacement, no multi-node scaling. Say that explicitly; conflating Compose with orchestration is a junior signal.

Same app, three networking models
# 1. Local: user-defined bridge, DNS by service name
services:
  api:  { build: ., ports: ["8080:8080"], depends_on: [db] }
  db:   { image: postgres:16, environment: [POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev] }
# api reaches the database at  db:5432  - resolved by Docker's embedded DNS

# 2. Kubernetes: Service DNS, stable across pod churn
#    api pod reaches  postgres.payments.svc.cluster.local:5432
#    -> ClusterIP -> kube-proxy iptables/IPVS -> one of the ready pod IPs

# 3. EKS with VPC CNI: the pod IP is a real VPC address
$ kubectl get pod api-7d9f -o wide
NAME       IP            NODE
api-7d9f   10.20.19.214  ip-10-20-16-33   # <-- from YOUR app subnet
# Consequence: a /24 app subnet holds ~251 PODS, not 251 nodes.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why can two containers both bind port 8080?

Each has its own network namespace, so each has its own complete port space — there is no conflict until you publish them to the same host port. In Kubernetes the same logic applies per pod, which is also why two containers in the same pod cannot both bind 8080: they share one network namespace.

What is host networking and when would I use it?

hostNetwork: true drops the network namespace so the pod uses the node's interfaces and ports directly. It removes a small amount of overhead and is used by infrastructure DaemonSets that must see node traffic — CNI agents, some ingress controllers, node exporters. For application workloads it is a bad default: you lose port isolation, collide with other pods, and weaken the security boundary.

How does a pod resolve a Service name?

CoreDNS runs in the cluster and the kubelet writes its address into each pod's /etc/resolv.conf, along with a search path of <ns>.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local. That search path is why postgres works from the same namespace but you need postgres.payments from another — and why a name with a dot in it can unexpectedly skip the search path entirely.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Security groups are stateful, instance-level (really ENI-level) firewalls. Stateful means you write one rule for the direction you care about and return traffic is automatically permitted — allow inbound 443 and the response goes back without an outbound rule. They are allow-only: there is no deny, so the default is deny-everything and every rule adds permission. Multiple groups on one ENI are additive, and rules are evaluated as a set rather than in order, so there is no precedence to reason about.

The feature that actually matters is that a security group rule can reference another security group as its source. So the database group says allow 5432 from sg-app, and that stays correct forever as instances scale, are replaced, and change IPs. It expresses the relationship — the app tier may reach the database — rather than a snapshot of addresses. Once you have used this you stop writing CIDR rules for internal traffic.

Network ACLs are stateless, subnet-level, and support both allow and deny. Stateless is the trap: because return traffic is not tracked, an inbound allow on 443 also needs an outbound allow on the ephemeral port range (1024–65535) or responses are dropped. Rules are numbered and evaluated in order, first match wins, which means insertion order matters and a broad low-numbered rule shadows everything below it.

The practical guidance: default to security groups for essentially everything. They are more expressive, harder to get wrong, and they carry the identity-style semantics that survive scaling. Reach for NACLs for the narrow cases they are actually good at — a blanket subnet-level deny of a specific CIDR during an incident, or a coarse guarantee that an isolated data subnet cannot talk to the internet regardless of what someone does to a security group.

Think of it as defence in depth with different granularities: NACL is the perimeter fence around a neighbourhood, security group is the lock on each door. Most of your security policy belongs on the doors.

Chained security groups, no IPs anywhere
sg-alb    ingress: 443 from 0.0.0.0/0
          egress:  8080 to sg-app

sg-app    ingress: 8080 from sg-alb          <-- source is a GROUP, not a CIDR
          egress:  5432 to sg-data
                   443  to 0.0.0.0/0         (outbound API calls via NAT)

sg-data   ingress: 5432 from sg-app
          egress:  (none)                     <-- database initiates nothing

Scale the app tier from 2 to 200 instances: no rule changes.
Replace every instance: no rule changes.
Compare with "allow 5432 from 10.20.16.0/20" - correct until someone
adds a subnet, and it also lets ANY pod in that subnet reach the database.

NACL on the data subnet (belt and braces):
  100 ALLOW 5432 from 10.20.16.0/20   |  100 ALLOW 1024-65535 to 10.20.16.0/20
  *   DENY  all                       |  *   DENY  all
  ^ inbound                              ^ outbound - required, because STATELESS
Follow-ups they will ask

What are the limits I should know?

Default 60 inbound and 60 outbound rules per security group, and 5 groups per ENI (both adjustable, with a combined cap). A referenced security group counts as one rule regardless of how many instances are in it — another argument for referencing groups over enumerating CIDRs, which is how teams hit the limit.

If security groups are allow-only, how do I block a specific attacking IP?

You cannot with a security group — that is exactly the NACL case. Add a low-numbered explicit deny on the subnet NACL, or better, block it at WAF on the load balancer where you also get rate-based rules and logging. NACL is the blunt instrument for when you need it now.

Does a security group protect me from traffic inside the same subnet?

Yes, and this is the key difference from a NACL. NACLs only evaluate traffic crossing the subnet boundary, so two instances in the same subnet talk freely regardless of NACL rules. Security groups are enforced at each ENI, so they apply to same-subnet traffic too — which is why they, not NACLs, are your lateral-movement control.

050/3

Indexes, registries, instances

How does a vector database find nearest neighbours without comparing against every vector? Explain HNSW and the recall-latency tradeoff.

Must coverExact search is O(n) per query, so production uses approximate nearest neighbour. HNSW builds a multi-layer navigable graph - coarse hops at the top, fine at the bottom - giving roughly log-time search at high recall, at the cost of memory and slow inserts. IVF partitions into clusters and searches only the nearest few, which is cheaper on memory but needs training. The knobs (efSearch, nprobe) trade recall against latency, and you must also handle metadata filtering, which can silently destroy recall if applied after the search.

StudyHNSW paper →

What is the difference between a tag and a digest, and why should a production deployment pin the digest? What else belongs in a container supply chain story?

Must coverA tag is a mutable pointer; latest can mean something different tomorrow, so identical manifests can produce different running code. A digest is the immutable sha256 of the manifest. Pin digests in production and let a bot raise the bump as a reviewable change. Around that: scan images for CVEs in CI, generate an SBOM, sign images and verify signatures at admission, and use a private registry with immutable tags enabled.

StudyOCI image spec →

Walk through choosing an EC2 instance type, then explain what an Auto Scaling group actually gives you beyond adding instances.

Must coverFamilies encode a ratio - c is compute-heavy, m balanced, r memory-heavy, and Graviton is usually cheaper per unit of work for JVM services. Match the ratio to your profile, then size. An ASG gives you three things: replacement of failed instances against a health check, distribution across AZs, and scaling policies. The health check source matters - switch it to ELB so an instance that is running but not serving gets replaced.

StudyEC2 Auto Scaling →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Exact nearest-neighbour search means comparing the query against every vector — O(n), which at 40 million vectors and 1,536 dimensions is billions of floating-point operations per query. Fine for 10,000 vectors, hopeless at scale. So production systems use approximate nearest neighbour: give up a small amount of recall in exchange for orders of magnitude less work.

HNSW — Hierarchical Navigable Small World — is the dominant algorithm. Build a multi-layer graph where each vector is a node linked to its near neighbours. The top layer is sparse with long-range links; each layer down is denser. Search starts at the top, greedily walks toward the query, drops a layer, refines, and repeats. It is a skip list generalised to metric space: coarse hops first, fine hops last, giving roughly logarithmic search time at 95–99% recall.

HNSW's costs are memory and write behaviour. The graph lives in RAM and the links themselves are substantial — often comparable to the vectors. Inserts are relatively expensive because they require finding neighbours and updating links, and deletes are typically soft: the node is tombstoned and only really removed on a rebuild. That matters for compliance — a deletion request may leave the vector present but unreturned until the index is rebuilt, and you need to know which your store does.

IVF is the main alternative: cluster the vectors with k-means, and at query time search only the nprobe nearest clusters. Much lower memory, cheap inserts, but it needs a training pass over representative data, and recall degrades when a query sits near a cluster boundary. Often combined with product quantisation (IVF-PQ), which compresses vectors into codes — big memory savings, some recall loss — which is how billion-scale indexes fit on reasonable hardware.

The knobs are the interview content. HNSW has M (links per node, build-time), efConstruction (build quality) and efSearch (candidates explored per query, the runtime recall/latency dial). IVF has nlist and nprobe. Raising efSearch or nprobe raises recall and latency together, monotonically — so tune it against a labelled set until recall stops improving, then stop, because the last two points of recall usually cost double the latency.

The tuning curve you should actually measure
HNSW, 40M vectors, M=32, efConstruction=200

efSearch   recall@10   p99 latency   notes
   16        0.87         4 ms       too lossy for a RAG generator
   64        0.96         9 ms       <-- knee of the curve
  128        0.975       17 ms
  256        0.982       33 ms       +0.7% recall for 2x latency
  512        0.986       68 ms       not worth it

Memory: 40M x 1536 dims x 4 bytes            = 245 GB  (vectors)
      + 40M x M x 2 x 4 bytes (graph links)  =  10 GB
  -> float32 does not fit one machine. Options:
       scalar quantise to int8   -> 61 GB, recall -1%
       Matryoshka truncate 512d  -> 82 GB, recall -2%
       shard across nodes        -> full recall, more moving parts
Follow-ups they will ask

When is a dedicated vector database actually necessary?

Later than vendors suggest. Under roughly a million vectors, pgvector on the Postgres you already run is usually the right answer — you get transactions, joins to your real metadata, one backup story, and one system to operate. Move to a dedicated store when you need billion-scale, sub-10ms at high QPS, or advanced hybrid and filtering features Postgres cannot match.

How does filtering interact with the ANN index?

Badly, if done naively. Post-filtering searches globally then discards non-matches, so a selective filter can return almost nothing. Pre-filtering restricts the candidate set first but can fragment the graph traversal. The best implementations do filtered traversal — checking the predicate during the walk. This is a real differentiator between vector stores and worth asking about explicitly.

What happens to recall as I add vectors over time?

HNSW degrades gradually with heavy churn, because tombstoned deletions leave dead nodes in the graph and incremental inserts produce a worse structure than a fresh build. Schedule periodic rebuilds and monitor recall against a fixed labelled query set — index quality drift is silent, and nobody notices until answer quality visibly drops.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A tag is a mutable, human-friendly pointer to a manifest. Nothing stops someone pushing a different image to v1.4.2 tomorrow. A digest is the SHA-256 of the manifest content — @sha256:abc123… — and it is immutable by construction: change any byte and it is a different digest.

The failure this creates is subtle and genuinely dangerous. Two pods created from the same Deployment at different times, both saying image: app:v1.4.2, can be running different code — because the second one pulled after the tag moved. Your rollout looks complete and consistent; it is not. Debugging that is miserable, because every piece of evidence says the versions match.

So production pins the digest, and something else keeps it current. The pattern is: CI builds, pushes with both a semantic tag and the digest, then a bot (Renovate, Argo CD Image Updater, or your pipeline) opens a pull request updating the digest in the manifest repository. The bump becomes a reviewable, revertible commit rather than an invisible side effect. That is also what makes GitOps meaningful — the repository states exactly what is running.

Around that sits the rest of the supply chain, and an interviewer will expect you to name the layers. Build: pinned base images, reproducible builds, no secrets in layers. Scan: Trivy or Grype in CI, failing on critical CVEs, plus continuous rescanning of already-published images because new CVEs are discovered against unchanged bytes. Attest: generate an SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX) so you can answer are we affected by this CVE in minutes rather than days. Sign: cosign signatures, ideally keyless via OIDC. Verify: an admission policy that rejects any image lacking a valid signature from your CI identity, and rejects any image not from your registry.

That last step is the one that converts the rest from paperwork into a control. Signing without verification at admission proves nothing — the check has to be enforced in the cluster, and it has to fail closed.

Pin, sign, verify
# CI: build, push, sign
docker buildx build -t $ECR/payments-api:1.4.2 --push .
DIGEST=$(crane digest $ECR/payments-api:1.4.2)
cosign sign --yes $ECR/payments-api@$DIGEST          # keyless, OIDC identity

# Manifest (what GitOps applies) - digest, not tag
spec:
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: 1234.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/payments-api@sha256:9f2c...

# Admission policy - the part that makes it real (Kyverno)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce        # fail closed
  rules:
    - name: verify-signature
      match: { any: [{ resources: { kinds: [Pod] } }] }
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences: ["1234.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/*"]
          attestors: [{ entries: [{ keyless: { subject: "https://github.com/org/*" }}]}]
    - name: no-other-registries
      match: { any: [{ resources: { kinds: [Pod] } }] }
      validate:
        pattern: { spec: { containers: [{ image: "1234.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/*" }] } }
Follow-ups they will ask

Is imagePullPolicy: Always a substitute for digests?

No, it is nearly the opposite. Always guarantees you re-resolve the tag on every pod start, which makes drift more likely — a pod restarting at 3am silently picks up whatever the tag points to now. With a digest, the pull policy barely matters because the content is fixed. Note also that :latest defaults to Always, which is one of several reasons not to use it.

Where do image pull secrets fit on EKS?

For ECR in the same account, nowhere — the node's IAM role grants pull access and the credential helper handles it. You need imagePullSecrets for third-party private registries (Docker Hub paid, Quay), and those secrets should come from Secrets Manager via the CSI driver rather than being committed. Cross-account ECR uses a repository policy, not a pull secret.

How do I answer are we affected by this new CVE?

With an SBOM per image stored alongside the artefact, plus a registry that rescans continuously. Then it is a query — which images contain this package at this version, and which of those are currently deployed. Without SBOMs the honest answer is a multi-day investigation, which is precisely the scenario Log4Shell made everyone live through.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Instance families encode a ratio of resources, not a quality tier. c is compute-optimised (2GB RAM per vCPU), m is general purpose (4GB), r is memory-optimised (8GB), i and d add fast local NVMe, g and p add GPUs, t is burstable with CPU credits. The generation number is the hardware age, and the suffix matters: g means Graviton (ARM), i means Intel, a means AMD, n means enhanced networking.

So the choice is: profile your workload, find its actual CPU-to-memory ratio, pick the family matching it, then size. A JVM service typically lands on m or r. And for almost any JVM workload, Graviton is the default recommendation — roughly 20% cheaper per hour with comparable or better performance, and since Java is architecture-neutral the migration is usually just building a multi-arch image. Say that in an interview; it shows current, cost-aware knowledge.

Avoid t family for production services with sustained load. Burstable instances earn CPU credits when idle and spend them under load; exhaust the balance and you are throttled to the baseline — sometimes 10 or 20% of a vCPU. The symptom is a service that performs fine for twenty minutes after deploy and then degrades catastrophically, which is a genuinely confusing incident if you do not know the mechanism.

An Auto Scaling group is not primarily a scaling tool. It gives you three things, and only the third is scaling. First, replacement: it maintains a desired count, so a failed instance is terminated and replaced automatically. Second, AZ distribution: given subnets in multiple zones it balances across them and rebalances after a zone recovers. Third, scaling policies — target tracking on a metric, step scaling, or scheduled.

The detail that separates people who have run this is the health check type. The default is EC2, which only checks that the hypervisor thinks the instance is alive — a JVM that has deadlocked, OOMed or is returning 500s to every request passes it forever. Set health check type to ELB so the load balancer's application-level check drives replacement, and set a health check grace period long enough for a JVM to start or the ASG will kill instances during boot in an endless loop.

An ASG that actually replaces broken instances
AutoScalingGroup:
  MinSize: 3            # n-1 across 3 AZs: lose one, still serve
  MaxSize: 12
  DesiredCapacity: 3
  VPCZoneIdentifier: [subnet-app-a, subnet-app-b, subnet-app-c]

  HealthCheckType: ELB               # <-- NOT the default 'EC2'
  HealthCheckGracePeriod: 300        # JVM start + warmup, or it kills itself

  MixedInstancesPolicy:
    Overrides: [m7g.large, m7g.xlarge, m6g.large]   # diversify -> spot capacity
    InstancesDistribution:
      OnDemandBaseCapacity: 3                       # baseline never on spot
      OnDemandPercentageAboveBaseCapacity: 20       # burst is 80% spot

  TargetTrackingPolicy:
    Metric: ALBRequestCountPerTarget    # not CPU - this is an IO-bound service
    TargetValue: 800

Warm-up matters for JVMs: a fresh instance is slow until JIT compiles.
Use a longer grace period + slow-start on the target group, or the new
instance takes full traffic while still interpreting bytecode.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not scale on CPU?

Because a typical Spring Boot service is IO-bound — blocked on the database or a downstream call. Under overload, latency and queue depth climb while CPU sits at 30%, so a CPU-based policy never fires and the service degrades without scaling. Scale on the thing that saturates: requests per target, in-flight requests, or queue depth.

What is the difference between a launch template and a launch configuration?

Launch configurations are the deprecated original — immutable, no versioning, no mixed instance types. Launch templates support versions, mixed instances, spot, and newer features. If you see launch configurations in an interview scenario, flagging them as legacy is a small easy point.

How does an ASG interact with a rolling deploy?

Through instance refresh: it replaces instances in batches honouring a minimum healthy percentage, optionally with a checkpoint to pause and verify. That gives you a rolling deploy without extra tooling. For anything needing traffic-percentage control or automatic metric-based rollback, use CodeDeploy blue/green against the target groups instead.

060/3

Week 1 synthesis: ship one service three ways

Design the smallest useful LLM feature in your payments service - a natural-language search over transaction history. What are the components, and where does it fail?

Must coverComponents: intent parse, structured filter extraction, query the real datastore, then a generation step that only summarises returned rows. The key design move is that the model must not invent numbers - it converts language to a query and narrates results, so every figure is traceable to a row. Failure modes: ambiguous date ranges, injection through transaction descriptions, latency budget, and cost per query at scale. State a fallback to plain filters when confidence is low.

StudyAnthropic - tool use →

Containerise a Spring Boot service properly, then explain how you would prove the image is production-ready before it goes anywhere near a cluster.

Must coverMulti-stage build, JRE base, non-root user, digest-pinned base, .dockerignore, health endpoint exposed. Prove it: build reproducibly in CI, scan for CVEs and fail on high, run the image locally against a compose stack and hit the health and readiness endpoints, check the image size and startup time, confirm it respects a memory limit by running it with one and watching it not get OOMKilled.

StudySpring Boot - container images →

Put that container on AWS behind a load balancer across two AZs, with no public database. Name every component and the traffic path.

Must coverRoute 53 to an internet-facing ALB in public subnets in two AZs, target group of instances or tasks in private subnets, ASG spanning both AZs, RDS Multi-AZ in private subnets. Security groups chained: ALB accepts 443 from the internet, app accepts its port only from the ALB security group, database accepts 5432 only from the app security group. NAT gateway per AZ for outbound. ACM certificate on the ALB, TLS terminated there.

StudyApplication Load Balancer →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The first move is to reject the obvious architecture. Natural-language search over transactions is not RAG — the data is structured, it is authoritative, and the answers contain money. So the model does not retrieve transaction text and summarise it. The model's job is translation: turn the question into a typed, validated query against the transaction store, then narrate the rows that come back.

Components, in order. A parse step with tool calling: a JSON schema with fields for date range, amount bounds, merchant, status, and free-text description match. Low temperature, no prose output. A validation and authorisation layer in your own code: reject anything malformed, clamp the date range, and — critically — inject the caller's account scope server-side rather than trusting a field the model produced. A query execution against the real datastore with the normal indexes and limits. A narration step that receives the returned rows and is instructed to summarise only what is present. Finally a rendering step that shows the actual table alongside the narration.

The single most important design property: every number a user sees comes from a row, not from the model. The model never does arithmetic, never states a total it was not given, and never fills a gap. Totals are computed in Java. This is what makes the feature acceptable in a payments context at all, and it is the sentence to lead with in an interview.

Failure modes worth naming unprompted. Ambiguous time expressions — last quarter means different things to different users, so echo the interpreted filter back visibly and let them correct it. Prompt injection through transaction descriptions, which are attacker-controlled free text a merchant can set — so descriptions reach the model as clearly delimited data and the model has no tool that could act on them. Empty results, where the model is tempted to be helpful and invent; instruct explicit no-results behaviour and test it. Latency, since this is two model calls plus a query — stream the narration. Cost per query, modelled up front.

And the fallback: when the parse step's confidence is low or validation fails, do not retry blindly — render the ordinary filter UI pre-populated with whatever was understood. Degrading to the deterministic path is a feature, not an admission of defeat.

Language in, typed query out, numbers from rows
// 1. Model produces ONLY this - never prose, never numbers
record TxnQuery(LocalDate from, LocalDate to, BigDecimal minAmount,
                BigDecimal maxAmount, String merchantContains,
                Status status, String freeText) {}

// 2. YOUR code decides what it is allowed to see
var q    = validate(model.parse(question));                  // clamp, reject junk
var rows = txnRepo.search(q, currentUser().accountIds());    // scope injected HERE
                                                             //   never from the model

// 3. Totals computed in Java, not generated
var total = rows.stream().map(Txn::amount).reduce(ZERO, BigDecimal::add);

// 4. Model narrates a fact sheet it cannot extend
var facts = "Rows returned: " + rows.size()
          + ". Total: " + total
          + ". Date range applied: " + q.from() + " to " + q.to()
          + ". Summarise ONLY these rows. State no figure not listed above."
          + " If rows is 0, say no matching transactions were found and stop.";
var answer = model.narrate(facts, rows);

// 5. UI renders the TABLE and the narration side by side.
//    The table is the source of truth; the prose is a convenience.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why two model calls instead of one that does everything?
