Agents, autoscaling, functions

What is an agent, and when is it the wrong choice? Describe the loop and how you keep it from running away.

Must coverAn agent is a model in a loop with tools, deciding its own next step rather than following a fixed pipeline. Use it when the sequence of steps genuinely cannot be known in advance. Use a workflow - deterministic code calling the model at fixed points - whenever it can, because workflows are testable, cheaper and debuggable. Controls: hard iteration cap, per-run token and cost budget, a timeout, tool allowlists per context, human approval for irreversible actions, and full trace logging of every tool call. Most production systems that call themselves agents are workflows, and that is the correct outcome.

StudyAnthropic - building effective agents →

How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decide, and why does CPU-based autoscaling fail for an IO-bound Spring service?

Must coverHPA reads metrics on an interval and computes desiredReplicas = ceil(current * (currentMetric / targetMetric)), with a tolerance band and stabilisation windows to damp flapping. It needs metrics-server for CPU and a custom or external metrics adapter for anything else. It fails for IO-bound services because the pod is blocked on the database, not burning CPU - queue depth grows and latency climbs while CPU sits at 20% and HPA does nothing. Scale on the thing that actually saturates: requests per second, in-flight requests, or SQS queue depth via KEDA. Also: HPA cannot scale nodes, so pair it with Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter.

StudyKubernetes - HPA →

Explain the Lambda execution model - cold starts, concurrency, and what breaks when a Spring Boot developer lifts a service into it unchanged.

Must coverLambda creates an execution environment per concurrent request; code outside the handler runs once per environment and is reused, so that is where connections and clients belong. A cold start is environment creation plus your init, and a Spring context is seconds of it - the usual fixes are SnapStart, provisioned concurrency, or not using Lambda for that workload. Concurrency is per-account and per-function; reserved concurrency protects a function, and unbounded concurrency will exhaust an RDS connection pool instantly, which is what RDS Proxy exists for. Timeout is capped at 15 minutes and payloads at 6MB synchronous.

StudyLambda - execution environment →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

An agent is a model in a loop with tools, where the model decides what to do next. That last clause is the entire definition. A workflow is deterministic code that calls the model at fixed points — you decide the steps, the model fills in the language-shaped parts.

The distinction matters because it is a spectrum of who holds control flow, and control flow is what you can test. In a workflow, the sequence is in your code: you can unit-test it, reason about its cost, bound its latency, and read the stack trace when it breaks. In an agent, the sequence is emergent — it differs run to run, cost is unbounded until you bound it, and debugging means reading a trace of decisions rather than a stack.

So the rule is: use a workflow whenever the steps can be known in advance, and reach for an agent only when they genuinely cannot. Most tasks that sound agentic are not. Extract fields from this document, validate them, route to a queue is a workflow with three model calls. Answer a question about our docs is a workflow: retrieve, generate. Building those as agents adds nondeterminism and cost for nothing.

Genuine agent territory is where the path depends on what you find: debugging an unfamiliar failure, multi-step research where each finding changes the next question, or an open-ended task over a large tool surface. Anthropic's own guidance is blunt about this — start with the simplest thing, add agency only when simpler patterns demonstrably fail — and repeating that framing in an interview signals you have read past the marketing.

Controls, and there should be several, because an agent without them is an unbounded liability. A hard iteration cap. A token and cost budget per run, enforced, with the run terminated when exceeded. A wall-clock timeout. Tool allowlists per context, so a customer-facing agent simply does not have the refund tool in its list. Human approval for irreversible actions, out of band, in a way the model cannot synthesise. Full tracing of every tool call with arguments and results, because without it you cannot investigate anything. And loop detection — the same tool with the same arguments twice means break out.

Close with the honest observation: most production systems that call themselves agents are workflows with one or two decision points, and that is the correct outcome. Saying that is a maturity signal, not a lack of ambition.

Same task, two architectures
// WORKFLOW - the sequence is in YOUR code. Testable, bounded, debuggable.
Dispute d = extract(document);              // model call 1, schema-constrained
Category c = classify(d);                   // model call 2, enum output
if (c == FRAUD) {
    var evidence = evidenceService.gather(d.txnId());   // plain code
    return summarise(d, evidence);          // model call 3
}
return route(d, c);
// cost: exactly 3 calls. latency: predictable. failure: a stack trace.

// AGENT - the model chooses. Use ONLY when the path is genuinely unknown.
var run = agent.run(task, tools, AgentLimits.builder()
    .maxIterations(8)                 // hard stop
    .maxTotalTokens(80_000)           // cost ceiling, enforced
    .maxWallClock(Duration.ofSeconds(45))
    .allowedTools(READ_ONLY)          // NO refund tool in this context, at all
    .requireApprovalFor(Set.of("issue_refund", "send_email"))
    .onRepeatedCall(BREAK)            // same tool + same args twice = loop
    .tracer(otelTracer)               // every call recorded, or you cannot debug
    .build());

// Decision rule, out loud:
//   Can I write the steps down?           -> workflow
//   Does step N+1 depend on step N's RESULT in a way I cannot enumerate?
//                                          -> agent, with the limits above
//   Is the action irreversible?            -> human in the loop regardless
Follow-ups they will ask

What are the standard workflow patterns before I reach for an agent?

Prompt chaining (output of one call feeds the next, with a validation gate between). Routing (a cheap classifier picks a specialised downstream path). Parallelisation (fan out independent subtasks, aggregate — or run the same task several times and vote). Orchestrator-workers (a model decomposes into subtasks that code then dispatches). Evaluator-optimiser (generate, critique, revise, up to N rounds). Between them these cover the large majority of real use cases.

How do I debug an agent that did something strange?

Only with a trace, which is why tracing is not optional. Record every iteration: the messages sent, the tool requested with full arguments, the result returned, token counts, and the model version. Then replay it. Without that you are guessing about a nondeterministic system, and the failure will not reproduce on demand.

Does giving the model more tools make it more capable?

Up to a point, then it degrades. Large tool sets increase the chance of picking the wrong one, consume context on every call, and make evaluation combinatorially harder. Keep the set small and contextual — expose the five tools relevant to the current task rather than fifty. If you genuinely need many, add a routing layer that selects a subset first.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The HPA is a control loop that runs roughly every 15 seconds. It reads a metric for the pods it targets and computes: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetricValue / targetValue). There is a tolerance band (10% by default) so small deviations do nothing, and stabilisation windows — 0 seconds to scale up, 300 seconds to scale down — so it reacts fast to load and slowly to its absence, avoiding flapping.

It needs a metrics source. CPU and memory come from metrics-server, which is not installed by default on all distributions. Anything else needs an adapter implementing the custom metrics API (Prometheus Adapter) or the external metrics API (KEDA, CloudWatch adapter).

Now why CPU fails for an IO-bound Spring Boot service. Such a service spends its time blocked — waiting on the database, on a downstream HTTP call, on Kafka. Under increasing load the thread pool fills, requests queue, and latency climbs — but the CPU is idle while threads are parked. So you get the pathological picture: p99 latency at 4 seconds, request queue depth rising, users timing out, and CPU at 25%, comfortably below a 70% target. The HPA does nothing. It is not misconfigured; it is measuring the wrong thing, because CPU is not the resource being exhausted. The exhausted resource is concurrency.

So scale on a saturation metric. Best options, in order: in-flight requests or thread pool utilisation (the thing actually running out); requests per second per pod, once you know a pod's safe capacity; queue depth for consumers, which is the cleanest signal of all because it directly measures unprocessed work. For a queue consumer, KEDA is the standard answer — it scales on SQS depth, Kafka lag, or almost any external system, and it scales to zero, which the HPA cannot.

Two further points that show operational experience. The HPA cannot create nodes. It changes replica count; if the cluster has no room, the new pods sit Pending until Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter provisions capacity — so end-to-end scale-up time is HPA reaction plus node provisioning (1–3 minutes) plus image pull plus JVM start. For a sharp morning spike, that total is often too slow, and the right answer is a scheduled pre-scale rather than a reactive one. And HPA and VPA conflict on the same resource: VPA changing requests moves the denominator the HPA is dividing by, so run VPA in recommendation mode only when an HPA is active on CPU or memory.

Scale on what actually saturates
# WRONG for an IO-bound service
metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 } }
# p99 = 4s, queue growing, users timing out, CPU = 25%  ->  HPA does nothing

# RIGHT - scale on concurrency / saturation
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: payments-api }
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 30
  metrics:
    - type: Pods                       # in-flight requests per pod
      pods:
        metric: { name: http_server_requests_active }
        target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "25" }
    - type: Pods                       # secondary: throughput
      pods:
        metric: { name: http_requests_per_second }
        target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "150" }
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 30 }]  # can double
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 600                               # slow, cautious
      policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 10,  periodSeconds: 60 }]
---
# Queue consumer: KEDA, and it scales to ZERO (HPA cannot)
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: settlement-worker }
  minReplicaCount: 0
  maxReplicaCount: 50
  triggers:
    - type: aws-sqs-queue
      metadata:
        queueURL: https://sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/.../settlements
        queueLength: "20"        # 20 messages per pod

# End-to-end scale-up time - be honest about it:
#   HPA reaction        ~15-30s
#   node provisioning   ~60-180s   (if no spare capacity)
#   image pull          ~10-40s
#   JVM start + warmup  ~30-90s
#   ----------------------------
#   ~2-5 minutes. For a known 09:00 spike, PRE-SCALE on a schedule instead.
Follow-ups they will ask

How do I pre-scale for a predictable daily spike?

A CronJob patching minReplicas before the spike and back after, or KEDA's cron scaler, which does exactly this natively. Reactive autoscaling always lags because provisioning takes minutes; for a spike you know the time of, scaling in advance is simply correct and much cheaper than keeping the peak capacity all day.

Why does my HPA keep oscillating?

Usually a scale-down window that is too short combined with a metric that drops as soon as capacity is added — you scale up, the metric falls, you scale down, the metric rises. Lengthen scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds to several minutes and cap the percentage per period. Oscillation is also a symptom of a metric that is a consequence of replica count rather than an independent measure of demand.

Can the HPA scale on a metric from outside the cluster?

Yes, via the external metrics API — CloudWatch, SQS depth, Kafka lag, a business metric like pending settlements. KEDA is the usual implementation because it ships dozens of scalers and adds scale-to-zero. Scaling a consumer on the depth of the queue it drains is the cleanest autoscaling signal there is, because it measures unprocessed work directly rather than a proxy for it.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Lambda creates an execution environment per concurrent request. Within one environment, invocations are serial — there is no threading model where one environment handles several requests at once. Ten concurrent requests means ten environments, each with its own memory and its own copy of your globals.

An environment has two phases. Init runs your code outside the handler: static blocks, class loading, connection setup. This happens once per environment and is billed but not counted against your timeout in the same way. Then invoke runs the handler, and the environment is kept warm for reuse — typically minutes — so subsequent requests skip init. This is why clients and connection pools belong outside the handler: creating an S3 client per invocation is the most common Lambda performance bug there is.

A cold start is environment creation plus your init. For a Node or Python function it is tens to low hundreds of milliseconds. For a Spring Boot application it can be 5–10 seconds, because you are building an application context, scanning classpaths, and creating hundreds of beans — inside a fresh JVM that has JIT-compiled nothing. That is the core of what breaks when someone lifts a service into Lambda unchanged. Mitigations: SnapStart, which snapshots the initialised JVM after init and restores from it (dramatic improvement, but you must handle state that must not be reused — random seeds, cached credentials, open connections — via runtime hooks); provisioned concurrency, which keeps N environments warm at a cost that partly defeats the point; a leaner framework (Micronaut, Quarkus) or a plain handler; or accepting that this workload should be a container on ECS instead.

Concurrency is the other thing that breaks. It is per-account per-region (default 1,000), shared across every function. Reserved concurrency guarantees a function that share and caps it — the cap is the important half. Because without it, a burst spawns hundreds of environments, and each one opens its own database connections. Three hundred concurrent Lambdas against an RDS instance with a 200-connection limit is an instant outage — for every other service using that database too, not just the Lambda. This is the classic serverless-meets-relational failure, and RDS Proxy exists precisely for it: it pools and multiplexes connections so Lambda concurrency is decoupled from database connections.

Then the hard limits to state: 15-minute maximum timeout, 6MB synchronous request and response payload (20MB for async), 10GB memory, and — worth knowing — CPU is allocated in proportion to memory, so a function that is CPU-bound gets faster by being given more memory, and is often cheaper as a result because it finishes sooner. That counter-intuitive tuning point is a good detail to offer.

What breaks on a naive lift-and-shift
// WRONG - client created per invocation, pool created per environment
public class Handler implements RequestHandler<Event, Response> {
    public Response handleRequest(Event e, Context ctx) {
        var s3 = S3Client.create();              // ~200ms, EVERY invocation
        var conn = DriverManager.getConnection(URL);   // new DB connection each time
        ...
    }
}

// RIGHT - init once per environment, reused across invocations
public class Handler implements RequestHandler<Event, Response> {
    private static final S3Client S3 = S3Client.create();       // init phase
    private static final DataSource DS = pool(2);               // SMALL pool
    static { warmUp(); }                                        // pay it once

    public Response handleRequest(Event e, Context ctx) { ... }
}

// The concurrency -> connection explosion
   300 concurrent invocations
 x   5 connections each (a typical Hikari default)
 = 1,500 connections  ->  RDS max_connections = 200  ->  everything fails,
                          including services that are nothing to do with Lambda

// Three fixes, applied together:
ReservedConcurrentExecutions: 50        // cap the blast radius
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 2   // tiny pool per environment
url: jdbc:postgresql://proxy.proxy-abc.eu-west-1.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/app
                                        // ^ RDS Proxy multiplexes

// Spring Boot cold start
   plain            ~6,000 ms    <-- unusable on a synchronous path
   + SnapStart        ~400 ms    <-- but handle non-reusable state in hooks
   + provisioned         ~0 ms   <-- paying for idle capacity

// Memory tuning is CPU tuning:
   512 MB  -> 3,200 ms  -> $0.0000267
  1024 MB  -> 1,500 ms  -> $0.0000250   <-- faster AND cheaper
Follow-ups they will ask

When should I not use Lambda?

Sustained high throughput, where per-request pricing overtakes an always-on instance. Anything needing more than 15 minutes. Long-lived connections — WebSockets, streaming responses, database-heavy request paths. Latency-critical synchronous paths with a JVM, unless you are using SnapStart or provisioned concurrency. And anywhere the local development and testing story matters more than the operational saving.

What is the difference between reserved and provisioned concurrency?

Reserved partitions your account's concurrency limit: it guarantees a function that much and prevents it exceeding it. It costs nothing and its main value is as a cap. Provisioned keeps environments initialised and warm, eliminating cold starts, and you pay for them whether used or not. Reserved is a safety control; provisioned is a latency purchase.

How do errors and retries work?

It depends entirely on the invocation type, which trips people up. Synchronous (API Gateway, ALB): no retry, the error is returned to the caller. Asynchronous (S3 events, EventBridge): Lambda retries twice with delay, then sends to an on-failure destination or DLQ if configured — otherwise it is lost. Poll-based (SQS, Kinesis): the source's semantics apply, so SQS redelivers until maxReceiveCount. Always configure a failure destination for async invocations; the default is silent loss.

Memory, placement, front doors

How do you handle conversation state and memory when the context window is finite and every turn re-sends the whole history?

Must coverThe model is stateless - memory is entirely your architecture. Short term: keep the transcript, and when it approaches the budget, summarise older turns into a running summary and keep the last N verbatim. Long term: extract durable facts and store them in a real database, retrieving relevant ones per turn like RAG - do not let the transcript be your database. Cost drives this: with prompt caching, a stable prefix is far cheaper, so keep the system prompt and any pinned context at the front and let variation accumulate at the end.

StudyAnthropic - long context tips →

Explain node selectors, affinity, anti-affinity, taints and tolerations, and topology spread constraints. Which do you actually need for a normal stateless service?

Must covernodeSelector is exact label matching. Affinity adds required and preferred rules with expressions; pod anti-affinity keeps replicas apart. Taints repel pods from nodes unless the pod tolerates them - that is how you reserve GPU or spot nodes. Topology spread constraints are the modern answer for even distribution across zones and nodes, with maxSkew and whether violation is a hard or soft constraint. For a normal service: topology spread across zones plus a soft anti-affinity per node. Reach for the rest only when you have a real placement requirement, because over-constrained pods sit Pending forever.

StudyKubernetes - assigning pods to nodes →

API Gateway or an Application Load Balancer in front of your service? And when should the API be asynchronous instead?

Must coverALB is a layer 7 load balancer - cheap per request, routes by host and path, good for a small number of long-lived services. API Gateway is an API product layer: per-client API keys and usage plans, throttling, request validation, WAF, authorizers, versioned stages, and per-request pricing that gets expensive at high volume. Choose ALB for internal high-volume service traffic, API Gateway for public or partner APIs needing governance. Go async - accept, enqueue, return 202 with a status URL - whenever the work exceeds a couple of seconds or the downstream cannot absorb the arrival rate; that converts a timeout into a queue.

StudyAPI Gateway developer guide →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start from the fact that determines everything: the model is stateless. Each call is independent, and the illusion of memory comes entirely from you re-sending the transcript. So memory is not a model feature you configure — it is an architecture you build, and its cost grows with every turn.

Short-term memory is the conversation transcript. The naive approach — append every turn forever — fails twice: it hits the context window, and it costs more on every single call because the whole history is re-sent as input tokens. A ten-turn conversation is not ten calls' worth of input; it is the sum of a growing prefix.

So manage it. Keep the last N turns verbatim, and when the transcript approaches a token budget, summarise the older portion into a running summary that replaces it. The summary must preserve decisions, entities, constraints and unresolved questions — not a prose précis of the chat. Keep the most recent turns intact because they carry the immediate referents (that one, the second option) that a summary destroys. Never blind-truncate from the front: dropping the turn where the user stated their account number produces a conversation that has silently forgotten the thing everything else depends on.

Long-term memory is a different mechanism entirely and people conflate the two. Durable facts — preferences, entitlements, prior decisions, corrections the user made — should be extracted into a real database and retrieved per turn like RAG, filtered by relevance to the current question. The transcript is a log; it is not a queryable store, and treating it as one means the model can only remember what fits in the window.

Then the cost architecture, which is where this connects to everything else. Prompt caching keys on a stable prefix, so the ordering rule is: system prompt, tool definitions, pinned long-term facts, then the summary, then recent turns, then the new message. Variation accumulates at the end. Put anything variable early — a timestamp, a per-request id, freshly retrieved chunks — and you invalidate the cache for everything after it, which in a long conversation is most of the tokens.

Two more practical points: memory is per-user data, so it inherits the retention, access control and deletion obligations of everything else — a memory store is a data store, with a subject access request path. And you need an explicit forget mechanism, because a wrong fact extracted into long-term memory is worse than no memory at all: it will be retrieved confidently, forever.

Two memories, one cache-friendly layout
// Context assembled per turn - order is deliberate, for the cache
[ system prompt        ]  2,000 tok   stable  ─┐
[ tool definitions     ]    800 tok   stable   │ CACHED PREFIX
[ long-term facts      ]    300 tok   stable  ─┘ (changes rarely)
        ---- cache breakpoint ----
[ rolling summary      ]    600 tok   turns 1-14, compressed
[ last 6 turns verbatim] 2,400 tok    immediate referents live here
[ new user message     ]     40 tok

// Short-term: compact, do not truncate
if (tokens(transcript) > SOFT_LIMIT) {
    var older  = transcript.subList(0, transcript.size() - KEEP_VERBATIM);
    var recent = transcript.subList(transcript.size() - KEEP_VERBATIM, size);
    // summarise for STATE, not for prose
    summary = model.summarise(older, "Preserve: decisions made, entities and IDs "
            + "mentioned, constraints stated, questions still unanswered. "
            + "Omit pleasantries and restatements.");
    transcript = List.of(summaryMessage(summary)) + recent;
}

// Long-term: a real store, retrieved by relevance - NOT the transcript
record Memory(String userId, String fact, String sourceTurnId,
              Instant learnedAt, double confidence) {}

var relevant = memoryStore.search(userId, currentQuestion, topK: 5);
// e.g. "prefers settlement reports in GBP", "authorised for merchant ACME-GB-0042"

// And a forget path, because a wrong remembered fact is worse than none:
memoryStore.revoke(userId, factId);   // user-triggered AND admin-triggered
Follow-ups they will ask

How do I decide what is worth promoting to long-term memory?

Be conservative. Extract only facts that are durable, user-specific and reusable — stated preferences, entitlements, corrections the user explicitly made. Do not extract anything inferred, anything transient (they seemed frustrated), or anything you cannot show the user. Attach a confidence and a source turn, expose the memories in the UI, and let the user delete them. A memory system users cannot inspect is a system that will confidently repeat a mistake forever.

What breaks when I summarise the middle of a conversation?

Referents and exact values. The second option becomes meaningless once the list is summarised away; an account number restated as their account is no longer usable in a tool call. Mitigate by keeping recent turns verbatim, by instructing the summariser to preserve identifiers and numbers literally, and by extracting entities into structured slots rather than relying on the prose summary to carry them.

Does prompt caching change how I structure the conversation?

Substantially, and it is the practical reason to care about ordering. A stable prefix is billed at a large discount on a cache hit, so a long system prompt plus tool definitions becomes cheap when it never changes. Concretely: no timestamps or request ids near the front, retrieved chunks after the stable block rather than before it, and the summary placed so that compaction invalidates as little as possible.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Five mechanisms, and the useful framing is that they answer different questions: where may this pod go, where should it prefer to go, which nodes reject pods by default, and how should replicas be distributed.

nodeSelector is exact label matching — the simplest and least expressive. Node affinity generalises it with operators (In, NotIn, Exists, Gt) and two strengths: requiredDuringScheduling (a hard constraint — unsatisfiable means Pending forever) and preferredDuringScheduling with a weight (a soft preference the scheduler tries to honour).

Pod affinity and anti-affinity place pods relative to other pods rather than to nodes, using a topologyKey to define what counts as together — same node, same zone, same rack. Anti-affinity keeps replicas apart. Be aware that requiredDuringScheduling pod anti-affinity is computationally expensive at scale, because the scheduler evaluates every candidate node against every existing pod; on large clusters it visibly slows scheduling, which is one reason topology spread constraints were introduced.

Taints and tolerations are the inverse relationship and this is the part people muddle. A taint is on the node and repels pods; a toleration is on the pod and says I can put up with that taint. Crucially, a toleration does not attract — it only permits. So reserving GPU or spot nodes takes two things: a taint so ordinary pods stay off, and a node selector or affinity so your pods actually land there. Effects are NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, and NoExecute, which additionally evicts pods already running — that is the mechanism behind node-pressure evictions and the not-ready timeouts.

Topology spread constraints are the modern answer to even distribution. maxSkew bounds the difference in pod count between the most and least populated topology domains; whenUnsatisfiable is DoNotSchedule (hard) or ScheduleAnyway (soft). They are more expressive and much cheaper to evaluate than anti-affinity for the common case of spread my replicas across zones.

For a normal stateless service, the answer is deliberately small: topology spread across zones with maxSkew: 1 and ScheduleAnyway, plus optionally a soft spread across nodes. Nothing else. Use ScheduleAnyway rather than DoNotSchedule so that when one zone is short of capacity you get an uneven deployment instead of Pending pods — availability beats symmetry. Reach for the heavier mechanisms only when you have a real requirement, because over-constrained pods sit Pending forever, and that is the failure mode of this whole topic: a manifest with hard anti-affinity, a hard zone constraint and a node selector describes a placement that may simply not exist.

Start here, and usually stop here
# The 90% case: spread across zones, tolerate imbalance
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway        # <-- availability > symmetry
      labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: payments-api } }
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname      # also spread across nodes
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway

# Reserving a node pool: taint AND selector - a toleration alone does NOTHING
#   node:  kubectl taint nodes gpu-1 workload=gpu:NoSchedule
spec:
  tolerations:                                  # permits me to be here
    - { key: workload, operator: Equal, value: gpu, effect: NoSchedule }
  nodeSelector: { workload: gpu }               # ATTRACTS me here
  #  ^ without this second half, the pod may still land on a normal node

# Spot with graceful eviction
  tolerations:
    - key: node.kubernetes.io/not-ready
      operator: Exists
      effect: NoExecute
      tolerationSeconds: 30       # evict fast when a spot node goes away

# The classic self-inflicted outage:
  affinity:
    podAntiAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:     # HARD
        - topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: payments-api } }
# replicas: 10, nodes: 6  ->  4 pods Pending FOREVER. The scheduler is correct;
# the constraint is impossible. Use preferred, or topology spread with skew.
Follow-ups they will ask

When is hard anti-affinity actually justified?

For quorum systems where two members on one node genuinely breaks the guarantee — etcd, ZooKeeper, a three-node Kafka controller quorum. There, Pending is the correct outcome, because scheduling two members together silently removes the fault tolerance you deployed three for. For a stateless API, soft is right: a temporarily co-located replica is a small risk, whereas an unschedulable pod is a certain capacity loss.

What are the built-in taints I should recognise?

node.kubernetes.io/not-ready and unreachable (added automatically, with a default 300-second toleration that governs how long pods linger on a dead node — shorten it for faster failover), memory-pressure, disk-pressure, pid-pressure, and unschedulable when a node is cordoned. Control-plane nodes carry a NoSchedule taint, which is why workloads do not land there.

Why are my pods Pending and how do I find out fast?

kubectl describe pod and read the scheduler event verbatim — it names the failed predicate and how many nodes failed each one, which is usually the whole answer. Ranked causes: insufficient CPU or memory on every node; an unsatisfiable hard affinity or topology constraint; a taint with no matching toleration; a PVC that cannot bind because the volume is in the wrong zone; and namespace ResourceQuota already exhausted. The message distinguishes all five.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

ALB is a layer 7 load balancer: host and path routing, header and query matching, TLS termination, WAF integration, native ECS and EKS target support. It is billed per hour plus LCUs, which at high volume works out to a small fraction of a cent per thousand requests. API Gateway is an API management product: per-client API keys and usage plans, request and response validation and transformation, per-method throttling, Lambda and JWT authorizers, versioned stages, SDK generation, caching, and detailed per-route metrics. It is billed per request, and at high volume that becomes the dominant cost.

So the decision is mostly about who your callers are. Internal, high-volume, service-to-service traffic: ALB. You already control the clients, you do not need API keys or usage plans, and the per-request pricing of API Gateway on tens of millions of calls is real money for governance you will not use. Public or partner APIs: API Gateway, because API keys, per-client quotas, request validation at the edge and a managed authorizer are exactly the features you would otherwise build badly yourself.

Do the arithmetic out loud in an interview — it lands well. At 50 million requests a month, API Gateway REST is on the order of $175 and an ALB is on the order of $20–30. At 5 million with twelve partner integrations needing separate quotas and keys, API Gateway is obviously right. HTTP APIs sit between the two: cheaper and lower-latency than REST APIs, with a reduced feature set (no request validation, no usage plans), and they are the sensible default for a straightforward proxy to Lambda.

Also mention the hybrid, because it is what large organisations actually run: API Gateway at the edge for public traffic, forwarding into a private ALB, so external callers get governance and internal callers go direct.

When to go asynchronous is the second half of the question and it is the more architectural one. Make the API async when the work exceeds a couple of seconds, when the downstream cannot absorb the arrival rate, or when the work must survive a client disconnect. The shape: validate, persist the request with an idempotency key, enqueue, and return 202 Accepted with a status URL. The client polls that URL, or you push completion over WebSocket or SSE, or you call a webhook.

The reason to state plainly: this converts a timeout into a queue. A synchronous API under overload fails — connections pile up, threads exhaust, the load balancer returns 504, and the work is simply lost. An async API under the same load grows queue depth, which is a metric you alarm on and scale against, and no work is lost. That is also why the 29-second API Gateway integration timeout is less of a constraint than it appears: anything approaching it should not have been synchronous in the first place.

The async shape, and why it beats a longer timeout
// SYNCHRONOUS - fine until it is not
POST /settlements/reconcile     ->  90 seconds of work
  ALB idle timeout 60s        -> 504
  API Gateway hard limit 29s  -> 504
  client retries              -> the work runs TWICE
  under load                  -> threads exhausted, requests LOST

// ASYNCHRONOUS - the same operation, safely
POST /settlements/reconcile
Idempotency-Key: 7f3a-...                  // client-supplied, required
  201 Accepted
  Location: /jobs/abc123
  { "jobId": "abc123", "status": "PENDING" }

  // server: conditional insert on the idempotency key, then enqueue
  //   duplicate key -> return the EXISTING jobId, do not enqueue again

GET /jobs/abc123
  { "status": "RUNNING", "progress": 0.4 }
  { "status": "SUCCEEDED", "result": "/settlements/reports/2026-08" }
  { "status": "FAILED", "error": { "code": "PARTNER_FILE_MALFORMED", ... } }

// What you gain, concretely:
//   overload        -> queue depth grows (alarm + scale), nothing is lost
//   client dies     -> work continues, result is still there
//   retry           -> idempotency key makes it a no-op
//   long work       -> no timeout anywhere in the path
//   observability   -> queue depth and job age are the SLIs

// Cost sanity check, 50M requests/month:
//   ALB                  ~ $25    (hourly + LCU)
//   API Gateway HTTP     ~ $50
//   API Gateway REST     ~ $175   + caching if enabled
Follow-ups they will ask

What about the client that really wants a synchronous response?

Give them one, up to a deadline: accept the request, wait on the job for a bounded time (say 3 seconds), and return the result if it completes or 202 with the status URL if it does not. That is long polling and it gives the common fast case a synchronous feel without making the slow case a failure. Never let the wait be unbounded — the deadline is the whole point.

Where does authentication go in each option?

API Gateway has first-class authorizers — a JWT authorizer validating a Cognito or OIDC token at the edge, or a Lambda authorizer for custom logic, with the result cached. An ALB can do OIDC authentication natively too, which is underused and works well for internal tools. Otherwise the ALB passes the request through and your service validates the token, which is fine and is what most internal service meshes do anyway.

How do I stop a client hammering the status endpoint?

Return a Retry-After header and honour it with throttling; make the status response cacheable for a couple of seconds; and prefer a push channel (WebSocket, SSE, or a webhook the client registers) for anything long-running. Polling every 100ms across thousands of clients is a self-inflicted load problem, and the status endpoint is often the first thing to fall over in an otherwise well-designed async system.

Streaming, shutdown, orchestration

Why do LLM features stream, and what does that mean for your Spring Boot service and its error handling?

Must coverTime to first token is what users perceive, and total generation can be many seconds, so streaming turns an unacceptable wait into an acceptable one. Server-sent events over a Flux or SseEmitter; the connection is long-lived, so ALB and Ingress idle timeouts must exceed it and response buffering must be disabled at every proxy. The hard part is errors: you have already sent 200 OK and half an answer, so failures must be carried in-band as an error event and rendered, not thrown. Also handle client disconnect by cancelling the upstream call, or you keep paying for tokens nobody will read.

StudyAnthropic - streaming messages →

A pod is being deleted. Walk through every step and explain exactly why in-flight requests still fail without a preStop hook.

Must coverOn delete, two things happen concurrently: the pod is removed from Service endpoints, and SIGTERM is sent. Endpoint removal must propagate to kube-proxy on every node and to the ingress controller, which takes time; meanwhile your app has already started shutting down. So traffic is still being routed to a socket that is closing - that is the race. Fix: a preStop hook sleeping 5-15 seconds so the app keeps serving while endpoints propagate, then graceful shutdown draining in-flight requests, with terminationGracePeriodSeconds longer than the sleep plus the drain. In Spring Boot, server.shutdown=graceful plus a shutdown phase timeout.

StudyKubernetes - pod lifecycle →

When do you reach for Step Functions instead of orchestrating in your own service? What does it give you that a Spring @Transactional method cannot?

Must coverWhen a business process spans multiple services and minutes to days, you need durable state you did not write - Step Functions persists every state transition, so a crash resumes rather than restarts. It gives you built-in retry with backoff per step, catch and fallback branches, parallel and map states, wait states, and a visual execution history that is genuinely the best debugging artefact in AWS. It is also where you implement the saga pattern with explicit compensating steps, because a distributed transaction has no rollback. Standard workflows are durable and billed per transition; Express are cheap, high-volume and short.

StudyAWS Step Functions →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Streaming exists because of a property of the technology: generation is sequential in the output length. A 600-token answer cannot arrive faster than 600 sequential decode steps. So total latency is fixed by output size, but time to first token is not — and time to first token is what a user perceives as responsiveness. Streaming converts a four-second blank screen into a 400ms first word followed by text appearing at reading speed, and users rate the second as dramatically faster despite identical total time.

Mechanically it is server-sent events: the provider streams deltas, and you forward them to the browser over a long-lived HTTP response. In Spring Boot that is a Flux<ServerSentEvent> on WebFlux, or an SseEmitter on MVC — and if you are on MVC, note that each emitter holds a servlet thread for the whole generation, so a few hundred concurrent streams exhausts the pool. That is the single strongest practical argument for a reactive stack on this path.

Then the infrastructure, which is where this actually breaks in production. Every proxy between you and the browser must be configured: idle timeouts must exceed the longest generation (ALB defaults to 60 seconds, which is often enough but not always), and response buffering must be disabled at every hop — nginx buffers by default, so a correctly implemented stream arrives as one lump at the end and everyone blames the application. Set X-Accel-Buffering: no or the equivalent, and test through the real ingress rather than against localhost.

Error handling is the genuinely hard part, and it is what separates a considered answer. You have already sent 200 OK and half an answer when the failure occurs. You cannot retroactively send a 500. So errors must be carried in band: emit a typed error event, have the client render it inline, and end the stream cleanly. Your exception handler is useless here — a thrown exception mid-stream just severs the connection and the user sees a truncated sentence with no explanation. This also means partial output has already been shown, so anything you would have validated before returning (schema conformance, a groundedness check, a PII scan) has already reached the user. For output that must be validated, either do not stream it, or stream to a buffer and validate before rendering — which gives up the latency benefit and should be an explicit decision.

Finally, cancellation. When the user closes the tab or navigates away, propagate that downstream and abort the upstream call. Otherwise you keep generating and paying for tokens nobody will read, which on an abandoned-heavy interface is a meaningful and completely invisible cost.

Streaming, with the parts people miss
@GetMapping(value = "/ask", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
public Flux<ServerSentEvent<String>> ask(@RequestParam String q) {
    return client.streamMessage(buildPrompt(q))
        .map(delta -> ServerSentEvent.builder(delta.text()).event("token").build())

        // errors AFTER 200 OK must be in-band - you cannot send a 500 now
        .onErrorResume(ex -> {
            log.error("stream failed mid-generation", ex);
            return Flux.just(ServerSentEvent.<String>builder()
                .event("error")
                .data("{\"code\":\"UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE\"," +
                      "\"message\":\"Answer interrupted. Please retry.\"}")
                .build());
        })
        .concatWith(Mono.just(ServerSentEvent.<String>builder()
                .event("done").data("{}").build()))

        // client disconnected -> stop paying for tokens nobody will read
        .doOnCancel(() -> upstream.abort())
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(60));
}

// Infrastructure - a correct implementation still fails without these
ALB          idle_timeout.timeout_seconds = 120       # > longest generation
nginx        proxy_buffering off;  proxy_read_timeout 120s;
response     X-Accel-Buffering: no
Spring MVC   -> each SseEmitter holds a SERVLET THREAD for the whole generation
                300 concurrent streams exhausts the pool. Use WebFlux here.

// Client
es.addEventListener("token", e => out.append(e.data));
es.addEventListener("error", e => showInlineError(JSON.parse(e.data)));
es.addEventListener("done",  e => es.close());
Follow-ups they will ask

Can I validate output if I am streaming it?

Not before the user sees it, and that is a real trade rather than a detail. Options: do not stream anything that must pass validation (structured extraction, anything with money in it); stream to a buffer, validate, then render — which keeps the server-side streaming but gives up the perceived latency; or stream the prose and deliver validated structured fields separately after. For a payments narration, I would stream the prose and render the numbers from the query result, which sidesteps the problem entirely.

How do I show a token count or cost when streaming?

The final message in the stream carries usage metadata, so emit a terminal done event with input and output tokens and record it there. Do not try to count tokens client-side — tokenisation is model-specific and your estimate will drift from what you are billed.

Is WebSocket better than SSE for this?

Not for one-way token streaming — SSE is simpler, works over plain HTTP/2, reconnects automatically with Last-Event-ID, and needs no protocol upgrade through your proxies. WebSocket earns its complexity when you need genuine bidirectional traffic mid-generation: interrupting the model, sending tool approvals, or a collaborative session. Start with SSE.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Deleting a pod starts two things concurrently and with no ordering between them, and that concurrency is the entire answer.

Path one: the pod's deletionTimestamp is set, the endpoint controller notices and removes the pod from the Service's EndpointSlices. That removal must then propagate — to kube-proxy on every node, which rewrites iptables or IPVS rules; to the ingress controller, which reloads or updates its upstreams; to any mesh sidecar; to a cloud load balancer's target group if you are using IP-target mode. That propagation takes hundreds of milliseconds to several seconds depending on cluster size, and Kubernetes does not wait for it.

Path two: the kubelet runs the preStop hook if there is one, then sends SIGTERM to PID 1 in each container, then waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30), then sends SIGKILL to anything still running.

So without a preStop hook: SIGTERM arrives immediately, your application closes its listener and begins draining — while nodes that have not yet received the endpoint update are still routing new connections to it. Those connections are refused, and the user sees a 502 from the ingress. The pod did everything right; the routing tables were simply stale. This is why teams see a small burst of 502s on every deploy and often never explain it.

The fix is a preStop hook that sleeps and does nothing else — 5 to 15 seconds. During that window the application is completely unaffected and keeps serving normally, which is exactly the point: it buys time for endpoint removal to converge everywhere. Only after the sleep does SIGTERM arrive, at which point no new traffic is being sent and the drain is safe. It feels wrong to add a deliberate delay to a shutdown path, and it is nonetheless the standard, correct pattern.

Then graceful shutdown in the application: stop accepting new requests, let in-flight ones finish, close connection pools and consumers cleanly. Spring Boot does this with server.shutdown=graceful and a shutdown phase timeout. And terminationGracePeriodSeconds must exceed sleep plus drain plus margin, or the kubelet SIGKILLs you mid-request — which reintroduces the failure you were fixing.

Two related things worth adding: for PID 1 to receive SIGTERM at all, your process must actually be PID 1 and must handle the signal (a shell-form ENTRYPOINT makes the shell PID 1 and it may not forward signals). And a PodDisruptionBudget governs voluntary disruptions only — node drains and autoscaler consolidation — so it complements this but does not replace it.

The race, and the sleep that fixes it
WITHOUT preStop
 t=0.000  delete: deletionTimestamp set  AND  SIGTERM sent   (concurrent!)
 t=0.010  app closes listener, starts draining
 t=0.050  endpoint controller updates EndpointSlice
 t=0.400  kube-proxy on node-7 finally rewrites its rules
          ^^^ ~390ms of NEW connections routed to a closed listener -> 502s

WITH preStop
 t=0.000  delete: endpoint removal begins propagating
 t=0.000  preStop starts: sleep 10        <- app STILL SERVING, untouched
 t=0.400  every kube-proxy, ingress and sidecar has converged
 t=10.00  preStop returns -> SIGTERM
 t=10.00  app stops accepting, drains in-flight requests
 t=22.00  process exits 0
 (grace period 45s > 10 sleep + ~12 drain + margin)

spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  containers:
    - name: api
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          exec: { command: ["sh","-c","sleep 10"] }   # does nothing, on purpose
---
# application.yaml
server.shutdown: graceful
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s

# Dockerfile: exec form, so the JVM is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app/app.jar"]        # correct
# ENTRYPOINT java -jar /app/app.jar              # shell form: sh is PID 1

# Verify it actually works, before you need it to:
$ kubectl delete pod api-7d9f & hey -z 30s -c 20 https://api.example.com/health
# non-2xx count must be ZERO
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not just make the application handle SIGTERM faster?

Because speed is the opposite of what helps. The problem is that traffic is still arriving after SIGTERM; shutting down faster widens the window of refused connections. The application must keep serving longer, which is precisely what the sleep provides. This inversion is why the pattern is unintuitive and why people try to fix it in the application first.

How long should the preStop sleep be?

5 seconds is usually enough on a small cluster, 10–15 on a large one or where an external load balancer with its own health-check interval and deregistration delay is in the path. Measure it: run a load test while deleting pods and increase the sleep until non-2xx responses hit zero. Then add margin, because propagation time grows with node count.

Does this apply to queue consumers too?

Differently, and it still matters. There is no ingress race, so the sleep is unnecessary — but SIGTERM must stop polling for new messages while allowing in-flight ones to finish and be acknowledged. Otherwise messages are redelivered, which is safe if you are idempotent and wasteful if you are not. Make sure the grace period exceeds your longest message processing time, or you get a SIGKILL mid-transaction on every deploy.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Reach for Step Functions when a business process spans several services and takes longer than a request — minutes, hours, or days — and must survive process restarts, deploys and failures. The core thing it gives you that your own code cannot easily is durable state you did not have to build: every state transition is persisted, so a crash mid-workflow resumes from where it was rather than starting over or leaving the world half-updated.

Contrast that with @Transactional honestly, because the comparison is the point of the question. A database transaction gives you atomicity across rows in one database. It gives you nothing across services: you cannot roll back an HTTP call to a partner, a message already published, or a refund already issued. The moment your process touches a second system, @Transactional stops being the right mental model — and worse, holding a transaction open across a network call is actively harmful, because you are pinning a database connection and holding locks for the duration of someone else's latency.

What Step Functions adds concretely: retry with backoff and jitter per state, declared rather than coded; catch blocks routing specific errors to fallback branches; parallel and map states for fan-out with a concurrency limit; wait states measured in days, which is how you model hold this for a 3-day dispute window without a scheduler; and callback patterns (waitForTaskToken) that pause the workflow until an external system or a human responds. Plus a visual execution history showing every input, output and error per state — genuinely the best debugging artefact in AWS, and worth saying so.

It is also where you implement the saga pattern. There is no distributed rollback, so a long-running business transaction is a sequence of steps each with an explicit compensating action: reserve funds → compensate by releasing; issue refund → compensate by reversing. Step Functions makes that structure visible in the definition rather than buried in exception handlers, which matters because compensation logic is exactly the code nobody tests.

Standard versus Express: Standard is durable, exactly-once state transitions, up to a year long, billed per transition, with full history — use it for business processes. Express is up to 5 minutes, at-least-once, billed on duration and memory, and cheap enough for high-volume event processing — use it for streaming and ingestion.

The honest counter-argument to give unprompted: Step Functions is infrastructure-as-JSON, poorly unit-testable, harder to review than Java, and it couples you to AWS. For a process with three steps and simple retries, an SQS queue with a state column in your database is simpler and better. The threshold is roughly: more than a handful of steps, genuine long waits, human approval, or a compensation story — then the durable orchestrator earns its complexity.

Saga with explicit compensation
{ "Comment": "Settlement with compensation",
  "StartAt": "ReserveFunds",
  "States": {
    "ReserveFunds": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
      "Retry": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["States.TaskFailed"],
                  "IntervalSeconds": 2, "MaxAttempts": 4,
                  "BackoffRate": 2.0, "JitterStrategy": "FULL" }],
      "Catch": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"], "Next": "Fail" }],
      "Next": "NotifyPartner" },

    "NotifyPartner": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
      "Catch": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["States.ALL"],
                  "Next": "ReleaseFunds" }],        // <-- COMPENSATE
      "Next": "AwaitConfirmation" },

    "AwaitConfirmation": {                           // human or external system
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke.waitForTaskToken",
      "TimeoutSeconds": 259200,                      // 3 days, no scheduler needed
      "Catch": [{ "ErrorEquals": ["States.Timeout"], "Next": "ReleaseFunds" }],
      "Next": "Settle" },

    "ReleaseFunds": { "Type": "Task", "Resource": "...", "Next": "Fail" },
    "Settle":       { "Type": "Task", "Resource": "...", "End": true },
    "Fail":         { "Type": "Fail" }
  } }

// What @Transactional could never do here:
//   - survive a deploy or crash mid-process        (durable state)
//   - wait 3 days for a partner                    (wait state)
//   - undo an HTTP call already made               (compensation, not rollback)
//   - retry ONE step with backoff, not the whole thing

// And what it does better for the simple case:
//   two rows in one database, one commit, fully unit-testable. Use it there.
Follow-ups they will ask

When would you use Step Functions over an SQS-driven state machine you write yourself?

When the process has real branching, needs long waits or human approval, requires per-step retry policies, or has compensation logic. Your own version means writing durable state, idempotent transitions, timers and a visualisation — all of which is work, and all of which is where bugs live. Below that threshold, a status column plus a queue is genuinely simpler and I would defend it.

How do you test a Step Functions workflow?

Test the Lambdas as ordinary units — that is where the business logic should live, keeping the state machine thin. For the machine itself, use the local test runner and the TestState API for individual states, and run end-to-end executions against a real state machine in a test account with stubbed downstreams. Accept that this is weaker than testing plain Java, and let that weakness push logic out of the definition and into code.

What are the limits that bite?

25,000 events in the history of a Standard execution (a long loop exhausts it — restart the execution to reset), a 256KB payload passed between states (pass an S3 pointer for anything larger, which is the standard workaround), and 1-year maximum duration. Express has none of the history limits but no full history either, only CloudWatch Logs.

Design the async processing path for settlement files: files land in S3, each has up to 500,000 rows, processing must be exactly-once from the business point of view and must not fall over on a bad file.

Must coverS3 event to SQS, not straight to compute, so you get buffering, retry and a DLQ. A dispatcher splits the file into batches and enqueues work items keyed by a deterministic id derived from file plus row range. Consumers are idempotent against a processed-items table with a conditional write - that is what makes it exactly-once in effect despite at-least-once delivery. Visibility timeout above p99, heartbeat extension for long batches, DLQ with an alarm and a documented replay path. Track progress in DynamoDB so a partial failure resumes. AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Instrument before you change anything. Both symptoms — p99 of 11 seconds and a 4x cost rise — are aggregates that hide the cause, and the temptation is to start optimising the thing you happen to suspect. Split latency into retrieval, prompt assembly, time to first token, and total generation. Log input tokens, output tokens, cached tokens, model version and retry count on every single request. Ten minutes of instrumentation usually makes the answer obvious.

What you almost always find, in order of impact. First: output tokens dominate both cost and latency. Output is typically several times the input rate per token, and it is the only part that is sequential — 800 tokens of answer is 800 decode steps. Cap max_tokens, instruct explicitly for brevity, and stop asking the model to restate the question before answering.

Second: the system prompt is large and uncached. If a 3,000-token system prompt plus tool definitions is re-sent uncached on every call, that is the single biggest line item and it is trivially fixable — enable prompt caching and order the context so the stable prefix comes first. Check that nothing variable (a timestamp, a request id) sits near the front silently invalidating it.

Third: you are retrieving too much. Twenty chunks where five would do costs tokens, adds latency, and measurably degrades quality by diluting the context. Add a reranker and cut k. Fourth: the largest model is doing work a small one handles — classification, routing, query rewriting, extraction. Route by task class. Fifth: retries are multiplying spend invisibly. A timeout that fires at 10 seconds on a call that would have completed at 11, retried three times, is 3x the cost and a worse p99 than simply waiting.

Then the structural fixes. Stream, which does not reduce total time but moves time-to-first-token to a few hundred milliseconds and changes what the p99 measures. Cache — exact-match first, since it is free and safe, then carefully-bounded semantic caching. Batch anything not interactive, because the Batch API is roughly half price for work that can wait.

And name the p99-specific cause, because a p99 of 11 seconds with a reasonable p50 is usually not everything is slow — it is a long tail. Common sources: a small fraction of requests with very long outputs; retries after timeouts; provider rate-limit backoff; and one slow retrieval path. Fix the tail by capping output length and by shedding or degrading rather than retrying, not by making the median faster.

Diagnose, then fix in this order
// Instrument first - one structured line per request
{ "requestId": "...", "model": "claude-...-20260514",
  "inputTokens": 9840, "cachedTokens": 0,        // <-- cache never hit. Why?
  "outputTokens": 820,                           // <-- expensive AND sequential
  "retrievalMs": 34, "assemblyMs": 6,
  "ttftMs": 1180, "totalMs": 9740,               // generation is 88% of the time
  "retries": 2 }                                 // <-- paying 3x for this request

// Fixes, in order of impact
1. output length      max_tokens 2000 -> 400, prompt for brevity   ~40% cost, ~50% latency
2. prompt caching     stable prefix first, breakpoint after tools   ~30% input cost
                      (verify: cachedTokens > 0 on the second call)
3. retrieval k        20 chunks -> 5 after reranking                ~25% input cost
                      (quality usually IMPROVES - less dilution)
4. model routing      classify/rewrite/extract -> small model       ~20% total
5. retry policy       timeout 10s on a p99 of 11s = retry storm
                      -> raise timeout, cap attempts at 1, add jitter

// Then structural
   stream            ttft 400ms (p99 measured on ttft, not total)
   exact-match cache  internal corpora repeat far more than you expect
   Batch API          ~50% off for anything not interactive

// The p99 tail is usually NOT "everything is slow":
   p50 1.9s / p99 11s  ->  look at the outputTokens distribution and the
   retry count on the slow requests. Cap the tail; do not optimise the median.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does retrieving fewer chunks improve quality?

Because context is not free attention. Marginally relevant passages compete with the right one, and models are known to attend less reliably to material in the middle of a long context. Five well-ranked chunks routinely beat twenty loosely-ranked ones on groundedness. This is also why a reranker is usually the best quality-per-effort change available: it fixes ordering, which is what the generator is most sensitive to.

How do I verify prompt caching is actually working?

Check cache_read_input_tokens in the usage on the second and subsequent calls — if it is zero, the prefix is not stable. The usual culprits are a timestamp or request id near the front, tool definitions built in a nondeterministic order (a HashMap rather than a list), or retrieved chunks placed before the system prompt. Also note cache entries expire, so low-traffic paths may never hit.

Is a cheaper model always worth trying?

Worth trying, always — measured against your eval set, never by impression. Small models are frequently indistinguishable on classification, extraction, routing and short summarisation, and an order of magnitude cheaper. They are noticeably worse on multi-step reasoning and long synthesis. Run the suite on both and route by task class rather than picking one model for everything.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Work outward from the symptom, and do not start with the application. Three symptoms are given and they have different causes; part of the skill is not conflating them.

First, the stuck rollout, because it is blocking everything and is the easiest to read. kubectl rollout status and then kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp. A stalled rollout almost always means new pods never reach Ready, which is the healthy failure mode — old pods are still serving. Do not force it. Read why: kubectl describe pod on a new pod tells you whether it is failing readiness, failing to schedule, or crashing.

Second, distinguish the restart causes, because they look identical in kubectl get pods and have opposite fixes. OOMKilled: true in the last state means the memory limit is below real usage — under 3x load, thread pools grew, direct buffers grew, and the non-heap portion pushed the process over. Exit 137 without OOMKilled, alongside a Killing container ... failed liveness probe event, means the liveness probe fired — usually because the probe endpoint shares an exhausted thread pool with the traffic, so the pod is slow rather than dead and you are killing healthy pods to no benefit.

Third, CPU throttling, which shows up nowhere obvious. It does not cause restarts and it produces no log lines — the only evidence is container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total rising. This is why that metric must already be on the dashboard: at 3am you cannot discover it by reading logs. Throttling under a 3x spike means your CPU limits are too tight for peak, and for a JVM it is doubly painful because GC threads get throttled too.

Fourth, did autoscaling even fire? kubectl describe hpa shows the current metric value and its decisions. Two common findings: the HPA is scaling on CPU for an IO-bound service, so it never triggers; or it scaled up correctly and the pods are Pending because the cluster has no room and node provisioning takes minutes. Those need different fixes.

The fix set, and I would state it as prevention rather than as this-morning's mitigation. Right-size requests and limits from observed p95 rather than guesses. Add a startup probe so the JVM gets time to boot and liveness can then be tight. Make liveness shallow and local, on a separate management port with its own connector. Scale on a saturation metric — in-flight requests or queue depth — not CPU. And for a spike that happens at 9am every single day, pre-scale on a schedule: reactive autoscaling takes minutes end to end, so for a known event it is simply the wrong tool.

The 9am triage, in order
# 1. Is the rollout the problem, or a victim?
kubectl rollout status deploy/api --timeout=30s
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -30
#   "1 of 6 updated replicas are available" -> new pods not Ready. GOOD failure.
#   Old pods still serving. Investigate; do NOT --force or delete them.

# 2. Why are pods restarting? Two different bugs, identical at a glance.
kubectl describe pod api-xxx | sed -n '/Last State/,/Ready/p'
#   Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137   -> memory limit too low
#   Exit Code: 137, no OOMKilled, event "failed liveness probe"
#                                       -> probe too tight / shared thread pool

# 3. Throttling: invisible without this metric
kubectl top pods                                    # shows usage, NOT throttling
# Prometheus:
rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total{pod=~"api-.*"}[5m]) > 0
#   > 0 means every thread froze until the next 100ms period. No errors. No logs.

# 4. Did the HPA do anything?
kubectl describe hpa api
#   "current CPU: 31% (target 70%)"  -> IO-bound; CPU will never trigger
kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending
kubectl describe pod <pending> | grep -A5 Events
#   "0/12 nodes are available: insufficient cpu" -> waiting on the node autoscaler

# 5. Mitigate NOW, then fix properly
kubectl scale deploy/api --replicas=18        # buy headroom immediately
kubectl rollout undo deploy/api               # if the new version is the cause

# Prevention
resources:  requests from observed p95; memory request == limit
startupProbe failureThreshold 30 / period 5s  # JVM gets 150s, then tight liveness
livenessProbe -> shallow, port 9090, separate connector
HPA metric   -> http_server_requests_active   # not CPU
schedule     -> CronJob patches minReplicas to 18 at 08:45, back at 10:30
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not just raise the memory limit and move on?

Because you have not established whether it is a leak or legitimate peak usage. Raising the limit on a leak buys you a longer interval between the same incident. Look at the memory trend across the pod's lifetime: sawtooth returning to a stable floor is normal GC and the limit is genuinely too low; a rising floor is a leak, and the fix is a heap dump, not a bigger number.

What if the rollout is stuck but you cannot tell why quickly?

Roll back first, diagnose after — kubectl rollout undo is fast and safe because the previous ReplicaSet is retained. Users are the priority at 3am; the root cause keeps until morning. The one thing to capture before rolling back is a kubectl describe and the logs of a failing pod, since those disappear with it.

How do you tell a bad deploy from a load problem?

Correlate with time. If restarts and latency began at the deploy timestamp, it is the deploy — roll back and confirm recovery. If they began with the traffic ramp and the deploy was hours earlier, it is capacity. When both happened at once, roll back anyway: it is the cheaper, more reversible experiment, and it eliminates one variable in about a minute.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The requirement to interrogate first is exactly-once, because it is not achievable at the delivery layer. Say that plainly: SQS is at-least-once, retries exist, and networks partition. What is achievable — and what the business actually means — is exactly-once effect: every row is applied to the ledger once regardless of how many times it is delivered. That is an idempotency property in the consumer, not a queue setting.

Ingest. The file lands in S3; the event notification goes to SQS, not directly to Lambda — buffering, controlled concurrency, per-message retry, and a DLQ. A dispatcher reads the file, records it in a control table with a row count and a checksum, and splits it into batches — say 5,000 rows each — enqueuing a work item per batch. It does not process rows itself; splitting and processing are separate concerns with different failure characteristics.

Idempotency. Every work item gets a deterministic id derived from content: fileId + rowRange, or a hash of the row itself for row-level granularity. Never the SQS message id, which changes on redelivery and would make every retry look new. The consumer's first action is a conditional write claiming that id in a processed-items table — attribute_not_exists(pk) in DynamoDB, or a unique constraint in Postgres. If the claim fails, it is a duplicate: acknowledge and return. That conditional write, not the queue, is what makes the system exactly-once in effect.

Not falling over on a bad file is the second half. Validate structurally at dispatch — if the header is wrong or the row count does not match the trailer, reject the whole file immediately with a clear operational error rather than half-processing it. Then, at row level, a bad row must never fail its batch: write it to a rejects file with the row number and the reason, and continue. A single malformed amount should not block 499,999 good rows, and this is exactly where naive implementations lose an entire night's processing.

Operational shape. Visibility timeout above p99 batch time with a heartbeat for long batches. maxReceiveCount of 4, DLQ with an alarm on any non-zero depth, and a documented redrive procedure. Progress tracked in the control table so a partial failure resumes rather than restarts, and so you can answer how far through are we without reading logs. Consumers scale on queue depth via KEDA, not CPU. And a reconciliation step at the end: count applied rows plus rejected rows and assert it equals the file's declared count — because the failure you most need to catch is the silent one where rows simply vanished.

500k rows, at-least-once delivery, exactly-once effect
S3 (file lands)
  -> S3 Event Notification -> SQS control-queue        (never straight to Lambda)
     -> DISPATCHER
          validate header + trailer row count          # reject bad files whole
          INSERT file_control(fileId, rowCount, checksum, status=SPLITTING)
          for each 5,000-row range:
              SendMessage(work-queue, { fileId, from, to,
                                        workId = fileId + "#" + from + "-" + to })
          UPDATE file_control SET status=DISPATCHED, batches=N

     -> WORK QUEUE (visibility 300s, maxReceiveCount 4, DLQ + alarm)
        -> WORKERS (KEDA: 1 pod per 20 messages, max 40)

// Worker: claim first, then work
try {
    ddb.putItem(r -> r.tableName("processed_batches")
        .item(Map.of("pk", s(workId), "ttl", n(ttl90d())))
        .conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk)"));   // THE guarantee
} catch (ConditionalCheckFailedException dup) {
    ack(); return;                       // already applied - safe no-op
}

int applied = 0, rejected = 0;
for (Row row : read(fileId, from, to)) {
    try {
        ledger.apply(row, idempotencyKey(fileId, row.number()));  // row-level too
        applied++;
    } catch (ValidationException bad) {
        rejects.write(fileId, row.number(), bad.getMessage());    // NEVER fail the batch
        rejected++;
    }
}
progress.record(fileId, from, to, applied, rejected);
ack();

// Final reconciliation - catches the silent failure
assert sum(applied) + sum(rejected) == file_control.rowCount;
// mismatch -> alarm, do NOT mark the file complete
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not process the whole file in one Lambda?

Two hard limits and one soft one: the 15-minute timeout, the memory ceiling for buffering, and the fact that a failure at row 480,000 loses everything before it unless you have checkpointing — at which point you have reinvented batching badly. Splitting gives you parallelism, bounded retry blast radius, and resumability, and it makes the work item the natural unit of idempotency.

How do you handle a file that is re-sent by the partner?

The fileId should derive from content — a hash — not from the filename, since partners reuse names. A genuine re-send then produces identical work ids and every batch is a no-op claim, which is the correct behaviour. A corrected re-send is a different file: it needs an explicit supersede path with reversing entries for the original, because silently applying both is how you double-count a settlement.

What does the DLQ replay path look like in practice?

Fix the bug, deploy, then redrive from the DLQ back to the source queue (the console and API both support this natively now). Because the workers claim by deterministic id, any message that was actually applied before failing is a safe no-op on replay — which is what makes redrive routine rather than frightening. Rehearse it once in staging so the runbook is not written during an incident.

Evaluation and the Platform

Judging output, regression gates and cost models - StatefulSets, storage, jobs and admission - ECS, EKS, ECR and deployment strategy.

Week 3 was about load. This week is about change: how you know a change is safe before it ships, and how you ship it without an outage.

190/3

Judging output, keeping state, choosing a runtime

Explain LLM-as-judge. When is it trustworthy, when is it not, and how do you stop your eval from drifting along with your system?

Must coverA stronger model grades outputs against a rubric, which scales far past human labelling. It is trustworthy for relative comparisons and for checking explicit criteria - is every claim supported by the provided context, does this follow the format. It is not trustworthy for absolute quality scores, and it has known biases: position bias, length bias, and self-preference for its own outputs. Controls: a fixed rubric with concrete pass criteria, randomised ordering, a held-out human-labelled set to calibrate the judge itself, and a frozen judge model version so scores stay comparable across releases.

StudyAnthropic - creating strong empirical evaluations →

Explain StatefulSets. What exactly do you get that a Deployment does not, and would you run PostgreSQL on Kubernetes?

Must coverStable ordinal identity (app-0, app-1) that survives rescheduling, stable per-pod DNS via a headless Service, one PersistentVolumeClaim per replica created from a volumeClaimTemplate and retained across restarts, and ordered rolling updates and scale-down. That is what clustered software needs to find its peers and its own data. Would I run Postgres on it: only with a mature operator handling failover, backup and upgrade - otherwise use RDS, because the operational surface you are taking on is the entire database, and Kubernetes gives you none of it for free.

StudyKubernetes - StatefulSets →

ECS, EKS or Fargate - talk me through the decision for a team of eight running twelve Java services.

Must coverFargate is a launch mode, not a competitor - it removes node management from either ECS or EKS at a per-vCPU premium and with fewer daemonset-style capabilities. ECS is AWS-native, far less to operate, integrates directly with ALB, IAM and CloudWatch, and has almost no learning curve. EKS is standard Kubernetes - portable, vastly richer ecosystem, and a genuine platform-team-sized operational cost: upgrades, add-ons, CNI, autoscaler. For eight engineers with no platform team, ECS on Fargate is the honest answer; EKS is right when you already have Kubernetes expertise or need its ecosystem.
