AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

LLM-as-judge means using a model — usually a strong one — to grade another model's output against a rubric. It exists because human labelling does not scale: you cannot have a person read 300 outputs on every pull request, but you can run a judge in CI in two minutes.

Where it is trustworthy. Relative comparisons — is A better than B — are reliable, because the judge only has to detect a difference rather than calibrate an absolute scale. And explicit, checkable criteria are reliable: is every factual claim in the answer supported by the provided context, does the output follow the requested format, does it refuse when the context is insufficient. These are close to reading comprehension, which models are genuinely good at.

Where it is not. Absolute quality scores — rate this 1–10 — are close to meaningless: the numbers are not stable across runs, not comparable across rubric versions, and cluster around 7 and 8 regardless of quality. And there are documented biases you must design around: position bias (the first option in a pairwise comparison wins more often), length bias (longer answers score higher irrespective of correctness), self-preference (a model rates its own outputs generously), and sycophancy toward whatever the rubric's phrasing implies is desirable.

Controls. Write a rubric with concrete pass criteria, not adjectives — cites at least one document id present in the retrieved set beats is well-sourced. Randomise ordering in pairwise comparisons and run both orders. Keep the judge as a binary or small-ordinal classifier per criterion rather than a scalar score. Use a different model family from the one under test where you can, to blunt self-preference.

Then the part that answers how do you stop the eval drifting. Two things. Pin the judge model version — an explicit version, never a floating alias — so a provider update does not silently move every score you have ever recorded; treat a judge upgrade as its own migration where you re-score history and compare. And calibrate the judge against a human-labelled subset: 50–100 items scored by a person, so you know the judge's agreement rate and its error direction. Re-run that calibration whenever the judge or rubric changes. Without it you have a number with unknown accuracy, and you will eventually ship a regression because the judge learned to like it.

Finally: use the judge only where you must. Anything checkable in code — schema validity, cited ids existing in the retrieved set, a number matching the source row, absence of PII — should be a deterministic grader. Those are exact, free, instant, and cannot drift. The judge is for the residue.

Deterministic first, judge for the residue
// Tier 1 - deterministic. Free, exact, cannot drift. Use wherever possible.
assertTrue(schema.validate(output));                        // shape
assertTrue(retrievedIds.containsAll(output.citations()));   // no invented sources
assertEquals(sourceRow.amount(), output.amount());          // numbers from data
assertFalse(PII.matcher(output.text()).find());             // leakage

// Tier 2 - judge, binary criteria, pinned version, fixed rubric
{
  "judge_model": "claude-...-20260514",     // EXPLICIT version, never an alias
  "temperature": 0,
  "criteria": [
    { "id": "grounded",
      "question": "Is EVERY factual claim in the answer supported by text in the
                   provided context? Answer only PASS or FAIL.",
      "type": "binary" },
    { "id": "answers_question",
      "question": "Does the answer address the user's question, as opposed to a
                   related topic? Answer only PASS or FAIL.",
      "type": "binary" },
    { "id": "correct_refusal",
      "question": "The context does not contain the answer. Did the response say
                   so rather than speculating? Answer only PASS or FAIL.",
      "type": "binary", "applies_when": "expected_refusal" }
  ]
}
// NOT: "rate the quality 1-10"  -> unstable, clusters at 7-8, meaningless

// Tier 3 - calibration. Without this you have an uncalibrated instrument.
human_labelled = 80 items
judge_agreement = 0.91        # track it; investigate the 9%
judge_bias      = "fails 6% of grounded answers that a human passes"
                              # known error direction -> read the threshold with it

// Drift guards
- judge model version pinned and recorded with every score
- rubric versioned in git; a rubric change re-scores history
- 20 golden items with known-correct grades, asserted every run
Follow-ups they will ask

Should the judge see the reference answer?

For groundedness, no — it should see the answer and the retrieved context only, because that is the actual question. For correctness against a known answer, yes, and it makes the judge far more reliable, since comparing two texts is easier than evaluating one. Where you have reference answers, prefer that setup; where you do not, keep the criteria to properties checkable from the context alone.

How many judge calls does this cost per CI run?

Roughly cases × criteria. 200 cases with three criteria is 600 calls — a few dollars and a couple of minutes with parallelism, which is fine for a merge gate. Keep it affordable by batching criteria into one call per case where the model can answer several binary questions reliably, and by running the full suite on merge with a smaller smoke subset on every push.

What if the judge and a human disagree on a specific case?

Treat it as information about the rubric, not about the judge. Most disagreements trace to an ambiguous criterion, and tightening the wording fixes a whole class of them. Keep every disagreement in the calibration set permanently — those are the cases that tell you when a judge upgrade changes behaviour, and they are much more valuable than easy cases where everyone agrees.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A StatefulSet gives you four guarantees a Deployment explicitly does not, and each maps to something clustered software genuinely needs.

Stable network identity. Pods are named by ordinal — redis-0, redis-1, redis-2 — and that name survives rescheduling to a different node. Combined with a headless Service (clusterIP: None), each pod gets its own DNS record, redis-0.redis.ns.svc.cluster.local. That is how peers find each other. A Deployment gives you random suffixes that change on every restart, so there is no stable address to put in a cluster configuration.

Stable storage. A volumeClaimTemplate creates one PersistentVolumeClaim per replica, bound to that ordinal, and — critically — retained when the pod is deleted or rescheduled. redis-1 always gets data-redis-1. A Deployment with a PVC gives every replica the same claim, which for EBS (ReadWriteOnce) deadlocks past one replica, and for a shared filesystem means every replica writing over the same data — silent corruption.

Ordered, controlled lifecycle. Scale-up is sequential and waits for each pod to be Ready; rolling updates go in reverse ordinal order, one at a time; scale-down removes the highest ordinal first. That ordering is what lets a quorum system stay above a majority throughout an upgrade — and it is why the readiness probe must mean joined the cluster and caught up, not merely port is open. A probe that returns Ready too early lets the controller move to the next pod and break quorum.

Partitioned rollouts. updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition updates only pods at or above an ordinal, which is how you canary a single replica and verify before releasing the rest.

Would I run PostgreSQL on Kubernetes? The honest answer is: only behind a mature operator, and usually not. A StatefulSet gives you identity and storage — it gives you nothing of what a database actually needs: leader election, automated failover with fencing, streaming replication setup, backup and point-in-time recovery, major version upgrades, connection pooling, and the ability to recover from a split brain. An operator like CloudNativePG or Zalando's encodes that, and they are genuinely good now.

But state the trade explicitly: choosing Kubernetes over RDS means you have taken on operating a database, including being the person paged for a failed failover at 3am, in exchange for portability, cost control at large scale, and the same deployment model as everything else. For a payments platform on AWS with a small team, RDS or Aurora is the right call and I would defend it — the differentiating engineering is not in operating Postgres. I would reconsider at large scale, with a platform team, or where multi-cloud or on-prem portability is a real requirement rather than an aspiration.

What the volumeClaimTemplate buys you
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata: { name: redis }
spec:
  serviceName: redis                 # MUST be a headless Service - peer DNS
  replicas: 3
  podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady  # or Parallel, if peers do not need ordering
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { partition: 0 }  # set to 2 to canary ONLY redis-2
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
      containers:
        - name: redis
          readinessProbe:            # must mean "in the cluster and caught up"
            exec:
              command: ["sh","-c","redis-cli ping && redis-cli info replication \
                                   | grep -q 'master_link_status:up'"]
            periodSeconds: 5
          volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /data }]
  volumeClaimTemplates:              # ONE PVC PER REPLICA, retained
    - metadata: { name: data }
      spec:
        accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
        storageClassName: gp3-wait   # volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
        resources: { requests: { storage: 20Gi } }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: redis }
spec:
  clusterIP: None                    # headless -> returns POD IPs, not a VIP
  selector: { app: redis }
---
# Result:
#   redis-0 -> pvc data-redis-0 -> redis-0.redis.ns.svc.cluster.local
#   redis-1 -> pvc data-redis-1 -> redis-1.redis.ns.svc.cluster.local
#   pod rescheduled to another node -> SAME name, SAME volume

# With a Deployment instead:
#   pod-7d9f2, pod-a13c8   (names change every restart -> no peer config)
#   all replicas share ONE pvc -> EBS is ReadWriteOnce -> replica 2 stuck Pending
#   ...or on a shared FS: three writers, one dataset. Silent corruption.

# NOTE: deleting the StatefulSet does NOT delete the PVCs. Deliberate - and a
# real cost leak. persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy now controls this.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why WaitForFirstConsumer on the StorageClass?

Because EBS volumes are AZ-scoped. With immediate binding, the PV is provisioned in some zone before the scheduler has chosen a node — and if the pod is then scheduled elsewhere, it can never mount its volume and sits Pending forever. WaitForFirstConsumer delays provisioning until the pod is scheduled, so the volume is created in the right zone. This is one of the most common StatefulSet failures on EKS.

How do I take a StatefulSet's backup?

Not with a volume snapshot alone — a snapshot of a database mid-write restores a torn file. You need application-consistent backups: the database's own tool (pg_basebackup, WAL archiving to S3) run as a CronJob, or a pre-snapshot hook that quiesces writes. Velero can orchestrate hooks around the snapshot. And test the restore on a schedule, because an untested backup has an unknown recovery time and an unknown success rate.

What is podManagementPolicy Parallel for?

It starts and stops all pods at once rather than in ordinal order, which is right when peers do not need to come up sequentially — a sharded cache, a set of independent workers with per-replica storage. It makes scale-up much faster. Keep OrderedReady for anything where a new member must join an existing quorum, since the ordering is precisely what protects the majority.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

First, correct the framing: Fargate is not a competitor to ECS or EKS — it is a launch mode for either. It removes node management (patching, scaling, right-sizing, capacity planning) at a per-vCPU and per-GB premium of roughly 15–25% over equivalent EC2, with some capability loss: no DaemonSets in the usual sense, no privileged containers, no GPU, and a smaller instance shape ceiling. So the real axis is ECS versus EKS, and then separately whether you manage nodes.

ECS is AWS-native orchestration. It is meaningfully simpler: task definitions and services, direct ALB integration, IAM task roles, CloudWatch logs, and Service Connect for discovery. There is no control plane to upgrade, no add-ons to keep compatible, no CNI to tune. A backend engineer can be productive in a day. The cost is expressiveness — no operators, no CRDs, a thinner ecosystem, and it is AWS-only.

EKS is standard, conformant Kubernetes. You get the entire ecosystem — Argo, Helm, operators, service meshes, KEDA, Kyverno — genuine portability, and a declarative model your team may already know. The cost is a platform team's worth of operational surface: control plane version upgrades on a roughly annual cadence with deprecated-API breakage, add-on lifecycle (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, CSI drivers), autoscaler configuration, IRSA setup, admission policy, and the observability stack. None of that is optional and none of it is free.

For eight engineers running twelve Java services, the honest recommendation is ECS on Fargate. Twelve services is not a scale that needs Kubernetes' expressiveness, and eight engineers cannot spare one to operate a cluster without visibly slowing product work. The Fargate premium is far cheaper than a fraction of an engineer. Say that plainly — interviewers are often testing whether you choose technology by fashion or by team capacity.

Then name what would change the answer, because a recommendation without conditions sounds dogmatic. Choose EKS if: the team already has real Kubernetes experience; you need the ecosystem specifically (operators for stateful workloads, Argo Rollouts for progressive delivery, KEDA for event-driven scaling); portability to another cloud or on-prem is a genuine requirement rather than a slide; or you are heading toward enough services and teams that self-service platform tooling starts to pay for itself — typically dozens of services and several teams.

Add the cost detail that shows you have actually run this: the EKS control plane is a flat charge per cluster per hour, which is negligible; the real cost is nodes and the engineering time. And on either platform, use Graviton for JVM workloads — around 20% cheaper for equal or better performance, and for Java it is usually just a multi-arch image build.

The decision, with the conditions attached
                        ECS + Fargate         EKS + Fargate      EKS + EC2
time to first deploy    ~1 day                ~1-2 weeks         ~2-4 weeks
ongoing ops burden      near zero             moderate           HIGH
  control plane upgrade  n/a                   ~annual, breaking API removals
  add-on lifecycle       n/a                   CNI, CoreDNS, CSI, autoscaler
  node patching          n/a                   n/a                yours
ecosystem               AWS only              full k8s           full k8s
portability             none                  real               real
compute premium         ~15-25%               ~15-25%            0
DaemonSets / GPU        no                    limited            yes

8 engineers, 12 Java services, no platform team
  -> ECS on Fargate. The Fargate premium is far cheaper than the fraction
     of an engineer that operating EKS actually consumes.

Change the answer if:
  - the team already runs Kubernetes competently
  - you need operators / Argo Rollouts / KEDA / a mesh specifically
  - multi-cloud or on-prem portability is a REQUIREMENT, not an aspiration
  - you are heading to dozens of services across several teams

Regardless of choice:
  - Graviton (arm64) for JVM workloads: ~20% cheaper, same or better perf
  - one image, promoted by digest through dev -> staging -> prod
  - EKS control plane cost is trivial; NODES and ENGINEERING TIME are the bill
Follow-ups they will ask

Is it hard to migrate from ECS to EKS later?

The container images and the twelve-factor discipline transfer unchanged, which is the majority of the work. What you rewrite is the orchestration layer: task definitions become Deployments, ECS services become Services plus Ingress, task roles become IRSA-annotated ServiceAccounts, and Service Connect becomes cluster DNS. It is real work but it is bounded and mechanical — so starting on ECS is not a trap, provided you keep application code free of platform-specific assumptions.

What about ECS on EC2 rather than Fargate?

Worth it when you need capabilities Fargate lacks (GPU, privileged containers, very large instance shapes, host-level agents) or when you are large enough that the Fargate premium exceeds the cost of managing an ASG — that crossover is usually in the tens of thousands of dollars a month. Below that, Fargate's operational saving generally wins.

Does EKS Auto Mode change this recommendation?

It moves the line, and it is worth acknowledging — AWS managing node provisioning, scaling and core add-ons removes a real slice of the burden. It does not remove control plane upgrades, deprecated-API breakage, or the need to understand Kubernetes when something goes wrong. For eight engineers I would still start with ECS, but it is a much closer call than it was two years ago, and saying so shows current knowledge.

Regression, volumes, registries

Prompt changes are code changes. Design the CI pipeline that stops a prompt edit from silently regressing production.

Must coverVersion prompts in git, never in a database edited by hand, and treat the model version and parameters as part of the artefact. On every PR run the eval suite: a labelled set of 100-300 cases with graders that are deterministic where possible (schema validity, required citation, regex on forbidden content) and judge-based where not. Gate on aggregate score plus a hard gate on any case in the critical set regressing. Snapshot diffs of outputs for human review. Then canary in production behind a flag with online metrics before full rollout.

StudyAnthropic - evaluation tool →

Explain PersistentVolume, PersistentVolumeClaim, StorageClass and access modes. What happens to the EBS volume when the pod moves to another AZ?

Must coverA PVC is the request, a PV is the actual volume, and a StorageClass provisions PVs dynamically with a given type and reclaim policy. Access modes matter: EBS is ReadWriteOnce, so exactly one node can mount it - which is why a Deployment with replicas above one and an EBS volume deadlocks. EFS is ReadWriteMany. And EBS is AZ-scoped: if the pod is rescheduled to another AZ it cannot mount the volume and sits Pending forever, which is why the topology-aware volumeBindingMode is WaitForFirstConsumer.

StudyKubernetes - persistent volumes →

How do images get from your CI to your cluster on AWS? Cover ECR, authentication, immutability, scanning and the pull path from private subnets.

Must coverCI authenticates to ECR with an IAM role (OIDC from GitHub Actions, no static keys), builds, pushes with an immutable tag plus the digest. Enable tag immutability and scan-on-push, and set a lifecycle policy or you pay for thousands of old images. Deployments reference the digest. From private subnets the pull needs either a NAT gateway or - better and cheaper at volume - VPC endpoints for ECR api and dkr plus S3, since layers live in S3. Cross-account pulls need a repository policy, and EKS nodes need the ECR read policy on their node role.

AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start from the premise the question is testing: a prompt is code. It changes behaviour in production, it has a version, it can regress, and it must be reviewable. Prompts edited in a database admin screen or a vendor console are unversioned production changes with no diff, no review and no rollback — that is the practice to argue against first.

So: prompts live in git, alongside the code that uses them, and the deployable artefact is the whole set — prompt template, model id with an explicit version, sampling parameters, tool schemas, and retrieval configuration (k, thresholds, embedding model). Pinning the model version matters because a floating alias means your artefact silently changes underneath you.

The pipeline. On every pull request touching any of those, run the eval suite. Structure the graders in tiers. Deterministic first: schema validity, cited ids present in the retrieved set, extracted numbers matching source rows, forbidden content absent, refusal produced where required. These are exact, fast and free, and they catch most real regressions. Judge-based second, with a pinned judge and binary criteria, for groundedness and relevance.

The gates. Two, deliberately different. An aggregate floor that fails the build — say overall score must not drop more than a point below the main branch's score. And a critical set where any single regression is an unconditional block, no override. The critical set is small (20–40 cases), covers the things that must never break — permissions, refusals on unanswerable questions, no PII in output, injection resistance — and it is what prevents someone shipping a plausible-looking improvement that quietly breaks a safety property.

Output diffs for human review. Numbers tell you that something changed; the diff tells you what. Render side-by-side old and new outputs for the cases whose grade changed, and put it in the PR. Reviewers catch tone and format regressions that no grader encodes.

Then canary in production, because offline evals are necessary and not sufficient — real inputs are messier than your set. Serve the new version to a small traffic percentage behind a flag, watch schema failure rate, latency, cost per request and the online quality signal, and ramp on green. Keep the previous version deployed so rollback is a flag flip rather than a deploy, and log the prompt version on every response so you can attribute a complaint to a specific version weeks later.

Finally, the loop that keeps the suite honest: every production failure becomes a permanent eval case. That is what stops the same bug shipping twice, and it is why a mature eval set looks like a scar record rather than a design document.

Prompt change as a reviewable, gated deploy
prompts/
  settlement_summary/
    v7.md                 # the template
    config.yaml           # model + params + tool schemas, PINNED
    CHANGELOG.md
evals/
  settlement_summary/
    cases.jsonl           # 240 cases, 32 marked critical
    graders.py

# config.yaml - the artefact is ALL of this, not just the text
model: claude-...-20260514        # explicit version, never an alias
temperature: 0
max_tokens: 400
retrieval: { k: 5, rerank: true, min_score: 0.35 }
embedding_model: voyage-3         # changing this invalidates the index

# .github/workflows/prompt-eval.yml
on: pull_request
    paths: ['prompts/**','evals/**','src/main/java/**/ai/**']
jobs:
  eval:
    - run: eval run --suite settlement_summary --baseline origin/main
    - run: eval gate
        --aggregate-min 0.92
        --regression-tolerance 0.01     # soft: fails the build
        --critical-must-pass             # hard: NO override
    - run: eval diff --format html --only-changed > diff.html
    - uses: actions/upload-artifact      # reviewers see WHAT changed, not just that

# Sample gate output
  aggregate      0.941 -> 0.936   (-0.005)  PASS  within tolerance
  groundedness   0.972 -> 0.981   (+0.009)  PASS
  citation_valid 1.000 -> 1.000            PASS
  CRITICAL       32/32 -> 31/32            FAIL  <-- blocks, no override
    eval-118 "user without finance role asks for payroll totals"
             expected: refusal      got: summarised the document
             ^ a permissions regression that the aggregate score hid

# Then production
  flag: prompt.settlement_summary.version = v7  (5% -> 25% -> 100%)
  every response logs promptVersion + modelVersion for attribution
  rollback = flag flip, because v6 is STILL DEPLOYED
Follow-ups they will ask

What goes in the critical set?

Things whose failure is a safety, security or compliance event rather than a quality dip: a user without permission must not receive restricted content; an unanswerable question must be refused; no PII in output; a known injection payload must not trigger a tool call; monetary figures must match the source exactly. Keep it small enough that every case is individually justified, and never let anyone override it — the moment it becomes overridable it stops working.

How do I evaluate a change to the retrieval config rather than the prompt?

With the same suite, because the pipeline is what you are testing, not the prompt in isolation. Changing k, the reranker, the chunker or the embedding model all change what reaches the generator, so they all go through the same gate. This is exactly why the eval suite must run the full path end to end rather than mocking retrieval — a mocked retriever tests a system you do not ship.

Is a canary really necessary if the evals pass?

Yes, and the reason is distribution. Your eval set is a sample someone curated; production inputs include phrasings, languages, lengths and edge cases nobody thought of. The canary is where you find those. It also catches operational regressions evals cannot see — latency, cost per request, and rate-limit behaviour under real concurrency.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Four objects, and the relationship between them is the answer. A PersistentVolumeClaim is a request for storage made by a workload — size, access mode, class. A PersistentVolume is the actual piece of storage. A StorageClass is a template describing how to provision one dynamically: which CSI driver, what parameters (volume type, IOPS, throughput, encryption), what reclaimPolicy, and what volumeBindingMode. In modern clusters you almost never create PVs by hand — you create a PVC referencing a StorageClass and the CSI driver provisions the PV.

Access modes are where most surprises live, and they are a property of the storage technology, not a preference you express. ReadWriteOnce means one node may mount it read-write — that is EBS. ReadWriteOncePod restricts it further to a single pod. ReadOnlyMany is many nodes read-only. ReadWriteMany is many nodes read-write, which EBS cannot do and EFS can.

The consequence people hit: a Deployment with replicas: 3 and one EBS-backed PVC. All three pods reference the same claim. The first pod mounts it; the other two are stuck Pending forever with a multi-attach error — or, if they land on the same node, they all write to one filesystem with no coordination, which is worse because it looks like it works. The correct shapes are: a StatefulSet with a volumeClaimTemplate (one volume per replica), or EFS if replicas genuinely need shared read-write, or — most often — no volume at all, because the state belongs in a database.

Now the AZ question, which is the core of it. An EBS volume exists in exactly one availability zone and cannot be mounted from another. So if a pod is rescheduled to a node in a different AZ, it cannot attach its volume and sits Pending indefinitely with a node-affinity conflict — the cluster has capacity, the pod is valid, and it will never run. The PV carries a nodeAffinity that pins it to its zone, which is what produces the message.

This is exactly why volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer exists and should be your default. With the older Immediate binding, the volume is provisioned as soon as the PVC is created — before the scheduler has picked a node — so it lands in an arbitrary zone and then constrains where the pod may run. With WaitForFirstConsumer, provisioning is deferred until the scheduler has chosen a node, and the volume is created in that node's zone. It inverts the dependency from storage-constrains-scheduling to scheduling-determines-storage.

The residual limitation is worth stating: once bound, the pod is pinned to that AZ for its lifetime. Lose the AZ and the pod cannot be rescheduled elsewhere with its data. That is not a Kubernetes flaw; it is what block storage means. Real availability for stateful workloads comes from application-level replication across zones — three StatefulSet replicas in three AZs, each with its own local volume — not from expecting a volume to follow a pod.

WaitForFirstConsumer, and why the default bites
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata: { name: gp3-wait }
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer      # <-- make this your default
reclaimPolicy: Delete                        # Retain for anything precious
allowVolumeExpansion: true                   # you WILL need to grow it
parameters:
  type: gp3
  iops: "3000"
  throughput: "125"
  encrypted: "true"
  kmsKeyId: arn:aws:kms:...

# With volumeBindingMode: Immediate  (the trap)
#   1. PVC created            -> EBS volume provisioned in eu-west-1a, NOW
#   2. PV gets nodeAffinity   -> zone == eu-west-1a
#   3. scheduler must now place the pod in 1a, whatever the capacity there
#   4. node in 1a dies        -> pod cannot move to 1b/1c
#      "0/9 nodes are available: 6 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict"
#      Pending. Forever. Cluster has capacity; the pod will never run.

# With WaitForFirstConsumer
#   1. PVC created            -> nothing provisioned yet
#   2. scheduler picks a node (considering CPU, memory, affinity, spread)
#   3. volume provisioned IN THAT NODE'S ZONE
#   -> storage follows scheduling, not the other way round

# The classic broken manifest
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: shared-data }   # ONE claim
# EBS is ReadWriteOnce -> pod 1 mounts, pods 2 and 3 Pending (multi-attach).
# Correct: StatefulSet + volumeClaimTemplate (one volume EACH), or EFS
#          (ReadWriteMany), or - usually - no volume: put the state in RDS.

# Residual limit, state it out loud:
#   a bound pod is pinned to its AZ for life. HA for stateful workloads comes
#   from replication ACROSS zones, not from volumes following pods.
Follow-ups they will ask

When is EFS the right choice over EBS?

When you genuinely need ReadWriteMany — several pods writing a shared directory — or when you want storage that is not AZ-pinned, since EFS is regional and mountable from any zone. The costs are real: significantly higher price per GB, higher and more variable latency, and NFS semantics that many applications handle badly (file locking especially). Never put a database on it. Good for shared uploads, static content, and legacy applications that assume a shared filesystem.

What does reclaimPolicy actually control?

What happens to the underlying volume when the PVC is deleted. Delete destroys it — convenient, and a data-loss footgun if someone deletes a namespace. Retain keeps the PV and the EBS volume, requiring manual cleanup, which also means orphaned volumes silently accrue cost. Use Retain for anything whose loss would be an incident, and pair it with a job that reports unbound retained volumes.

How do I grow a volume that is full?

Set allowVolumeExpansion: true on the StorageClass in advance — you cannot add it retroactively to already-provisioned volumes in a useful way — then edit the PVC's requested size. The CSI driver expands the EBS volume and the filesystem online for most modern setups. You cannot shrink. Note EBS enforces a cooldown between modifications of the same volume, so repeated small growth attempts will be rejected; size the increase generously.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The path is: CI authenticates to ECR, builds, pushes, and the cluster pulls. Each hop has a control worth naming.

Authentication from CI. Use OIDC federation, not stored credentials. GitHub Actions presents a signed OIDC token; a role in your account trusts that provider with a condition on the repository and branch, and returns short-lived STS credentials. No access key exists anywhere — nothing to rotate, nothing to leak. The condition matters: without pinning sub to your specific repo and ref, any repository on GitHub can assume the role, which is a real and frequently-made misconfiguration.

Push and immutability. Enable tag immutability on the repository so a tag can never be overwritten — this removes an entire class of drift where v1.4.2 means different bytes on different days. Enable scan on push (basic, or Inspector-backed enhanced scanning which continuously rescans existing images as new CVEs are published — that continuous part is what actually matters, since a clean image today is not clean next month). Push both a semantic tag and record the digest; deployments reference the digest.

Lifecycle policy is not optional. Without one you accumulate every image ever built, and at a few hundred MB each across a dozen services with per-commit builds, that becomes a meaningful monthly line item for artefacts nobody will ever pull. Keep the last N tagged images per service and expire untagged ones after a few days.

The pull path from private subnets is the part that separates people who have run this. Nodes in private subnets need to reach ECR, and by default that means NAT — where you pay per gigabyte processed, on every image layer, on every cold node. Container images are large and node churn (autoscaling, spot reclamation, upgrades) makes this constant. The fix is VPC endpoints: interface endpoints for ecr.api and ecr.dkr, plus a gateway endpoint for S3 — because ECR stores the actual layers in S3, and people configure the two ECR endpoints, see pulls still failing or still traversing NAT, and are baffled. That S3 gateway endpoint is the detail worth stating explicitly.

Permissions. On EKS the node role needs AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly and the kubelet's credential provider handles the token exchange — no imagePullSecrets for same-account ECR. Cross-account pulls need a repository policy on the ECR side granting the other account's principals; this is how a shared build account publishes once and dev, staging and production all pull the identical digest, which is exactly the promotion model you want.

Add: use ECR pull-through cache for Docker Hub and public registries, so you are insulated from upstream rate limits and outages and your base images are scanned and cached in your own account.

CI to cluster, with no stored credentials
# 1. CI auth: OIDC, no secrets. Note the CONDITION.
{ "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::1234:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com" },
  "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com" },
    "StringLike":   { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub":
                      "repo:acme/payments-api:ref:refs/heads/main" } } }
                      # ^ omit this and ANY GitHub repo can assume the role

# 2. Repository settings
imageTagMutability: IMMUTABLE          # a tag can never be overwritten
imageScanningConfiguration: { scanOnPush: true }
# + Inspector enhanced scanning: CONTINUOUS rescan as new CVEs appear

# 3. Lifecycle policy - without this you pay for every build, forever
{ "rules": [
  { "rulePriority": 1, "selection": { "tagStatus": "untagged",
      "countType": "sinceImagePushed", "countUnit": "days", "countNumber": 7 },
    "action": { "type": "expire" } },
  { "rulePriority": 2, "selection": { "tagStatus": "tagged",
      "tagPrefixList": ["v"], "countType": "imageCountMoreThan", "countNumber": 30 },
    "action": { "type": "expire" } } ] }

# 4. Pull path from PRIVATE subnets - three endpoints, not two
com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.ecr.api    (interface)
com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.ecr.dkr    (interface)
com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.s3         (GATEWAY - free, and REQUIRED:
                                    ECR stores layers in S3. Everyone forgets it.)
# Without them: every layer of every pull is billed as NAT data processing,
# on every cold node, forever.

# 5. Cross-account promotion: build once, pull the same digest everywhere
{ "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "AWS": ["arn:aws:iam::STAGING:root","arn:aws:iam::PROD:root"] },
  "Action": ["ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer","ecr:BatchGetImage",
             "ecr:BatchCheckLayerAvailability"] }
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is my pull still going through NAT after adding the ECR endpoints?

Almost always the missing S3 gateway endpoint. The ECR API endpoints handle authentication and manifest resolution; the layer blobs themselves are served from S3. Add the gateway endpoint (it is free) and confirm the private subnets' route tables actually reference it — a gateway endpoint works by adding a route, so a subnet whose route table was not associated silently keeps using NAT.

Should CI push directly to the production account's registry?

No — push once to a shared build or artefact account and let environment accounts pull cross-account by digest. That gives you one artefact promoted unchanged through environments, which is the property you actually want: what you tested in staging is bit-for-bit what runs in production. Pushing separately per environment means three different builds and three chances to differ.

How do you handle base image updates across twelve services?

A bot (Renovate or Dependabot) opens a pull request per service when the pinned base digest changes, so each bump is reviewed, tested by that service's pipeline, and revertible. Combine with continuous scanning so a new CVE in an already-deployed image raises an alert rather than waiting for the next build. The failure mode to avoid is a floating base tag that changes silently — it makes builds irreproducible and hides exactly this class of change.

Guardrails, batch work, deployment strategy

What guardrails go around a customer-facing LLM feature in a regulated payments company? Be concrete about input and output.

Must coverInput: authenticate and authorise before the model sees anything, strip or tokenise PII, classify for abuse and out-of-scope intent with a cheap model, and rate limit per user. Output: schema validation, a grounding check that every factual claim maps to retrieved context, a blocklist and PII scan on the way out, and never let generated text drive a side effect without a typed, permission-checked tool call. Around both: full audit logging of prompt, retrieved context, output and user, with retention that satisfies compliance, plus a kill switch flag and a deterministic fallback path.

StudyAnthropic - reduce hallucinations →

Explain Jobs, CronJobs and DaemonSets. How do you stop a CronJob from stacking up when a run overruns its schedule?

Must coverA Job runs pods to completion with completions and parallelism, and backoffLimit before it gives up; use an indexed Job for partitioned work. A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule - concurrencyPolicy Forbid stops overlapping runs, Replace kills the old one, and startingDeadlineSeconds prevents a storm of catch-up runs after a control-plane outage. Always set ttlSecondsAfterFinished or completed pods accumulate until the namespace is unusable. DaemonSets run one pod per node and are how log shippers, CNI and node exporters get everywhere.

StudyKubernetes - CronJob →

Compare rolling, blue/green and canary deployments on AWS. Which would you use for a payments API and how do you roll back?

Must coverRolling replaces instances gradually - cheapest, but both versions serve simultaneously so the API and the database schema must be backward compatible. Blue/green stands up a full parallel environment and switches the listener or DNS - instant rollback, double the cost during the window, and stateful concerns (in-flight sessions, schema) do not switch cleanly. Canary shifts a small traffic percentage and watches metrics before proceeding. For payments: canary with automatic rollback on error rate and latency alarms, plus expand-contract schema migrations so rollback is genuinely possible - the deploy strategy is worthless if the database has already moved forward.

StudyAWS - deployment strategies →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Organise the answer as input guardrails, output guardrails, and the wrapper around both — and be explicit that in a regulated context every one of them is enforced in code, never in the prompt.

Input. Authenticate and authorise before the model sees anything, so retrieval and tools are already scoped to what this user may access. Strip or tokenise PII — replace a card number with a token, call the model, detokenise on the way out if needed; the model never sees a PAN, which also keeps the request out of PCI scope for that data. Classify the incoming request with a cheap model for abuse, out-of-scope intent and obvious injection, and reject early. Rate limit per user and per tenant, and cap input size, because unbounded input is both a cost attack and a context-stuffing attack.

Output. Validate against the schema. Run a grounding check — every factual claim must map to retrieved context, and every monetary figure must equal a value from the system of record rather than from generated text. Scan for PII on the way out, because retrieved context can contain it even when the input did not. Apply a blocklist for prohibited content — competitor comparisons, legal or financial advice, promises about outcomes. And the structural rule: generated text must never drive a side effect. Actions happen only through typed, permission-checked tool calls, so there is no path from the model said to the system did.

Around both. Full audit logging: the prompt, the retrieved chunk ids, the output, the user, the model version, the prompt version, tied to a request id, retained under the same policy as the underlying data — which means the log inherits the data's classification, so it is encrypted, access-controlled and covered by deletion requests. A kill switch: a feature flag that disables the AI path and falls back to the deterministic experience, tested, so that turning it off during an incident is routine rather than a deploy. And a documented deterministic fallback for every path, because the feature is unavailable is an acceptable outcome and the feature invented a number is not.

The framing to close on, because it is what a regulator or a security reviewer actually wants to hear: the model is inside the trust boundary but is never a trust authority. Every control that matters — authorisation, validation, audit, limits — sits in code that runs regardless of what the model produced. Prompt instructions reduce the frequency of bad output; they are not controls, and I would not present them as such.

Guardrails as code, not as prompt text
public Answer ask(User user, String question) {
  // ---- INPUT ----
  rateLimiter.check(user.id(), tenant.id());                  // cost + abuse
  require(question.length() <= 2_000, "input too long");
  var intent = cheapModel.classify(question);                 // small, fast
  if (intent.isAbusive() || intent.isOutOfScope()) return Answer.declined(intent);

  var redacted = pii.tokenise(question);                      // model never sees a PAN
  var chunks   = retriever.search(redacted, aclFilter(user)); // scoped BEFORE the model

  // ---- MODEL ----
  var raw = model.generate(SYSTEM_V7, chunks, redacted,
                           Tools.forContext(user, READ_ONLY));// no write tools here

  // ---- OUTPUT ----
  var out = schema.parse(raw);                                // shape
  require(chunks.ids().containsAll(out.citations()),          // no invented sources
          "ungrounded citation");
  for (Money m : out.figures())                               // numbers from the
      require(ledger.contains(m), "figure not in source");    //   system of record
  require(!pii.detect(out.text()), "PII in output");          // retrieved leakage
  require(!blocklist.matches(out.text()), "prohibited content");

  // ---- AUDIT + FALLBACK ----
  audit.record(requestId, user, redacted, chunks.ids(), out,
               MODEL_VERSION, PROMPT_VERSION);                // same retention as data
  return pii.detokenise(out, user);
}

// Kill switch - tested, and a flag flip, not a deploy
if (!flags.enabled("ai.settlement-assistant", user)) return deterministicSearch(q);

// The line to say out loud:
//   the model is INSIDE the trust boundary but is never a trust AUTHORITY.
//   Prompt instructions lower the failure rate; they are not controls.
Follow-ups they will ask

Is a second model checking the first model's output a real control?

It is a mitigation, not a control — it lowers the rate and it can fail in correlated ways with the thing it is checking. It is worth having for fuzzy properties like tone and groundedness. It is not what you present to an auditor. Anything checkable deterministically (a figure matching a ledger row, a cited id existing, a schema conforming) must be checked deterministically, because that check has a known, provable failure rate of zero.

How do you handle PII that is legitimately needed in the answer?

Tokenise on the way in and detokenise on the way out, with the mapping held server-side and scoped to the request. The model reasons over CARD_TOKEN_7 and the user sees the real value, so the sensitive data never enters the prompt, the provider's systems, or your prompt logs. Where detokenisation is needed, re-check the user's entitlement at that point rather than assuming the earlier check still holds.

What does the kill switch actually turn off?

The AI path specifically, falling back to the deterministic experience — keyword search instead of semantic, a filter form instead of natural language, raw records instead of a summary. It must be per-feature and ideally per-tenant, it must not require a deploy, and it must be exercised regularly. A switch nobody has flipped since it was written is an untested code path, and it will be tested for the first time during an incident.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Job runs pods until a target number succeed. completions is how many successes you need, parallelism how many run concurrently, and backoffLimit how many failures before the Job is marked failed. An indexed Job (completionMode: Indexed) gives each pod an ordinal in an env var, which is how you partition work statically — pod 3 processes shard 3 — without a queue.

CronJob creates Jobs on a cron schedule. It is a controller over Jobs, not a separate execution mechanism, so everything about Jobs applies.

DaemonSet runs exactly one pod per node (optionally filtered by selector or tolerations), and adds one automatically when a node joins. That is how log shippers, CNI agents, node exporters, and CSI node plugins get everywhere. It is also why every node must have room for your DaemonSets before it has room for workloads — a detail that bites when right-sizing small instances.

Now the stacking question. concurrencyPolicy controls what happens when a run is still going at the next scheduled time. Allow (the default) starts another anyway — so a job that normally takes 4 minutes on a 5-minute schedule will, on a slow day, run two, then three, then compound until the namespace quota or the database gives out. Forbid skips the new run and logs it. Replace kills the running Job and starts fresh. For anything writing to a shared store, Forbid is the right default, and Allow should be a deliberate decision backed by the job being safely concurrent.

Two companions to that. startingDeadlineSeconds bounds how late a missed run may start — without it, a control plane outage or a suspended CronJob can produce a burst of catch-up executions the moment it recovers, all at once. And if more than 100 schedules are missed without this set, the controller gives up scheduling entirely and logs an error, which is a genuinely confusing silent failure. Set it to something like one schedule interval.

And the one that causes real operational pain: ttlSecondsAfterFinished. Completed Jobs and their pods are retained indefinitely by default. A CronJob every five minutes produces 288 Jobs a day; after a month the namespace is full of completed pods, kubectl get pods is unusable, and etcd is carrying tens of thousands of dead objects. Set a TTL, and set successfulJobsHistoryLimit and failedJobsHistoryLimit — keeping a few failures for diagnosis and almost no successes.

Finally, the failure semantics worth knowing: a Job's pod restartPolicy must be Never or OnFailure, never Always. With Never, each failure creates a new pod, so you keep the logs of failed attempts — which is usually what you want.

A CronJob that cannot stack, flood, or accumulate
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata: { name: settlement-reconcile }
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  timeZone: "Europe/London"          # otherwise UTC - and DST WILL surprise you
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid          # <-- the stacking fix
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 300       # do not run a missed job an hour late,
                                     #     and avoid the >100-missed dead-stop
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 1      # keep almost no successes
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3          # keep a few failures to diagnose
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 240     # hard stop BELOW the 5-minute schedule
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 600   # <-- the accumulation fix
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never       # each attempt is a new pod -> logs survive
          containers:
            - name: reconcile
              resources:
                requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }
                limits:   { memory: "512Mi" }

# Without concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
#   09:00 run starts, takes 12 minutes (slow partner file)
#   09:05 second run starts   -> two writers
#   09:10 third run starts    -> three
#   ...   quota exhausted, or duplicated ledger entries. Both are bad.

# Without ttlSecondsAfterFinished
#   288 Jobs/day x 30 days = 8,640 Job objects + their pods, in etcd, forever

# Indexed Job: static partitioning without a queue
spec:
  completions: 12
  parallelism: 4
  completionMode: Indexed        # JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX=0..11 in each pod
Follow-ups they will ask

Should a CronJob or an application scheduler own recurring work?

CronJob when the work is a self-contained batch that can run anywhere and you want it visible to the platform — resource-isolated, independently scalable, restartable, and monitorable with the same tools as everything else. An in-application scheduler (Quartz, ShedLock) when the work needs the application's context and connection pools, or must coordinate across replicas — and note that an in-app scheduler in a 3-replica Deployment runs three times unless you add distributed locking, which is a very common bug.

How do I alert when a CronJob silently stops running?

Not by watching for failures — the dangerous case is that nothing runs at all, which produces no failure to alert on. Alert on absence: a Prometheus rule on kube_cronjob_status_last_successful_time being older than your expected interval, or a dead-man's-switch where the job pings a heartbeat endpoint and you alert when the ping stops. Missing-work alerts are the ones teams forget to build.

What if the job must not run twice even across clusters?

CronJob's Forbid only guards within one CronJob object. For a global guarantee you need an external lock — a conditional write to DynamoDB or a Postgres advisory lock taken at the start of the job and held for its duration, with a TTL so a crashed holder does not block forever. That is also the answer for a job scheduled in two regions for availability, where exactly one must actually execute.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Rolling replaces instances or tasks in batches. It is the cheapest — no duplicate environment — and it is what ECS and Kubernetes do natively. The constraint it imposes is that both versions serve simultaneously, so the API must be backward compatible and any schema change must work for both. Rollback is another rolling deploy, so it takes as long as the deploy did.

Blue/green stands up a complete parallel environment, tests it, then switches traffic at once — an ALB listener change, a target group swap, or a DNS change. The advantage is a genuinely instant rollback: switch the listener back. The costs are double infrastructure during the window, and the fact that stateful things do not switch cleanly — in-flight requests, sticky sessions, and above all the database, which is shared and has already moved forward.

Canary shifts a small percentage of real traffic to the new version, watches metrics for a defined period, then proceeds or aborts. It is the only one of the three that limits blast radius: a bad deploy affects 5% of users for five minutes rather than everyone immediately. CodeDeploy supports this natively for ECS and Lambda with linear or canary traffic-shifting configurations and CloudWatch alarms as the abort trigger.

For a payments API: canary with automatic rollback, driven by alarms on error rate and p99 latency, with a bake period long enough for a real signal — several minutes, not thirty seconds. Define the abort criteria numerically before the deploy, not by watching a dashboard, because a human watching graphs at 2am is not a control.

Then the part that makes or breaks all of it, and it is the answer to how do you roll back: the deployment strategy is worthless if the database has already moved forward. If your deploy ran ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN, rolling back the code does not roll back the data, and the old version now queries a column that no longer exists. So every schema change must be expand-contract: expand (add the new nullable column, deploy code writing both and reading old), migrate and backfill, flip reads behind a flag, and only contract — dropping the old column — in a much later, separate release once you are certain you will not roll back.

That gives you the property you actually want: at every point in the sequence, the previous version of the application still works against the current schema. Rollback is then a code-only operation, which is fast and safe. Without it, your rollback plan is a restore from backup, and that is measured in hours.

Canary, plus the migration discipline that makes rollback possible
# CodeDeploy canary on ECS - abort criteria defined BEFORE the deploy
DeploymentConfig: CodeDeployDefault.ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes
AutoRollbackConfiguration:
  enabled: true
  events: [DEPLOYMENT_FAILURE, DEPLOYMENT_STOP_ON_ALARM]
Alarms:
  - api-5xx-rate      > 0.5%   for 2 consecutive minutes
  - api-p99-latency   > 800ms  for 2 consecutive minutes
  - dlq-depth         > 0

#   10% -> bake 5 min -> alarms clean -> 100%
#   alarm fires at any point -> automatic revert to the old task set
#   blast radius of a bad deploy: 10% of users, ~5 minutes

# ---- The half that actually determines whether rollback works ----

# Release 1 - EXPAND. Old version still works. Rollback is free.
ALTER TABLE settlement ADD COLUMN currency_code char(3) NULL;   -- nullable, instant
-- code: writes BOTH currency (old) and currency_code (new); reads currency

# Release 1.5 - BACKFILL, in bounded batches, watching replica lag
UPDATE settlement SET currency_code = lookup(currency)
WHERE currency_code IS NULL AND id BETWEEN :lo AND :hi;         -- never one big UPDATE

# Release 2 - FLIP reads behind a flag. Old version STILL works.
-- code: reads currency_code, still writes both

# Release 3 - CONTRACT. Only once you will never roll back past release 2.
ALTER TABLE settlement DROP COLUMN currency;

# The invariant, stated:
#   at EVERY point, version N-1 of the application works against the CURRENT
#   schema. Therefore rollback is a code-only operation: fast, safe, boring.
#
# Without it: rollback means restoring a database. Hours, not minutes.
# Index changes on a large table: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, or you lock writes.
Follow-ups they will ask

How long should the canary bake?

Long enough to see a statistically meaningful sample at that traffic percentage — for a low-volume API, 10% for five minutes may be a handful of requests, which proves nothing. Compute it from your request rate: you want enough requests that a 1% error rate would be visible. For low-traffic services, shift a larger percentage or bake longer; for high-traffic ones, a small percentage for a few minutes is plenty.

Blue/green with a shared database — is that even blue/green?

Only for the compute tier, and it is worth being precise about that. The database is shared, so it is a single point of coupling that does not switch. That is fine, provided the schema is backward compatible — which brings you straight back to expand-contract. Anyone proposing blue/green as a way to avoid thinking about migrations has misunderstood what switches.

What about feature flags instead of deployment strategies?

They are complementary and arguably more powerful: deploy the code dark, then enable behaviour per user, tenant or percentage without any deploy at all. Rollback is a flag flip in seconds. Use both — canary for the infrastructure change (new image, new task definition) and flags for the behaviour change. The cost is flag debt, so give every flag an owner and a removal date.

Cost of intelligence, isolation, service networking

Build the cost model for an LLM feature serving 50,000 requests a day. What are the levers, in order of size?

Must coverCost is input tokens plus output tokens at different rates, and output is typically several times more expensive per token. Compute it explicitly: tokens per request times requests times rate. Levers by size - first, model choice, since a small model is often an order of magnitude cheaper and adequate for routing, extraction and classification; second, output length, because it is the expensive side; third, prompt caching on a stable prefix, which can cut input cost dramatically for RAG and long system prompts; fourth, retrieving fewer and better chunks; fifth, caching whole responses for repeated queries. Then batch anything that is not interactive.

StudyAnthropic - pricing and token counting →

How do namespaces, ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges give you multi-tenancy? What does a namespace explicitly not isolate?

Must coverA namespace scopes names and is the unit RBAC and quota attach to. ResourceQuota caps aggregate requests, limits and object counts per namespace; LimitRange sets defaults and per-pod bounds so a pod with no requests still gets sensible ones. What a namespace does not give you: network isolation - all pods can reach all pods unless you add NetworkPolicy; node isolation - workloads share kernels unless you taint dedicated nodes; nor protection from a noisy neighbour on the same node beyond cgroup limits. Namespaces are soft multi-tenancy; hostile tenants need separate clusters.

StudyKubernetes - resource quotas →

How do services find each other on ECS or EKS, and what does a service mesh add that you cannot get from Kubernetes Services alone?

Must coverOn ECS, Service Connect or Cloud Map gives DNS-based discovery; on EKS, a ClusterIP Service plus cluster DNS. That gives you name resolution and round-robin, and nothing else. A mesh adds a sidecar or node proxy that intercepts all traffic and gives you mutual TLS between every service without touching application code, retries, timeouts and circuit breaking as configuration, traffic splitting for canaries, and consistent L7 telemetry. The cost is a real one - extra hop latency, sidecar memory per pod, and a new control plane to operate - so adopt it for mTLS and traffic policy at scale, not for observability alone.

StudyKubernetes - service networking →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Build it from units, not from a price list, because the model is what survives when prices change. Cost = (input tokens × input rate) + (output tokens × output rate), per request, times requests. The critical asymmetry: output tokens are typically 3–5× the price of input tokens, and they are also the only sequential part, so output length drives cost and latency together.

Do the arithmetic explicitly. 50,000 requests a day with a 2,000-token system prompt, 4,000 tokens of retrieved context, a 100-token question and a 500-token answer is 6,100 input and 500 output per request — about 305 million input and 25 million output tokens a month. Then apply rates. Doing this out loud, with numbers, is what an interviewer is listening for.

The levers, in order of size. One: model choice. A small model is often an order of magnitude cheaper and entirely adequate for classification, routing, extraction, query rewriting and short summarisation. Routing those away from the large model is usually the single biggest saving available, and it typically improves latency too.

Two: output length. The expensive side, and the easiest to overspend on. Cap max_tokens, instruct for brevity, and stop asking for restatements and preambles. Halving output length is close to halving the expensive half of the bill.

Three: prompt caching. With a stable prefix — system prompt, tool definitions, pinned reference material — cache reads are heavily discounted. For RAG with a long system prompt this frequently cuts input cost substantially, and it is a configuration change plus careful ordering, not a redesign. Verify it works by checking cached-token counts rather than assuming.

Four: retrieve fewer, better chunks. Five reranked chunks instead of twenty cuts input tokens by most of the retrieved portion and usually improves quality by reducing dilution. Five: cache whole responses — exact-match first, since it is free and safe, then bounded semantic caching where the query space is narrow. Internal corpora repeat far more than people expect.

Then batch anything non-interactive: the Batch API is roughly half price for work tolerant of latency — nightly summaries, backfills, bulk classification, eval runs. And put a per-user and per-tenant budget in place with hard enforcement, because without it a single automated client or a retry loop can multiply spend overnight, and you will discover it on the invoice.

Close with the honest framing: at 50,000 requests a day the inference bill is often smaller than one engineer's salary, so optimise it, but do not let it drive the architecture at the expense of quality or delivery speed. The cost that scales dangerously is not this one — it is the one that grows with an agent loop's iteration count or an unbounded retry policy.

Model it in units, then pull the levers in order
BASELINE  50,000 requests/day
  system prompt         2,000  in
  retrieved (20 chunks) 4,000  in
  question                100  in
  answer                  500  out
  ------------------------------------
  per request           6,100  in  /  500 out
  per month           305 M    in  /  25 M out
  (output is ~4x the unit price, so it is roughly half the bill at 1/12 the volume)

AFTER, in order of impact
  1. route classify/rewrite/extract -> small model      ~ -35%  (biggest single win)
  2. max_tokens 500 -> 250, prompt for brevity          ~ -20%
  3. prompt caching: stable 2,800-token prefix          ~ -25%  of input cost
     (verify: cache_read_input_tokens > 0 on call #2)
  4. rerank, 20 chunks -> 5                             ~ -15%  and quality UP
  5. exact-match response cache (internal corpus)       ~ -10%  at ~12% hit rate
  6. Batch API for nightly summaries + eval runs        ~ -50%  on that slice

GUARDS - the thing that actually prevents a bad month
  per-user daily token budget, enforced at the client (429, not a surprise bill)
  per-tenant monthly cap with alerting at 50/80/100%
  agent loops: maxIterations AND maxTotalTokens, both enforced
  retries: capped at 1, with jitter  <-- an uncapped retry storm is the
                                         classic way a bill triples overnight

Sanity check to state out loud:
  cost per request, and cost per user per month. If the second number is
  smaller than a coffee, stop optimising and go improve the quality.
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the most common invisible cost?

Retries and agent loops. A timeout set slightly below your p99 causes a retry on requests that would have succeeded, tripling the cost of your slowest traffic — and it is invisible unless you log retry counts. In an agent loop, the entire transcript is re-sent every iteration, so cost grows superlinearly with steps. Log input tokens per iteration and the curve is immediately obvious.

Does prompt caching help conversational traffic?

Yes, and more than people expect, provided you order the context so the growing part is at the end. System prompt, tools and pinned facts stay stable across every turn of a conversation, so they hit cache from the second turn onward. What breaks it is putting a timestamp, request id or freshly retrieved chunks near the front — everything after the first changed token is uncacheable.

When is fine-tuning a cost optimisation?

When it lets you use a much smaller model for a narrow, high-volume task, or when it removes thousands of few-shot example tokens from every request. Then the saving is real and recurring against a one-off training cost. It is not a cost win for general tasks, and it adds a data pipeline, a versioning burden, and a re-tuning obligation every time the base model improves — so compute the payback period before proposing it.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A namespace is a scope for names and the attachment point for policy. It gives you three things: RBAC boundaries, resource quotas, and a place to hang default policies. It does not give you isolation in the sense most people assume, and being precise about that gap is the point of this question.

ResourceQuota caps aggregate consumption in a namespace: total CPU and memory requests and limits, counts of objects (pods, services, PVCs), and storage per StorageClass. Its important side effect: once a ResourceQuota constrains CPU or memory, every pod in that namespace must specify requests and limits, or it is rejected outright. That is a useful forcing function — it turns please set resources from a review comment into an admission failure.

LimitRange complements it by setting defaults and per-object bounds: a default request and limit applied to containers that omit them, plus minimum and maximum values. Without a LimitRange, a quota-enforced namespace simply rejects unannotated pods; with one, they get sensible defaults instead. Use both — LimitRange for the default, ResourceQuota for the ceiling.

Now what a namespace does not isolate, which is the substance of the answer.

Network. By default every pod can reach every other pod in the cluster, across all namespaces. A namespace is not a network boundary until you add NetworkPolicy with a default-deny — and that requires a CNI that enforces it, which the AWS VPC CNI alone does not.

Kernel. Pods from different namespaces share nodes and therefore share a kernel. A container escape crosses namespaces trivially. Pod Security admission, seccomp and dropped capabilities reduce the risk; they do not remove it.

Noisy neighbours. Quotas bound what a namespace may request; they do not stop a Burstable pod from consuming spare CPU, saturating node network or disk IO, or filling the node's ephemeral storage. Two teams on one node still interfere.

Cluster-scoped resources. CRDs, ClusterRoles, StorageClasses, PersistentVolumes, admission webhooks and node labels are all shared. A team with permission to install a CRD or a webhook can affect everyone.

DNS and the API server. One CoreDNS and one API server serve all namespaces, so a team generating enormous watch load or DNS query volume degrades everyone.

So the conclusion to state plainly: namespaces are soft multi-tenancy — good for organising trusted teams within one organisation, with quotas, RBAC and NetworkPolicy layered on. For hostile or regulated tenancy, the boundary is a separate cluster, and possibly a separate account. Anyone proposing namespaces as a security boundary between untrusted tenants has misread what they are.

Namespace as a policy attachment point, with its limits
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata: { name: team-quota, namespace: payments }
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "40"
    requests.memory: 80Gi
    limits.memory: 80Gi
    pods: "120"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "12"
    count/services.loadbalancers: "2"     # each one is a real, billed NLB/ALB
# Side effect: with CPU/memory quota set, a pod WITHOUT requests+limits is
# REJECTED at admission. Good - it forces resource discipline.
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata: { name: team-defaults, namespace: payments }
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:        { cpu: "500m", memory: 512Mi }   # applied if omitted
      defaultRequest: { cpu: "100m", memory: 256Mi }
      max:            { cpu: "4",    memory: 8Gi }     # nobody grabs a whole node
---
# WITHOUT this, the namespace is not a network boundary at all
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: default-deny, namespace: payments }
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
# then add explicit allows, INCLUDING egress to kube-dns (the classic omission)

# What a namespace still does NOT isolate:
#   network      -> until NetworkPolicy + an enforcing CNI (Calico/Cilium)
#   kernel       -> shared node, shared kernel; escape crosses namespaces
#   node IO      -> disk, network, ephemeral storage: no quota
#   cluster-wide -> CRDs, ClusterRoles, webhooks, StorageClasses, PVs
#   control plane-> one API server, one CoreDNS, shared by everyone

# Soft multi-tenancy: trusted teams, one org.
# Hostile/regulated tenancy: separate CLUSTER, and probably separate ACCOUNT.
Follow-ups they will ask

How do I stop one namespace exhausting node ephemeral storage?

Set ephemeral-storage requests and limits — they are quota-able and enforced like memory, with the pod evicted when it exceeds the limit. Add a quota on requests.ephemeral-storage at the namespace level. Also configure kubelet eviction thresholds and image garbage collection, because the usual cause is not application data but accumulated images and container logs.

Is one big cluster with namespaces or many small clusters better?

Fewer clusters for efficiency — better bin-packing, lower fixed cost, one place to apply policy, one upgrade. More clusters for isolation — hard blast radius, independent upgrade cadence, regulatory separation. The practical middle ground most organisations land on is a cluster per environment per region, with namespaces separating teams inside it, and separate clusters only where a failure or compliance boundary genuinely demands it.

What is hierarchical namespaces and is it worth it?

The Hierarchical Namespace Controller lets namespaces have parents, propagating RBAC, NetworkPolicies and quotas down the tree — useful when one team owns many namespaces and you want policy inherited rather than copied. It is a real solution to a real problem, but it is an additional controller to operate. For most organisations, a GitOps repository that templates the standard policy set into each namespace achieves the same outcome with less machinery.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Baseline first. On ECS, Service Connect (or the older Cloud Map integration) registers tasks and gives you a DNS name plus a managed Envoy proxy for basic retries and connection management. On EKS, a ClusterIP Service plus CoreDNS gives you a stable name resolving to a virtual IP, load-balanced in the kernel by kube-proxy. Both give you the same two things: name resolution and connection-level load balancing. Nothing else.

What that leaves out is substantial, and it is the case for a mesh. Mutual TLS between every service, with automatic certificate issuance and rotation, without touching application code — in a payments environment that is often the deciding feature, because the alternative is implementing mTLS in twelve services and operating a certificate lifecycle yourself. Retries, timeouts, circuit breaking and outlier ejection as configuration rather than as library code that differs between your Java services and anything else. Traffic splitting by percentage or header for canaries, without a second Deployment and replica-count arithmetic. And consistent L7 telemetry from both sides of every call — golden signals for every service pair, with no instrumentation effort.

A related and underrated point: kube-proxy balances per connection, not per request. With HTTP keep-alive and especially gRPC, a client pins to one backend for the connection's lifetime, so traffic skews badly and scaling out does not help. A mesh proxies at L7 and balances per request, which fixes this properly. It is one of the most common real reasons teams adopt one.

Now the costs, stated honestly because an interviewer is checking whether you have actually run a mesh. Every pod gains a sidecar consuming 50–100MB of memory and some CPU — across 500 pods that is real capacity. Every call gains two extra hops (out through the local proxy, in through the remote one), adding low-single-digit milliseconds. You gain a control plane to operate and upgrade, and its failure modes are subtle. Debugging becomes harder before it becomes easier: a connection failure could now be the app, the sidecar, the policy, or the control plane. And sidecar lifecycle used to fight with pod lifecycle — native sidecars in recent Kubernetes fix the worst of it, but ordering during shutdown is still something to verify.

So the recommendation: adopt a mesh for mTLS everywhere and consistent traffic policy at scale — not for observability alone, which OpenTelemetry gives you more cheaply. Before that threshold, prefer Argo Rollouts for progressive delivery and a resilience library or gateway for retries and circuit breaking. And consider Cilium's eBPF mode or Istio's ambient mode as sidecar-free alternatives, which remove most of the per-pod overhead — mentioning that shows current knowledge.

What you get for the sidecar you pay for
BASELINE (Service + CoreDNS, or ECS Service Connect)
  name resolution                        yes
  L4 load balancing                      yes - PER CONNECTION
  mTLS                                   no
  retries / timeouts / circuit breaking  in each app's own library code
  traffic splitting by %                 only via replica-count ratios
  per-service-pair L7 metrics            only if you instrument for it

WITH A MESH
  mTLS everywhere, certs rotated         yes, zero app changes  <-- often the reason
  L7 load balancing                      PER REQUEST (fixes gRPC/keep-alive skew)
  retries/timeouts/CB as config          yes, uniform across languages
  canary by weight or header             yes, declarative
  golden signals for every call          yes, both sides, free

COST
  ~50-100 MB + CPU per pod (x 500 pods = real capacity)
  ~2 extra hops per call (low single-digit ms)
  a control plane to run and upgrade
  harder debugging: app? sidecar? policy? control plane?

# Declarative, language-agnostic - this is the actual value
kind: DestinationRule
spec:
  host: payments-api
  trafficPolicy:
    tls: { mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL }
    connectionPool: { http: { http2MaxRequests: 1000 } }
    outlierDetection:                       # eject failing pods automatically
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5
      interval: 10s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s

DECISION RULE
  need mTLS everywhere or uniform policy across many services  -> mesh
  need canaries only                                           -> Argo Rollouts
  need tracing/metrics only                                    -> OpenTelemetry
  fewer than ~15 services, one language                        -> resilience library
  worried about sidecar overhead                               -> Cilium eBPF /
                                                                  Istio ambient
Follow-ups they will ask

Can I get mTLS without a full mesh?

Yes — Cilium can do transparent encryption at the node level with WireGuard or IPsec, which encrypts pod-to-pod traffic without sidecars and without per-workload identity. That covers encryption in transit but not workload identity and authorisation. If your requirement is a compliance checkbox for encryption, this is much cheaper. If it is service A may call service B and nothing else may, you need identity-aware policy, which is what a mesh provides.

What breaks first when adopting a mesh?

Anything that does not speak the protocol the proxy expects: raw TCP mistaken for HTTP, non-standard ports without a declared protocol, and headless services. Then startup ordering — the app connecting to a dependency before its sidecar is ready — which native sidecars largely fix. And database connections through the proxy often need explicit exclusion, since long-lived connections and connection pooling interact badly with proxy timeouts.

Is a mesh worth it for twelve services?

Usually not, unless mTLS is a hard requirement. Twelve services is a scale where a resilience library plus OpenTelemetry plus Argo Rollouts covers the same ground with far less operational surface, and where the mesh's control plane is a disproportionate addition. The economics change with many teams and many languages, where the mesh's value is uniformity — one policy model instead of twelve library configurations.
