Model selection, admission, load balancers

Prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning - how do you decide? Give the decision rule and the cost of getting it wrong.

Must coverOrder of attempt: prompt engineering, then RAG, then fine-tuning, and stop as soon as it works. Prompting fixes format and behaviour. RAG fixes knowledge - anything the model could not know, anything that changes, anything needing citation. Fine-tuning fixes style, format adherence and narrow task performance, and reduces prompt length; it does not reliably teach facts, and it freezes you to a base model, adds a data pipeline, and must be redone when the base model improves. The wrong move is fine-tuning to inject knowledge - expensive, unverifiable and stale on day one.

StudyAnthropic - prompt engineering overview →

What is an admission controller? Explain validating versus mutating webhooks and give two policies you would enforce in a payments cluster.

Must coverAdmission runs after authentication and authorisation but before the object is persisted. Mutating webhooks change the object - injecting a sidecar, defaulting labels; validating webhooks accept or reject it. Pod Security admission is the built-in one enforcing baseline or restricted profiles per namespace. Policies I would enforce: reject images not from our ECR and not digest-pinned, reject any pod without resource requests, reject privileged and hostNetwork pods, and require a team label for cost allocation. Implement with Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper. Critical operational point: a failing webhook with failurePolicy Fail can block all deployments cluster-wide, so scope it and exempt kube-system.

StudyKubernetes - admission controllers →

ALB versus NLB versus Gateway Load Balancer, and explain target groups, health checks, and connection draining.

Must coverALB is layer 7 - host and path routing, HTTP header rules, TLS termination, WAF integration, and it terminates the client connection. NLB is layer 4 - preserves the source IP, handles millions of connections at very low latency, supports static IPs and non-HTTP protocols, and is what you want for gRPC or raw TCP. GWLB is for inserting third-party appliances. Targets are registered in target groups with their own health check - the health check path must be shallow and must not check downstream dependencies. Deregistration delay is the drain window; set it above your longest request or you cut connections during deploys.

StudyElastic Load Balancing →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

There is a strict order of attempt, and the discipline is to stop as soon as it works rather than proceeding to the most impressive-sounding option. Prompt engineering → RAG → fine-tuning. Each step up costs more, takes longer, and adds permanent maintenance.

Prompting fixes behaviour and format. Tone, structure, refusal conditions, step-by-step reasoning, output schema. It is free, instant to iterate, and reversible. A surprising amount of what people attribute to model capability is actually prompt quality — clear instructions, a couple of good examples, an explicit output contract. Always exhaust this first, and measure it against your eval set rather than by impression.

RAG fixes knowledge. Anything the model could not have known (your internal policies, this customer's transactions), anything that changes (prices, procedures, product state), and anything that must be cited. It gives you provenance, freshness through re-indexing, per-user access control at retrieval time, and the ability to delete a document and have it genuinely gone.

Fine-tuning fixes style, format adherence and narrow task performance. It teaches the model to behave a particular way consistently — a specific classification taxonomy, a rigid output format, a domain-specific writing style — and it lets you drop long few-shot examples from every request, which is a real cost saving at volume. It can also make a smaller, cheaper model competitive with a larger one on one specific task.

The wrong move — and the one interviewers are listening for — is fine-tuning to inject knowledge. It is expensive, requires thousands of examples, produces knowledge you cannot verify or cite, cannot be updated without retraining, and is stale the day training finishes. Worse, in a regulated context: you cannot delete a fact from weights. If a customer exercises a deletion right and their data was in your fine-tuning corpus, the only remedy is retraining from a cleaned dataset. That single point is the strongest practical argument for RAG over fine-tuning on customer data, and it is worth stating explicitly.

The other cost of fine-tuning is lock-in to a base model. Your adapter is tied to a specific version; when a better base model ships, you re-tune, re-evaluate and re-deploy. Given how fast base models improve, teams that fine-tuned early frequently find that the current base model, well prompted, beats their tuned older one.

So the decision rule: is the gap in knowledge, or in behaviour? Knowledge → RAG. Behaviour → prompt first, then fine-tune only if prompting demonstrably plateaus and you have the evaluation infrastructure to prove the tuned model is better.

Decision rule, and what each one cannot do
SYMPTOM                                   -> TRY
"it does not know our refund policy"         RAG        (knowledge, changes, cite it)
"it does not know this customer's balance"   TOOL CALL  (authoritative, live, audited)
"the format is inconsistent"                 PROMPT, then schema-constrained output
"the tone is wrong"                          PROMPT
"it will not follow our 14-category taxonomy PROMPT + few-shot, then FINE-TUNE
 consistently, at 2M calls/month"                       (behaviour + cost at volume)
"we want a small model to match a large one  FINE-TUNE  (narrow task, real saving)
 on ONE narrow task"

ANTI-PATTERN
"fine-tune it on our documents so it knows them"
  - needs thousands of examples, not documents
  - cannot cite  -> unusable where provenance is required
  - stale on day one, no incremental update
  - CANNOT DELETE A FACT FROM WEIGHTS
      -> a subject deletion request means RETRAINING from a cleaned corpus
  - locks you to a base model version you will want to leave

COST / TIME
  prompt      hours     $0        fully reversible
  RAG         weeks     infra     reversible, auditable, deletable
  fine-tune   weeks     training  + permanent data pipeline, re-tune per base model

TEST BEFORE COMMITTING
  baseline: best prompt + RAG, scored on the eval suite
  candidate: fine-tuned model, same suite
  the bar is BEATING THE BASELINE, not beating nothing.
Follow-ups they will ask

How much data does fine-tuning actually need?

For parameter-efficient tuning on a narrow task, often a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality examples — quality and consistency matter far more than volume, and a thousand carefully-labelled examples beat ten thousand noisy ones. The real work is building that dataset in exactly the input-output shape production uses, deduplicating it, and holding out a genuine test split created before any tuning.

Can I combine RAG and fine-tuning?

Yes, and it is a legitimate advanced pattern: fine-tune for the output format and domain style, retrieve for the facts. The model learns how to answer and the retriever supplies what to say. Just make sure you have measured that the fine-tuning adds something on top of a well-prompted baseline with the same retrieval — otherwise you have taken on a training pipeline for nothing.

What about continued pre-training rather than fine-tuning?

That is for teaching a model a genuinely new domain, vocabulary or language, and it needs a very large corpus and serious compute — it is a research-team activity, not an application-team one. For essentially every enterprise use case the answer is RAG plus prompting, occasionally with a light fine-tune. Being able to distinguish the three, and to say that the third is almost never the right call, is itself a good signal.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Admission control is the third stage of the API request pipeline: authentication (who are you), authorisation (may you do this), then admission (should this specific object be allowed, and should it be modified first) — all before anything is persisted to etcd. That ordering matters: admission is the last place you can reject an object, and the only place you can change it.

Mutating webhooks run first and can modify the object — injecting a sidecar, adding default labels, setting a securityContext, adding a topology spread constraint. Validating webhooks run after all mutations and can only accept or reject, so they see the final object. That order is why you can mutate a default in and then validate that it is present.

There is also the built-in Pod Security admission controller, which enforces the privileged, baseline or restricted profiles per namespace via labels, in enforce, audit or warn modes. It replaced PodSecurityPolicy, it costs nothing to enable, and labelling namespaces restricted gets you most of the container hardening story for free.

Policies I would enforce in a payments cluster, and each should come with the failure it prevents. Only images from our ECR, pinned by digest — prevents running unreviewed third-party images and eliminates tag drift. Verified signature from our CI identity — makes the whole signing chain meaningful, since signing without verification proves nothing. Resource requests and limits required — prevents BestEffort pods and unschedulable guesswork. No privileged, no hostNetwork, no hostPID, no hostPath mounts — these are container-escape vectors. runAsNonRoot with a read-only root filesystem. A team and cost-centre label on every workload — unglamorous, and it is what makes cost attribution possible at all.

Implement with Kyverno (policies written as Kubernetes YAML, much lower barrier) or OPA Gatekeeper (Rego, more expressive, steeper). Kyverno is the pragmatic default for most teams.

Now the operational point that separates someone who has run this. A webhook is on the critical path of every matching API write. With failurePolicy: Fail, if the webhook pod is down, unreachable, or its certificate has expired, every matching create and update in the cluster is rejected — including, potentially, the deployment that would fix it. Teams have locked themselves out of their own clusters this way. Mitigations: always exempt kube-system and your policy controller's own namespace; scope rules narrowly to the specific resources and operations you care about rather than matching everything; run the webhook with multiple replicas and a PodDisruptionBudget; set a short timeoutSeconds; and roll new policies out in audit or Warn mode first, measure what they would have blocked, and only then switch to Enforce.

Enforce the rule, and do not lock yourself out
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: { name: payments-baseline }
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce      # start as Audit, measure, THEN enforce
  background: true                      # also report on EXISTING objects
  rules:
    - name: only-our-registry-by-digest
      match: { any: [{ resources: { kinds: [Pod] } }] }
      exclude: { any: [{ resources: { namespaces: [kube-system, kyverno] } }] }
      validate:
        message: "images must come from our ECR and be pinned by digest"
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - image: "1234.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/*@sha256:*"

    - name: verify-ci-signature          # makes signing MEAN something
      match: { any: [{ resources: { kinds: [Pod] } }] }
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences: ["1234.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/*"]
          attestors: [{ entries: [{ keyless:
              { subject: "https://github.com/acme/*",
                issuer: "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" }}]}]

    - name: require-resources
      match: { any: [{ resources: { kinds: [Pod] } }] }
      validate:
        message: "requests and limits are required"
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - resources:
                  requests: { memory: "?*", cpu: "?*" }
                  limits:   { memory: "?*" }

    - name: no-host-namespaces
      match: { any: [{ resources: { kinds: [Pod] } }] }
      validate:
        pattern:
          spec:
            "=(hostNetwork)": "false"
            "=(hostPID)": "false"
            containers:
              - "=(securityContext)":
                  "=(privileged)": "false"
---
# Free, built-in, and covers most container hardening:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: payments
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest

# THE OPERATIONAL TRAP
#   failurePolicy: Fail + webhook down = EVERY matching write rejected,
#   including the deploy that would fix the webhook. Teams have bricked clusters.
#   -> exempt kube-system and the policy namespace
#   -> narrow the `rules` match; do not match every resource
#   -> multiple replicas + PDB + short timeoutSeconds
#   -> Audit mode first, always
Follow-ups they will ask

Should failurePolicy be Fail or Ignore?

Fail for genuine security controls — a policy that can be bypassed by killing a pod is not a control. Ignore for convenience mutations like label defaulting, where availability matters more than the guarantee. The way to make Fail safe is not to weaken it but to make the webhook highly available and narrowly scoped, and to always exempt the namespaces you would need to recover through.

How do I apply a new policy to workloads that already exist?

Admission only sees new writes, so existing objects are unaffected until they are next updated. Kyverno's background: true scans existing resources and produces PolicyReports, which gives you the list of what is currently non-compliant without breaking anything. Fix the reported workloads, then switch to Enforce — doing it in the other order blocks the very deploys that would fix them.

What is a validating admission policy and does it replace webhooks?

It is the in-tree, CEL-based alternative that now graduates the common cases into the API server itself — no webhook pod, no certificate, no availability risk, and much lower latency. For simple structural validation it is strictly better and worth preferring. Webhooks remain necessary for mutation, for anything needing external data (an image signature lookup, an inventory call), and for complex cross-object logic.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

ALB is layer 7. It parses HTTP, so it can route on host, path, header, query string, method and source IP; it terminates the client connection and opens its own to the target, which means it can rewrite, redirect, and integrate with WAF and Cognito. It supports HTTP/2 and gRPC to targets, and it is what you want in front of a normal web API.

NLB is layer 4. It forwards TCP and UDP without parsing, which gives it three properties ALB does not have: it preserves the client source IP (no X-Forwarded-For needed, the target sees the real address), it supports static IPs and Elastic IPs per AZ — which matters enormously when a partner has to allowlist your address — and it handles enormous connection counts at very low added latency. Use it for non-HTTP protocols, for extreme throughput, when a client needs a fixed IP to allowlist, or when you are fronting your own proxy layer.

Gateway Load Balancer is a different animal entirely: it transparently inserts third-party virtual appliances — firewalls, IDS, DPI — into the traffic path using GENEVE encapsulation. It appears in this comparison mainly so you can say what it is and that it is not a general-purpose load balancer.

Target groups hold the registered targets — instances, IPs, Lambda functions, or another ALB behind an NLB — with a protocol, port and their own health check. The health check configuration is where real incidents come from, so be specific: the path must be shallow and local. A health check hitting /actuator/health that verifies the database means that when the database blips, every target fails health simultaneously, the load balancer removes all of them, and you get 503s with no healthy targets — turning a degraded dependency into a complete outage. Use a readiness-style endpoint that reflects can this instance serve, not is the whole system well.

Connection draining — deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds, default 300 — is the window during which a deregistering target finishes in-flight requests before the load balancer closes connections. Set it above your longest normal request; set it too low and every deploy cuts requests mid-flight, which shows as a small burst of 502s that nobody explains. Set it absurdly high and deploys crawl.

Two more details that show real experience: the ALB idle timeout (default 60s) must exceed the application's own keep-alive idle timeout, or the ALB reuses a connection the target is closing and you get intermittent 502s — one of the most common and most confusing production bugs on AWS. And slow start on the target group gives a newly registered target a ramp-up period, which matters a great deal for a JVM that is still interpreting bytecode and would otherwise take a full share of traffic while cold.

Choosing, and the two settings that cause most incidents
                       ALB (L7)          NLB (L4)         GWLB
protocol               HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC   TCP/UDP/TLS      GENEVE
routing                host/path/header  port only        n/a (appliances)
client source IP       X-Forwarded-For   PRESERVED        n/a
static / Elastic IP    no                YES              n/a
WAF integration        yes               no               n/a
latency added          ~ms               ~microseconds    n/a
use when               normal web API    partner must     inserting firewalls
                                         allowlist an IP; / IDS transparently
                                         raw TCP; huge
                                         connection counts

TargetGroup:
  HealthCheckPath: /actuator/health/readiness    # SHALLOW - not a deep check
  HealthCheckPort: 9090                          # management port
  HealthyThresholdCount: 2
  UnhealthyThresholdCount: 3
  HealthCheckIntervalSeconds: 10
  Matcher: { HttpCode: "200" }
  TargetGroupAttributes:
    deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds: 60     # > longest request, or deploys cut it
    slow_start.duration_seconds: 60              # JVM warms up before full traffic
    load_balancing.algorithm.type: least_outstanding_requests
                                                 # better than round_robin for
                                                 # variable request cost

# INCIDENT 1 - deep health check
#   /actuator/health includes the DB. DB blips for 20s.
#   -> ALL targets unhealthy at once -> 503, no healthy targets
#   -> a 20-second degradation becomes a full outage.

# INCIDENT 2 - the keep-alive race (very common, very confusing)
   ALB idle timeout        60s
   app server idle timeout 60s   <-- SAME. Race condition.
   -> ALB reuses a connection the target is closing -> intermittent 502
   FIX: app idle timeout MUST exceed the ALB's
        server.tomcat.keep-alive-timeout: 70s      (ALB 60s)
Follow-ups they will ask

How do I know whether a 502 is my app or the load balancer?

ALB access logs, which record elb_status_code and target_status_code separately. A 502 with target_status_code - means the ALB never got a valid response — connection reset or malformed reply, which points at the keep-alive race or a target dying mid-request. A 502 with a target status code means the target actually responded that way. That distinction is usually the whole investigation.

Can I put an ALB behind an NLB?

Yes, and it is a standard pattern: the NLB gives you the static IPs a partner allowlists and the ALB gives you L7 routing behind it. You pay for both and add a hop. The alternative — an ALB with a Global Accelerator in front — also provides static anycast IPs and improves global latency, and is often the better answer if fixed IPs are the only reason you were reaching for the NLB.

What does least_outstanding_requests actually change?

Round robin sends the next request to the next target regardless of how busy it is, which is fine when every request costs the same and badly wrong when they do not — one target stuck on a slow query keeps receiving work. Least outstanding requests routes to the target with the fewest in-flight requests, which naturally avoids the busy one. For a service with variable request cost it is a meaningful, free improvement to tail latency.

Week 4 synthesis: from prototype to platform

Your RAG prototype works in a notebook. Write the plan to get it to production in a bank. What are the twelve things that must exist that do not exist today?

Must coverAuth and per-user retrieval filtering; PII handling and a data classification decision; audit logging of prompt, context and output; an eval suite in CI with a regression gate; prompt versioning in git; cost controls - caching, model routing, per-user rate limits; latency budget with streaming; a deterministic fallback and a kill switch; monitoring on groundedness, refusal rate, latency and spend; a red-team pass for injection through ingested documents; a document lifecycle covering re-embedding and deletion; and a written statement of what the system must never do, enforced at the tool boundary rather than in the prompt.

StudyAnthropic - security and compliance →

Write the full manifest set for a stateful service - say a Redis-backed rate limiter - and justify every object to a reviewer who thinks a Deployment is enough.

Must coverStatefulSet for stable identity and per-replica volumes, headless Service for peer discovery, plus a normal Service for clients, PVC template with a StorageClass using WaitForFirstConsumer, PodDisruptionBudget so a node drain cannot take quorum, anti-affinity or topology spread so replicas are not co-located, ConfigMap for the config file, resource requests equal to limits for Guaranteed QoS, and probes that check the actual protocol rather than TCP. Explain that a Deployment gives shared identity and shared claim semantics, which for anything with per-replica state is silent data corruption.

StudyKubernetes - StatefulSet basics →

Design the deployment pipeline for twelve services onto ECS Fargate across dev, staging and production accounts. Cover accounts, artefacts, promotion and rollback.

Must coverSeparate AWS accounts per environment under an Organization, with SCPs - blast radius and IAM clarity are the whole reason. Infrastructure as code (CDK or Terraform) with per-environment parameters, plan reviewed in PR.
