AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Treat it as a deploy with one extra property: you cannot diff the behaviour statically. A code change can be reviewed line by line; a prompt or model change can only be reviewed by observing outputs. So the pipeline substitutes measurement for reading.

Offline first. The eval suite must pass — aggregate score above the floor, and no regression in the critical set, which blocks unconditionally. Then generate an output diff for the cases whose grade changed and put it in the pull request, because numbers say that something changed and only the diff says what. Reviewers reliably catch tone and format regressions no grader encodes.

Shadow next. Run the new version against a copy of live traffic without serving its output. This is the step that catches what evals cannot: real inputs are messier, longer, in more languages, and full of edge cases nobody curated. Compare schema failure rate, latency, cost per request, and output length distribution between old and new. Shadowing costs you double inference on the sampled slice and it is worth it — it is the only way to see production behaviour with zero user risk.

Then canary. A small traffic percentage behind a flag, segmented so you compare like with like — random assignment by user, not by time of day or by cohort, or you will attribute a difference in users to a difference in versions. Watch the metrics that break callers first: schema validation failure rate, provider error rate, latency percentiles, cost per request; then the quality signals: online groundedness on a sampled basis, thumbs-down rate, and rephrase rate.

Ramp on green — 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% with a bake period at each step long enough to see a statistically meaningful sample. For a low-volume feature, 5% for five minutes is a handful of requests and proves nothing, so compute the bake from your request rate rather than picking a round number.

Two things that make rollback real. The old version must still be deployed, not deleted — rollback is then a flag flip in seconds rather than a redeploy. And log the prompt version and model version on every response, so when a complaint arrives three weeks later you can attribute it to a specific version rather than guessing.

Finally, the model-specific concern: model deprecation is a forced version of this process. Providers retire versions on a schedule, so plan for a migration a few times a year — run the suite against the successor, examine the regressions, adjust, canary. Pinning versions is what makes that planned work rather than an unannounced behaviour change.

Offline, shadow, canary, ramp — with rollback that actually works
1. OFFLINE   eval suite in CI
     aggregate >= 0.92, regression tolerance 0.01     (soft: fails the build)
     critical set 32/32                                (hard: no override)
     + OUTPUT DIFF for changed cases, attached to the PR
       numbers say THAT it changed; the diff says WHAT

2. SHADOW    new version runs on a copy of live traffic, output DISCARDED
     compare old vs new on REAL inputs:
       schema_failure_rate    0.002  ->  0.001   ok
       p99 latency            5.4s   ->  5.6s    ok
       output tokens (median)  318   ->  511     <-- 60% more expensive. Investigate
                                                     BEFORE any user sees it.
     costs double inference on the sampled slice; zero user risk

3. CANARY    flag, RANDOM assignment BY USER (not by time, not by cohort)
     ai.settlement_summary.version = v8  for 5% of users
     gate on, in order:
       schema_failure_rate   (breaks callers)
       provider_error_rate
       p99 latency, cost/request
       online groundedness (sampled judge), thumbs_down, rephrase_rate

4. RAMP      5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%
     bake time computed from REQUEST RATE, not a round number:
       enough requests that a 1% error rate would be visible
       low-volume feature: 5% for 5 min is a handful of requests -> proves nothing

ROLLBACK THAT ACTUALLY WORKS
  v7 stays DEPLOYED, not deleted     -> rollback = flag flip, seconds
  every response logs:
      { "promptVersion": "settlement_summary@v7",
        "modelVersion": "claude-...-20260514" }
  -> a complaint three weeks later is attributable to a specific version

MODEL DEPRECATION is this same process, forced on a provider's schedule.
  Pinning versions makes it PLANNED work a few times a year instead of an
  unannounced behaviour change you discover from user complaints.
Follow-ups they will ask

Is shadowing worth the doubled inference cost?

On a sampled slice, almost always — you only need a few percent of traffic to see the distribution. It catches the class of problem evals systematically miss: real inputs that are longer, multilingual, malformed, or adversarial in ways nobody curated. The output-length regression in the example above is a real pattern; it costs nothing to catch in shadow and is embarrassing to discover from an invoice.

How do you canary a change that affects retrieval rather than the prompt?

Identically, because the unit under test is the pipeline, not the prompt. Version the retrieval configuration (k, reranker, embedding model, thresholds) as part of the same artefact and flag it the same way. The one difference is that an embedding model change requires a parallel index, so the canary is comparing two indexes — which is more expensive and needs planning, but the process is the same.

What if a regression only shows up days later?

That is what the version stamp on every response is for: you can retroactively segment complaints by version and see whether the new one is over-represented. It also argues for a longer soak at partial rollout for anything touching quality rather than availability — slow-burn regressions in tone or thoroughness do not appear in five minutes. Keep the previous version deployed for the whole soak, not just the ramp.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Order: control plane first, then node groups, then add-ons — and never skip a minor version. Kubernetes supports a limited version skew (the kubelet may be up to three minors behind the API server, but not ahead), so upgrading node groups before the control plane breaks that contract. And skipping a version means skipping its deprecation warnings and its migration path.

Before starting, the single most important check: deprecated and removed APIs. Removed APIs are the number one cause of upgrade breakage, and the failure is silent until something needs to reconcile. Run pluto or kubent against your manifests and against what is live in the cluster, because a Helm chart in the release history can hold an old API version even when your current manifests are clean. On EKS, the console surfaces API deprecation insights from actual API server usage, which is the most reliable source because it reflects what is really being called.

Then compatibility of everything you did not write: every controller, operator, CRD, CSI driver, CNI, ingress controller and admission webhook has its own supported version matrix. This is usually where the real work is — the cluster upgrade is a button; the add-on upgrades are a project.

Node upgrade means cordon, drain, replace. That makes PodDisruptionBudgets load-bearing in both directions: without one, a drain can evict every replica of a service simultaneously; with one that is too strict (maxUnavailable: 0, or a budget that cannot be satisfied at the current replica count), the drain hangs forever and the upgrade stalls. Both failure modes are common, and the second is more confusing because nothing is broken — it simply never finishes.

The surprises, worth naming unprompted: pods with local storage (emptyDir) block eviction unless annotated safe-to-evict; bare pods with no controller are never rescheduled, so draining destroys them; single-replica workloads have no safe drain at all; long terminationGracePeriodSeconds multiply across a large node group into hours of drain time; and an admission webhook with failurePolicy: Fail that becomes unavailable mid-upgrade can block every write in the cluster, including the ones needed to recover.

How you know it is safe: validate on a staging cluster that is genuinely the same version, same add-on set and same workload shapes — a staging cluster two versions behind proves nothing. Then upgrade a canary node group first, watch a real workload on it, and only then proceed. And have a documented path back, accepting the honest constraint that the EKS control plane cannot be downgraded — so the rollback plan for a control-plane problem is a new cluster from infrastructure as code with GitOps reconciling workloads onto it, which is only credible if you have rehearsed it.

Check APIs first; PDBs decide whether the drain works
ORDER (never skip a minor)
  1. control plane   (API server, scheduler, controller-manager)
  2. add-ons         (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI - matched to version)
  3. node groups     (kubelet may be BEHIND the API server, never ahead)

# 1. THE CHECK THAT MATTERS MOST - removed APIs
$ pluto detect-all-in-cluster -o wide
$ kubent
# also check HELM RELEASE HISTORY, not just current manifests - an old release
# secret can carry a removed apiVersion and break the next `helm upgrade`
$ aws eks list-insights --cluster-name prod        # from REAL API server usage

# 2. Add-on compatibility matrix - this is where the actual work is
   VPC CNI / CoreDNS / kube-proxy / EBS CSI / ingress-nginx / cert-manager
   / ArgoCD / Karpenter / Kyverno / every operator and CRD

# 3. PDBs are load-bearing in BOTH directions
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1        # correct
# maxUnavailable: 0        -> drain HANGS FOREVER, upgrade stalls, nothing "broken"
# no PDB at all            -> drain evicts every replica at once -> outage

# Drain surprises
  emptyDir volumes         -> blocks eviction
      annotation: cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "true"
  bare pods (no controller)-> evicted and NEVER rescheduled. Gone.
  replicas: 1              -> no safe drain exists. Scale to 2 first.
  long grace periods       -> multiply across the node group into hours
  webhook failurePolicy:Fail, webhook pods drained
                           -> EVERY write in the cluster rejected, including
                              the ones needed to recover. Exempt kube-system,
                              run >=2 replicas with a PDB.

# Dry run the drain before the upgrade window
$ kubectl drain ip-10-20-16-33 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data \
      --dry-run=server

# HOW YOU KNOW IT IS SAFE
  staging cluster at the SAME version + SAME add-ons + SAME workload shapes
  then ONE canary node group, watch a real workload, then proceed
  rollback: the EKS control plane CANNOT be downgraded.
    -> the plan is a NEW cluster from IaC + ArgoCD reconciling workloads.
       Only credible if rehearsed.
Follow-ups they will ask

How often should you upgrade?

Stay within the supported window and upgrade roughly every four to six months — EKS supports each version for about fourteen months standard, with extended support available at extra cost. Falling behind is the expensive path: the further behind you are, the more skipped deprecations accumulate and the larger each upgrade becomes. Frequent small upgrades are dramatically less risky than infrequent large ones, and the discipline of doing them regularly is what keeps the add-on matrix current.

What is the safest node upgrade strategy?

Blue/green node groups rather than in-place. Create a new node group on the new version, cordon the old one, drain it gradually while watching, and delete it once empty. That gives you an instant rollback — uncordon the old group — which an in-place rolling replacement does not. It costs double node capacity during the window, which is a cheap insurance premium for a production cluster.

What breaks most often in practice?

Removed APIs in Helm chart history, add-ons pinned to an old version by a chart nobody has updated, and PodDisruptionBudgets that make drains impossible. Behind those, the CNI is the most impactful add-on to get wrong because a version mismatch can break pod networking cluster-wide. None of these are exotic — which is why the pre-flight checklist, run every time, is worth more than any amount of cleverness during the window.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A runbook is written for someone who did not build the service and is being woken at 3am. That single constraint determines everything about it: no assumed context, no obviously you would check, and every command copy-pasteable.

Open with what the service does in two sentences, and what breaks for users when it is down. That is what lets the responder judge severity and decide whether to escalate immediately or investigate. Settlement API — merchants cannot see or reconcile payouts; funds movement is unaffected tells someone instantly that this is serious but not a money-loss event.

Then the dashboard link and the three metrics that matter — not twenty. If the responder has to choose which graph to look at, you have not done the work.

Then, per alert: what the alert actually means in plain language; the likely causes ranked by frequency, because at 3am you want the common case first; the exact commands or console links to check each one; and the mitigation. Crucially, the mitigation should be a reversible operational action, not a code fix: roll back, scale up, fail over, disable a feature flag, drain a zone. Nobody should be writing code at 3am, and a runbook that ends in fix the bug has not helped.

Escalation path with names and dependency owners — who to call for the database, for the partner integration, for the network — because half of incident time is often spent finding the right person.

Known false alarms, explicitly. If the batch job at 02:00 always trips the latency alert for four minutes, say so. Otherwise every new responder investigates it from scratch, and worse, they learn to ignore the alert generally.

And a what not to do section, which is the part most runbooks omit and the part that prevents the worst outcomes. Name the destructive action someone will reach for under pressure: do not restart the database, do not delete the DLQ to clear the alarm, do not scale the consumers past N or you will exhaust the connection pool, do not re-run the settlement job without checking the idempotency table. These are the mistakes that turn an incident into a much longer incident.

Finally, test it. Have someone who did not write the service follow it during a game day. An untested runbook is fiction — the commands have drifted, the dashboard was renamed, the escalation contact left. Reviewing runbooks after every incident, and exercising them on a schedule, is what keeps them true.

Written for someone who has never seen this service
# RUNBOOK: settlement-api

## What it does
Serves merchant settlement views and drives the nightly reconciliation.
IF DOWN: merchants cannot view or reconcile payouts. Funds movement is NOT
affected - no money is at risk. Sev-2 unless combined with a ledger alert.

## Dashboard  https://.../settlement-api        Three metrics:
  1. 5xx rate            (users are failing)
  2. p99 latency         (users are suffering)
  3. SQS queue depth     (work is backing up)

## ALERT: SettlementApi5xxHigh
Means: >0.5% of requests failing for 2+ minutes.
Likely causes, MOST COMMON FIRST:
  1. bad deploy (~60%)
       aws deploy list-deployments --application-name settlement-api --max-items 3
       -> deployed in the last 30 min? ROLL BACK FIRST, diagnose after.
          aws deploy stop-deployment --deployment-id <id> --auto-rollback-enabled
  2. RDS failover or connection exhaustion (~25%)
       CloudWatch RDS: DatabaseConnections, and check for a recent failover event
       -> if connections are pinned near max: kubectl rollout restart deploy/settlement-api
          (recycles the pool; it does NOT fix the leak - raise a ticket)
  3. partner API degraded (~10%)
       X-Ray service map -> partner.notify span duration
       -> flip flag settlement.partner_notify=off  (degrades gracefully, no data loss)
  4. AZ impairment (~5%)
       Athena on ALB logs: p99 by target, grouped by AZ
       -> zonal shift:  aws arc-zonal-shift start-zonal-shift ...

## KNOWN FALSE ALARMS
  02:00-02:06 nightly batch trips p99 latency. Expected. Do not investigate.
  Monday 09:00 brief 5xx spike during cache warm. Self-resolves in <90s.

## DO NOT
  - do NOT restart the RDS instance. Failover is 60-120s of full outage and
    almost never the right first action.
  - do NOT purge the DLQ to clear the alarm. Those are unprocessed settlements.
  - do NOT scale consumers above 40 - it exhausts the RDS connection pool and
    takes down every other service on that database.
  - do NOT re-run the settlement job without checking processed_batches first.

## ESCALATE
  database:  #db-oncall     partner integration: #payments-partners
  network:   #platform      business owner (comms): J. Patel

## Last tested: 2026-08-12 game day (T. Okafor followed it cold, 2 corrections made)
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you keep runbooks from going stale?

Two mechanisms. Review the runbook as a mandatory item in every post-incident review for that service — the incident just told you what was wrong with it. And exercise it on a schedule with someone who did not write it, which finds the drift that reading never does: renamed dashboards, changed commands, departed contacts. Put the last-tested date at the top so a responder knows how much to trust it.

Should the runbook contain the diagnosis or just the actions?

Actions first, diagnosis second. At 3am the goal is to restore service, not to understand it — so lead with mitigation, and put the deeper investigation in a separate section for the morning. Ranking causes by frequency serves the same purpose: it gets the responder to the likely fix quickly rather than making them work through a decision tree.

What makes an alert worth a runbook entry?

If it pages, it needs an entry — and if you cannot write a bounded remediation for it, that is strong evidence it should not page. Writing the runbook is a useful forcing function on alert quality: an alert whose runbook says investigate is not actionable, and it should become a ticket or be deleted. That review often removes a third of a team's pages.

And you deleted a customer's data on request. The honest framing: an LLM feature is a system with moving parts you do not own, so it needs an owner and a maintenance budget.

AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Answer with the actual list, because the point of the question is that an LLM feature is not a thing you ship, it is a system you maintain — and most teams do not budget for that.

Model deprecation. The version you pinned reached end of life. You ran the eval suite against the successor, found two regressions — it became more verbose and started hedging on questions it previously answered — adjusted the prompt, re-evaluated, shadowed, canaried, rolled out. That is a week of work and it happens a couple of times a year. Pinning made it planned; not pinning would have made it an unannounced behaviour change discovered from complaints.

Corpus drift. Documents changed, the corpus grew 40%, and retrieval quality slid because chunks that used to be uniquely relevant now have near-duplicates competing with them. You retuned k, added a reranker, and re-measured recall on the labelled set.

Cost. Usage grew faster than expected. You added prompt caching, routed classification and query rewriting to a small model, and capped output length. Spend per request fell by half while volume tripled.

New failure classes. The weekly triage surfaced patterns nobody anticipated — users asking multi-part questions, questions about documents that exist but are not indexed. Each became an eval case and, in two instances, a product change.

A dependency changed a document format. A partner switched PDF templates; the parser produced fragments; average chunk length dropped from 380 tokens to 74 and retrieval quality for that source collapsed. Nobody noticed for nine days because there was no alarm on chunk statistics. There is now.

Someone attempted an injection through an uploaded file. It failed, because tools run as the calling user — but it went into the red-team suite and prompted a review of what content reaches the context.

And you deleted a customer's data on request, across source, index, logs and caches, and produced evidence of it.

The honest framing to close on: this is a system with moving parts you do not own — the model, the corpus, and the users' behaviour all change without you doing anything. So it needs a named owner and a standing maintenance budget, the way a database does. A team that ships an AI feature and reassigns everyone has not finished; they have started an unowned liability.

Six months of maintenance nobody budgets for
MONTH  EVENT                          WORK                          PREVENTABLE?
-----  -----------------------------  ----------------------------  ------------
  1    corpus grew 40%                retune k, add reranker,       partly - alarm
       retrieval quality slid         re-measure recall@10          on recall
  2    usage 3x, spend 3x             prompt caching, small-model   yes - model the
                                      routing, cap max_tokens       cost up front
  3    partner changed PDF template   fix parser, re-ingest         YES - alarm on
       avg chunk length 380 -> 74     9 DAYS before anyone noticed  chunk stats
  4    injection attempt via upload   failed (tools run as user);   no - expected;
                                      added to red-team suite       this is working
  5    MODEL DEPRECATED               eval vs successor, 2          no - but PINNING
       (pinned version EOL)           regressions, adjust prompt,   made it planned
                                      shadow, canary, roll out      work, not a
                                      ~1 week                       surprise
  6    subject deletion request       delete across source, index,  no - but the
                                      logs, caches + evidence       DESIGN made it
                                                                    an operation,
                                                                    not a project

# The alarms that would have caught month 3 on day one - cheap, and almost
# nobody has them:
index.avg_chunk_length   per source, daily   -> alert on >30% change
index.chunk_count        per source, daily
retrieval.recall_at_10   frozen eval set, daily
ingest.failures          any non-zero -> alert  (silent ingest failure is how
                                                 an index quietly goes stale)

# THE FRAMING
#   the model changes without you.
#   the corpus changes without you.
#   user behaviour changes without you.
#   -> an LLM feature needs a NAMED OWNER and a standing maintenance budget,
#      the way a database does. Shipping it and reassigning the team does not
#      finish the work; it creates an unowned liability.
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the maintenance cost as a proportion of the build?

For a RAG feature in a regulated environment, budget roughly 20–30% of an engineer ongoing after launch — model migrations a few times a year, weekly triage, corpus and parser maintenance, and eval-set upkeep. That is comparable to owning a moderately complex service, which is the right mental model. Teams that budget zero end up with a feature that degrades silently until someone escalates it.

Which of those six was most avoidable?

The parser change. A daily check on chunk count and average chunk length per source would have caught it within a day instead of nine, and it is three metrics and one alert. It is the classic example of a cheap monitoring gap costing far more in degraded quality than the monitoring would have cost to build — and it is invisible in every conventional dashboard, because no service errored and no latency moved.

Does this argue against building AI features at all?

No — it argues for scoping them honestly. The maintenance is real and it is manageable, and the same is true of any integration with a third-party API or a data pipeline. What it argues against is treating an AI feature as a one-off project with no owner, which is how most of them are staffed. Say the maintenance cost out loud during planning; it is far easier to fund then than after the first silent degradation.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Design it as three signals with one correlation key, and be explicit about what you deliberately do not build — the cost ceiling makes that half of the answer.

Metrics. Prometheus, or Amazon Managed Prometheus if you would rather not run it, scraping Micrometer endpoints via ServiceMonitors. Use recording rules to precompute the expensive aggregations dashboards use, and a retention split: high-resolution data for a couple of weeks, downsampled for long-term trends. Keep label cardinality bounded — no user id, no request id, no unbounded path — because cardinality, not scrape volume, is what kills a Prometheus.

Logs. Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet, structured JSON, one backend. Drop DEBUG at the shipper so you never pay to ingest it, and set retention on every log group. Log volume is usually the largest observability line item, and both of those levers are configuration rather than engineering.

Traces. The OpenTelemetry Java agent injected by the operator, so twelve services get tracing with an annotation and no code change. The collector does the expensive thinking: attribute scrubbing to remove PII, and tail sampling — keep 100% of errors and everything over a latency threshold, plus 1% baseline. Without tail sampling, tracing at full volume genuinely can cost more than the services being traced.

Dashboards from one template. A single parameterised service dashboard driven by a label, not twelve bespoke ones. Twelve hand-built dashboards diverge, and when you need to compare two services during an incident you cannot. One template also means improving it improves everything.

Alert on symptoms, not causes. Latency, error rate, saturation — the things users feel. High CPU with healthy latency needs no human; a deadlocked connection pool takes you down at 5% CPU. Cause metrics belong on the dashboard for diagnosis, not in the alert rules.

What I would deliberately not do, and this is the part that shows judgement under a cost ceiling. Not log successful requests individually — the trace covers it, and per-request logging at volume is enormous. Not put high-cardinality labels on metrics. Not run a second overlapping vendor because someone likes their UI. Not build custom dashboards per team before the shared one is proven insufficient. And not enable CloudWatch data events or full-fidelity tracing account-wide by default.

Close with the correlation point, because it is what makes the three worth more than the sum: the trace id goes in every log line and as an exemplar on metrics. Then a latency spike leads to a trace, and the trace leads to exactly the log lines emitted during it. That single field costs nothing and is the difference between three tools and one system.

Three signals, one trace id, an explicit not-doing list
METRICS   Prometheus (or AMP) + ServiceMonitors
  scrape /actuator/prometheus
  recording rules for expensive dashboard queries
  retention: 15d high-res  ->  downsampled long-term (Thanos/AMP)
  CARDINALITY DISCIPLINE: no user_id, no request_id, no unbounded path label
      http_requests_total{service,method,status,route}   route is TEMPLATED

LOGS      Fluent Bit DaemonSet -> one backend
  structured JSON to stdout, multiline parser for Java stack traces
  DROP DEBUG AT THE SHIPPER (never pay to ingest it)
  retention set on EVERY log group, enforced by a Config rule

TRACES    OTel Java agent, injected by the operator (one annotation per service)
  collector: scrub PII attributes, then TAIL SAMPLE
      100% errors | 100% > 2s | 1% baseline
  without tail sampling this can cost more than the services it traces

DASHBOARDS  ONE parameterised template, $service as a variable
  twelve bespoke dashboards diverge and cannot be compared during an incident

ALERTS    on SYMPTOMS, with recording rules behind them
- alert: HighErrorRate
  expr: sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])) by (service)
        / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) by (service) > 0.01
  for: 5m
- alert: HighLatency          # p99 from a recording rule
  expr: service:http_p99:5m > 1.5
  for: 10m
# NOT: high CPU (a cause). High CPU with healthy latency needs no human.
#      A deadlocked pool takes you down at 5% CPU and never trips a CPU alert.

DELIBERATELY NOT DOING
  x  per-request logging of SUCCESSFUL requests (traces cover it; volume is huge)
  x  high-cardinality metric labels
  x  a second overlapping vendor because someone prefers the UI
  x  bespoke dashboards before the shared one is proven insufficient
  x  CloudWatch data events / full-fidelity tracing on by default

THE CORRELATION KEY - costs one field, worth more than any single signal
  every log line carries trace.id (Micrometer MDC)
  metrics carry exemplars pointing at representative traces
  -> latency spike -> trace -> exactly the log lines from that request
Follow-ups they will ask

Self-hosted Prometheus or Amazon Managed Prometheus?

AMP if you would rather not operate a time-series database with its storage, retention and high-availability concerns — it is a genuine operational saving and it integrates with Grafana and alerting cleanly. Self-hosted when you want full control, local recording rules, or cost predictability at very large volume. For a twelve-service platform with a cost ceiling and no dedicated platform team, AMP plus managed Grafana is usually the right call.

How do you stop teams adding metrics with unbounded cardinality?

Make it hard rather than forbidden: provide a shared instrumentation library with the approved label set, review new metrics in code review, and alert on Prometheus's own series count and ingestion rate so you catch it within hours rather than when the server falls over. Then teach the alternative — high-cardinality context belongs in logs and traces, and the Embedded Metric Format or exemplars connect them.

What is the minimum viable version of this?

For a small team: structured JSON logs to stdout with a shipper and retention set, the four golden signals as metrics with three symptom-based alerts, and the OTel agent with aggressive tail sampling. That is a couple of days of work and covers the overwhelming majority of incidents. Everything else — recording rules, exemplars, custom dashboards, long retention — is refinement you add when a specific investigation proves you needed it.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start from a user-facing SLI, not an internal one. For a payments API: the proportion of requests that return a successful response in under 300 milliseconds, measured at the load balancer — measured there because that is closest to what the client experienced, and it includes queueing and connection time your application metrics never see.

Then the SLO: 99.9% over a rolling 30 days. That is an error budget of about 43 minutes of failure per month, and framing it as a budget is what makes it useful — it is a quantity you are permitted to spend, which turns reliability from a moral argument into an engineering trade-off. Ship fast while budget remains; slow down and fix things when it is exhausted.

Derive alerting from burn rate, not from thresholds. A threshold alert on error rate above 1% fires at 3am for a two-minute blip that consumed 0.1% of the budget, and it fires again and again as the metric oscillates. A burn-rate alert asks at this rate, how fast am I consuming the month's budget?

The standard shape is multi-window, multi-burn-rate. A fast burn — consuming 2% of the budget in an hour, which is a 14.4× burn rate — pages immediately, because at that rate the entire month is gone in three days. A slow burn — 10% in six hours, a 6× rate — opens a ticket, because it is real but not urgent. Each condition uses a long window and a short window ANDed together, so the alert fires promptly and, crucially, resolves promptly when the problem stops rather than staying lit for an hour.

That gives you urgency proportional to consequence, and it stops the flapping that trains people to ignore alerts.

Why alerting on CPU is wrong: it is a cause, not a symptom. High CPU with healthy latency needs no human — the service is working and using the capacity you paid for. Meanwhile a database deadlock, a connection pool exhaustion, or a downstream timeout will take you down completely at 5% CPU and never trip a CPU alert. So CPU alerts produce both false positives and false negatives, which is the worst combination available.

Cause metrics — CPU, memory, queue depth, connection counts, throttling — belong on the dashboard for diagnosis, because once you are paged they tell you why. They just should not be the thing that pages you.

One caveat worth adding: for very low-traffic services, ratio-based SLIs are statistically noisy — a handful of requests makes the error rate jump to 20%. Use longer windows, or a minimum-volume condition, so you do not page on three failed health checks at 4am.

Error budget, burn rate, and why CPU is the wrong signal
SLI  proportion of requests: HTTP 2xx/3xx AND target_processing_time < 300ms
     measured at the ALB (closest to what the client experienced)
SLO  99.9% over a rolling 30 days
     ERROR BUDGET = 0.1% x 30 days = ~43 minutes of failure per month

BURN RATE = how fast you are consuming the budget
  1x   = exactly on budget, exhausted at day 30
  14.4x = 2% of the budget in 1 hour  -> whole month gone in ~50 hours  -> PAGE
  6x    = 10% of the budget in 6 hours -> ticket

# Multi-window, multi-burn-rate. The short window makes it RESOLVE quickly too.
- alert: ErrorBudgetFastBurn
  expr: (slo:error_ratio:1h  > (14.4 * 0.001))
    and (slo:error_ratio:5m  > (14.4 * 0.001))
  for: 2m
  labels: { severity: page }

- alert: ErrorBudgetSlowBurn
  expr: (slo:error_ratio:6h  > (6 * 0.001))
    and (slo:error_ratio:30m > (6 * 0.001))
  for: 15m
  labels: { severity: ticket }

# Low-traffic caveat: ratios are noisy at low volume
  and sum(rate(requests_total[5m])) > 1        # minimum-volume guard,
                                               # or you page on 3 failed requests

WHY CPU IS WRONG
  high CPU + healthy latency        -> no human needed. It is working.
  deadlocked pool at 5% CPU         -> total outage. CPU alert NEVER fires.
  => false positives AND false negatives. The worst combination.

  CPU, memory, queue depth, connections, CFS throttling
    -> ON THE DASHBOARD, for diagnosis once you are paged
    -> NOT in the alert rules

WHAT THE BUDGET BUYS YOU (the real value)
  budget remaining  -> ship features, take risks, deploy on Fridays
  budget exhausted  -> freeze features, spend the sprint on reliability
  -> reliability becomes an ENGINEERING TRADE-OFF with a number,
     not an argument between two people with opinions.
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you pick the SLO target?

From what users actually need and what you can afford, not from how many nines sound impressive. Each additional nine is roughly an order of magnitude more expensive. Start by measuring current performance for a month — if you are already at 99.95%, setting 99.9% gives you budget to spend; setting 99.99% commits you to work nobody has funded. And check it against the dependencies: an SLO tighter than what RDS or a partner API offers is arithmetically unachievable.

What do you do when the error budget is exhausted?

Whatever you agreed in advance, which is the entire point of writing it down. The usual policy is a feature freeze on that service until the budget recovers, with the team's effort going to reliability work. It only functions if leadership agreed beforehand — negotiating it mid-incident is how error budgets become decorative. The policy is more valuable than the number.

Should every service have an SLO?

Every service with users, internal or external. For internal services the consumer is another team, and the SLO is the contract between you — which is far more useful than an informal expectation. What does not need an SLO is a batch job with no latency requirement or an internal tool where an hour of downtime is an inconvenience; there, a simple availability alert is proportionate and an SLO is ceremony.

Week 07

Scale and Distribution

Rate limits, routing and caching - autoscaling, GitOps and mesh traffic - CloudFront, Route 53, multi-region and data transfer.

The week where every answer needs a number attached. Vague scale answers are the most common reason a strong candidate stalls at the senior bar.

370/3

Throughput

You are rate-limited by the provider at peak. Design the client so a spike degrades instead of failing.

Must coverProviders limit both requests and tokens per minute, so the constraint is often tokens, not calls. Build a token-aware client-side limiter that admits work against your known quota rather than discovering the limit by getting 429s. Retry with exponential backoff plus full jitter, honouring Retry-After, and cap total attempts. Put a bounded queue in front with a deadline - work that will miss its deadline is shed early rather than adding load. Then tiering: interactive traffic gets priority, background work goes to a separate queue at lower priority or to the Batch API at half the cost. Degrade to a smaller model or a non-AI path rather than returning an error.

StudyAnthropic - rate limits →

Explain cluster autoscaling. Compare Cluster Autoscaler with Karpenter and say what makes pods sit Pending forever.

Must coverCluster Autoscaler works on node groups: it sees unschedulable pods and increases the ASG desired count, so every node in a group is the same shape and you must predefine the shapes. Karpenter provisions individual right-sized nodes directly from the pending pods' actual requirements, consolidates underused nodes, and handles spot diversification - much better bin-packing and faster. What makes pods sit Pending forever: requests larger than any available instance type, a nodeSelector or affinity nothing satisfies, a taint with no matching toleration, an EBS volume bound to an AZ with no capacity, or hitting the pod-per-node limit of the VPC CNI, which is driven by ENI limits per instance type.

StudyKarpenter →

Explain CloudFront and when an edge cache genuinely helps an API rather than just adding a hop.

Must coverCloudFront terminates TLS at the edge and, even for uncacheable requests, moves the handshake close to the user and carries the rest over AWS's backbone rather than the public internet - which measurably helps global clients. It genuinely caches when responses are shareable: static assets, public reference data, and GETs you can key correctly. The design work is the cache key - include only headers, cookies and query strings that change the response, or you fragment the cache to a hit rate of zero. Use origin request policies to control what reaches the origin, and invalidate by versioned paths rather than by wildcard invalidations, which are slow and metered.

StudyAmazon CloudFront →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The first thing to know is that providers limit on two axes — requests per minute and tokens per minute — and for RAG workloads the binding constraint is almost always tokens, not calls. A service making 40 requests a minute with 8,000-token prompts is using 320,000 tokens a minute, and it will be throttled long before any request-count limit matters. Teams that only count requests are surprised by this.

So build a token-aware admission controller on your side, rather than discovering the limit by collecting 429s. Track a rolling window of tokens consumed, estimate the cost of an incoming request before sending it, and admit only if it fits within your known quota. That turns rate limiting from a failure you react to into a queue you manage — and a queue you manage can be prioritised, which a 429 storm cannot.

Retries: exponential backoff with full jitter, honouring Retry-After when the provider sends it, and a hard cap on attempts. Without jitter, every throttled client retries at the same moment and you get a synchronised thundering herd that keeps you throttled. And cap attempts low — an uncapped retry policy under a sustained rate limit multiplies both your cost and your latency while achieving nothing.

A bounded queue with a deadline in front. Every request carries the time by which its answer is worthless; when the queue is deep enough that a request cannot be served before its deadline, shed it immediately rather than accepting it and adding load. Fast rejection is a feature — it lets the caller fall back now instead of timing out in twenty seconds.

Then tiering, which is what makes it degrade rather than fail. Interactive user-facing traffic gets priority admission. Background work — nightly summaries, bulk classification, eval runs — goes to a separate queue at lower priority, or better, to the Batch API at roughly half the price, where latency is explicitly not a concern. That separation alone often removes the contention entirely, because most of the token volume in a mature system is not interactive.

And degrade rather than error. When capacity is short: drop to a smaller and cheaper model, which usually has separate quota; reduce retrieved context so each request costs fewer tokens; shorten max_tokens; or fall back to the deterministic path — keyword search instead of semantic, raw records instead of a summary — with a visible indication that the enhanced experience is temporarily unavailable.

The framing to state: a spike should change the quality of the answer, not whether there is one.

Admit by tokens, shed by deadline, degrade by tier
// Providers limit REQUESTS/min AND TOKENS/min. Tokens bind first for RAG.
//   40 req/min x 8,000 tokens = 320,000 TPM  <-- throttled long before any
//                                                request-count limit matters

class TokenBudgetLimiter {
    private final int tokensPerMinute;                  // your KNOWN quota
    private final RollingWindow window = new RollingWindow(Duration.ofMinutes(1));

    boolean tryAdmit(int estimatedTokens) {             // estimate BEFORE sending
        return window.sum() + estimatedTokens <= tokensPerMinute * 0.9;  // headroom
    }
}

// Priority admission - interactive wins, background waits or batches
enum Tier { INTERACTIVE, BACKGROUND }

Answer handle(Request r) {
    if (r.tier() == BACKGROUND && !limiter.hasSpareCapacity())
        return batchApi.submit(r);           // ~50% cheaper, latency irrelevant

    if (!queue.offerBefore(r, r.deadline()))  // SHED EARLY if it cannot be served
        return degraded(r, "capacity");       //   in time. Fast rejection is a
                                              //   feature: the caller falls back
                                              //   NOW instead of timing out.
    ...
}

// Retries: full jitter, honour Retry-After, CAP ATTEMPTS LOW
RetryPolicy.builder()
    .maxAttempts(2)                                   // not 5. Uncapped retries
    .backoff(Backoff.exponentialWithFullJitter(       // under sustained throttling
        Duration.ofMillis(500), Duration.ofSeconds(8)))//   multiply cost and
    .respectRetryAfterHeader(true)                     //   latency for nothing
    .retryOn(RateLimitException.class, TimeoutException.class)
    .build();
// without jitter: every client retries at the same instant -> synchronised
//                 thundering herd -> you stay throttled

// DEGRADE, in order
Answer degraded(Request r, String reason) {
    if (canUseSmallModel(r))  return smallModel.answer(r);   // separate quota
    if (canReduceContext(r))  return answer(r.withTopK(2).withMaxTokens(150));
    return deterministicFallback(r);      // keyword search, raw records,
                                          // + a visible "enhanced view
                                          //   temporarily unavailable"
}

// The principle:
//   a spike should change the QUALITY of the answer, not WHETHER there is one.
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you estimate tokens before sending?

Use the provider's token-counting endpoint where one exists, or a local tokenizer for the model family — both are accurate enough for admission control. A character-count heuristic (roughly four characters per token for English) is fine as a fallback and errs in the right direction if you add headroom. You are making an admission decision, not billing, so a few percent of error is acceptable.

Should you request a quota increase or engineer around the limit?

Both, in that order. Request the increase early — before launch, with your projected tokens per minute — because it is free and it takes time to process. Then engineer around it anyway, because quotas are per-account and shared across features, and traffic grows. A team whose entire capacity plan is we asked for more quota has no answer when the spike exceeds the new number too.

What is the right behaviour when the queue is full and there is no fallback?

Return a clear, fast error with a Retry-After header, and make sure the calling service treats it as a degraded-but-known state rather than an exception. Never hold the connection hoping capacity appears — that converts your capacity problem into the caller's thread-pool problem and propagates the failure upstream. Shedding load is a deliberate act of protection, and it should look like one to the caller.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Cluster Autoscaler works at the level of node groups. It watches for unschedulable pods, simulates whether adding a node from a given group would let them schedule, and increases that ASG's desired count. Because every node in a group is one shape, you must predefine the shapes — and pods that need something no group provides simply never schedule. Scale-down removes nodes it can drain and that are under a utilisation threshold.

Karpenter works from the pods. It reads the pending pods' actual requirements — CPU, memory, architecture, zone, taints — and provisions an individual node right-sized for them, choosing from a wide set of instance types directly through the EC2 API. No node groups to define. It also consolidates: continuously repacking workloads onto fewer or cheaper nodes and terminating the rest, which Cluster Autoscaler does not do — it only removes nodes that are already nearly empty.

The practical differences: Karpenter provisions in well under a minute versus a few minutes, packs far better because the node fits the pods rather than the pods fitting the node, and handles spot diversification natively across many instance types so a single capacity pool draining does not take you out. Teams commonly see double-digit percentage cost reductions on the switch. Cluster Autoscaler remains the portable, multi-cloud option and is perfectly adequate for uniform workloads.

Now what makes pods sit Pending forever, which is the more valuable half of the answer because it is a debugging skill. kubectl describe pod prints the scheduler's verdict per predicate, and it is almost always one of six things.

Requests larger than any available instance type — a pod asking for 32Gi when the largest configured node offers 30Gi allocatable will never schedule, and no autoscaler can fix it. An unsatisfiable nodeSelector, affinity or topology spread with DoNotSchedule. A taint with no matching toleration, which is how a pod fails to reach the GPU or spot pool it was meant for. An EBS volume bound to an AZ with no capacity, or already bound to a zone the pod cannot be scheduled into — the volume node affinity conflict message. A namespace ResourceQuota already exhausted, which is namespace-scoped and therefore easy to miss when the cluster looks empty. And on EKS specifically, the VPC CNI's pod-per-node limit, driven by how many ENIs and secondary IP addresses the instance type supports — a small instance may cap at 8 or 17 pods regardless of its CPU and memory, and prefix delegation is the standard fix.

Add one more that catches people: the node has capacity but not allocatable capacity — kubelet reservations, system reservations and eviction thresholds mean a 16Gi node offers perhaps 14.5Gi to pods.

Two autoscalers, and six reasons for Pending
CLUSTER AUTOSCALER              KARPENTER
scales node GROUPS (ASGs)       provisions INDIVIDUAL nodes from pending pods
shapes predefined by you        picks instance types from EC2 directly
scale-up ~2-4 min               scale-up <60s
removes near-empty nodes only   CONSOLIDATES: repacks onto fewer/cheaper nodes
spot: per-group                 spot: diversified across many types natively
portable across clouds          AWS-focused (and now other providers)

apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      requirements:
        - { key: kubernetes.io/arch, operator: In, values: ["arm64"] }   # Graviton
        - { key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type, operator: In, values: ["spot","on-demand"] }
        - { key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-family, operator: In,
            values: ["m7g","c7g","r7g"] }            # diversify -> spot resilience
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized     # <-- the cost lever
    consolidateAfter: 1m
  limits: { cpu: "2000" }                            # a ceiling, so a bug cannot
                                                     #   provision the whole region

# --------- WHY PODS SIT PENDING FOREVER ---------
$ kubectl describe pod stuck-7d9f | grep -A15 Events
  Warning FailedScheduling  0/12 nodes are available:
    3 Insufficient memory,
    4 node(s) had untolerated taint {workload: gpu},
    5 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict.

1. requests > largest allocatable      32Gi requested, node offers 30Gi allocatable
                                       -> NO autoscaler can fix this
2. unsatisfiable affinity / topology   hard anti-affinity, replicas > nodes
   spread (DoNotSchedule)
3. taint with no toleration            the GPU/spot pool rejects it
4. EBS volume in the wrong AZ          "volume node affinity conflict"
                                       -> StorageClass WaitForFirstConsumer
5. namespace ResourceQuota exhausted   cluster looks empty; the NAMESPACE is full
                                       $ kubectl describe quota -n payments
6. EKS VPC CNI pod-per-node limit      driven by ENIs/secondary IPs per instance
                                       type. m5.large caps at 29 pods regardless
                                       of CPU/memory. Fix: ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION

# And the one that catches everyone:
#   ALLOCATABLE != CAPACITY. kubelet + system reservations + eviction thresholds
#   mean a 16Gi node offers ~14.5Gi to pods.
$ kubectl describe node ip-10-20-16-33 | grep -A6 Allocatable
Follow-ups they will ask

Can Karpenter and Cluster Autoscaler run together?

Only with care, and generally you should not. If both manage the same capacity they fight — one provisions, the other decides the node is underutilised and removes it. The supported migration path is to run Karpenter for new capacity while scaling the old managed node groups down to a small static baseline, then remove Cluster Autoscaler entirely. Overlapping ownership of node lifecycle is a reliable source of confusing behaviour.

How do you stop consolidation from disrupting production constantly?

PodDisruptionBudgets are the primary control — consolidation respects them, so a budget of maxUnavailable: 1 means it moves one replica at a time. Add consolidateAfter so it waits before acting, and use the karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt annotation on pods that genuinely must not move mid-work, such as long batch jobs. Without PDBs, consolidation is doing exactly what you asked and it will feel like chaos.

What is the fastest way to diagnose Pending?

kubectl describe pod and read the FailedScheduling event literally — it counts how many nodes failed each predicate, which usually identifies the cause without further investigation. If the message says insufficient resources, check allocatable rather than capacity, and check whether a ResourceQuota is the real limit. If it says volume node affinity conflict, it is the AZ. The scheduler is remarkably informative; the mistake is skipping past the event text.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

CloudFront is a CDN, and its cache is only half of what it does. The other half is that it terminates TLS at an edge location physically close to the user, then carries the request to your origin over AWS's own backbone rather than the public internet. That matters even for entirely uncacheable requests: a TLS handshake is multiple round trips, and doing those over 20ms to a nearby edge instead of 180ms to a distant region is a large, measurable win for global clients. Connection reuse from edge to origin compounds it.

So the first honest statement is: for a global audience, CloudFront helps even at a 0% cache hit rate. For a single-region audience hitting a single-region origin, it mostly adds a hop and you should be able to say so rather than reflexively recommending it.

Where it genuinely caches is where responses are shareable: static assets (always, with content-hashed filenames), public reference data (currency lists, fee schedules, product catalogues), and GETs you can key correctly. Anything personalised is not shareable and should be marked private or no-store — caching a per-user response at a shared edge is a data leak, and it is a real incident that has happened to real companies.

The design work is the cache key, and this is where most CloudFront deployments fail. By default, including every header, cookie and query string in the key fragments the cache so badly that the hit rate approaches zero — every request is unique, so nothing is ever reused, and you have added a hop for no benefit. Use cache policies to include only what genuinely changes the response: perhaps Accept-Encoding, a locale header, and two specific query parameters. Use a separate origin request policy to forward things the origin needs but that must not be part of the key — the Authorization header being the canonical example.

Invalidation is slow and metered, so do not design around it. Use versioned paths — /assets/app.9f2c4a.js — so a new deployment produces new URLs and the old objects simply age out. Wildcard invalidations should be an emergency tool, not a deployment step.

Two extras worth mentioning: origin shield adds a regional caching layer so many edges do not all miss through to your origin simultaneously, which protects against a cache-clear stampede. And CloudFront Functions handle cheap edge logic — header rewriting, redirects, normalising the cache key — at a fraction of Lambda@Edge's cost and latency.

Cache keys decide whether any of this works
WHY IT HELPS EVEN AT 0% HIT RATE (global audience)
  client -> nearest edge      ~15 ms RTT   TLS handshake happens HERE
  edge   -> origin            AWS backbone, reused connections
  vs. client -> distant region ~180 ms RTT x several handshake round trips

# THE CACHE KEY - where most deployments quietly fail
# BAD (legacy behaviour): forward everything
#   key = url + ALL headers + ALL cookies + ALL query strings
#   -> every request unique -> hit rate ~0% -> you added a hop for nothing

# GOOD: include ONLY what changes the response
CachePolicy:
  ParametersInCacheKeyAndForwardedToOrigin:
    HeadersConfig:        { HeaderBehavior: whitelist, Headers: [Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language] }
    CookiesConfig:        { CookieBehavior: none }
    QueryStringsConfig:   { QueryStringBehavior: whitelist, QueryStrings: [page, size] }
    EnableAcceptEncodingGzip: true
  DefaultTTL: 3600
  MinTTL: 0
  MaxTTL: 86400

# Things the ORIGIN needs but must NOT be in the key:
OriginRequestPolicy:
  HeadersConfig: { HeaderBehavior: whitelist, Headers: [Authorization, X-Request-Id] }
#  ^ Authorization forwarded, but NOT part of the cache key

# PERSONALISED RESPONSES - never shareable
Cache-Control: private, no-store        # per-user data at a shared edge is a LEAK

# INVALIDATION - do not design around it
  /assets/app.9f2c4a.js                 # versioned path: new deploy = new URL,
                                        # old objects age out. No invalidation.
  aws cloudfront create-invalidation --paths "/*"    # emergency only: slow, metered

# EXTRAS
  Origin Shield        one regional cache layer in front of the origin, so many
                       edges do not all miss through simultaneously
  CloudFront Functions header rewrites, redirects, cache-key normalisation
                       - much cheaper and faster than Lambda@Edge

# HONEST CAVEAT
#   single-region audience + single-region origin -> CloudFront mostly adds a hop.
#   Say so rather than recommending it reflexively.
Follow-ups they will ask

Can you cache authenticated API responses at all?

Sometimes, and carefully. If a response depends only on a coarse attribute — a tenant id or a role — you can include that in the cache key and share it among users with the same value, which is legitimate and effective for reference data. Never key on the raw Authorization header, since every token differs and the hit rate collapses. And be extremely deliberate: an incorrect key on authenticated content serves one user's data to another.

What does a low cache hit rate usually mean?

An over-inclusive cache key, nine times out of ten — forwarding all cookies or all query strings. After that: TTLs too short, or an origin sending Cache-Control: no-cache it did not intend to. Check the CacheHitRate metric and the x-cache response header, and normalise the key with a CloudFront Function if clients send query parameters in inconsistent orders.

Global Accelerator or CloudFront?

CloudFront for HTTP where caching is possible or where you want WAF and edge functions. Global Accelerator for non-HTTP protocols, for static anycast IP addresses that partners can allowlist, and for fast regional failover — it routes over the AWS backbone but does not cache. They solve overlapping problems for different traffic shapes, and the tell is whether the protocol is HTTP and whether anything is cacheable.

380/3

Routing and placement

Design a model router: which requests go to a small model, which to a large one, and how do you avoid the router becoming the bottleneck?

Must coverRoute on task class, not on a model judging difficulty - classification, extraction, routing and short summarisation go to the small model; multi-step reasoning and synthesis go to the large one. Where the class is genuinely unknown, use a cheap classifier or a heuristic on input length and the presence of tools, not a large-model call, or the router costs what it saves. Add a confidence-based escalation: the small model returns a structured answer plus a self-reported grounding flag, and you re-run on the large model only when it fails validation. Measure the escalation rate - if it is above roughly 30% the routing is not paying for itself.

StudyAnthropic - model comparison →

Helm or Kustomize, and how does GitOps change who can deploy? Explain the ArgoCD reconciliation model.

Must coverHelm is templating plus a package and release lifecycle - right for third-party software you install. Kustomize is overlay-based patching with no templating language - right for your own services across environments, because the base is valid YAML you can read. Many teams use both: Helm for vendor charts, Kustomize for their own. GitOps inverts the deployment direction: CI writes the desired state to a git repo, and an in-cluster controller pulls and reconciles continuously - so CI needs no cluster credentials, drift is corrected automatically, and git history is the audit log. ArgoCD compares live state to the manifest and reports Synced or OutOfSync, with sync waves for ordering and health checks before promotion.

StudyArgo CD - core concepts →

Explain Route 53 routing policies and how you would fail over a service between two regions. What is the real limit of DNS failover?

Must coverSimple, weighted (percentage shifting, good for canaries and migrations), latency-based (lowest-latency region per client), geolocation and geoproximity, failover (primary with health-checked secondary), and multi-value. Cross-region failover is usually failover or latency routing with health checks against a deep endpoint, not a ping. The real limit is that DNS is cached: resolvers and especially JVM clients ignore your TTL, so failover takes minutes rather than the TTL you set - Java caches DNS by security policy, and networkaddress.cache.ttl must be set explicitly. So DNS failover is a coarse tool; for fast failover use a global load balancer with anycast, or client-side retry across endpoints.

StudyRoute 53 - routing policies →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Route on task class, not on perceived difficulty. The distinction matters: task class is known from the code path — you are calling the model to classify, to extract, to rewrite a query, or to synthesise an answer — so routing is free and deterministic. Difficulty is a property of the input that you would have to infer, and inferring it is where routers go wrong.

Small model: classification, intent detection, extraction into a schema, query rewriting, short summarisation, routing decisions, and safety pre-screening. These are the bulk of calls in a mature system and a small model is typically an order of magnitude cheaper and noticeably faster. Large model: multi-step reasoning, synthesis across several documents, anything user-facing where quality is the product, and anything involving tool orchestration.

Where the class is genuinely unknown, do not use a large-model call to decide — that is the failure mode the question is pointing at. If your router costs as much as the call it is routing, it has achieved nothing. Use a heuristic instead: input length, whether tools are involved, whether retrieval returned high-confidence context, the endpoint the request came from. Or a genuinely cheap classifier — a small model, or even a fine-tuned embedding classifier at effectively zero marginal cost.

The pattern that works best is confidence-based escalation. Run the small model with a structured output that includes a self-reported confidence or a grounding flag, then validate deterministically — is the schema valid, are the cited ids real, do the figures match the source. If validation fails or confidence is below threshold, re-run on the large model. You pay for the small call plus, occasionally, a large one, and the quality floor is set by the large model rather than the small one.

Then measure the escalation rate, and this is the number that tells you whether the design is earning its keep. If escalation runs above roughly 30%, you are paying for both models on most requests plus the added latency, and you would be better off calling the large model directly. Below 10% and the routing is clearly paying. That single metric turns an architectural opinion into an empirical question.

Two operational notes. Version and evaluate each route separately — the small model's extraction task has its own eval set and its own regression gate, because a change that is fine for synthesis may break extraction. And keep the fallback path warm: if the small model's provider or quota fails, route to the large one rather than failing, since a more expensive answer is better than none.

Route by task class; escalate on failed validation
// ROUTE BY TASK CLASS - known from the code path, so routing is FREE
enum Task { CLASSIFY, EXTRACT, REWRITE_QUERY, SUMMARISE_SHORT,   // -> SMALL
            SYNTHESISE, REASON_MULTISTEP, TOOL_ORCHESTRATE }     // -> LARGE

Model modelFor(Task t) {
    return switch (t) {
        case CLASSIFY, EXTRACT, REWRITE_QUERY, SUMMARISE_SHORT -> SMALL;
        case SYNTHESISE, REASON_MULTISTEP, TOOL_ORCHESTRATE    -> LARGE;
    };
}
// NOT: ask a large model "is this hard?" -> the router costs what it saves

// CONFIDENCE-BASED ESCALATION - the pattern that actually works
record Extraction(Dispute data, double confidence, boolean allFieldsFound) {}

Extraction extract(String doc) {
    var small = SMALL.extract(doc);                    // cheap, fast

    boolean ok = schema.valid(small)                   // deterministic checks
              && small.allFieldsFound()
              && small.confidence() >= 0.85
              && figuresMatchSource(small);

    if (ok) { metrics.counter("route.small.kept").increment(); return small; }

    metrics.counter("route.escalated").increment();    // <-- WATCH THIS NUMBER
    return LARGE.extract(doc);                         // quality floor = large model
}

// THE METRIC THAT DECIDES WHETHER THIS IS WORTH IT
   escalation rate  < 10%   routing clearly pays
                     10-30% marginal; measure cost AND latency
                     > 30%  you pay for BOTH models on most requests, plus the
                            extra latency. Call the large model directly.

// COST SHAPE, 50k requests/day
   all large                                    100%
   70% small (no escalation) + 30% large         ~40%
   70% small + 30% escalating (small THEN large) ~55%   <-- still a win, but
                                                            watch the latency

// OPERATIONAL
//  - each route has its OWN eval set and regression gate
//    (a prompt change fine for synthesis can break extraction)
//  - keep the fallback warm: small model unavailable -> route to large,
//    never fail. A more expensive answer beats no answer.
Follow-ups they will ask

Can a fine-tuned small model replace the large one entirely for a route?

For a narrow, high-volume, well-defined task — often yes, and that is one of the few genuinely good reasons to fine-tune. A small model tuned on a few thousand examples of your specific extraction task can match a large prompted model at a fraction of the cost. The bar is beating the prompted baseline on your eval set, and the ongoing cost is that you now own a training pipeline and must re-tune when the base model improves.

Does routing add meaningful latency?

Only if you route by making a model call, which is why heuristic routing matters. Task-class routing is a switch statement — zero latency. Confidence-based escalation adds the small call's latency on the escalated fraction, which is why the escalation rate matters for latency as well as cost. Keep the small model's call fast and the median improves, because most requests never touch the large one.

How do you stop the two routes drifting apart in behaviour?

Shared prompt components and a shared output schema, so both routes produce the same shape and the downstream code does not branch. Then run both against the same eval set and record their scores separately — you want to know the gap, because it tells you whether the small model is still adequate as both models evolve. A silently widening gap is how a routing decision made a year ago becomes a quality problem.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Helm is templating plus a release lifecycle. It renders Go templates with values, tracks installed releases with revision history, and supports rollback. Its strength is packaging: installing third-party software with one command and a values file. Its weakness is that the templates are not valid YAML — they are text with control flow — so you cannot read a chart and know what it produces without rendering it, and complex charts become genuinely hard to reason about.

Kustomize is overlay-based: a base of real, valid YAML plus patches per environment. No templating language, no logic. Its strength is that everything you read is the actual manifest, and the diff between environments is explicit. Its weakness is that it cannot express conditional structure or loops, so it is poor for distributing configurable software to strangers.

So the sensible split, and it is what most teams converge on: Helm for third-party charts you install, Kustomize for your own services across environments. Argo CD supports both, and Helm can render into Kustomize if you want a single pipeline.

GitOps inverts the direction of deployment, and that inversion is the substance of the question. In push-based CI/CD, the pipeline holds cluster credentials and applies changes — so CI is a highly privileged system, credentials must be distributed to it, and if someone runs kubectl by hand the cluster silently diverges from the repository with nothing to detect it.

In GitOps, CI's job ends at writing the desired state to a git repository. An in-cluster controller pulls from that repository and reconciles. Consequences: CI needs no cluster credentials at all — a compromised runner cannot touch production; drift is corrected automatically, so a manual change is reverted rather than accumulating; and git history is the deployment audit log, with author, reviewer, timestamp and diff, which is stronger evidence than any API log because it shows intent and approval.

It also changes who can deploy: deployment permission becomes merge permission on a repository, governed by branch protection and review rules you already have — so access control moves from cluster RBAC, which is awkward to reason about, to code review, which everyone understands.

Argo CD's model is a continuous comparison between the desired state (repository) and live state (cluster), reporting each Application as Synced or OutOfSync and separately as Healthy or Degraded. Sync can be manual or automatic, with prune to delete removed resources and selfHeal to revert manual changes. Sync waves order resources within an application, and health checks gate promotion — Argo waits for a Deployment to be genuinely available before proceeding to the next wave, which is what makes multi-component rollouts safe.

CI writes git; the cluster pulls
HELM                              KUSTOMIZE
Go templates + release lifecycle  overlays patching valid YAML
packages third-party software     your own services across environments
rollback via release history      rollback via git revert
templates are NOT valid YAML      everything you read is the real manifest
good: distributing to strangers   good: 3 environments, 1 base
bad: complex charts are opaque    bad: no conditionals, no loops

# Typical split
charts/            Helm: ingress-nginx, cert-manager, kube-prometheus-stack
services/payments/
  base/            deployment.yaml service.yaml ingress.yaml  (valid YAML)
  overlays/dev/    kustomization.yaml + patch: replicas 1, small resources
  overlays/prod/   kustomization.yaml + patch: replicas 6, PDB, HPA, prod domain

# --------- GITOPS: the direction is reversed ---------
PUSH (traditional CI/CD)
  CI holds cluster credentials -> kubectl apply
  - CI is a highly privileged system; a compromised runner reaches production
  - manual kubectl changes silently diverge, forever, undetected

PULL (GitOps)
  CI -> commit desired state to a git repo   (CI has NO cluster credentials)
  in-cluster controller -> pull + reconcile continuously
  - a compromised CI runner cannot touch the cluster
  - drift is REVERTED automatically
  - git history IS the audit log: author, reviewer, timestamp, diff, PR thread
  - "who may deploy" becomes "who may merge" - branch protection you already have

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
spec:
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/k8s-manifests
    targetRevision: main
    path: services/payments/overlays/prod
  destination: { server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, namespace: payments }
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true          # resource removed from git -> deleted from cluster
      selfHeal: true       # manual kubectl change -> REVERTED
    syncOptions: [CreateNamespace=true]
---
# Ordering within an application
metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"     # migrations Job runs BEFORE the app
# Argo waits for each wave to be HEALTHY before starting the next.

# STATUS MODEL - two independent axes
  Synced / OutOfSync   does live state match git?
  Healthy / Degraded   is the workload actually working?
# OutOfSync + Healthy = someone changed the cluster by hand (selfHeal reverts it)
# Synced + Degraded   = git is correct and the app is broken -> your bug
Follow-ups they will ask

Where do secrets go in a GitOps repository?

Not in it. Use the External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver so the repository contains only a reference to a secret in AWS Secrets Manager, and the real value never enters git. Where something genuinely must live in the repo — bootstrap credentials for the operator itself — use SOPS or Sealed Secrets so it is encrypted at rest and only the cluster can decrypt. A plaintext secret in git is permanent, because git history is.

Does GitOps make emergency changes harder?

Slightly, and deliberately. The emergency path is a commit to the repository, which with a pre-approved break-glass process takes a minute or two rather than seconds. Do not disable selfHeal to allow manual changes — that removes the property you adopted it for. Instead make the emergency merge path fast and audited: a break-glass branch rule, two approvals, and an automatic ticket to review afterwards.

One repository or one per service?

A single manifests repository for a small organisation — one place to look, atomic cross-service changes, simpler Argo configuration. Split when merge contention becomes real or when teams need genuinely independent access control, using the app-of-apps pattern so a root Application points at per-team repositories. Do not split before you have to; the coordination cost of many repositories arrives long before the benefits do.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The policies. Simple — one record, no logic. Weighted — split traffic by percentage across records, which is how you do a gradual migration or a cross-region canary. Latency-based — send each client to the region with the lowest measured latency from their resolver, which is the usual choice for a multi-region active-active service. Geolocation — route by the client's country or continent, which is how you enforce data residency. Geoproximity — route by distance with an adjustable bias. Failover — a primary with a health-checked secondary. Multi-value — return several healthy records for simple client-side spreading.

Cross-region failover is usually failover or latency-based routing with health checks. Two important details: the health check must hit a deep endpoint that actually verifies the region can serve — not a static file, or you fail over to a region whose database is unreachable. And health checks come from multiple global locations, with the record considered unhealthy only when enough of them agree, which is what prevents a single network path problem from triggering a failover.

Now the real limit, and it is the substance of the question: DNS is cached, and you do not control the cache. You set a TTL of 60 seconds; recursive resolvers may honour it or not, corporate resolvers frequently extend it, and browsers keep their own cache. So a DNS failover that theoretically takes one minute routinely takes five to fifteen in practice.

And for a Java service the problem is worse and specific: the JVM caches DNS resolutions according to a security property, and historically caches successful lookups indefinitely when a security manager is present, with a default of a few seconds otherwise depending on version. Many applications never set networkaddress.cache.ttl, so a JVM client will keep connecting to the old region long after DNS has moved. Combined with a connection pool holding open sockets, the client can be pinned to a dead region for a very long time. That is the concrete, testable failure — and setting the TTL explicitly plus bounding connection maxLifetime is the fix.

So the honest conclusion: DNS failover is a coarse, slow tool suited to disaster recovery, not to fast failover. For seconds-level failover you need something else — Global Accelerator, which uses anycast IP addresses so the failover happens in the network with no DNS change at all; or client-side retry across multiple endpoints, which is what well-designed SDKs do; or Route 53 Application Recovery Controller for a controlled, deliberate shift with readiness checks.

Finally, a caution worth adding: avoid a failover mechanism that depends on the failing region. If your health check, your DNS updates, or your failover automation live in the region that is down, the mechanism fails with it. Static stability — the failover path already provisioned and requiring no control-plane call — is the property you want.

The policies, and why DNS failover is slower than its TTL
POLICY          USE
simple          one target, no logic
weighted        gradual migration, cross-region canary (10/90 -> 50/50 -> 100/0)
latency         multi-region active-active: each client to its fastest region
geolocation     DATA RESIDENCY: EU users must hit the EU stack
geoproximity    distance-based with a bias dial
failover        primary + health-checked secondary  (DR)
multi-value     return several healthy records; simple client-side spreading

# Failover record + a DEEP health check
HealthCheck:
  Type: HTTPS
  ResourcePath: /health/deep        # verifies DB reachable, not a static file
  RequestInterval: 10               # fast checks
  FailureThreshold: 3
  Regions: [eu-west-1, us-east-1, ap-southeast-1]   # multiple vantage points,
                                                    # so one bad path != failover

# ---------- THE REAL LIMIT ----------
you set     TTL 60s
resolvers   may extend it; corporate resolvers frequently do
browsers    keep their own cache
=> a "60-second" failover routinely takes 5-15 minutes in practice

# And for a JVM client it is worse and SPECIFIC:
#   the JVM caches DNS per a security property. Many apps never set it.
#   Combined with a connection pool holding open sockets, the client stays
#   pinned to the DEAD region long after DNS moved.
-Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl=5                       # or in java.security:
networkaddress.cache.ttl=5
networkaddress.cache.negative.ttl=1
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime: 600000  # recycle connections
# TEST THIS. It is the difference between a 2-minute and a 30-minute failover.

# FOR SECONDS-LEVEL FAILOVER, DNS IS THE WRONG TOOL
