Follow-ups they will ask

Would you use one index or three?

Three read replicas of one logical index, with a single write path. Retrieval must be in-region for latency, and the corpus is read-heavy with infrequent writes, so replication is straightforward. Where residency rules differ by market, they become genuinely separate indexes with separate content — which is more work but is a requirement rather than a choice, and conflating the two cases is how residency violations happen.

How do you handle multiple languages?

Two decisions. For retrieval, either a multilingual embedding model over a multilingual corpus, or translate queries to the corpus language and answer in the user's — measure both, because multilingual embeddings vary a lot by language pair. For evaluation, you need labelled cases per language; a suite that is entirely English tells you nothing about the Japanese experience, and quality in non-English languages is routinely and invisibly worse.

What breaks first at this scale?

Usually cost, then evaluation coverage. Cost, because per-request spend that seemed trivial at pilot scale multiplies by a large user base and grows with adoption. Evaluation coverage, because the eval set was built from one market's questions and stops predicting quality as the user base broadens. Both are foreseeable, which is why per-region measurement and a modelled cost per user per month belong in the design rather than in the retrospective.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Argue both sides properly, because the honest answer depends on facts about the organisation rather than on a principle.

The case for more clusters. A cluster is a genuine failure domain — a bad admission webhook, an etcd problem, a botched upgrade or a CRD conflict is contained. It allows independent upgrade cadence, so one region can be upgraded and observed before the others. It satisfies data residency cleanly, because workloads processing EU data run in an EU cluster with no path to elsewhere. It removes quota and noisy-neighbour contention at the control plane level — one team's runaway informer cannot degrade another's API server. And it simplifies RBAC, because cluster-scoped resources are no longer shared.

The case for fewer. Operational surface multiplies per cluster: upgrades, add-on lifecycle (CNI, CoreDNS, CSI drivers, autoscaler, ingress, policy engine), monitoring, cost. Bin-packing is better in a larger cluster, so utilisation is higher and the fixed overhead — system DaemonSets on every node, control plane charges — is amortised. And policy is applied in one place rather than N.

My recommendation: cluster per environment per region is the right granularity once you actually serve multiple regions — but on one condition, and the condition is the substance of the answer. Everything must be GitOps-driven, so adding a cluster is a directory rather than a project. If a new cluster means a week of hand-configuration, you will end up with clusters that drift, and drifted clusters are worse than a single large one. With an Argo CD app-of-apps structure and cluster bootstrap in Terraform, a new region is a pull request.

Then the distinction that resolves most of the argument: namespaces separate teams; clusters separate failure domains. Teams within one organisation, in one region, are soft multi-tenancy — namespaces with ResourceQuotas, RBAC and default-deny NetworkPolicy handle that well. Splitting clusters per team is a common mistake: it multiplies operational cost to solve a problem namespaces already solve, and it usually reflects a lack of confidence in the namespace controls rather than a real isolation requirement.

So push back on the platform team's proposal by asking what it is for. If the answer is regional residency and independent upgrades, agree. If it is team isolation, the cheaper and better answer is to fix the namespace controls.

Namespaces separate teams; clusters separate failure domains
MORE CLUSTERS                        FEWER CLUSTERS
hard failure domain                  less operational surface
  (bad webhook, etcd, upgrade,         upgrades, add-ons, monitoring, cost
   CRD conflict is CONTAINED)          all multiply per cluster
independent upgrade cadence          better bin-packing -> higher utilisation
data residency, cleanly              fixed overhead amortised
                                       (system DaemonSets per node,
no control-plane contention             control plane charge per cluster)
simpler cluster-scoped RBAC          policy applied in ONE place

RECOMMENDATION
  cluster per ENVIRONMENT per REGION, once you actually serve multiple regions
  CONDITION: everything GitOps-driven, so a new cluster is a DIRECTORY,
             not a project.

clusters/
  prod-eu-west-1/     bootstrap.yaml   apps/   <- new region = a PR
  prod-us-east-1/     bootstrap.yaml   apps/
  staging-eu-west-1/  bootstrap.yaml   apps/
  dev-eu-west-1/      bootstrap.yaml   apps/

# Argo app-of-apps: one root Application per cluster, pointing at its directory.
# Terraform module for cluster + node pools + add-ons, parameterised per region.
# If adding a cluster takes a WEEK OF HAND-CONFIGURATION, clusters will DRIFT -
# and drifted clusters are worse than one large one.

# THE DISTINCTION THAT RESOLVES THE ARGUMENT
  namespaces separate TEAMS          -> ResourceQuota + RBAC + default-deny
                                        NetworkPolicy. Soft multi-tenancy,
                                        appropriate for one organisation.
  clusters separate FAILURE DOMAINS  -> region, environment, regulatory boundary,
                                        genuinely hostile tenancy

# PUSH BACK BY ASKING WHAT IT IS FOR
  "regional residency + independent upgrades"  -> agree, do it
  "team isolation"                             -> namespaces already do this.
                                                  Fix the controls instead; a
                                                  cluster per team multiplies
                                                  cost to solve a solved problem.
Follow-ups they will ask

How many clusters is too many?

When you can no longer confidently state that they are all on the same version with the same add-on set — that is the practical threshold, and it arrives sooner than people expect without automation. With strong GitOps and templated bootstrap, dozens are manageable. Without it, four is already painful. The number is a function of your automation, not an absolute.

How do you handle cluster-wide services with many clusters?

Decide per service whether it is per-cluster or central. Per-cluster: ingress controllers, cert-manager, the CNI, the policy engine — they must be local. Central: observability backends, the container registry, the GitOps control plane (one Argo CD managing many clusters), and secret storage. The mistake is running a central service that becomes a hard dependency of every cluster's data path, which reintroduces the shared failure domain you split clusters to avoid.

What about a single cluster spanning regions?

Do not. etcd requires low-latency consensus between members, and stretching it across regions produces a cluster that is slow in normal operation and prone to split-brain during a network event. Kubernetes explicitly targets a single failure domain per cluster. Multi-region means multiple clusters with a federation or GitOps layer above them, which is the well-trodden path.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Take the numbers seriously first, because they dictate the choices. RPO 5 seconds rules out backup-and-restore and any batched replication — it requires continuous, near-synchronous replication. RTO 2 minutes rules out provisioning compute on demand; capacity must already exist. So this is a warm standby, and both numbers point at the same architecture.

Data layer: Aurora Global Database. A writer in the primary region and a read-only secondary in the standby, replicating at the storage layer with typical lag well under a second — comfortably inside a 5-second RPO, provided you measure and alarm on the lag rather than assuming it. Managed planned failover is clean; unplanned promotion takes roughly a minute. That is the single most important component and it is what makes the RPO achievable at all.

Compute: warm in both regions. Infrastructure as code deployed identically, with the standby's ECS service or node group running at reduced capacity — enough to serve immediately and scale out under load. Not zero, because provisioning from cold does not fit two minutes.

Routing: Route 53 health-checked failover with a low TTL and deep health checks from multiple vantage points — plus the honest caveat that DNS caching means the client-observed RTO exceeds the mechanism's. Mitigate with client-side retry across endpoints, and for genuinely fast failover consider Global Accelerator, where the shift happens in the network with no DNS involved.

What you lose on unplanned failover — and this must be stated explicitly, because it is the question's real substance. Transactions committed in the primary but not yet replicated are gone. At sub-second lag that is a small window, but it is not zero, and in payments a lost transaction is not an abstraction. Therefore the design must make replay safe: an idempotency key on every write so a re-submitted transaction is a no-op; a transactional outbox that can be re-driven so events corresponding to lost writes are regenerated; and a reconciliation process against the partner's or scheme's records after failover, because the authoritative record of what actually happened may be theirs.

And what does not fail over automatically, which is where most real gaps live: SQS queues are regional, so messages in the dead region are stranded until it returns; ElastiCache is regional, so you fail over into a cold cache and the resulting miss storm can overwhelm the newly-promoted database — a very common way a technically successful failover still causes an outage; EventBridge schedules exist per region, so both firing is a double-execution bug and neither firing is a silent gap; in-flight Step Functions executions do not migrate; and every WebSocket or streaming connection drops.

Finally: KMS multi-region keys, or the standby cannot decrypt anything — a failure you cannot fix during the incident.

Warm standby, and an explicit statement of what is lost
REQUIREMENT   RPO 5s  ->  rules out backups and batched replication
              RTO 2min ->  rules out provisioning compute on demand
              => WARM STANDBY

DATA      Aurora Global Database
            writer eu-west-1  |  read-only secondary eu-west-2
            storage-layer replication, typical lag <1s
            MEASURE IT: alarm on AuroraGlobalDBReplicationLag > 3s
            unplanned promotion ~60s
COMPUTE   same IaC both regions; standby ECS service at 20-30% capacity, WARM
          (not zero - cold provisioning does not fit 2 minutes)
ROUTING   Route 53 failover, TTL 60, deep health checks from >=3 regions
          + client-side retry across endpoints
          (consider Global Accelerator: failover in the NETWORK, no DNS)
SECRETS   Secrets Manager cross-region replication
KEYS      KMS MULTI-REGION KEYS  <-- without these the standby cannot decrypt
                                     ANYTHING. Not fixable during the incident.
IMAGES    ECR cross-region replication

# ---- WHAT YOU LOSE ON UNPLANNED FAILOVER ----
# Transactions committed in the primary but NOT YET REPLICATED are GONE.
# Sub-second window, but not zero. In payments that is not an abstraction.
# THEREFORE the design must make REPLAY SAFE:

  1. idempotency key on EVERY write
     ddb.putItem(... conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk)"))
     -> a re-submitted transaction is a safe no-op

  2. transactional outbox that can be RE-DRIVEN
     -> events for lost writes are regenerated when the write is replayed

  3. RECONCILIATION against the scheme's / partner's records after failover
     -> the authoritative record of what actually happened may be THEIRS

# ---- WHAT DOES NOT FAIL OVER (where the real gaps are) ----
  SQS queues        regional. Messages in the dead region are STRANDED.
  ElastiCache       regional. You fail over into a COLD CACHE -> miss storm
                    can overwhelm the newly-promoted database.
                    <-- very common way a "successful" failover still causes
                        an outage. Plan for it: warm the cache, or rate-limit
                        cache-miss traffic to the DB.
  EventBridge       schedules exist per region. Both firing = double execution.
  schedules         Neither firing = silent gap. Decide explicitly.
  Step Functions    in-flight executions do NOT migrate.
  WebSocket/SSE     all connections drop.

# REHEARSE QUARTERLY. An untested plan has an unknown RTO.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not active-active to get RPO to zero?

Because with a shared writable ledger, active-active means either distributed consensus across regions — which adds cross-region latency to every write and defeats the purpose — or last-writer-wins, which silently discards financial transactions. The safe active-active shape is regional partitioning, where each account has a home region, and that is worth doing if the traffic pattern supports it. For a single global writer, active-passive with a stated RPO is the honest design.

How do you avoid the cold-cache stampede on failover?

Three options, usually combined. Keep the standby's cache warm by replaying a sample of read traffic to it continuously. Put request coalescing in front of the cache so a thousand simultaneous misses for one key produce one database query. And rate-limit or shed cache-miss traffic to the database during the first minutes after promotion, accepting slower responses rather than overwhelming the writer. Deciding this in advance is what separates a two-minute failover from a twenty-minute one.

What about the scheduled jobs firing in both regions?

Make the decision explicit and enforce it with a lock rather than with configuration. Have the schedule fire in both regions but have each execution take a cross-region lock — a conditional write to a Global Table with a TTL — so exactly one proceeds. That is resilient to failover in both directions and does not require someone to remember to enable a rule in the standby. Configuration-based approaches fail silently in exactly the moment you need them.

Week 08

Data and Durability

Fine-tuning, index migration and versioning - operators, backups and stateful upgrades - outbox, CDC, backup and chaos.

Derived data is where AI systems rot and where distributed systems lose correctness. This week is about the copies of your data you forgot you made.

430/3

Changing the model, extending the cluster, moving the data

When you do decide to fine-tune, what does the process actually involve? Cover data, method and evaluation.

Must coverData is the whole job: a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality examples in exactly the input-output shape you will use in production, deduplicated, with a held-out test split created before any tuning. Method is usually parameter-efficient (LoRA-style adapters) rather than full fine-tuning - far cheaper, and the adapter is a small artefact you can version and swap. Evaluate against the same suite you use for the prompted baseline, and the bar is beating that baseline, not beating nothing. Watch for catastrophic forgetting on adjacent tasks and for overfitting to the quirks of your labellers. Then version it like code: dataset hash, base model version, adapter artefact, eval scores.

StudyAmazon Bedrock - custom models →

What is a CustomResourceDefinition and what is an operator? Give an example where writing one is justified.

Must coverA CRD extends the Kubernetes API with your own object type, so kubectl get yourthing works and RBAC applies to it. An operator is a controller watching that type and running a reconcile loop that drives real state toward the spec - it encodes the operational knowledge a human would apply. Justified when the thing you manage has non-trivial lifecycle: a database needing leader election, backup, failover and version upgrade, or provisioning cloud resources alongside a workload. Not justified for anything a Helm chart plus a Job can do. The discipline is that reconcile must be idempotent, level-triggered rather than edge-triggered, and must tolerate being interrupted at any point.

StudyKubernetes - operator pattern →

Explain the transactional outbox pattern and why you need it when a service writes to a database and publishes an event.

Must coverWriting to the database and publishing to a broker are two systems, so there is no atomic commit across them - crash between the two and you either have a state change nobody heard about or an event for a change that rolled back. The outbox: in the same local transaction as the business write, insert a row into an outbox table. A separate relay - polling, or change data capture via DMS or Debezium reading the transaction log - publishes those rows and marks them sent. That gives at-least-once delivery with guaranteed correspondence to committed state, so consumers must be idempotent. On AWS, DynamoDB Streams gives you the same property natively for DynamoDB writes.

StudyAWS - transactional outbox pattern →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The data is the job — say that first, because people imagine fine-tuning is a compute problem and it is overwhelmingly a dataset problem. You need a few hundred to a few thousand examples in exactly the input-output shape production will use, including the same system prompt and the same schema, or the model learns a task you will not actually give it.

Quality dominates volume. A thousand carefully-labelled, consistent examples beat ten thousand noisy ones, and inconsistency between labellers is the most common cause of a fine-tune that underperforms — the model faithfully learns the disagreement. So: a written labelling guide, measured inter-annotator agreement, and deduplication. And create the held-out test split before any tuning, from a different time period if possible, or you will evaluate against data the model effectively memorised.

Method. In practice, parameter-efficient fine-tuning — LoRA-style adapters that train a small number of additional parameters while the base weights stay frozen. Far cheaper, far faster, and the artefact is a small adapter file you can version, store and swap, rather than a full model copy. Full fine-tuning is rarely justified for application work. On AWS this is Bedrock custom models or SageMaker; the mechanics matter less than the discipline around them.

Evaluation is where most attempts fail honestly. The bar is not does the tuned model work — it is does it beat the best prompted baseline on the same eval suite, including cost and latency. Teams routinely fine-tune, see good numbers, and never compare against a well-engineered prompt with good few-shot examples, which frequently matches it. Run both.

Then watch for two specific failure modes. Catastrophic forgetting: the model gets better at your task and worse at adjacent ones — instruction following, refusals, formats you did not train on — so your eval suite must include tasks you did not tune for. And overfitting to labeller quirks: if two annotators always resolved ambiguity the same way, the model learns that convention as if it were ground truth.

Version it like code, and be specific about what a version comprises: the dataset hash, the base model version, the training hyperparameters, the adapter artefact, and the eval scores. Without that you cannot reproduce a model, explain a regression, or answer an auditor.

And name the permanent obligations you have just taken on: you must re-tune when the base model is deprecated, you now own a data pipeline, and — critically in a regulated context — a deletion request against training data means retraining, because weights cannot be unlearned.

The dataset is the work; the baseline is the bar
# 1. DATA - in the EXACT production shape, including the system prompt
{"messages":[
  {"role":"system","content":"<the production system prompt, verbatim>"},
  {"role":"user","content":"Merchant writes: 'charged twice on the 3rd, want it back'"},
  {"role":"assistant","content":"{\"reason\":\"DUPLICATE\",\"amountMinor\":null,
     \"transactionDate\":\"2026-03-03\",\"confidence\":0.9}"}]}

  1,200 examples | deduplicated | written labelling guide
  inter-annotator agreement measured: 0.91
  <-- LABELLER INCONSISTENCY is the most common cause of a weak fine-tune.
      The model faithfully learns the disagreement.

  TEST SPLIT CREATED FIRST, from a LATER time period than the training data
  (otherwise you evaluate against what it effectively memorised)

# 2. METHOD - parameter-efficient (LoRA-style adapters)
   base weights frozen; a small adapter is trained
   artefact = a small file you can version, store and SWAP
   full fine-tuning is rarely justified for application work

# 3. EVALUATION - the bar is BEATING THE BASELINE, not beating nothing
                      prompted    fine-tuned    delta
  extraction F1         0.87        0.94        +0.07   <-- the win
  schema valid          0.96        0.999       +0.04
  cost per call         1.00x       0.18x       (small model now viable)
  p50 latency           820ms       210ms
  ---- tasks NOT tuned for (catastrophic forgetting check) ----
  instruction following 0.95        0.88        -0.07   <-- REGRESSION
  refusal correctness   0.92        0.79        -0.13   <-- SERIOUS
# -> tuned model wins on the task and LOST safety behaviour.
#    Either mix general instruction data into training, or keep the tuned model
#    ONLY on the extraction route and never on the conversational one.

# 4. VERSION IT LIKE CODE
model_version: extraction-v3
  dataset_hash:   sha256:7a91...          # exactly which examples
  base_model:     claude-...-20260514     # explicit
  hyperparams:    { epochs: 3, lr: 1e-4, rank: 16 }
  adapter:        s3://models/extraction-v3.safetensors
  eval_scores:    { f1: 0.94, schema: 0.999, refusal: 0.79 }

# PERMANENT OBLIGATIONS YOU JUST ACCEPTED
  re-tune when the base model is deprecated (a few times a year)
  you now own a data pipeline and a labelling process
  a DELETION REQUEST against training data means RETRAINING - weights cannot
  be unlearned. In a regulated context this is the decisive cost.
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you know the dataset is big enough?

Plot a learning curve: train on 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of the data and score each on the held-out set. If the curve has flattened, more data will not help and the remaining gap is a task or method limitation. If it is still climbing steeply, labelling more is the highest-value work available. This takes an afternoon and prevents both premature satisfaction and pointless labelling.

Can you fine-tune on outputs from a larger model?

Distillation — generating training data with a large model and tuning a small one on it — is a legitimate and widely used technique, and it works well for narrow tasks. Two cautions: check the provider's terms, since some prohibit training competing models on their outputs; and the small model inherits the large one's mistakes, so the generated data needs review and filtering rather than blind acceptance. Where you have real labelled data, prefer it.

What is the honest failure rate of fine-tuning projects?

High, and the most common outcome is not a broken model but an unnecessary one — a tuned model that matches a well-engineered prompt, at the cost of a permanent pipeline. That is why the baseline comparison is not a formality: it is the decision. The second most common failure is a dataset built too quickly, with inconsistent labels, producing a model that is confidently wrong in the specific ways the labellers were.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A CustomResourceDefinition extends the Kubernetes API with a new object type. Once registered, your type behaves like a built-in: kubectl get postgresclusters works, RBAC applies to it, it is stored in etcd, and it can be validated with an OpenAPI schema. A CRD on its own is inert — it is a place to put data.

An operator is the thing that makes it mean something: a controller watching that resource type and running a reconcile loop that drives real-world state toward the declared spec. It encodes the operational knowledge a human would otherwise apply — if the primary is unreachable, promote a replica, update the endpoint, fence the old one, and record it.

Three properties of a correct reconcile loop, and these are what an interviewer is listening for. It must be level-triggered, not edge-triggered: it looks at current state versus desired state and acts, rather than reacting to an event — so a missed event is self-correcting. It must be idempotent: reconciling twice does the same thing as reconciling once. And it must be interruptible at any point, because the operator pod will be killed mid-reconcile and must resume safely, which means state lives in the cluster (status subresource, finalizers) rather than in the operator's memory.

When writing one is justified. When the thing you manage has a non-trivial lifecycle that a human currently performs from a runbook — a database needing leader election, failover, backup, point-in-time recovery and version upgrade; a Kafka cluster needing partition rebalancing; provisioning cloud resources whose lifecycle must be tied to a workload's. The test is: is there a runbook of conditional steps that someone follows at 3am? If yes, that is an operator. If the answer is apply this YAML, it is not.

When it is not justified — and this matters more, because writing an operator is a serious commitment. Anything a Helm chart plus a Job can do. Anything with no ongoing lifecycle beyond create and delete. And anything where the real motivation is a nicer YAML interface, which is a templating problem, not a controller problem.

A concrete example I would give: AWS Controllers for Kubernetes or Crossplane managing an S3 bucket or an RDS instance whose lifecycle is tied to a namespace — so deleting the namespace reclaims the cloud resource. That is genuine lifecycle management, and it is a good illustration because the alternative (Terraform in a separate pipeline) has a real drift problem the operator solves.

One caution to add: an operator is privileged software running permanently in your cluster. It needs broad RBAC, it can be a single point of failure for the workloads it manages, and a buggy reconcile loop can delete production data enthusiastically and repeatedly. Prefer a mature community operator over writing your own.

Level-triggered, idempotent, interruptible
# The CRD: a place to put data. Inert on its own.
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata: { name: settlementjobs.payments.acme.com }
spec:
  group: payments.acme.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names: { kind: SettlementJob, plural: settlementjobs, shortNames: [sj] }
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      subresources: { status: {} }        # status is where the loop keeps state
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              required: [sourceBucket, schedule]
              properties:
                sourceBucket: { type: string }
                schedule:     { type: string }
                partnerId:    { type: string }
---
# The operator: a reconcile loop with three required properties
func (r *Reconciler) Reconcile(ctx context.Context, req Request) (Result, error) {
    var sj v1.SettlementJob
    if err := r.Get(ctx, req.NamespacedName, &sj); err != nil {
        return Result{}, client.IgnoreNotFound(err)
    }

    // LEVEL-TRIGGERED: compare CURRENT to DESIRED. Not "react to an event".
    // A missed event is self-correcting on the next resync.
    current := r.observe(ctx, &sj)          // what actually exists right now

    // IDEMPOTENT: CreateOrUpdate, never blind Create
    if _, err := ctrl.CreateOrUpdate(ctx, r.Client, desiredCronJob(&sj), mutate);
       err != nil { return Result{}, err }

    // INTERRUPTIBLE: state lives in the CLUSTER, not in operator memory
    sj.Status.LastReconciled = metav1.Now()
    sj.Status.Phase = phaseFrom(current)
    if err := r.Status().Update(ctx, &sj); err != nil { return Result{}, err }

    // Finalizer: cleanup runs even if the operator restarts mid-delete
    return Result{RequeueAfter: 5 * time.Minute}, nil   // periodic resync
}

# JUSTIFIED WHEN                      NOT JUSTIFIED WHEN
a RUNBOOK of conditional steps        a Helm chart + a Job can do it
exists that a human follows at 3am    lifecycle is just create and delete
  (failover, backup, PITR, upgrade,   the real motivation is "nicer YAML"
   partition rebalance)                 (that is a templating problem)
cloud resource lifecycle tied to a
workload (ACK / Crossplane: delete
the namespace -> reclaim the bucket)

# CAUTION
#   an operator is PRIVILEGED software running permanently in your cluster.
#   Broad RBAC, a single point of failure for what it manages, and a buggy
#   reconcile loop can delete production data enthusiastically and repeatedly.
#   Prefer a MATURE COMMUNITY OPERATOR over writing your own.
Follow-ups they will ask

What is a finalizer and why does it matter?

A string on an object that prevents deletion until the controller removes it. When someone deletes the resource, Kubernetes sets a deletionTimestamp instead of removing it, the operator sees this, performs external cleanup — deleting the S3 bucket, deregistering from a partner — and then removes the finalizer to let deletion complete. It is the mechanism for cleanup that must happen outside the cluster. It is also a classic way to wedge a namespace: if the operator is gone, the finalizer is never removed and the object cannot be deleted.

How do you test an operator?

With envtest, which runs a real API server and etcd without a full cluster, so you can assert on reconcile behaviour quickly. Test the properties specifically: reconcile twice and assert the same outcome (idempotency), reconcile from several partial states (interruptibility), and reconcile after deleting a managed resource behind its back (level-triggered self-healing). Those three tests catch the majority of operator bugs, and none of them are obvious from ordinary unit-test habits.

Operator or Terraform for cloud resources?

Terraform when the resource is long-lived infrastructure with its own lifecycle — VPCs, clusters, shared databases — and reviewed change is what you want. An operator (ACK or Crossplane) when the resource's lifecycle is genuinely tied to a workload, so it should be created and destroyed with the namespace. The failure mode of mixing them is two systems believing they own the same resource, so draw the boundary explicitly and enforce it with tags.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The problem is the dual write: you need to change your database and publish an event, and those are two different systems with no atomic commit between them. There is no distributed transaction available, so one of two things happens on a crash between the steps — a state change nobody heard about (the write committed, the publish did not), or an event for a change that rolled back (you published first, then the transaction failed). Both are corruption from a consumer's point of view, and the second is worse because it is unrecoverable by retry.

Trying to fix it with ordering does not work. Publish-then-commit gives phantom events; commit-then-publish gives lost events; and wrapping the publish in the transaction achieves nothing, because a broker acknowledgement cannot be rolled back.

The outbox pattern resolves it by making the intent to publish part of the same local transaction as the business write. You insert a row into an outbox table alongside the state change — one database, one commit, fully atomic and fully testable. A separate relay then reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them, marking them sent.

That relay can be a poller — simple, adds a little latency, and needs care to avoid two instances publishing the same row, which a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED handles cleanly. Or it can be change data capture reading the database's transaction log — DMS or Debezium — which adds no query load, has lower latency, and requires no polling loop, at the cost of operating the CDC pipeline.

The guarantee you get is at-least-once publication that corresponds exactly to committed state. Not exactly-once: the relay can publish and crash before marking the row sent, so the event is republished. Therefore consumers must be idempotent — an event id checked against a processed-events table with a conditional write. That consequence is not a footnote; it is the contract, and a design that omits it has moved the bug rather than fixed it.

On AWS there is a case where you get this for free: DynamoDB Streams. Because the stream is derived from the transaction log itself, every record corresponds to a committed change, in order per partition key — so for DynamoDB writes the outbox is built in. That is a genuinely good reason to reach for DynamoDB for event-heavy write paths.

One practical detail worth adding: put the ordering key and the full event payload in the outbox row, not just an id — otherwise the relay must read the entity again and may see a later state, publishing an event that does not match the transaction it came from.

One local transaction, then a relay
// THE PROBLEM - two systems, no atomic commit
@Transactional
void settle(Settlement s) {
    repo.save(s);                       // commits...
    eventBridge.putEvents(event(s));    // ...and this fails -> event LOST
}                                       // or: publish first, tx rolls back
                                        //     -> PHANTOM event, unrecoverable

// THE OUTBOX - intent to publish is part of the SAME local transaction
@Transactional
void settle(Settlement s) {
    repo.save(s);
    outbox.insert(new OutboxRow(
        UUID.randomUUID(),              // eventId - the consumer's idempotency key
        "PaymentSettled",
        s.getAccountId(),               // ORDERING KEY
        json(s),                        // FULL PAYLOAD - not just an id (see below)
        Instant.now(),
        null));                         // sentAt
}   // one database, one commit, atomic, and fully unit-testable

// RELAY option A: poller. Simple. SKIP LOCKED prevents double-publish.
@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)
void relay() {
    var sql = "SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE sent_at IS NULL "
            + "ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED";
    for (var r : jdbc.query(sql, MAPPER)) {
        eventBridge.putEvents(toEntry(r));      // may publish then crash...
        jdbc.update("UPDATE outbox SET sent_at = now() WHERE id = ?", r.id());
    }                                            // ...so it republishes. Fine.
}

// RELAY option B: CDC - reads the transaction log. No query load, lower latency.
//   DMS or Debezium -> MSK / Kinesis -> EventBridge
//   cost: a pipeline to operate

// THE GUARANTEE, stated precisely
//   AT-LEAST-ONCE publication corresponding EXACTLY to committed state.
//   NOT exactly-once: relay publishes, crashes before marking sent -> republish.
//   => CONSUMERS MUST BE IDEMPOTENT. This is the contract, not a footnote.
try {
    ddb.putItem(r -> r.tableName("processed_events")
        .item(Map.of("pk", s("EVT#" + eventId), "ttl", n(ttl30d())))
        .conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk)"));
    handle(event);
} catch (ConditionalCheckFailedException dup) { /* safe no-op */ }

// WHY THE FULL PAYLOAD IN THE ROW
//   store only an id -> the relay must re-read the entity -> it may see a LATER
//   state -> it publishes an event that does not match the transaction it
//   came from. Snapshot the payload at write time.

// FREE ON AWS: DynamoDB Streams IS an outbox - derived from the transaction log,
// every record corresponds to a committed change, ordered per partition key.
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you keep the outbox table from growing forever?

Delete sent rows on a schedule — a partitioned table with a retention window, or a simple delete job keeping a few days for debugging and replay. Do not delete immediately on publish: keeping a short history lets you re-drive events after a consumer bug, which is one of the pattern's practical benefits. Monitor unsent row age; a rising oldest-unsent timestamp is the clearest signal the relay has stopped.

Does the outbox preserve ordering?

Per key, if you make it so. Include an ordering key (account id, aggregate id) in the row, publish with that as the message group id on a FIFO queue or the partition key on a stream, and process in order within the key. Global ordering across all events is neither achievable at scale nor usually needed. The relay reading by created_at gives you a reasonable global approximation, but do not build consumers that depend on it.

When would you skip the outbox?

When losing an event is genuinely acceptable — a metrics ping, a cache invalidation that has a TTL fallback, a best-effort notification. Then a direct publish with a retry is simpler and fine. The outbox earns its complexity when a consumer's correctness depends on hearing about every committed change, which in payments is essentially always.

440/3

Keeping derived data honest

You need to change embedding models. Your index has 40 million vectors. How do you migrate without downtime or a quality cliff?

Must coverVectors from different models are not comparable, so you cannot mix them in one index - that is the constraint everything follows from. Build the new index alongside the old, backfilling from the source documents, not from the old vectors, since embeddings are not invertible. Keep ingest dual-writing to both during the backfill. Evaluate the new index against your labelled retrieval set and tune k and thresholds, because the score distribution and the right threshold will differ. Then shift read traffic by percentage with the eval running online, and keep the old index until you are confident. Budget for it honestly: the backfill is a large compute and cost event, and it is why the embedding model choice is stickier than it looks.

StudyAnthropic - embeddings →

How do you back up a Kubernetes cluster, and what does backing up the cluster actually not cover?

Must coverVelero snapshots the API objects in selected namespaces plus the underlying volume snapshots, on a schedule with retention, into S3 - and can restore into a different cluster, which is the real test. What it does not cover: the desired state should already be in git, so object backup is a convenience, not the source of truth; and application-consistent data is not guaranteed by a volume snapshot alone - a database mid-write needs a pre-snapshot hook to flush and quiesce, or you restore a corrupt file. Also not covered: cluster-level configuration outside the API (node groups, IAM, add-on versions), which belongs in infrastructure as code. Test restores on a schedule; an untested backup is a hypothesis.

StudyVelero →

Explain change data capture and when you would use MSK or Kinesis instead of SQS.

Must coverCDC reads the database transaction log and emits every committed change as an event - no application code, no dual-write problem, complete ordering per key. On AWS that is DMS or Debezium into MSK. Choose a log (MSK, Kinesis) over a queue (SQS) when you need any of: replay from an offset, multiple independent consumer groups reading the same stream at their own pace, strict ordering within a key, or retention as a source of truth for rebuilding projections. Choose SQS when you want simple work distribution with per-message retry and a DLQ, and you never need to re-read. The operational cost is real: MSK is a cluster to run, and consumer group rebalancing and lag monitoring become your problem.

StudyAmazon MSK →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Lead with the constraint that makes this hard: vectors from different embedding models are not comparable. There is no shared coordinate system and no conversion function — you cannot transform old vectors into new ones. So the migration is a full rebuild from source documents, and everything else follows from that single fact.

Build the new index alongside the old, backfilling from the source documents, not from stored chunks or old vectors. If you kept only vectors and not the source text, this migration is much worse — which is a good argument, made in advance, for retaining chunk text or making chunking deterministically reproducible from versioned sources.

Dual-write during the backfill. New and changed documents go to both indexes while the historical backfill runs, or the new index is stale before it is complete. Reconcile at the end by comparing document counts and checksums per source.

Then re-tune, because the numbers change. This is the step people miss. A different model produces a different score distribution — cosine similarities may cluster in a different band entirely — so your minimum-score threshold, your k, and any filtering behaviour must be re-derived. A threshold of 0.35 that meant relevant under the old model may mean everything or nothing under the new one. Evaluate against your labelled retrieval set: measure recall@k, sweep the threshold, and pick the new operating point empirically.

Shift read traffic by percentage with evaluation running online — 5%, 25%, 50% — comparing retrieval and end-to-end answer quality between the two indexes on live queries. Keep the old index until you are confident, because rebuilding it again would be another multi-day operation.

Budget for it honestly, because that is part of the answer: 40 million chunks is 40 million embedding calls. Even in batch, that is a substantial compute and cost event measured in hours to days and hundreds to thousands of pounds, plus double the index storage and memory during the overlap. Use the batch API, parallelise, and rate-limit against your quota.

And close with the lesson: the embedding model is a stickier choice than it appears on day one. That is worth knowing when you pick one — favour a model with a stable versioning policy and, if available, Matryoshka support so you can change dimensions without changing models. It is also a reason to keep source text and make ingest reproducible, so that when this does become necessary it is expensive rather than impossible.

Rebuild from source, re-tune the thresholds, shift by percentage
CONSTRAINT: vectors from different models are NOT comparable.
            No conversion exists. Migration = full rebuild from SOURCE.

PHASE 1  build alongside
  new index (model-B), empty
  backfill workers read SOURCE DOCUMENTS -> chunk -> embed(model-B) -> upsert
  ingest DUAL-WRITES to both indexes throughout, or B is stale before it is done
  40M chunks / batch API / parallel workers / rate-limited to quota
  -> hours to days, hundreds to thousands of GBP, 2x storage during overlap

PHASE 2  reconcile
  per source: document_count(A) == document_count(B)
              checksum of doc_id set matches
  -> if not, find the gap BEFORE shifting traffic

PHASE 3  RE-TUNE - the step people miss
  score distributions DIFFER between models:
     model-A  relevant results score 0.72-0.89, threshold 0.35 worked
     model-B  relevant results score 0.31-0.52  <-- the SAME threshold now
                                                    admits everything
  against the labelled retrieval set:
     sweep min_score:  0.10 0.15 0.20 0.25 ...  -> pick the new operating point
     sweep k:          3 5 8 10 15              -> recall@k vs precision
     re-check filter behaviour (pre- vs post-filter recall)

PHASE 4  shift reads by percentage, evaluating ONLINE
  5% -> compare recall proxies + end-to-end answer quality on live queries
  25% -> 50% -> 100%
  KEEP INDEX A until confident. Rebuilding it is another multi-day operation.

# IF YOU STORED ONLY VECTORS AND NOT SOURCE TEXT, this migration is far worse.
# -> retain chunk text, OR make chunking deterministically reproducible from
#    versioned source documents. Decide this on day one.

# THE LESSON
#   the embedding model is a STICKIER choice than it looks.
#   favour: a stable versioning policy, and Matryoshka support (change
#   dimensions without changing models).
Follow-ups they will ask

Can you avoid the rebuild by running both models in parallel permanently?

You can run two indexes and fuse their results — which is a legitimate hybrid — but it doubles storage, memory and query cost forever, and it complicates every subsequent change. It is reasonable as a transitional state during the shift, and as a permanent architecture it is usually paying an ongoing tax to avoid a one-off cost. Migrate properly and retire the old index.

How do you decide the migration is worth it at all?

Measure first, on a sample. Build the new index over 1–2% of the corpus, evaluate recall@k against your labelled set, and compare. If the improvement is a point or two of recall, it almost certainly does not justify a multi-day rebuild plus re-tuning plus risk. If it is a large jump — or if the old model is being deprecated, which is often the actual forcing function — then proceed. Never migrate on a benchmark score published by a vendor; measure on your own corpus.

What breaks in production during the shift?

Mostly threshold-dependent behaviour that nobody remembered was threshold-dependent: the no relevant context found short-circuit, any confidence-based routing, and caches keyed on retrieval results. Also anything that stored a vector id externally, since ids differ between indexes. Grep for every place a similarity score or a vector id crosses a boundary before you start — that list is usually longer than expected.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Velero is the standard tool. It snapshots the Kubernetes API objects in selected namespaces — Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, CRDs and custom resources — into an object store, and separately triggers volume snapshots through the CSI driver for PersistentVolumes. It supports schedules, retention, label selectors and namespace mapping, and — the property that makes it a real backup rather than a copy — it can restore into a different cluster. That is also the only meaningful test of it.

Now what backing up the cluster does not cover, which is the substance of the question.

It should not be your source of truth. If you run GitOps, the desired state already lives in git with history, review and attribution. Restoring API objects from a backup is a convenience for a fast rebuild; the authoritative recovery path is point Argo CD at the repository and let it reconcile. A team whose only record of what should be running is a Velero backup has a configuration management problem, not a backup problem.

It does not give you application-consistent data. A CSI volume snapshot is crash-consistent — it captures the disk as it was at an instant, which for a database mid-write is a torn state. Restoring it is equivalent to recovering from a power cut: often survivable, sometimes corrupt. Application consistency requires pre- and post-snapshot hooks that quiesce writes and flush buffers, or better, using the database's own backup mechanism (WAL archiving, pg_basebackup) and treating the volume snapshot as secondary.

It does not cover cluster-level configuration outside the API: the node groups, the IAM roles and IRSA trust relationships, the VPC and subnets, the add-on versions, the control plane settings. All of that belongs in infrastructure as code. A Velero restore into an empty account restores nothing useful, because there is no cluster to restore into.

So the honest recovery model has three layers: infrastructure as code rebuilds the cluster, git plus GitOps restores the workloads, and Velero or database-native backups restore the data. Velero's most valuable role is often the middle-ground case — recovering one accidentally deleted namespace quickly — rather than full disaster recovery.

And the discipline that makes any of it real: test restores on a schedule, into a different cluster, with an automated integrity check, recording the elapsed time. An untested backup is a hypothesis with an unknown success rate and an unknown RTO.

Three layers, and the snapshot that is not application-consistent
# Velero: API objects + volume snapshots, restorable INTO A DIFFERENT CLUSTER
velero schedule create daily-payments \
  --schedule="0 2 * * *" \
  --include-namespaces payments,payments-data \
  --snapshot-volumes \
  --ttl 720h                                   # 30 days

# APPLICATION CONSISTENCY - a raw CSI snapshot is CRASH-consistent, not
# application-consistent. Restoring a database mid-write is a power-cut recovery.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  annotations:
    pre.hook.backup.velero.io/container: postgres
    pre.hook.backup.velero.io/command: '["/bin/sh","-c","psql -c \"SELECT pg_backup_start(''velero'');\""]'
    post.hook.backup.velero.io/container: postgres
    post.hook.backup.velero.io/command: '["/bin/sh","-c","psql -c \"SELECT pg_backup_stop();\""]'
# BETTER: use the database's own mechanism (WAL archiving to S3, pg_basebackup)
#         and treat the volume snapshot as secondary.

# ---- WHAT VELERO DOES NOT COVER ----
NOT the source of truth      desired state is in GIT. Restore = point Argo at
                             the repo and reconcile. A Velero backup as your
                             only record of what should run is a configuration
                             management problem, not a backup problem.
NOT app-consistent by default see hooks above
NOT cluster-level config     node groups, IAM roles, IRSA trust, VPC, subnets,
                             add-on versions, control plane settings
                             -> INFRASTRUCTURE AS CODE
                             (a Velero restore into an empty account restores
                              nothing: there is no cluster to restore INTO)

# ---- THE HONEST THREE-LAYER RECOVERY MODEL ----
  layer 1  Terraform/CDK      -> rebuild the cluster + node pools + IAM + add-ons
  layer 2  git + Argo CD      -> reconcile all workloads (the real source of truth)
  layer 3  Velero / DB-native -> restore the DATA

# Velero's most valuable everyday role is layer 2's gap: recovering ONE
# accidentally deleted namespace in minutes.
velero restore create --from-backup daily-payments-20260829020000 \
  --include-namespaces payments

# ---- THE DISCIPLINE ----
# Monthly, automated, into a DIFFERENT cluster:
#   1. restore
#   2. run an integrity check against the restored data
#   3. RECORD THE ELAPSED TIME  <-- this is your measured RTO
# An untested backup is a hypothesis with an unknown success rate.
Follow-ups they will ask

Do you need to back up etcd directly?

On a managed control plane like EKS, no — AWS operates etcd and you have no access to it. On a self-managed control plane, yes, and it is the single most important backup you have, since it contains the entire cluster state. Even then, prefer git as the source of truth for workloads: an etcd restore brings back everything including the broken thing you were trying to escape, whereas reconciling from git gives you a clean, reviewed state.

How do you back up a StatefulSet's data properly?

Use the application's own backup mechanism wherever one exists — continuous WAL archiving to S3 for Postgres, snapshots plus AOF for Redis — because those are designed for consistency and point-in-time recovery. Volume snapshots are a coarser secondary layer. And back up to a different account, not just a different region, so a compromised or mistaken deletion in the production account cannot destroy the backups with it.

What is the most common backup failure?

Discovering at restore time that something essential was excluded — a namespace not in the include list, a CRD not captured, a Secret in kube-system, or a volume whose StorageClass had no snapshot support configured. All of these are found instantly by a real restore test and never by reading the backup configuration. That is why the monthly restore is the control, and the backup schedule is merely the prerequisite.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Change data capture reads the database's transaction log — the WAL in Postgres, the binlog in MySQL — and emits every committed change as an event. Three properties follow from that and they are why it is attractive: no application code changes, since you are reading what the database already writes; no dual-write problem, because the log is the record of committed state; and complete ordering per key, because that is how the log is written. On AWS that is DMS or Debezium, typically into MSK.

The trade is that CDC events are row changes, not business intent. You get this row's status column went from PENDING to SETTLED, not PaymentSettled. Consumers must reconstruct meaning from schema-level changes, which couples them to your internal schema — so a column rename becomes a breaking change for every downstream team. That coupling is the main argument for an outbox producing deliberately-designed events instead, and it is worth stating so the answer is not one-sided.

Now: log versus queue. Choose a log — MSK or Kinesis — when you need any of four things. Replay from an offset: a consumer with a bug can re-read the last week after a fix, without you rebuilding anything. Multiple independent consumer groups reading the same stream at their own pace, so adding a fifth consumer does not affect the other four. Strict ordering within a key, guaranteed by partition. And retention as a source of truth, so downstream projections can be rebuilt from scratch.

Choose a queue — SQS — when you want simple work distribution with per-message retry, a dead-letter queue, and no cluster to operate, and you will never need to re-read. The tell is a question: will anyone ever want to read this history again? Queues consume; logs retain.

Then the operational cost, stated honestly, because this is where teams underestimate. MSK is a cluster: brokers, storage, partition planning, and consumer group rebalancing — which pauses consumption and is a real source of production surprises — plus consumer lag as a metric you must monitor and alert on, since a lagging consumer is invisible until the retention window expires and data is genuinely lost. Kinesis removes the broker management but brings its own model of shards, per-shard limits, and resharding.

So the recommendation shape: SQS by default, because most work distribution genuinely does not need replay; a log when replay, multiple consumers or per-key ordering is a real requirement; and be explicit that adopting MSK is taking on a distributed system to operate.

Log versus queue, and what CDC gives you for free
CDC: read the transaction log. No app changes, no dual write, ordered per key.
  Postgres WAL / MySQL binlog
    -> DMS or Debezium
      -> MSK / Kinesis
        -> consumers

  BUT: events are ROW CHANGES, not business intent.
    CDC gives:   { table: "settlement", op: "U",
                   before: { status: "PENDING" }, after: { status: "SETTLED" } }
    outbox gives:{ type: "PaymentSettled", settlementId: ..., amountMinor: ... }
  -> CDC couples consumers to your INTERNAL SCHEMA. A column rename becomes a
     breaking change for every downstream team. That is the argument FOR an
     outbox with deliberately designed events.

CHOOSE A LOG (MSK / Kinesis) WHEN YOU NEED
  replay from an offset          consumer had a bug -> re-read last week, no
                                 backfill project needed
  multiple consumer GROUPS       each at its own pace; adding a 5th consumer
                                 does not affect the other 4
  strict ordering within a key   guaranteed by partition
  retention as source of truth   rebuild projections from scratch

CHOOSE A QUEUE (SQS) WHEN
  simple work distribution, per-message retry, DLQ, no cluster to operate,
  and you will NEVER need to re-read.

THE TELL: "will anyone ever want to read this history again?"
          queues CONSUME. logs RETAIN.

# OPERATIONAL COST, honestly - this is where teams underestimate
  MSK       brokers, storage, partition count planning (hard to change later)
            CONSUMER GROUP REBALANCING - pauses consumption; a real source of
              production surprises (a slow consumer triggers a rebalance,
              which slows everyone, which triggers another)
            CONSUMER LAG - must be monitored and ALERTED. A lagging consumer is
              invisible until the retention window expires and data is GENUINELY
              LOST. This is the metric people forget.
  Kinesis   no brokers, but shards, per-shard limits (1MB/s in, 2MB/s out),
            and resharding

# Alert that matters most on either:
#   consumer lag (records or seconds behind) approaching the retention window
Follow-ups they will ask

Can you get replay with SQS?

Not natively — a consumed message is gone. The usual workarounds are archiving every message to S3 as it is published and replaying from there, or using EventBridge with an archive, which supports replaying a time range to targets. Both work and both are less convenient than an offset. If replay is a first-class requirement rather than an occasional rescue, that is the signal to use a log.

How do you size partitions in MSK?

From your required parallelism, since consumer parallelism within a group is capped by partition count — you cannot have more active consumers than partitions. Choose a number comfortably above your expected peak consumer count, because increasing partitions later breaks key-to-partition mapping and therefore ordering for existing keys. Over-provisioning partitions is cheap; under-provisioning is a migration.

Is DMS a reasonable long-term CDC solution or just for migrations?

It is genuinely used for ongoing replication, and it is the low-operational-effort choice on AWS. Debezium is more capable and more configurable — better transformation, better schema handling, richer connector ecosystem — at the cost of running it yourself on MSK Connect or Kubernetes. For straightforward table-to-stream replication, DMS is usually adequate and much less work.
