Versioning everything

How do you version an AI system so that any past answer can be explained? List everything that must be pinned.

Must coverPin and record on every response: model id and explicit version (never a floating alias), sampling parameters, the prompt template version from git, the tool schema version, the embedding model version, the index snapshot or document versions retrieved, and the application version. Store the request id linking them. That is what lets you answer a complaint from three months ago, and it is what lets you reproduce a regression. The two people miss are the embedding model - because the index silently encodes it - and the retrieved document versions, since the source may have been edited since. Treat the whole set as one deployable artefact with a version of its own.

StudyAnthropic - model deprecations →

How do you run a stateful upgrade - say a three-node Redis or Kafka on Kubernetes - without losing data or quorum?

Must coverStatefulSet rolling updates go one pod at a time in reverse ordinal order, waiting for each to become Ready before proceeding - so the readiness probe must actually mean joined the cluster and caught up, not just port open, or you break quorum by moving on too early. Use a PodDisruptionBudget with maxUnavailable 1 so a node drain cannot take a second replica concurrently. Use partitioned rollouts to canary a single ordinal and verify before releasing the rest. Back up before starting, verify the restore path, and check version compatibility both ways so you can roll back. And accept that some upgrades are not rollback-safe once the on-disk format changes - know which those are before you start.

StudyKubernetes - StatefulSet update strategies →

Explain how you would do a zero-downtime schema migration on Aurora for a table with 400 million rows.

Must coverExpand-contract, always. Expand: add the new nullable column or new table, deploy code that writes both and reads the old - fully backward compatible, so rollback is free. Backfill in batches with a bounded rate, monitoring replica lag, never one big UPDATE that holds locks and blows up the undo log. Then flip reads to the new column behind a flag and verify. Contract: only after the old path is unused and you are certain you will not roll back, drop the old column in a separate later release. For the DDL itself, know which operations are online in your engine version - in modern PostgreSQL adding a nullable column is instant, adding a NOT NULL with a default is too, but adding an index must be CONCURRENTLY or it locks writes.

StudyAurora PostgreSQL best practices →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The requirement is: any past answer must be explainable. That means reproducible — you can reconstruct exactly what the system saw and why it said what it said. Everything that can vary must therefore be recorded, and there are more varying parts than people list.

Pin and record on every response: the model id with an explicit version — never a floating alias, because an alias makes the question unanswerable by construction; the sampling parameters (temperature, top-p, max tokens); the prompt template version from git; the tool schema version, since a changed tool description changes behaviour; the embedding model version; the retrieval configuration (k, thresholds, reranker); the ids and versions of the documents actually retrieved; and the application version.

The two people miss are worth calling out specifically. First, the embedding model — because the index silently encodes it, and if you rebuilt the index six months ago with a different model, the retrieval behaviour changed for reasons invisible in any prompt or code diff. Second, the retrieved document versions, because the source may have been edited since. If you record only document ids and the document has been updated twice, you can no longer see what the model actually read — and the policy said something different then is the most common legitimate explanation for a complaint about a past answer.

Treat the whole set as one deployable artefact with a version of its own. That is the framing that makes it manageable: settlement-assistant@v14 resolves to a specific model version, prompt, tool schemas, retrieval config and embedding model. One identifier on the response, one lookup to expand it. Without that, you either store a dozen fields per request or you cannot reproduce anything.

Two practical consequences. Reproduction is not the same as identical output — sampling is stochastic, so you can reproduce the inputs exactly and get slightly different text. Be precise about that in a compliance conversation: you can evidence what the system was given and what it produced, and you can demonstrate the behaviour is consistent, but you cannot promise bit-identical regeneration. Claiming otherwise is a claim you cannot support.

And the retention of versions must match the retention of answers. If you keep audit records for seven years, the prompt template from six years ago must still be resolvable — so prompt versions live in git and are never deleted, and the artefact manifest is archived alongside. A version identifier pointing at something that no longer exists is not an audit trail.

One artefact version, expandable to everything
// ONE identifier on the response; one lookup to expand it.
{ "requestId": "req_9f2c4a1b",
  "artefactVersion": "settlement-assistant@v14",     // <-- the whole set
  "retrievedDocs": [                                  // ids AND VERSIONS
     { "docId": "fees-guide",     "version": 12 },
     { "docId": "chargeback-ops", "version": 4  } ] }

// The manifest that v14 resolves to - archived, immutable, never deleted
settlement-assistant@v14:
  model:            claude-...-20260514      # EXPLICIT version, never an alias
  temperature:      0
  maxTokens:        400
  promptTemplate:   settlement_summary@v7    # git tag
  toolSchemas:      settlement-tools@v3      # a changed DESCRIPTION changes behaviour
  embeddingModel:   voyage-3                 # <-- MISSED #1: the index encodes it
  indexSnapshot:    idx-2026-08-01           #     silently
  retrieval:        { k: 5, minScore: 0.35, rerank: cohere-v3 }
  appVersion:       payments-api@2.14.3

// MISSED #2: document VERSIONS, not just ids.
//   record only ids -> the doc has since been edited twice -> you can no longer
//   see what the model actually read.
//   "the policy said something different then" is the most common LEGITIMATE
//   explanation for a complaint about a past answer.

// REPRODUCTION IS NOT IDENTICAL OUTPUT - be precise in a compliance conversation
//   you CAN evidence: exactly what the system was given, and what it produced
//   you CAN demonstrate: behaviour is consistent across re-runs
//   you CANNOT promise: bit-identical regeneration (sampling is stochastic,
//                       and provider-side numerics drift)
//   Claiming otherwise is a claim you cannot support.

// RETENTION MUST MATCH
//   audit records kept 7 years -> the v7 prompt template from 6 years ago must
//   still resolve. Prompt versions live in git and are NEVER deleted; the
//   artefact manifest is archived alongside the audit record.
//   A version identifier pointing at something that no longer exists is not
//   an audit trail.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why is the tool schema a versioned artefact?

Because the schema text is part of the prompt. Field names, descriptions and enum values are read by the model and materially change which tool it picks and what arguments it produces. A one-word change to a tool description can shift behaviour as much as a prompt edit — so it goes through the same eval gate and carries the same version discipline. Teams that version prompts but not tool schemas have a gap that eventually produces an unexplainable change.

How do you handle a model version that no longer exists?

You cannot re-run it, and that is a limitation to state honestly rather than engineer around. What you retain is the recorded input and output, which is what an auditor actually needs — evidence of what happened, not the ability to recreate it. Record the deprecation date alongside the version so the audit trail shows why re-execution is unavailable after that point, and note that this is another argument for storing the full output rather than only a hash where classification allows.

Does this apply to a simple non-RAG feature too?

Yes, minus the retrieval fields. Model version, parameters, prompt version and application version are the irreducible set for anything using a model in a path that affects customers. It is four fields on a log line, and it is the difference between answering a complaint in ten minutes and being unable to answer it at all.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A StatefulSet rolling update goes one pod at a time, in reverse ordinal order, waiting for each pod to become Ready before proceeding to the next. That ordering is the safety mechanism — and it only works if Ready means what you need it to mean.

So the first and most important point: the readiness probe must mean joined the cluster and caught up, not the port is open. A TCP check passes on a Redis loading its dataset from disk, on a Kafka broker still catching up on partitions, on a Postgres replica still replaying WAL. If the probe returns Ready early, the controller proceeds to the next pod and you have two members down at once — quorum lost, on a three-node cluster, during what looked like a routine upgrade. The probe is the entire safety property; get it wrong and the ordering guarantee is worthless.

A PodDisruptionBudget with maxUnavailable: 1 handles the other direction. The rolling update respects ordinality, but a node drain during a cluster upgrade does not know about your quorum — the PDB is what stops the eviction API taking a second member while one is already down. Without it, a cluster upgrade and a StatefulSet upgrade can overlap disastrously.

Partitioned rollouts are how you canary. Setting partition: 2 on a three-replica set updates only pod-2 and leaves 0 and 1 alone. You verify the new version genuinely works — joined, replicating, serving — then lower the partition to release the rest. That is the single most useful StatefulSet feature and it is underused.

Back up before starting, and verify the restore path, not merely that a backup exists. And check version compatibility in both directions: can the new version read data written by the old, and — the one that matters for rollback — can the old version read data written by the new.

Because that leads to the honest constraint to state unprompted: some upgrades are not rollback-safe. Once a node has written data in a new on-disk format, or once a cluster-wide feature flag or protocol version has been bumped, downgrading is not supported and the recovery path is restore from backup. Know which upgrades those are before you start, because the point of no return is usually crossed silently — often by the first upgraded node writing a single record.

Finally, sequence it: one pod, verify at the application level (not just Ready), then proceed. And do it during a window where you can tolerate the recovery, not on a Friday afternoon.

Readiness carries the whole safety property
# The ordering guarantee is worthless if readiness lies.
readinessProbe:
  exec:
    command:
      - sh
      - -c
      - |
        redis-cli ping | grep -q PONG || exit 1
        # AND: actually in the cluster and caught up
        redis-cli info replication | grep -q 'master_link_status:up' || exit 1
        redis-cli info persistence | grep -q 'loading:0' || exit 1
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3
# A TCP check passes on a node that is LOADING and serving nothing.
# -> controller proceeds to the next pod -> TWO members down -> QUORUM LOST
#    during what looked like a routine upgrade.

# CANARY ONE ORDINAL FIRST - the most useful and most underused feature
spec:
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      partition: 2          # replicas 0 and 1 untouched; ONLY redis-2 updates
# verify redis-2 at the APPLICATION level, then:
#   kubectl patch sts redis -p '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"partition":0}}}}'
---
# Node drains do not know about your quorum. The PDB does.
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: redis } }
# without it: a cluster upgrade draining nodes can take a SECOND member while
# the StatefulSet rollout already has one down.

# SEQUENCE
  1. back up AND verify the restore path (not just that a backup exists)
  2. check compatibility BOTH WAYS:
       new version reads old data?   (upgrade works)
       OLD version reads NEW data?   (ROLLBACK works)  <-- the one that matters
  3. partition: N-1  -> update one ordinal
  4. verify at the application level: joined, replicating, serving real traffic
  5. lower the partition one step at a time
  6. never rely on "Ready" alone as the verification

# THE HONEST CONSTRAINT - state it unprompted
#   Some upgrades are NOT rollback-safe. Once a node writes data in a new
#   on-disk format, or a cluster-wide feature flag / protocol version is
#   bumped, downgrade is unsupported and recovery = RESTORE FROM BACKUP.
#   The point of no return is usually crossed SILENTLY - often by the first
#   upgraded node writing a single record.
#   Know which upgrades those are BEFORE you start.
Follow-ups they will ask

What is podManagementPolicy Parallel and when is it safe?

It starts and stops all pods simultaneously rather than in ordinal order. Safe when replicas are independent — a sharded cache, workers with per-replica storage, anything where a new member does not need to join an existing quorum. Unsafe for anything with consensus, because simultaneous restarts are exactly the scenario ordering exists to prevent. Note it affects scaling and creation; the rolling update strategy is separate.

How do you handle a StatefulSet upgrade that requires a specific order — say, replicas before the primary?

The controller only knows reverse ordinal order, so encode the requirement in the topology: make the highest ordinal the one that should be upgraded first, and use partitioned rollouts to control each step manually. For anything with genuine role-dependent ordering — a primary that must be upgraded last, or a coordinated protocol switch — that is exactly the case for an operator, which can implement the real sequence rather than approximating it with ordinals.

What goes wrong most often in practice?

A readiness probe that only checks the port, and a missing or over-strict PodDisruptionBudget. Those two account for most quorum-loss incidents during maintenance. Behind them: assuming rollback is possible when the on-disk format changed, and discovering the backup was never restore-tested at exactly the moment it is needed.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Expand-contract, always — and the reason to lead with that phrase is that it is the only pattern where rollback remains possible at every step, which is the actual requirement behind zero downtime.

Expand. Add the new column as nullable with no default, or add the new table. In modern PostgreSQL, adding a nullable column is a metadata-only change and effectively instant even at 400 million rows — no table rewrite, no long lock. Then deploy code that writes both the old and new columns and reads the old. At this point the schema and both application versions are mutually compatible, so rollback is free.

Backfill in bounded batches. Never a single UPDATE over 400 million rows: it holds locks for the duration, generates enormous WAL, bloats the table with dead tuples, blows up autovacuum, and — the part that bites in production — pushes replica lag through the roof, which breaks read-your-writes and can trigger failovers. Instead iterate over primary key ranges in batches of a few thousand, committing each, with a sleep between batches and a check on replication lag that pauses when it exceeds a threshold. Make the batch job resumable and idempotent, because it will be interrupted.

Flip reads behind a feature flag and verify. Still writing both, so rollback is still a flag flip.

Contract — drop the old column — only in a separate, later release, once you are certain you will not roll back past the flip. This is the step people collapse into the first one, and doing so is precisely what makes rollback impossible.

Then the DDL specifics, because online depends on the operation and the engine version. Adding a nullable column: instant. Adding NOT NULL with a constant default: instant in PostgreSQL 11 and later, a full rewrite before that. Adding a constraint: use NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT separately, so the long scan does not hold an exclusive lock. Adding an index: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, or you lock writes for the whole build — on 400 million rows that is many minutes of outage.

And the operational detail that catches people even with correct DDL: a migration waits for a lock, and while it waits it queues every subsequent query behind it. A long-running read or an idle-in-transaction session can turn an instant DDL into a full outage. So set lock_timeout to a few seconds and retry, rather than letting the migration block indefinitely.

Expand, backfill, flip, contract — rollback safe throughout
-- RELEASE 1: EXPAND. Old code still works. Rollback is free.
SET lock_timeout = '3s';                     -- do NOT wait behind a long read
ALTER TABLE settlement ADD COLUMN currency_code char(3);   -- nullable: INSTANT
-- app v2: writes BOTH currency and currency_code; reads currency

-- RELEASE 1.5: BACKFILL in bounded batches, watching replica lag
DO $$
DECLARE lo bigint := 0; hi bigint; lag interval;
BEGIN
  LOOP
    SELECT lo + 5000 INTO hi;
    UPDATE settlement SET currency_code = lookup(currency)
     WHERE id >= lo AND id < hi AND currency_code IS NULL;
    COMMIT;
    SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() INTO lag;
    WHILE lag > interval '5 seconds' LOOP       -- PAUSE, do not drown the replica
      PERFORM pg_sleep(2);
      SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() INTO lag;
    END LOOP;
    PERFORM pg_sleep(0.05);
    lo := hi;
    EXIT WHEN lo > (SELECT max(id) FROM settlement);
  END LOOP;
END $$;
-- NEVER one UPDATE over 400M rows: locks held for the duration, enormous WAL,
-- table bloat, autovacuum overwhelmed, REPLICA LAG through the roof
-- (breaks read-your-writes and can trigger a failover)

-- RELEASE 2: FLIP READS behind a flag. Old code STILL works.
-- app v3: reads currency_code, still writes both

-- RELEASE 3: CONTRACT. Only once you will never roll back past release 2.
ALTER TABLE settlement DROP COLUMN currency;

-- ---- DDL: what is actually online ----
ADD COLUMN nullable                 instant (metadata only)
ADD COLUMN NOT NULL DEFAULT const   instant in PG 11+; FULL REWRITE before
ADD CONSTRAINT                      use NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT
                                    separately (the scan takes a weak lock)
CREATE INDEX                        CONCURRENTLY, or you lock WRITES for the
                                    whole build - minutes of outage on 400M rows
DROP COLUMN                         instant (marks it dropped; space reclaimed
                                    by a later VACUUM FULL / pg_repack)

-- THE OPERATIONAL DETAIL THAT CATCHES PEOPLE
--   a migration WAITING for a lock QUEUES every subsequent query behind it.
--   One long-running read, or an idle-in-transaction session, turns an
--   "instant" DDL into a full outage.
--   -> SET lock_timeout, and RETRY. Never let a migration block indefinitely.
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you run the migration in a Kubernetes deployment?

As a separate Job or an Argo sync hook that runs to completion before the application rollout, not as an init container. With three replicas, three init containers race to run the same migration, which most migration tools serialise with an advisory lock — turning it into a slow, confusing startup rather than a clean step. A pre-sync Job runs exactly once, fails loudly, and blocks the rollout if it fails, which is what you want.

What if the backfill is still running when you need to deploy?

That is fine and it is one of the benefits of the pattern — the backfill is decoupled from any release. Application code writes both columns, so new rows are already correct; the backfill only fills history. Make it resumable from a checkpoint and idempotent so it survives restarts and redeploys, and monitor its progress as an ordinary job with an expected completion time.

How do you verify the backfill was complete and correct?

A reconciliation query counting rows where the new column is null but should not be, plus a sampled comparison of old and new values — run as an automated check, not a manual one, and gate the read-flip on it. And keep both columns for a while after the flip so a discrepancy discovered later is still diagnosable. Dropping the old column is the step that destroys your ability to verify, which is another reason to delay it.

Proving durability

Design the data pipeline that keeps your retrieval index in sync with twelve source systems. What are the correctness properties you need?

Must coverProperties: eventual convergence (every source change eventually reflected), idempotency (reprocessing the same change is harmless), ordering per document (a delete must not be overtaken by a stale update - use a version or timestamp and reject out-of-order writes), and completeness (you can prove nothing was silently dropped). Architecture: per-source connectors emitting change events with a document id and version into a stream, a normaliser, chunk and embed workers, and an upsert into the index keyed by document id so re-processing replaces rather than duplicates. Add a reconciliation job that periodically diffs source counts and checksums against the index - drift is not hypothetical, and without reconciliation you will not know.

StudyAWS - data pipeline patterns →

How do you test that your cluster actually survives a node failure? Describe a game day.

Must coverAnnounce it, do it in business hours, and have a rollback. Start with a single pod delete and watch the Service endpoints and the client error rate - if a single pod delete causes errors, you have a graceful shutdown problem, not a resilience problem. Then cordon and drain a node and watch whether PDBs let it drain and whether the scheduler finds room. Then terminate a node abruptly, which is different, because the kubelet does not get to shut down cleanly and pods stay Terminating until the node controller times out - measure that gap, because it is your real failure detection time. Finally kill an AZ's worth of nodes and see whether topology spread actually spread you. Record the observed RTO and fix the largest gap.

StudyKubernetes - node lifecycle →

What is AWS Fault Injection Service for, and what would you inject into a payments platform first?

Must coverFIS runs controlled experiments - terminating instances, adding latency or packet loss, throttling API calls, failing over RDS - with a stop condition tied to a CloudWatch alarm so the experiment aborts if real users are affected. That stop condition is what separates chaos engineering from an outage. First experiments, in order: kill one task or pod and prove no errors; fail over the RDS writer and measure how long the connection pool takes to recover, which is where most Java services fail badly; inject 200ms of latency into a downstream dependency and confirm your timeouts and circuit breakers fire before the caller's timeout; then throttle an AWS API and see whether your retries have jitter or stampede. Always start with a hypothesis you expect to hold.

AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

State the correctness properties first, because they are what the design must guarantee, and a pipeline described without them is just a diagram.

Eventual convergence — every source change is eventually reflected in the index. Idempotency — reprocessing the same change is harmless, so retries and replays are safe. Ordering per document — a delete must not be overtaken by a stale update, which is the property that silently breaks in a parallel pipeline. Completeness — you can prove nothing was dropped, rather than assume it.

Architecture. Per-source connectors emit change events carrying a docId, a version or timestamp, an operation (upsert or delete) and the source's ACLs. Twelve sources means twelve connectors with different mechanisms — webhooks where available, polling with an etag or a modified-since cursor otherwise, CDC where the source is a database you control. Normalise them all into one internal event shape immediately, so the rest of the pipeline is source-agnostic.

Then a normaliser, chunk-and-embed workers, and an upsert keyed by document id — delete all existing chunks for that document version, then write the new ones — so reprocessing replaces rather than duplicates. Duplicated chunks from a re-run are one of the most common and most damaging silent failures, because retrieval then returns two contradictory versions of the same policy.

Ordering per document is enforced with a version check, not with a sequential pipeline: store the version on the chunks and reject any write whose version is lower than what is already indexed. That makes parallel processing safe and makes out-of-order delivery — which will happen — harmless. It is the same conditional-write discipline as idempotency, applied to ordering.

And the piece that is almost always missing: reconciliation. A periodic job that diffs the source against the index — document counts and a checksum of the id set per source — and reports drift. Drift is not hypothetical: connectors fail silently, webhooks are dropped, a permission change hides documents from the connector's account, a parser starts returning empty text. Without reconciliation you will not know, and the failure mode is that the assistant quietly answers from a stale corpus for weeks.

Add two alarms that cost nothing and catch most of it: ingest failure rate above zero, and chunk-count or average-chunk-length change per source beyond a threshold, which is what catches a parser breaking when a partner changes a template.

Four properties, and the reconciliation nobody builds
PROPERTIES the design must guarantee
  eventual convergence   every source change eventually reflected
  idempotency            reprocessing the same change is harmless
  ORDERING PER DOCUMENT  a delete must not be overtaken by a stale update
  completeness           you can PROVE nothing was dropped

PIPELINE
  12 connectors (webhook | poll+etag | CDC)
    -> normalise to ONE internal event shape immediately
       { docId, version, op: UPSERT|DELETE, acl[], sourceUrl, fetchedAt }
    -> queue (per-source, so one broken source cannot block the others)
      -> parse -> chunk -> embed -> UPSERT

// IDEMPOTENCY + ORDERING, both from one conditional write
void upsert(DocEvent e) {
    int indexed = index.currentVersion(e.docId());
    if (e.version() <= indexed) {              // ORDERING, without a serial pipeline
        metrics.counter("ingest.stale_skipped").increment();
        return;                                 // out-of-order delivery WILL happen
    }
    index.deleteByDocId(e.docId());             // IDEMPOTENCY: replace, never append
    index.insertAll(chunk(e).stream()
        .map(c -> c.withVersion(e.version()).withAcl(e.acl())).toList());
}
// duplicated chunks from a re-run are the most damaging silent failure:
// retrieval returns TWO CONTRADICTORY VERSIONS of the same policy.

// RECONCILIATION - almost always missing, and the reason indexes rot
@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 3 * * *")
void reconcile() {
    for (var source : sources) {
        var src = source.listDocIdsAndVersions();     // authoritative
        var idx = index.listDocIdsAndVersions(source.id());
        var missing = difference(src.keySet(), idx.keySet());
        var extra   = difference(idx.keySet(), src.keySet());   // deleted at source,
                                                                // still indexed
        var stale   = src.entrySet().stream()
            .filter(e -> idx.getOrDefault(e.getKey(), -1) < e.getValue()).toList();
        report(source, missing, extra, stale);
        if (!missing.isEmpty() || !extra.isEmpty()) alert(source);
    }
}
// DRIFT IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL: connectors fail silently, webhooks are dropped,
// a permission change hides docs from the connector's account, a parser starts
// returning empty text. Without this you answer from a stale corpus for weeks.

// TWO ALARMS THAT COST NOTHING
  ingest.failures > 0                             -> alert
  chunk_count / avg_chunk_length per source
    changed > 30% day over day                    -> alert
    (catches a partner changing a PDF template)
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you handle a source that has no change notification at all?

Poll with the narrowest cursor the source supports — a modified-since filter, an etag, or a sequence number — and fall back to a full listing on a slower cadence to catch deletes, which most incremental APIs do not report. Deletes are the hard part: a document removed at source often produces no event anywhere, so the periodic reconciliation is the only thing that catches it. That is a second reason reconciliation is not optional.

Should each source have its own queue?

Yes. One queue per source means a broken or slow connector accumulates depth in isolation rather than blocking the other eleven, and it lets you tune concurrency per source — some APIs rate-limit aggressively. It also makes the metrics legible: per-source lag and failure rates tell you which connector to fix, where a shared queue tells you only that ingest is unhappy.

What do you do when reconciliation finds drift?

Fix forward automatically where it is safe: missing documents are re-fetched and indexed, extra documents are deleted, stale ones re-processed. Alert on the rate rather than on any single discrepancy, because a small amount of transient drift is normal in a distributed pipeline. What matters is a persistent or growing gap for one source, which means the connector is broken rather than merely behind.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A game day is an announced, business-hours experiment with a rollback. That framing matters: doing it unannounced or at night is not braver, it just produces a worse experiment and less learning, because the people who could explain what they are seeing are not there.

Start with a single pod delete, and treat this as a real test rather than a warm-up. Delete one pod while running load, and watch the client error rate. If a single pod delete causes errors, you do not have a resilience problem — you have a graceful shutdown problem, and there is no point testing node failure until it is fixed. The usual cause is the endpoint-propagation race: no preStop sleep, so traffic is still routed to a pod that has already closed its listener. Fix that first.

Then cordon and drain a node. This tests the voluntary path: do PodDisruptionBudgets let the drain proceed, or do they block it forever? Does the scheduler find room elsewhere, or do pods sit Pending because the cluster has no headroom? Both outcomes are common and both are things you want to discover deliberately.

Then terminate a node abruptly, and this is the genuinely different test. On an abrupt loss the kubelet does not get to shut anything down cleanly. The node controller must notice the node has stopped heartbeating, mark it NotReady, and only after a toleration period (300 seconds by default) begin evicting its pods. So pods sit in Terminating and their endpoints remain in the routing tables — meaning a slice of your traffic is blackholed for that whole window. Measure that gap: it is your real failure-detection time, and it is usually far longer than people assume. Shortening the tolerationSeconds for not-ready and unreachable is the lever.

Then kill an AZ's worth of nodes and check whether topology spread actually spread you, whether the remaining zones have capacity (which is the n-1 sizing question made concrete), and how long the node autoscaler takes to replace them.

Record the observed RTO at each step and fix the largest gap. The output of a game day is not a pass; it is a ranked list of measured weaknesses. And the discipline that makes it worth repeating: write down the hypothesis before each step — we expect zero errors and full recovery within 90 seconds — so the experiment can actually fail, rather than being a demonstration.

Escalating experiments, with the number you are measuring
RULES: announced | business hours | a stop condition | a written hypothesis
       per step (so the experiment can FAIL, rather than be a demonstration)

STEP 1  single pod delete            hypothesis: ZERO client errors
  hey -z 120s -c 50 https://api.example.com/health &
  kubectl delete pod payments-api-7d9f
  -> ANY non-2xx = a GRACEFUL SHUTDOWN problem, not a resilience one.
     Usual cause: no preStop sleep -> endpoint propagation race.
     FIX THIS BEFORE going further. Node tests are meaningless until it passes.

STEP 2  cordon + drain a node        hypothesis: drain completes < 2 min, 0 errors
  kubectl cordon ip-10-20-16-33
  kubectl drain ip-10-20-16-33 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
  -> does the PDB let it proceed, or block FOREVER (maxUnavailable: 0)?
  -> do pods reschedule, or sit Pending for lack of headroom?

STEP 3  ABRUPT node termination      hypothesis: full recovery < 60s
  aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-xxxx     # no clean shutdown
  -> node controller must notice missed heartbeats -> NotReady
  -> pods stay Terminating for tolerationSeconds (DEFAULT 300s)
  -> ENDPOINTS REMAIN -> a slice of traffic is BLACKHOLED for that whole window
  MEASURE THAT GAP. It is your real failure-detection time, and it is almost
  always longer than people assume.
  Lever:
    tolerations:
      - { key: node.kubernetes.io/not-ready,   operator: Exists,
          effect: NoExecute, tolerationSeconds: 30 }
      - { key: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable, operator: Exists,
          effect: NoExecute, tolerationSeconds: 30 }

STEP 4  kill an AZ's worth of nodes  hypothesis: serve at reduced capacity, no errors
  -> did topology spread ACTUALLY spread you? (check before, not after)
  -> do the remaining zones have capacity? (n-1 sizing, made concrete)
  -> how long does the node autoscaler take to replace them?

OUTPUT: a ranked list of MEASURED gaps, not a pass.
  observed  single pod delete       0 errors        OK
            drain                   1m40s           OK
            abrupt node loss        4m10s blackhole <-- LARGEST GAP. Fix first.
            AZ loss                 recovered, 62% capacity  <-- size for n-1
Follow-ups they will ask

Why does abrupt node loss take so much longer than a drain?

Because a drain is cooperative — the API server knows immediately and removes endpoints as pods terminate gracefully. An abrupt loss must be inferred from missed heartbeats, which takes the node-monitor grace period, and then pods are evicted only after their not-ready toleration expires. Nothing knows the node is gone until the timers fire, so traffic keeps being routed there. Shortening the tolerations trades faster detection against more churn on transient network blips.

Is it safe to do this in production?

Safer than not doing it, provided you have a stop condition and start small. The failures you find in a controlled window during working hours are failures you would otherwise find at 3am with no preparation. Start in staging to shake out the obvious, then move to production — because staging never reproduces production's traffic, scale or timing, and the interesting failures only appear there.

What do you do if the game day causes a real incident?

Stop the experiment, run the incident, and treat it as a successful game day — you found a genuine failure under controlled conditions with the right people already watching. Then write it up like any incident. The only bad outcome is not having a stop condition, so define in advance the metric that aborts the exercise and make sure whoever is running it can abort without escalation.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

AWS Fault Injection Service runs controlled failure experiments against real infrastructure — terminating instances, stopping ECS tasks, injecting CPU or memory pressure, adding network latency or packet loss, throttling AWS API calls, and forcing RDS or Elasticache failover. It integrates with IAM so the blast radius is scoped by role, and with resource tags so you target exactly what you intend.

The feature that makes it chaos engineering rather than an outage is the stop condition: a CloudWatch alarm attached to the experiment template that aborts it automatically if real users are affected. Without that you are not running an experiment, you are causing an incident and hoping. Say that explicitly — it is the difference an interviewer is listening for.

What I would inject first, in order, and each with a hypothesis stated before running it.

One: kill one ECS task or pod and assert zero client errors. If that fails, you have a graceful shutdown or connection draining problem, and every subsequent experiment is meaningless until it is fixed. It is the cheapest test and the most commonly failed.

Two: force an RDS failover and measure how long the application takes to recover — not how long AWS takes. This is where most Java services fail badly: the JVM has cached the DNS resolution, HikariCP holds sockets to an instance that no longer exists, and the service is down for minutes after a 90-second failover. That gap between AWS recovered and we recovered is the single most valuable number this exercise produces.

Three: inject 200ms of latency into a downstream dependency and confirm your timeouts and circuit breakers fire before the caller's timeout. The failure you are looking for is a timeout budget that is not nested properly — your client waits 30 seconds while the caller gave up at 10, so you burn threads producing responses nobody will read.

Four: throttle an AWS API and see whether your retries have jitter and a cap, or whether they stampede. An unjittered retry storm turns a brief throttle into a sustained one.

And the discipline that makes it engineering: always start with a hypothesis you expect to hold. The purpose is to build evidence that the system behaves as designed; when it does not, you have found something real. An experiment where you already expect failure is not an experiment — fix the known problem first.

A stop condition is what separates this from an outage
{
  "description": "RDS failover - measure APPLICATION recovery, not AWS recovery",
  "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::1234:role/fis-experiment",
  "targets": {
    "db": { "resourceType": "aws:rds:cluster",
            "resourceTags": { "Environment": "prod", "ChaosEligible": "true" },
            "selectionMode": "ALL" }
  },
  "actions": {
    "failover": { "actionId": "aws:rds:failover-db-cluster",
                  "targets": { "Clusters": "db" } }
  },
  "stopConditions": [                          # <-- THE defining feature
    { "source": "aws:cloudwatch:alarm",
      "value": "arn:aws:cloudwatch:eu-west-1:1234:alarm:api-5xx-critical" }
  ]
}
# Without a stop condition you are not running an experiment.
# You are causing an incident and hoping.

ORDER, each with a hypothesis stated BEFORE running
1  kill one ECS task / pod          H: zero client errors
   -> fails? graceful shutdown / deregistration delay problem.
      Every later experiment is meaningless until this passes.

2  force RDS failover               H: recover within 120s of AWS promotion
   -> THE MOST VALUABLE NUMBER: the gap between "AWS recovered" and "we recovered"
   -> where most Java services fail badly:
        JVM cached the DNS resolution      -Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl=5
        HikariCP holds dead sockets        connection-timeout, max-lifetime,
                                           keepalive-time
        no failover-aware driver           jdbc:aws-wrapper:postgresql://...

3  inject 200ms downstream latency  H: circuit breaker opens before the caller
                                       times out
   -> looking for a badly NESTED timeout budget:
        caller waits 10s | you wait 30s  -> you burn threads producing responses
                                            nobody will read
   -> every timeout must be SHORTER than its caller's

4  throttle an AWS API              H: retries back off with jitter and a cap
   -> unjittered retries turn a brief throttle into a sustained one

# ALWAYS start with a hypothesis you EXPECT TO HOLD.
# The purpose is evidence that the system behaves as designed.
# An experiment you expect to fail is not an experiment - fix the known
# problem first.
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you get permission to run this in production?

By starting small, announcing it, and showing results. Run the single-task-kill experiment first — it is nearly risk-free with a stop condition and it either proves resilience or finds a real bug cheaply. Present the measured numbers to whoever is nervous; a concrete we recover from a task loss in 4 seconds with zero errors builds far more confidence than an argument. Escalate the experiments as trust accumulates.

What is the difference between FIS and just terminating things yourself?

Scoping, automation and the stop condition. FIS targets by tag with IAM-scoped blast radius, runs the actions in a controlled sequence, aborts automatically on an alarm, and produces an auditable record of what was injected and when. Doing it by hand works for a one-off, but it does not scale to a scheduled programme and it has no automatic abort — which is exactly the property that makes it safe to run regularly.

What should be a recurring experiment rather than a one-off?

Anything protecting a property that can regress silently: the single-task kill (graceful shutdown regresses whenever someone changes a deployment), the RDS failover (connection pool and driver settings drift), and the AZ evacuation. Run them monthly or quarterly on a schedule, in a non-peak window, and treat a newly failing experiment exactly like a failing test — because that is what it is.

The cost of durability

Everything in your AI pipeline is now duplicated - source, chunks, vectors, logs, evals. How do you keep storage and refresh costs sane?

Must coverStore the source once and treat everything else as derived and rebuildable, which means you can delete a derived store rather than back it up. Chunks do not need to be stored separately if you can re-derive them deterministically from a versioned source plus a chunker version - store the chunker version instead. Vectors dominate memory cost, so pick dimensions deliberately, use quantisation (scalar or product) where recall allows, and keep only the current index rather than every historical one. Logs are the sleeper: full prompt-and-response traces at volume are enormous, so sample successful requests, keep all failures, and set short retention with an export of the sampled set to cheap storage.

StudyAnthropic - token counting →

How do you run production workloads on spot instances without users noticing?

Must coverOnly stateless, interruptible workloads, and never the whole fleet - a base on on-demand or a Savings Plan, the burst on spot. Diversify across many instance types and AZs so a single capacity pool draining does not take you out; Karpenter does this well. Handle the two-minute interruption notice: a node termination handler cordons and drains on the warning, and your pods must shut down gracefully within that window, which brings you back to preStop hooks and drain timeouts. PodDisruptionBudgets keep the drain from taking too many replicas. And have capacity headroom, because the interruption and the replacement are not simultaneous. For batch, checkpoint so a lost node costs work, not the job.

Explain AWS Backup and how you would prove you can restore. What is the difference between a snapshot and a backup?

Must coverAWS Backup centralises policy - backup plans with schedules, lifecycle to cold storage, retention, and cross-region and cross-account copy - across RDS, EBS, DynamoDB, EFS and more, with Backup Vault Lock making them immutable so ransomware or a compromised admin cannot delete them. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy in the same account and often the same region - convenient, but it shares the blast radius of what it protects, which is why a backup must be in another account. Proving restore: a scheduled restore test into an isolated account, running an automated integrity check against the restored data, and recording the elapsed time as your measured RTO. Anything else is an assumption.

AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The organising principle: store the source once, and treat everything else as derived and rebuildable. That single decision changes what you must back up, what you must retain, and what you can simply delete when it becomes expensive — because a derived store you can regenerate does not need a backup, it needs a rebuild procedure.

Chunks. You often do not need to store them separately at all. If chunking is deterministic from a versioned source document plus a chunker version, you can re-derive them — so store the chunker version rather than the output. Where you do keep chunk text (for reranking, or for display), keep only the current version and rely on the source for history.

Vectors dominate memory cost, and that is where the real money is. Three levers, in order of value. Dimensions: pick deliberately rather than taking the model's maximum, and use Matryoshka truncation where the model supports it — keeping the first 512 of 1,536 dimensions often costs a point or two of recall for two-thirds less memory. Quantisation: scalar quantisation to int8 cuts memory by four with roughly a point of recall; product quantisation goes much further with a larger loss. Keep only the current index — not every historical build — with a documented rebuild procedure instead of an archive.

Measure the trade rather than assuming it: run recall@k on your labelled set at each configuration and pick the point where recall stops mattering for your generation quality.

Logs are the sleeper cost, and they are the item teams consistently underestimate. Full prompt-and-response traces at volume are enormous — a 6,000-token prompt is roughly 25KB, and at a million requests a day that is tens of gigabytes daily before you add tool calls and retrieval detail. The fix is tiering: keep everything for failures, refusals and flagged interactions; sample successes at a few percent; and keep a minimal permanent record (request id, user, timestamps, versions, token counts, outcome) for everything. Set short retention on the full traces and export the sampled set to cheap storage.

Eval sets are small and are the last thing to economise on — they are the most valuable data you have per byte.

And the framing that makes this a design conversation rather than a cleanup exercise: decide the retention and rebuild story for each derived store when you create it, not when the bill arrives. A store with no documented rebuild procedure becomes one you are afraid to delete, which is how the cost becomes permanent.

Source once; everything else derived, tiered, or rebuildable
STORE            KEEP?              STRATEGY
source documents  YES, authoritative  backed up, versioned, retention per policy
parsed text       usually NO          re-derive from source + parser version
chunks            current only        deterministic from (source@version,
                                      chunker@version) -> store the VERSION,
                                      not the output
VECTORS           current index only  the big one - see below
prompt/response   TIERED              see below
                  traces
eval sets         YES, all            tiny, and the most valuable data per byte
caches            ephemeral           TTL; never back up

# VECTORS - where the money is. Measure recall at each step; do not assume.
  40M chunks x 1,536 dims x 4 bytes (float32)   = 245 GB
  + Matryoshka truncate to 512 dims             =  82 GB   recall -1.5%
  + scalar quantise to int8                     =  20 GB   recall -1.0% more
  (+ HNSW graph links, roughly 10-15% on top)

  measure on YOUR labelled set:
     dims  quant   memory   recall@10
     1536  fp32     245 GB    0.962
      512  fp32      82 GB    0.947
      512  int8      20 GB    0.938   <-- often the right operating point
      256  int8      10 GB    0.901   <-- too lossy; generation notices

  keep ONE index, not every historical build. Document the REBUILD procedure
  instead of keeping an archive.

# LOGS - the sleeper cost
  6,000-token prompt  ~25 KB per request
  x 1M requests/day   ~25 GB/day  before tool calls and retrieval detail
  TIER IT:
    failures, refusals, flagged      100%    90 days
    successes                        2-5%    30 days, then export to S3 Glacier IR
    minimal record (id, user, ts,    100%    per compliance retention
      versions, tokens, outcome)             (tiny: ~200 bytes)

# THE DESIGN RULE
#   decide the RETENTION and the REBUILD PROCEDURE for each derived store
#   WHEN YOU CREATE IT, not when the bill arrives.
#   A store with no documented rebuild becomes one you are afraid to delete -
#   which is how the cost becomes permanent.
Follow-ups they will ask

Is quantisation safe for a production RAG system?

Scalar quantisation to int8 usually costs about a point of recall for a four-times memory reduction, which is an easy trade for most corpora — and many vector stores now do it transparently. Product quantisation is more aggressive and needs measurement, because the loss varies a lot by corpus and by how tightly clustered your embeddings are. Always validate against your labelled set and against end-to-end answer quality, not just against a recall number, since a small recall drop concentrated on your hardest queries matters more than the average suggests.

Should you keep chunk text if you can re-derive it?

Keep it if you display it, rerank on it, or need to show a user exactly what was retrieved. Re-deriving on every query means re-parsing the source, which is slow. The usual shape is: keep current chunk text in the index alongside the vector (it is small relative to the vector), and rely on versioned sources for anything historical. What you should not keep is every historical chunk version — that is what the source is for.

What is the biggest storage mistake teams make?

Full-fidelity prompt logging with no retention, driven by a reasonable instinct that you will want the detail. Six months later it is the largest line item in the feature's cost and nobody has queried anything older than two weeks. Tier it from day one — full traces for failures, sampled for successes, minimal record forever — and you keep all the investigative value at a fraction of the cost.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Only stateless, interruptible workloads, and never the whole fleet. The correct shape is a baseline on on-demand (or covered by a Savings Plan) with the burst on spot — so a capacity event degrades your headroom rather than your service.

Diversify aggressively. Spot capacity is per instance type per availability zone, so a single pool draining takes you out if that is all you asked for. Ask for many instance families and sizes across every zone. Karpenter does this well: give it a broad requirement set and it will choose from dozens of pools, and its capacity-type requirement lets one NodePool serve both spot and on-demand with a fallback.

Handle the two-minute notice. AWS sends a spot interruption warning roughly two minutes before reclaiming an instance, and there is also a rebalance recommendation that arrives earlier as a softer signal. A node termination handler — or Karpenter's native interruption handling via an SQS queue fed by EventBridge — cordons and drains the node on that signal. Two minutes is enough only if your pods actually shut down within it, which brings you straight back to preStop hooks, graceful shutdown and a terminationGracePeriodSeconds comfortably under 120 seconds. A workload with a 300-second grace period will simply be killed.

PodDisruptionBudgets keep the drain from taking too many replicas at once — and this is where a subtlety matters: a spot reclaim is an involuntary disruption from the cluster's point of view once the instance is gone, but the drain triggered by the warning is voluntary, so the PDB applies to it and can slow the drain past the two-minute window. Keep budgets permissive enough to drain quickly.

Have real capacity headroom, because the interruption and the replacement are not simultaneous — the node goes away in two minutes and a replacement takes one to three to become useful. Pause pods with a negative priority class give you instant capacity during that gap.

For batch, checkpoint. Then an interruption costs one work item rather than the whole run — which is what makes spot genuinely attractive for anything long-running.

The honest boundary: do not put stateful workloads, quorum members, or anything with long non-checkpointable work on spot. And be explicit that spot is a cost and availability decision, not just a cost one — you are trading a small amount of reliability for a large amount of money, and the trade is only sound if the handling above is genuinely in place.

Baseline on-demand, burst on spot, drain in under two minutes
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata: { name: spot-burst }
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      requirements:
        - { key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type, operator: In, values: ["spot"] }
        - { key: kubernetes.io/arch, operator: In, values: ["arm64"] }
        - { key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-family, operator: In,
            values: ["m7g","m6g","c7g","c6g","r7g"] }      # MANY pools
        - { key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-size, operator: In,
            values: ["large","xlarge","2xlarge"] }          # x sizes x zones
      taints:
        - { key: capacity, value: spot, effect: NoSchedule }  # opt-in only
  disruption: { consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized }
---
# Baseline stays on-demand. A capacity event degrades HEADROOM, not the service.
kind: NodePool
metadata: { name: baseline-ondemand }
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      requirements:
        - { key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type, operator: In, values: ["on-demand"] }
  limits: { cpu: "200" }
---
# Workload: tolerate spot, and BE ABLE TO LEAVE IN UNDER 2 MINUTES
spec:
  tolerations:
    - { key: capacity, operator: Equal, value: spot, effect: NoSchedule }
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60        # MUST be well under 120
  containers:
    - name: worker
      lifecycle:
        preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh","-c","sleep 5"] } }
# a 300s grace period means the pod is simply KILLED at the 2-minute mark.

# INTERRUPTION HANDLING - Karpenter consumes these via SQS/EventBridge
#   EC2 Spot Interruption Warning      ~2 min notice   -> cordon + drain
#   EC2 Instance Rebalance Recommendation  earlier     -> proactive replacement
#   AWS Health / scheduled maintenance

# PDB SUBTLETY
#   the reclaim itself is INVOLUNTARY, but the drain triggered by the warning
#   is VOLUNTARY -> the PDB applies and can slow it past the 2-minute window.
#   Keep budgets permissive enough to drain fast: maxUnavailable: 1 on a
#   10-replica service is fine; maxUnavailable: 1 on a 2-replica service is not.

# HEADROOM: the node leaves in 2 min; a replacement takes 1-3 min to be useful.
#   -> pause pods with a negative PriorityClass fill that gap instantly.

# BATCH: checkpoint, so an interruption costs ONE ITEM, not the run.

# DO NOT PUT ON SPOT
#   stateful workloads | quorum members | long non-checkpointable work
#   Spot is a COST AND AVAILABILITY decision, not just a cost one.
Follow-ups they will ask

What percentage of the fleet can safely be spot?

There is no universal number — derive it from what you can lose. If the on-demand baseline alone can serve your p50 traffic, then spot can carry the rest and a mass reclaim degrades to slower responses rather than an outage. A common shape is a baseline sized for typical load with 60–80% of peak burst on spot. For batch and CI, 100% spot is entirely reasonable with checkpointing.

How do you know spot is actually saving money?

Attribute it: tag spot and on-demand capacity separately and compare the effective hourly rate against what the same workload would cost on-demand. The saving is real and large, but it is offset by the headroom you must carry and by any engineering time spent handling interruptions — so a small cluster where spot handling is a week of work may not repay it. At scale it repays comfortably.

What happens if spot capacity is unavailable when you need to scale?

You do not get nodes, and pods sit Pending. That is why the fallback matters: configure a NodePool ordering or a Karpenter requirement that allows on-demand when spot cannot be fulfilled, so scale-up degrades to a more expensive node rather than to no node. A spot-only configuration with no fallback turns a capacity event into a scaling failure at exactly the moment you need to scale.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Start with the distinction, because it is the part people conflate. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy, typically in the same account and often the same region. It is convenient and fast to restore from — and it shares the blast radius of the thing it protects. An attacker or a mistaken administrator with permissions in that account can delete the resource and its snapshots in the same breath. A backup is a copy held under separate control: a different account, ideally a different region, with independent permissions and immutability.

AWS Backup centralises the policy layer. You define a backup plan — schedule, lifecycle to cold storage, retention — and assign resources to it by tag, across RDS, EBS, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, S3 and more. That tag-based assignment is what makes it scale: a new resource tagged Backup=daily is covered automatically rather than by someone remembering.

It also does cross-region and cross-account copy as part of the plan, which is how you get the separation above without writing orchestration. And Backup Vault Lock makes the recovery points immutable for a defined period — in compliance mode, nobody can delete them early, including the account root and AWS itself. That is the specific control against ransomware and against a compromised administrator, and it is the thing worth naming because it is what turns a backup from a copy into a guarantee.

Now proving restore, which is the substance of the question. A backup you have never restored has an unknown success rate and an unknown recovery time — so you do not have a backup, you have a hypothesis.

The proof is a scheduled, automated restore test into an isolated account: restore the most recent recovery point, run an automated integrity check against the restored data (row counts, checksums, a canary query returning a known value, and for a database, that the application can actually connect and read), record the elapsed time, and tear it down. AWS Backup has restore testing plans that automate exactly this and produce an auditable record.

The elapsed time you record is your measured RTO — not an estimate, a measurement. And run it often enough that it reflects current data volume, because restore time grows with the data and last year's number is optimistic.

One more thing worth adding: test the restore of the thing you would actually need. Restoring a database is common practice; restoring the IAM roles, KMS keys, parameter store values and networking that the database needs in order to be usable is what people discover is missing during the real event.

Immutable, cross-account, and restore-tested on a schedule
SNAPSHOT vs BACKUP
  snapshot  same account, often same region. Fast. SHARES THE BLAST RADIUS -
            an attacker or a mistaken admin deletes the resource AND its
            snapshots in the same breath.
  backup    separate control: different ACCOUNT, ideally different region,
            independent permissions, IMMUTABLE.

# Plan: tag-based assignment is what makes it scale
BackupPlan:
  Rules:
    - RuleName: daily
      TargetBackupVault: prod-vault
      ScheduleExpression: "cron(0 2 * * ? *)"
      Lifecycle: { MoveToColdStorageAfterDays: 30, DeleteAfterDays: 365 }
      CopyActions:
        - DestinationBackupVaultArn: arn:aws:backup:eu-west-2:5555:backup-vault:dr-vault
          Lifecycle: { DeleteAfterDays: 365 }     # CROSS-REGION and CROSS-ACCOUNT
BackupSelection:
  ListOfTags:
    - { ConditionType: STRINGEQUALS, ConditionKey: Backup, ConditionValue: daily }
# a NEW resource tagged Backup=daily is covered automatically - not by someone
# remembering

# VAULT LOCK - the control that makes it a guarantee, not a copy
aws backup put-backup-vault-lock-configuration \
  --backup-vault-name prod-vault \
  --min-retention-days 30 --max-retention-days 365 \
  --changeable-for-days 3                    # after 3 days: IRREVERSIBLE
# COMPLIANCE mode: nobody can delete early. Not an admin. Not root. Not AWS.
# This is the specific control against ransomware and a compromised admin.

# ---- PROVING RESTORE ----
# A backup never restored has an UNKNOWN success rate and an UNKNOWN RTO.
# You do not have a backup; you have a hypothesis.

RestoreTestingPlan:
  ScheduleExpression: "cron(0 4 ? * SUN *)"       # weekly
  RecoveryPointSelection: { Algorithm: LATEST_WITHIN_WINDOW, ... }
  # restores into an ISOLATED account, runs validation, records duration, tears down

# The validation must be REAL:
  row counts match the source within the replication window
  checksum of a sampled key range
  a canary query returning a KNOWN value
  the application can CONNECT and read (not just: the instance exists)

# RECORD THE ELAPSED TIME. That is your MEASURED RTO, not an estimate.
# Re-run often enough that it reflects CURRENT data volume - restore time grows
# with the data, and last year's number is optimistic.

# AND TEST THE THING YOU WOULD ACTUALLY NEED
#   restoring the database is common practice.
#   restoring the IAM roles, KMS keys, parameter values and networking it needs
#   to be USABLE is what people find missing during the real event.
Follow-ups they will ask

Does Vault Lock stop you fixing a mistake?

In compliance mode, yes, and that is deliberate — you cannot shorten retention or delete recovery points until the retention expires, which also means an over-long retention becomes an over-long cost. Governance mode allows a specifically privileged role to override, which is a reasonable middle ground for most organisations. Use compliance mode where a regulator requires demonstrable immutability, and note the three-day grace period before the lock becomes irreversible.

How do you restore data encrypted with a KMS key?

The restoring account must have access to the key, which for cross-account restores means either a multi-region key with a policy granting the DR account, or re-encrypting the copy with a key in the destination. This is the single most common cross-account restore failure and it cannot be fixed during an incident — the key policy has to be right before the copy is made. Test it as part of the restore drill specifically.

What is the difference between this and point-in-time recovery?

PITR (available for RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB) lets you restore to any second within a retention window, which is what you want for oops, we deleted the wrong rows twenty minutes ago. Scheduled backups give you discrete recovery points with long retention and cross-account immutability, which is what you want for ransomware, account compromise and compliance. They address different failures — use both, and know which one each scenario calls for.

Week 8 synthesis: durable systems

Design the data architecture for an AI feature over payment transactions, where records are immutable, retention is seven years, and every answer must be auditable.

Must coverSource of truth is the transaction store, append-only, with the AI system holding no authoritative copy. Retrieval works over a derived index built from a versioned view of that data, with the version recorded on every answer. Numbers in answers must come from tool calls that query the real store, never from generated text, so every figure is traceable to a row id - that is what makes it auditable. Retention: source under the seven-year policy, derived index rebuildable and therefore short-lived, and prompt-and-response audit records under the same seven-year policy with field-level redaction. Deletion requests propagate to source, index and logs, with a documented job proving it.

Your cluster is gone - region-wide EKS failure. Walk me through recovery and say honestly how long it takes.

Must coverPrerequisites decide the answer: the cluster itself is infrastructure as code, all workloads are in git and reconciled by ArgoCD, images are in a replicated registry, secrets are in Secrets Manager replicated cross-region, and persistent data is either in a managed service with cross-region replication or covered by Velero backups in an S3 bucket replicated cross-region. Recovery: apply the cluster IaC in the second region (10-20 minutes), point ArgoCD at the same repo and let it reconcile (minutes), restore volumes if any, then shift DNS. Honest RTO: 30-60 minutes if it has been rehearsed, and unbounded if it has not. If that is too slow, the answer is a warm cluster already running, not a faster restore.

StudyEKS - disaster recovery →

Compare event sourcing, CDC and the outbox pattern. When would you actually use event sourcing in a payments system?

Must coverOutbox solves one problem: atomically recording that an event should be published alongside the state change. CDC derives events from the transaction log without touching application code - great for integration, but the events are row changes, not business intent. Event sourcing makes the event log the source of truth and current state a projection - which gives you a complete, replayable audit history and temporal queries for free. Use it where the history is the product: a ledger, an account balance, a dispute trail. Do not use it broadly, because you inherit schema evolution of events forever, projection rebuild cost, and a much harder query story. In payments, event-source the ledger and use plain CRUD plus outbox everywhere else.
