AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Lead with the invariant, because it determines everything: the AI system holds no authoritative copy of anything. The transaction store is the source of truth, it is append-only, and the AI layer is strictly derived. That framing is what makes the seven-year retention and the auditability requirements tractable.

Retrieval works over a derived index built from a versioned view of the transaction data and the surrounding policy documents, with the index version recorded on every answer. Because it is derived, it needs no seven-year retention of its own and no backup — it needs a documented rebuild procedure. That is a large simplification and it is worth stating explicitly.

Numbers come from tool calls, never from generated text. This is the load-bearing design decision. The model translates a question into a typed query, your code executes it against the ledger, and the model narrates rows it was given. Every figure a user sees is traceable to a row id, which is precisely what makes the answer auditable. A system where the model produces a total is not auditable, no matter how good the model is — say that plainly, because in a payments context it is the point.

Immutability is schema and permissions, not a database choice. The ledger table grants INSERT only to the application role; corrections are reversing entries, never mutations. So what was true in March 2023 is answerable by construction.

Retention, in three tiers. The source under the seven-year policy, with lifecycle tiering to Glacier for cold years and an immutable cross-account backup. The derived index short-lived and rebuildable. And the audit record of every AI interaction — request id, user, prompt, retrieved ids and versions, tool calls, output, model and prompt versions — under the same seven-year policy, because it concerns the same regulated data. That audit record inherits the classification, so it is encrypted with a customer-managed key, tightly access-controlled, and structured with a subject identifier.

Deletion then has a defined path: source, index, caches and audit logs, with field-level redaction on the audit record so the auditable skeleton survives while personal content goes. And note the genuine tension — a seven-year retention obligation and a deletion right conflict, and the resolution is usually that the regulatory retention wins for the transaction record while derived and log copies are redacted. That is a legal determination, not an engineering one, and the right move is to build the mechanism and let compliance set the policy.

Finally: because records are immutable and history is the product, this is one of the few genuine cases for event sourcing the ledger — the log is the audit trail.

Source authoritative, index derived, figures from rows
INVARIANT: the AI system holds NO authoritative copy.

  [ transaction ledger ]  append-only, 7-year retention, source of truth
     |                    REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE FROM app_role;
     |                    corrections = reversing entries, never mutations
     |
     +--> [ derived index ]   policy docs + transaction metadata
     |      DERIVED: no backup, no 7-year retention.
     |      Needs a documented REBUILD PROCEDURE instead.        <-- big saving
     |      version recorded on every answer
     |
     +--> [ tool: query_ledger ]   <-- EVERY FIGURE COMES FROM HERE
              typed query, executed by YOUR code, scoped to the caller

// The load-bearing decision
var rows  = ledger.query(validated(parsedQuery), caller.accountIds());
var total = rows.stream().map(Txn::amountMinor).reduce(0L, Long::sum);  // in Java
var text  = model.narrate(factSheet(rows, total));   // narrates; never computes
// -> every figure a user sees is traceable to a ROW ID.
//    A system where the MODEL produces a total is not auditable, however
//    good the model is.

// AUDIT RECORD - 7 years, because it concerns the same regulated data
{ "requestId": "...", "userId": "...", "timestamp": "...",
  "question": "<tokenised>",
  "toolCalls": [ { "name": "query_ledger",
                   "rowIds": ["txn_9f2c","txn_a13d"],      // TRACEABILITY
                   "resultHash": "sha256:..." } ],
  "retrieved": [ { "docId": "fees-guide", "version": 12 } ],
  "artefactVersion": "settlement-assistant@v14",
  "output": "...", "classification": "RESTRICTED" }
// encrypted with a CMK | tight IAM | structured with a SUBJECT IDENTIFIER
// so a deletion request can reach it

RETENTION
  source ledger    7 years, S3/Aurora + lifecycle to Glacier + immutable
                   cross-account backup (Vault Lock)
  derived index    current only, rebuildable
  audit record     7 years, same classification as the source
  full AI traces   90 days (debugging), then only the minimal record

DELETION - and the honest tension
  a 7-year RETENTION obligation and a deletion RIGHT conflict.
  Usual resolution: regulatory retention wins for the TRANSACTION RECORD;
  derived copies and log content are redacted.
  -> that is a LEGAL determination. Build the mechanism; let compliance set
     the policy.

// Because records are immutable and history IS the product, this is one of the
// few genuine cases for EVENT SOURCING the ledger: the log IS the audit trail.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not let the model read the ledger directly through retrieval?

Because retrieved text is not authoritative and cannot be reconciled. A chunk containing a transaction is a snapshot of what the indexer saw, possibly stale, possibly truncated, and the model may misread or blend figures from adjacent rows. A typed query returns current, complete, scoped rows with ids. In a payments context the difference is between an answer you can defend to an auditor and one you cannot.

How do you handle questions about data older than the index?

Make the time range an explicit parameter the model extracts, and route historical queries to the ledger directly rather than to retrieval — the ledger holds seven years, the index need not. If the question requires policy context from that period too, retrieve by effective date so you return the policy version in force then, not the current one. Blending a 2019 transaction with a 2026 fee schedule is a very plausible and very wrong answer.

What does the auditor actually ask for?

Usually three things: show me how this specific answer was produced; show me that a user could not see data they were not entitled to; and show me that the control was in place continuously rather than today. The first is the audit record with row ids and versions. The second is the ACL filter applied inside the query, plus a test proving it. The third is AWS Config history on the encryption, access and retention settings — which is why those three questions should shape the design rather than be answered after it.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The answer depends entirely on what was in place beforehand, so state the prerequisites first — because they are the recovery plan.

Prerequisites. The cluster itself is infrastructure as code, parameterised by region. All workloads are in git and reconciled by Argo CD, so the repository is the authoritative desired state. Images are in a cross-region replicated registry. Secrets are in Secrets Manager with cross-region replication, reached by IRSA. Persistent data is either in a managed service with cross-region replication, or covered by Velero backups in a cross-region replicated S3 bucket. And DNS is managed so it can be repointed.

Recovery sequence. Apply the cluster IaC in the second region — 10 to 20 minutes for an EKS control plane plus node groups. Install the bootstrap add-ons (they are in the IaC). Point Argo CD at the same repository with the new cluster as its destination, and let it reconcile — minutes, and it brings up everything in dependency order via sync waves. Restore volumes with Velero if any workload is stateful. Then shift DNS.

The honest RTO: 30 to 60 minutes if it has been rehearsed, and unbounded if it has not. That second clause is the important half of the answer. An unrehearsed rebuild always finds something — an IAM role that only exists in the primary region, a KMS key that is not multi-region so nothing can be decrypted, a Terraform module with a hardcoded subnet id, a secret that was created by hand and never replicated, a webhook certificate that must be regenerated.

And if that is too slow, the answer is not a faster restore — it is a warm cluster already running. That is the honest trade to put in front of whoever sets the RTO: a rebuild is cheap and slow; a standing second cluster is expensive and fast. There is no engineering that makes a cold rebuild take two minutes.

Two refinements worth adding. Static stability: the recovery must not depend on anything in the failed region, including your CI system, your artefact registry's primary, or the Argo CD instance itself if it ran in that cluster — a Argo CD that lived only in the dead cluster is a recovery plan that died with it. And the data is the real constraint: stateless workloads recover in minutes, but a database restore from backup is measured in the size of the data, which is why managed cross-region replication rather than backup-and-restore is what actually determines your RTO for anything stateful.

The prerequisites are the plan; the rehearsal is the proof
PREREQUISITES - these ARE the recovery plan
  cluster        Terraform/CDK, parameterised by region
  workloads      git + Argo CD (the repo is the authoritative desired state)
  images         ECR cross-region replication
  secrets        Secrets Manager cross-region replication, reached by IRSA
  KMS            MULTI-REGION KEYS  <-- without these, nothing decrypts. Not
                                        fixable during the incident.
  data           managed service with cross-region replication, OR Velero
                 backups in a cross-region replicated bucket
  DNS            managed, repointable
  ARGO CD        runs OUTSIDE the workload cluster, or is bootstrapped from IaC
                 <-- an Argo CD that lived only in the dead cluster is a
                     recovery plan that died with it

SEQUENCE
  1. terraform apply -var region=eu-west-2          ~10-20 min (EKS + node groups)
  2. bootstrap add-ons (in the IaC: CNI, CoreDNS, CSI, ingress, cert-manager)
  3. Argo CD -> same repo, new cluster destination   ~5-10 min
        sync waves bring things up in dependency order
  4. Velero restore for stateful volumes             (size-dependent)
  5. shift DNS / Global Accelerator endpoint

HONEST RTO
  30-60 minutes IF REHEARSED
  UNBOUNDED if not.

WHAT AN UNREHEARSED REBUILD ALWAYS FINDS
  an IAM role that only exists in the primary region
  a single-region KMS key -> nothing decrypts
  a Terraform module with a hardcoded subnet or AZ id
  a secret created by hand, never replicated
  an admission webhook certificate that must be regenerated
  a container image tag that only exists in the primary registry

IF 30-60 MINUTES IS TOO SLOW
  the answer is NOT a faster restore. It is a WARM CLUSTER ALREADY RUNNING.
  There is no engineering that makes a cold rebuild take two minutes.
  Put the trade in front of whoever sets the RTO:
     cold rebuild   cheap, 30-60 min, rehearsed quarterly
     warm standby   ~2x cost, minutes, continuously exercised

THE REAL CONSTRAINT IS DATA
  stateless workloads recover in minutes.
  a database restore is measured in the SIZE OF THE DATA.
  -> for anything stateful, managed cross-region REPLICATION (not backup-and-
     restore) is what actually determines your RTO.
Follow-ups they will ask

Where should Argo CD run?

Not inside the only cluster it manages. Either a dedicated management cluster in a separate region, or an instance that is itself bootstrapped from IaC in minutes. The app-of-apps pattern makes this cheap: the new Argo CD reads the same repository and reconciles everything. A control plane that shares the failure domain of what it controls is a recurring architectural mistake, and it is exactly the one that turns a 30-minute recovery into an improvised one.

How often should you rehearse a full cluster rebuild?

Quarterly is a reasonable cadence, and it does not need to be a disaster simulation — building a fresh cluster from IaC into a test account and letting Argo reconcile is the same exercise with none of the risk. Do it after any significant change to the IaC or the add-on set, since that is when regressions appear. Record the elapsed time each run; a rising number is telling you the plan is drifting.

What is the single most common blocker?

Something created by hand that nobody remembers. A secret, an IAM trust policy, a DNS record, a KMS grant, a webhook certificate — created once during initial setup, never captured in code, and invisible until the rebuild. The way to find them is the rehearsal, and the way to stop them accumulating is to make console changes in production impossible rather than merely discouraged.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Three patterns that get conflated, and the distinction is what the event actually is.

The outbox solves exactly one problem: atomically recording the intent to publish alongside a state change, so a crash cannot produce a lost or phantom event. The events are yours to design — proper business events with a versioned contract. It does not change how you store state; you still have ordinary tables.

Change data capture derives events from the database's transaction log without touching application code. Cheap to adopt and it has no dual-write problem, but the events are row changes, not business intent — status went PENDING to SETTLED rather than PaymentSettled. That couples consumers to your internal schema, so a column rename becomes a breaking change for every downstream team.

Event sourcing is categorically different: the event log becomes the source of truth and current state is a projection derived by replaying it. You do not store a balance; you store every credit and debit and fold them. That gives you a complete, replayable audit history for free, temporal queries (what was this balance on 3 March), and the ability to build a new read model retroactively over historical data.

When to actually use it: where the history is the product. A ledger, an account balance, a dispute trail, an audit-heavy regulatory record. In those cases you were going to build an append-only history anyway, and event sourcing is the honest way to do it rather than bolting an audit table onto mutable state.

When not to, which matters more because event sourcing is over-recommended. You inherit event schema evolution forever — every event ever written must remain readable by every future version of the code, so upcasting old event versions becomes permanent work. Projection rebuild cost grows with history, so snapshots become necessary. Querying is much harder: there is no ad-hoc SQL over current state unless you maintain a projection for it, and every new question may need a new projection. And it is genuinely hard to onboard people onto.

So in a payments system: event-source the ledger, and use plain CRUD plus an outbox everywhere else. Merchant profiles, configuration, dispute workflow state — these are ordinary entities where current state is what matters and history is a nice-to-have. Applying event sourcing uniformly is the mistake; applying it to the one aggregate whose history genuinely is the business is the right call.

Three patterns, and the one bounded context that earns event sourcing
OUTBOX          fixes the DUAL-WRITE problem. You design the events.
                state stored normally. Cheapest correct option.
CDC             derives events from the transaction log. No app changes.
                Events are ROW CHANGES -> couples consumers to your SCHEMA.
EVENT SOURCING  the LOG IS the source of truth. State is a PROJECTION.

// Ordinary CRUD + outbox - merchant profile
UPDATE merchant SET contact_email = ? WHERE id = ?;      -- current state
INSERT INTO outbox (...) VALUES ('MerchantUpdated', ...); -- same transaction

// EVENT SOURCED - the ledger. You do not store a balance.
events for account ACC-123:
  { seq: 1, type: AccountOpened,     at: 2024-01-04, currency: GBP }
  { seq: 2, type: FundsCredited,     at: 2024-03-01, amountMinor: 250000 }
  { seq: 3, type: FeeCharged,        at: 2024-03-01, amountMinor: -1250 }
  { seq: 4, type: SettlementPaidOut, at: 2024-03-02, amountMinor: -200000 }

balance(t) = fold(events where at <= t)     // temporal query, FREE
audit trail = the event log itself           // not a separate table
new read model = replay history into it      // retroactively

// snapshots, because replay cost grows with history
  { accountId: ACC-123, upToSeq: 48210, balanceMinor: 48750 }
  -> load snapshot + replay events after it

WHAT YOU INHERIT, FOREVER
  event schema evolution: EVERY event ever written must stay readable by
    every future version -> upcasting v1 -> v2 -> v3 is permanent work
  projection rebuild cost grows with history -> snapshots are mandatory
  no ad-hoc SQL over current state unless a projection exists for it
    -> every new question may need a new projection
  genuinely hard to onboard people onto

# IN A PAYMENTS SYSTEM
  EVENT-SOURCE:  the ledger. History IS the product. You were going to build
                 an append-only audit trail anyway - this is the honest way.
  CRUD + OUTBOX: merchant profiles, configuration, dispute workflow state,
                 notification preferences. Current state is what matters.

# The mistake is applying event sourcing UNIFORMLY.
# The right call is applying it to the ONE aggregate whose history is the
# business.
Follow-ups they will ask

Can you get most of the benefit without full event sourcing?

Often, yes — an append-only audit table written in the same transaction as the state change gives you history and traceability without the projection and schema-evolution burden. What you do not get is the guarantee that state and history cannot diverge, since they are separate writes. For a ledger that guarantee is the point; for a dispute workflow, an audit table is proportionate and much cheaper.

How do you handle a bug that wrote incorrect events?

You do not edit the log — that destroys the property you adopted it for. You write compensating events that correct the effect, exactly as a ledger writes reversing entries, and you rebuild the projections. If the events are genuinely malformed rather than merely wrong, you version the event type and upcast the bad ones on read. Both approaches preserve the immutable history, which is what an auditor will ask about.

What is CQRS and does event sourcing require it?

CQRS separates the write model from the read model — different shapes optimised for their purpose. Event sourcing almost forces it, because the write side is a log and the read side must be a projection. But CQRS does not require event sourcing: you can have a normalised write database and denormalised read replicas without any event log. Conflating the two is common, and being able to separate them is a good signal.

Week 09

Design Rounds

Six full-length design questions per lane, run at interview pace, including a migration, a hard tradeoff and an incident review.

Stop optimising for knowing more. From here the marginal point comes from structure, from stating tradeoffs out loud, and from finishing in time.

490/3

Design round: the assistant

Design an AI assistant that answers merchant questions about their settlements, disputes and fees. 5,000 merchants, 40 questions a day each. 45 minutes.

Must coverStructure the whole round: requirements and non-goals, the two or three numbers that constrain the design, high-level components, then depth on the one or two pieces the interviewer pulls on, then failure and cost. Key design calls here - this is not RAG over documents, it is natural language over structured data, so the model translates to a typed query against the settlement store and narrates results; RAG handles only the policy and how-it-works questions. Numbers: 200k questions a day, roughly 2-3 QPS average with a business-hours peak of maybe 10. Per-merchant authorisation enforced in the query layer. Cost per question modelled explicitly.

StudyAnthropic - tool use →

Design the Kubernetes platform that hosts that assistant plus twenty other services for a 60-engineer organisation. What does a team get on day one?

Must coverFrame it as a product with users. Day one a team gets: a repo template with a Dockerfile, a Helm or Kustomize base, and a CI pipeline; a namespace with quota, RBAC and default NetworkPolicy; automatic ingress with TLS and a DNS name; dashboards, alerts and log routing without writing config; and secrets wired from Secrets Manager via IRSA. The platform enforces through admission (image provenance, resource requests, security context) rather than through documentation. Deployment is GitOps only. The measure of the platform is time from empty repo to production URL, and how much of the above a team can get wrong.

StudyEKS best practices →

Design the AWS architecture for a payment gateway handling 3,000 transactions per second at peak, with regulatory data residency in two countries.

Must coverResidency first, because it partitions everything: separate regional stacks with no cross-border data flow, routed by geolocation, with a shared control plane holding no regulated data. Per region: ALB into ECS or EKS across three AZs, Aurora with Multi-AZ and read replicas, DynamoDB for idempotency keys and hot lookups, SQS and EventBridge for async, ElastiCache for the fraud-check cache. 3,000 TPS with a 200-byte record is trivial bandwidth but real database write load - so partition, keep the synchronous path to the minimum (authorise, persist, respond) and push settlement, notification and reporting to the async path. Idempotency keys on every write. State the p99 latency budget and allocate it hop by hop.

AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Narrate the structure before you draw anything — I'll spend five minutes on requirements and scale, ten on the high level, then go deep wherever you want, and leave ten for failure and cost. That single sentence is worth points on its own, because it shows you have run these rounds rather than only attended them.

Requirements (5 min). Who asks — merchant staff, not consumers. What they ask — why is this settlement short, when will I be paid, what was this fee. Non-goals, stated explicitly: it does not move money, it does not raise disputes, it advises. Then the constraint that shapes everything: answers contain money, so every figure must be traceable to a row.

Numbers (2 min). 5,000 merchants × 40 questions a day = 200,000 questions a day, about 2.3 per second average, with a business-hours peak of perhaps 10–15 per second concentrated in a few morning hours. That is modest QPS — so the design problems are correctness, cost per question and permissions, not throughput. Say that conclusion out loud; deriving the numbers and then not using them is a common miss.

The key architectural call (this is what the round is really testing). This is not RAG over documents for the majority of questions. Settlement data is structured and authoritative, so the model's job is translation: parse the question into a typed, validated query, execute it against the settlement store with the merchant's scope injected server-side, compute totals in code, and have the model narrate rows it was given. RAG handles only the second class of question — policy, fee schedules, how does this work — where the answer genuinely lives in prose and should be cited.

So there is a router at the front: data question, policy question, or both. That routing decision is cheap (a small model or a classifier) and it determines which pipeline runs.

Then go deep wherever they push — usually per-merchant authorisation, or the grounding guarantee. Have both ready: scope injected in your code and never taken from model output; ACL filters inside the retrieval query for the policy path; and a validation step asserting that every figure in the output appears in the returned rows.

Close with failure, cost and evaluation. Fallback to the ordinary filter UI when parsing confidence is low. Cost modelled per question with caching and small-model routing. Two eval suites — exact-match on parsed queries, groundedness on narration — plus a permissions suite. And name what you would build second, not first: multi-turn conversation, proactive alerts.

45 minutes, allocated out loud
0-5    REQUIREMENTS
  users     merchant staff (not consumers)
  questions "why is this settlement short?" | "when will I be paid?"
            "what was this fee?" | "how do chargebacks affect payouts?"
  NON-GOALS it does not move money, does not raise disputes. It ADVISES.
  CONSTRAINT answers contain MONEY -> every figure traceable to a row

5-7    NUMBERS
  5,000 merchants x 40/day = 200,000 questions/day
  = 2.3 QPS average; business-hours peak ~10-15 QPS
  -> modest throughput. The problems are CORRECTNESS, COST/QUESTION,
     and PERMISSIONS. Say this conclusion out loud.

7-17   HIGH LEVEL - and the key call
  router (small model / classifier)
    |
    +-- DATA question (majority)   <-- NOT RAG. Structured + authoritative.
    |     parse -> TypedQuery {dateRange, settlementId, feeType, status}
    |     validate + inject merchantId server-side  <-- never from the model
    |     execute against settlement store
    |     totals computed IN CODE
    |     model NARRATES the returned rows; renders the table alongside
    |
    +-- POLICY question            <-- RAG. Answer lives in prose, cite it.
          hybrid retrieval over fee schedules + merchant guide
          effective-date filter (the version in force THEN)
          + citations the merchant can click

17-32  DEEP DIVE (wherever they push - have both ready)
  authorisation  merchantId injected in code; ACL filter INSIDE the retrieval
                 query; re-checked at render
  grounding      assert every figure in the output appears in the returned rows
                 (deterministic, not a judge)

32-42  FAILURE / COST / EVAL
  fallback       low parse confidence -> render the ordinary filter UI,
                 pre-populated with what was understood
  cost           ~5,500 in + 350 out per question; prompt caching on the
                 system prompt; small model for routing and parsing;
                 exact-match cache (merchants ask the same things)
  eval           suite 1: question -> TypedQuery, EXACT MATCH per field
                 suite 2: narration groundedness (figures match rows)
                 suite 3: permissions - merchant A cannot elicit merchant B

42-45  WHAT I WOULD BUILD SECOND, NOT FIRST
  multi-turn conversation | proactive "your settlement is short" alerts
  | bulk export | non-English

# Say the tradeoffs OUT LOUD and WRITE THE NUMBERS DOWN.
# A silent design round scores badly regardless of the design.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not just do RAG over everything, including the transaction data?

Because retrieved text is a stale, truncated snapshot and the model may blend figures from adjacent rows. A typed query returns current, complete, scoped rows with ids. In a payments context that is the difference between an answer you can defend and one you cannot — and it is the single most important call in this design, so I would lead with it rather than let the interviewer surface it.

How do you handle a question that spans both pipelines?

Run both and compose. Why is my settlement short and what is the policy on holdbacks? needs the rows and the policy section. The router returns a set of intents rather than one, the orchestrator executes each pipeline, and the narration step receives both the fact sheet and the retrieved policy with a clear instruction about which is authoritative for figures. Keep the composition in code, not in an agent loop.

What would make you say no to building this?

If the settlement data model could not express the questions merchants actually ask — if why is this short requires reasoning across systems nobody has joined, then the AI feature is papering over a data problem and will produce confident, unverifiable answers. I would want to see that a competent analyst can answer these questions from the available data before automating the explanation of them.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Frame it as a product with users — the users are the sixty engineers, and the measure of success is how quickly and how safely they get from an empty repository to a production URL. That framing is what separates a platform answer from an infrastructure answer.

What a team gets on day one. A repository template with a Dockerfile that already follows the rules (multi-stage, non-root, digest-pinned base), a Kustomize base with sensible defaults, and a CI pipeline that builds, tests, scans and pushes by digest. A namespace provisioned with a ResourceQuota, RBAC bound to their identity-provider group, and a default-deny NetworkPolicy. Automatic ingress with TLS from cert-manager and a DNS name derived from the service name. Observability without configuration — a ServiceMonitor, log routing, the OpenTelemetry agent injected by annotation, and a templated dashboard that appears because the service exists. Secrets wired from Secrets Manager via a ServiceAccount with IRSA, so no credential is ever in the repository.

Deployment is GitOps only. Merge to main, CI writes the new digest to the manifests repository, Argo reconciles. No human has cluster write access in production, which makes who deployed what a git question.

The platform enforces through admission, not documentation. This is the design principle to state explicitly: policies that reject images not from your registry or not digest-pinned, pods without resource requests, pods without a securityContext, and workloads without a team label. A rule in a wiki is advisory; a rule in Kyverno is a rule. Run new policies in audit mode first, then enforce.

The measure of the platform is two numbers, and offering them unprompted is the strongest part of this answer: time from empty repository to production URL — target under a day — and how much a team can get wrong, which should be very little, because the defaults are correct and the dangerous options are rejected at admission.

Add the honest constraint: a platform for sixty engineers needs owners. Two to four people, treating it as a product with a roadmap and support, or it becomes a set of half-maintained templates that teams route around. And say what you would deliberately not build first: a custom internal developer portal, a service mesh, multi-cluster federation — none of which pay for themselves at sixty engineers.

A platform is a product; its metric is time-to-URL
DAY ONE, a team gets:
  repo template        Dockerfile (multi-stage, non-root, digest-pinned)
                       Kustomize base + overlays
                       CI: build, test, scan (fail on HIGH), push by DIGEST
  namespace            ResourceQuota | LimitRange | RBAC bound to IdP group
                       default-deny NetworkPolicy + allow-dns
  ingress              automatic: <service>.<env>.acme.internal
                       TLS from cert-manager, no ticket
  observability        ServiceMonitor + log routing + OTel agent by annotation
                       + a TEMPLATED dashboard that exists because the service does
  secrets              ServiceAccount with IRSA -> Secrets Manager via CSI driver
                       nothing sensitive in the repo, ever
  deployment           GitOps only. Merge -> CI writes the digest -> Argo reconciles.
                       NO human has cluster write access in production.

ENFORCE THROUGH ADMISSION, NOT DOCUMENTATION   <-- the design principle
  reject: image not from our ECR, or not digest-pinned
  reject: no resource requests / limits
  reject: privileged, hostNetwork, hostPID, hostPath
  reject: no runAsNonRoot, no seccompProfile
  reject: no team / cost-centre label
  (roll out in Audit mode -> fix what it reports -> Enforce)
# a rule in a wiki is ADVISORY. A rule in Kyverno is a RULE.

THE METRIC - offer this unprompted
  time from EMPTY REPO to PRODUCTION URL          target: < 1 day
  how much a team can GET WRONG                   target: very little

HONEST CONSTRAINTS
  a platform for 60 engineers needs 2-4 OWNERS treating it as a product with a
  roadmap and support - otherwise it becomes half-maintained templates that
  teams route around
  golden path must have an ESCAPE HATCH, or teams fork it silently

DELIBERATELY NOT BUILDING FIRST
  x  a custom internal developer portal    (a good README + templates first)
  x  a service mesh                        (unless mTLS is a hard requirement)
  x  multi-cluster federation              (one cluster per env per region)
  x  bespoke dashboards per team           (one template, parameterised)
  none of these pay for themselves at 60 engineers.
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you stop the golden path from becoming a cage?

Provide an escape hatch and make using it visible rather than forbidden: a team can override a default, but the override is explicit in their manifest, reviewed, and reported. Teams fork platforms silently when the platform says no with no path forward — so the goal is that deviating is possible and obvious, which also gives you the signal about what the defaults are getting wrong.

What is the first thing you would build?

The paved path for one real service, end to end — repository to production URL, with a real team using it. Not the abstractions, not the portal. Building the general platform before proving one concrete path is how platform teams spend six months and deliver something nobody adopts. The second service tells you what to generalise; the third tells you whether you generalised correctly.

How do you measure whether the platform is working?

Adoption and lead time, not feature count. What proportion of services are on the golden path, how long from merge to production, how many deploys per day, and how many platform-related support requests per week — a rising support load usually means a missing default rather than a training problem. Also track how many services have drifted off the path, because that number tells you where the platform is failing its users.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Lead with residency, because it partitions everything else. Two countries with regulatory data residency means two independent regional stacks with no cross-border data flow — not one global system with a filter. Traffic is routed by geolocation, each stack holds its own data end to end, and any shared control plane holds no regulated data. Getting this the wrong way round — designing globally then trying to constrain it — is the mistake this question is testing.

Then the numbers. 3,000 transactions per second at peak with a 200-byte record is trivial bandwidth — under a megabyte a second — so this is not a network problem. It is a database write problem: 3,000 writes per second sustained, plus the reads and the index maintenance. That is the constraint to design around, and stating it explicitly is what shows you did the estimation rather than recited an architecture.

Per region. Route 53 geolocation → CloudFront/WAF → ALB in public subnets across three AZs → ECS or EKS in private subnets → Aurora PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ and read replicas for reporting → DynamoDB for idempotency keys and hot lookups → ElastiCache for the fraud-check and BIN lookup cache → SQS and EventBridge for everything asynchronous.

The critical design move: keep the synchronous path minimal. Authorise, persist, respond — and push settlement, notification, reporting, reconciliation and analytics onto the async path. That is what makes 3,000 TPS achievable on a single writer, because you are not doing five things per transaction inside the request. Say this as a deliberate decision with a reason, not as a diagram.

Idempotency on every write, keyed on the client's idempotency key with a conditional put — because at this volume retries are constant and a duplicate authorisation is a real financial event.

State the latency budget and allocate it hop by hop: if the p99 target is 300ms, spend it explicitly — 20ms edge, 5ms ALB, 30ms fraud cache, 40ms authorisation logic, 60ms database write, 20ms response, leaving headroom. That allocation is what turns it should be fast into a design you can test against.

Then scale the writer. If 3,000 TPS exceeds a single Aurora writer, the answers in order are: move everything non-essential off the synchronous path (usually enough); use Aurora Limitless or partition by merchant; or move the highest-volume append path to DynamoDB with a stream into the relational store for reporting. Present them as an ordered set rather than jumping to sharding.

Residency partitions first; then keep the sync path short
RESIDENCY FIRST - it partitions everything else
  Route 53 geolocation
    -> stack-UK  (eu-west-2)   all UK data, end to end
    -> stack-DE  (eu-central-1) all DE data, end to end
  NO cross-border data flow. Shared control plane (CI, IaC, monitoring config)
  holds NO REGULATED DATA.
  # designing globally and then trying to constrain it is the mistake here.

NUMBERS
  3,000 TPS x 200 bytes = 600 KB/s   -> NOT a network problem
  3,000 WRITES/s sustained + reads + index maintenance
  -> it is a DATABASE WRITE problem. Design around that.

PER REGION
  Route 53 (geo) -> CloudFront + WAF -> ALB (public, 3 AZs)
    -> ECS/EKS (private, 3 AZs, HPA on in-flight requests)
      -> Aurora PostgreSQL  writer + 2 readers, Multi-AZ
      -> DynamoDB           idempotency keys, hot lookups
      -> ElastiCache        fraud rules, BIN lookups
      -> SQS / EventBridge  EVERYTHING asynchronous

THE CRITICAL MOVE - keep the SYNCHRONOUS path minimal
  SYNC:   validate -> idempotency claim -> fraud check (cache) -> authorise
          -> persist -> respond                          ~5 steps
  ASYNC:  settlement, notification, reporting, reconciliation, analytics,
          partner notification, ledger projection
  -> this is what makes 3,000 TPS achievable on one writer.
     Not a diagram: a deliberate decision, with a reason.

IDEMPOTENCY on every write - at this volume retries are CONSTANT
  ddb.putItem(... conditionExpression("attribute_not_exists(pk)"))
  key = client Idempotency-Key header (required)

LATENCY BUDGET, allocated hop by hop (p99 target 300ms)
  edge + TLS            20 ms
  ALB                    5 ms
  fraud cache lookup    30 ms
  authorisation logic   40 ms
  DB write (sync commit)60 ms
  response              20 ms
  -------------------------
  175 ms   -> 125 ms headroom for GC pauses, retries, tail
# this is what turns "it should be fast" into something you can TEST AGAINST

IF 3,000 TPS EXCEEDS ONE WRITER - in this order
  1. move everything non-essential OFF the sync path      (usually enough)
  2. Aurora Limitless, or partition by merchant id
  3. move the highest-volume append path to DynamoDB, stream into the
     relational store for reporting
Follow-ups they will ask

Why Aurora rather than DynamoDB for the primary store?

Because authorisation involves multi-row transactions, referential integrity, and ad-hoc queries during investigation and reconciliation that nobody designed for in advance. DynamoDB is better on raw write throughput and predictable latency, so it earns the idempotency table and hot lookups. The honest position is a mix, chosen per access pattern — and being able to say why each store is there is more valuable than picking one.

How do you handle the shared control plane without violating residency?

It holds configuration and code, never regulated data: CI, infrastructure as code, container images, dashboards and alert definitions. Metrics and logs need care — a log line containing a PAN or a customer identifier is regulated data, so log aggregation stays in-region and only aggregate, non-identifying metrics leave. That distinction is usually where residency designs quietly leak.

What is the first thing you would load-test?

The synchronous write path at 1.5× peak, with realistic idempotency-key collision rates and a cold cache — because the failure modes that matter are database write saturation, connection pool exhaustion and the fraud-cache miss path, and all three only appear under sustained concurrency. Testing the happy path at average load tells you almost nothing about whether the design holds.

Design round: the pipeline

Design a document-understanding pipeline: 50,000 PDFs a day, extract structured fields, 99% accuracy required on six critical fields.

Must cover99% on critical fields is the whole design constraint - a model alone will not get you there reliably, so architect for human-in-the-loop. Pipeline: S3 landing, SQS, classification by document type, extraction with a schema per type, then a confidence and validation layer - cross-field checks, arithmetic checks, lookups against known values. High confidence auto-approves; anything below threshold routes to a review queue with the extracted values pre-filled and the source region highlighted. Corrections feed the eval set. Report the auto-approval rate as the business metric and accuracy on the auto-approved subset as the quality gate. 50k a day is 0.6/s average - batch it, do not build for real time.

Design the Kubernetes side of that pipeline: bursty batch work, GPU-free, must not starve the online services sharing the cluster.

Must coverSeparate the workloads by node pool with taints and tolerations so batch never lands on the nodes serving online traffic - that is the isolation that actually holds. Use PriorityClasses so online pods preempt batch under contention. Drive the workers from queue depth with KEDA rather than CPU, scaling to zero when idle. Run the batch pool on spot with a node termination handler and checkpointing so interruption costs one item, not the run. Set resource requests equal to limits on the online tier for Guaranteed QoS, and leave batch Burstable so it soaks up spare capacity without holding it. Cluster autoscaler or Karpenter provisions the batch pool on demand.

Must cover20M rows in an hour is about 5,500 rows per second sustained - comfortably parallel work, so the design is about partitioning and idempotency, not raw throughput. Files land in S3, an event goes to SQS, a splitter writes partitioned chunks back to S3 keyed by a hash of the matching key so all candidates for a key land in one partition. Workers process partitions independently against the internal ledger, writing matches and exceptions to separate stores. Use S3 plus Athena or a Glue job if the shape is truly batch-analytic - be willing to say that a Spark or Athena job is the right tool rather than forcing a microservice. Exceptions go to a queue with a workflow for human resolution, and the SLA is measured from file arrival to exception published.

AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The design constraint is the accuracy number, and it should be the first thing you say: 99% on six critical fields is not achievable by a model alone, reliably, across 50,000 varied documents a day. So the architecture is not extract with a model — it is extract, then verify, then route the uncertain cases to a human. Anyone who designs a pure extraction pipeline here has not engaged with the requirement.

Pipeline. S3 landing → SQS (buffer, retry, DLQ) → classification by document type, because an invoice and a settlement advice need different schemas and different validation → extraction with a per-type JSON schema and tool-calling so output is constrained → a confidence and validation layer → then either auto-approve or route to review.

The validation layer is where the accuracy comes from, and it is mostly deterministic rather than model-based. Cross-field checks: do the line items sum to the stated total. Arithmetic checks: does tax equal the rate times the net. Lookups against known values: is this merchant id real, is this currency valid, is this date within a plausible range. Format checks. And the model's own per-field confidence, which is a weaker signal but useful in combination. A document that passes all of these is very likely correct; one that fails any is routed to a human.

Human-in-the-loop, designed properly. The review queue shows the extracted values pre-filled, with the source region of the document highlighted for each field, so a reviewer confirms rather than re-reads. That single UI decision is the difference between ten seconds and two minutes per document, and at this volume it determines whether the operation is viable. Corrections feed the eval set.

The metrics that matter. Report the auto-approval rate as the business metric — what proportion needs no human — and accuracy on the auto-approved subset as the quality gate. Those two together are the whole story: you can always hit 99% by sending everything to humans, so the engineering goal is maximising auto-approval at 99% accuracy. Frame it that way explicitly.

And do the arithmetic on the rate: 50,000 a day is 0.6 per second average. This is a batch workload. Do not build for real time — build for throughput and cost, with a completion SLA measured in hours rather than a latency target measured in seconds.

99% comes from verification and humans, not from the model
CONSTRAINT: 99% on six critical fields is NOT achievable by a model alone.
            -> architecture = extract, VERIFY, route the uncertain to a human.

S3 landing -> SQS (buffer, retry, DLQ)
  -> CLASSIFY document type      (invoice | settlement advice | remittance | ...)
  -> EXTRACT with a per-type JSON schema, tool-calling constrained
  -> VALIDATE  <-- where the accuracy actually comes from, mostly DETERMINISTIC
       cross-field   sum(lineItems) == statedTotal
       arithmetic    tax == round(net * rate, 2)
       lookup        merchantId exists | currency is ISO-4217 valid
       range         invoiceDate within [today-3y, today+30d]
       format        IBAN checksum, reference pattern
       model         per-field confidence >= 0.9   (weakest signal; use in
                                                     combination, not alone)
  -> ROUTE
       ALL checks pass  -> AUTO-APPROVE
       ANY check fails  -> REVIEW QUEUE

REVIEW UI - this determines whether the operation is VIABLE
  extracted values PRE-FILLED
  SOURCE REGION OF THE DOCUMENT HIGHLIGHTED per field   <-- the key decision
  reviewer CONFIRMS rather than re-reads
  -> 10 seconds per document instead of 2 minutes
  corrections feed the eval set automatically

METRICS - frame it this way explicitly
  AUTO-APPROVAL RATE          the BUSINESS metric   (target: climb over time)
  accuracy ON THE AUTO-APPROVED SUBSET   the QUALITY GATE (must hold >= 99%)
# you can always hit 99% by sending everything to humans.
# the engineering goal is MAXIMISING AUTO-APPROVAL *AT* 99% ACCURACY.

  month 1   auto-approve 55%,  accuracy on those 99.3%   -> 22,500/day reviewed
  month 6   auto-approve 82%,  accuracy on those 99.2%   ->  9,000/day reviewed
  (improvement comes from: better validation rules, per-type prompts, and
   corrections promoted into the eval set)

THROUGHPUT
  50,000/day = 0.6 per second average
  -> THIS IS A BATCH WORKLOAD. Do not build for real time.
     Build for throughput and cost; SLA in HOURS, not a latency target.
     Use the Batch API where the provider offers it (~50% cheaper).
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you set the confidence threshold?

Empirically, from a labelled set, by plotting accuracy against auto-approval rate as you sweep the threshold. You will get a curve; pick the point where accuracy on auto-approved documents meets your 99% requirement, and read off the auto-approval rate that gives you. Then re-derive it whenever the model, the prompt or the document mix changes — a threshold set once and never revisited is how this quietly drifts below the requirement.

What if a document type is consistently poor?

Segment the metrics by type and treat it as its own problem — usually it needs a dedicated prompt, a dedicated schema, or a preprocessing step (better OCR, layout parsing, table extraction). Route that type to review at 100% until it is fixed rather than letting it drag the aggregate down. Per-type reporting is essential for the same reason per-region reporting is: an aggregate hides the segment that is failing.

Where does the model add the most value here?

On the unstructured, variable-layout documents where a rules-based or template-based extractor fails — which is most real-world documents from many partners. For fixed-layout documents from a single source, a deterministic template extractor is more accurate, cheaper and easier to reason about. Being willing to say this subset does not need a model is a stronger answer than applying it uniformly.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The requirement is that bursty batch work must not starve the online services sharing the cluster, and there are three independent mechanisms for that. Naming all three, and being clear that they do different things, is the substance of the answer.

One: node-pool isolation with taints and tolerations. This is the isolation that actually holds. Batch nodes carry a taint so ordinary workloads never land on them, and batch pods carry both a toleration and a node selector so they land there and nowhere else. Now batch and online workloads do not share a kernel, a page cache, a network interface or a disk — which matters because cgroup CPU and memory limits do not isolate disk I/O or network bandwidth, and a batch job reading gigabytes from S3 will degrade a co-located latency-sensitive service in ways no resource limit prevents.

Two: PriorityClasses. Online pods get a high priority, batch a low one, so under genuine cluster-wide contention the scheduler preempts batch pods to make room for online ones. This is the safety net for the case where node pools are exhausted or misconfigured.

Three: QoS. Online tier with requests equal to limits, so it is Guaranteed and evicted last; batch Burstable, so it soaks up spare capacity without holding a reservation it does not need.

Scaling: KEDA on queue depth, not CPU. The work arrives as messages, so queue depth is a direct measure of unprocessed work — the cleanest autoscaling signal available. And KEDA scales to zero, which the HPA cannot, so an idle pipeline costs nothing and Karpenter removes the nodes entirely.

Spot for the batch pool, with a node termination handler and checkpointing so an interruption costs one document rather than the run. Given 50,000 documents a day at 0.6 per second average, this is exactly the workload spot exists for.

And two details worth adding. The batch pool needs its own resource ceiling — a Karpenter limit or a namespace quota — so a bug in the dispatcher cannot provision unbounded nodes. And the online tier should keep a small amount of pause-pod headroom, because when batch scales from zero the node provisioning takes minutes, and you do not want that contention to be resolved by preempting something that matters.

Three isolation mechanisms; scale on the queue
# 1. NODE POOLS - the isolation that actually holds
kind: NodePool                                    # Karpenter
metadata: { name: batch-spot }
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      taints:
        - { key: workload, value: batch, effect: NoSchedule }
      requirements:
        - { key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type, operator: In, values: ["spot"] }
        - { key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-family, operator: In,
            values: ["c7g","c6g","m7g","m6g"] }     # diversify spot pools
  limits: { cpu: "500" }        # CEILING: a dispatcher bug cannot provision
                                #          unbounded nodes
  disruption: { consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized }
# WHY node pools, not just limits: cgroups do NOT isolate disk I/O or network.
# A batch job pulling GBs from S3 degrades a co-located latency-sensitive
# service in ways no CPU or memory limit prevents.
---
# 2. PRIORITY - the safety net under cluster-wide contention
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: { name: online-critical }
value: 1000
---
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: { name: batch-low }
value: 100                       # preempted to make room for online pods
---
# 3. WORKLOAD: taint toleration AND node selector (a toleration alone only
#    PERMITS; it does not ATTRACT)
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: doc-extract-worker }
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      priorityClassName: batch-low
      tolerations:
        - { key: workload, operator: Equal, value: batch, effect: NoSchedule }
      nodeSelector: { workload: batch }
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 90        # < spot's 120s notice
      containers:
        - name: worker
          resources:                            # Burstable: soaks up spare
            requests: { cpu: "1", memory: "2Gi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "4", memory: "2Gi" }
---
# 4. SCALE ON THE QUEUE, and to ZERO
kind: ScaledObject                                # KEDA
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: doc-extract-worker }
  minReplicaCount: 0                              # HPA cannot do this
  maxReplicaCount: 60
  cooldownPeriod: 300
  triggers:
    - type: aws-sqs-queue
      metadata:
        queueURL: https://sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/.../doc-extract
        queueLength: "30"                         # 30 messages per pod

# 5. CHECKPOINT, so a spot interruption costs ONE DOCUMENT, not the run
#    (claim each document with a conditional write before processing)

# 6. ONLINE TIER keeps pause-pod headroom - batch scaling from zero takes
#    minutes to provision nodes, and you do not want that contention resolved
#    by preempting something that matters.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why not just use resource limits and share the nodes?

Because cgroups isolate CPU and memory and nothing else. Disk I/O, network bandwidth, page cache and CPU cache are shared, and a batch job that saturates any of them degrades a latency-sensitive neighbour without exceeding a single limit. Separate node pools are the only mechanism that isolates those. It costs some bin-packing efficiency and it buys predictable online latency, which is the right trade for a payments platform.

How do you stop batch consuming the whole cluster budget?

Two ceilings. A Karpenter NodePool limits block caps the total CPU it may provision, so a runaway dispatcher hits a wall rather than the account's quota. And a namespace ResourceQuota caps aggregate requests. Alert on approaching either, because hitting the ceiling silently means work queues up with no obvious cause.

Does scale-to-zero cause problems?

It adds cold-start latency to the first item after an idle period — node provisioning plus image pull plus JVM start, so one to three minutes. For a batch pipeline with an SLA in hours that is irrelevant and the saving is real. For anything with a latency expectation, keep a minimum of one replica. The mistake is applying scale-to-zero to a workload someone is waiting on.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Do the arithmetic first, because it changes the architecture. 20 million rows in an hour is about 5,500 rows per second sustained — comfortably parallel work, not extreme throughput. So the design problem is partitioning and idempotency, not raw speed. Say that conclusion out loud.

Then be willing to say that microservices may be the wrong tool. This is a batch-analytic matching problem over three files and a ledger, and an AWS Glue or Spark job, or Athena over Parquet, is very likely the right answer — it does joins over tens of millions of rows for a few pounds and finishes in minutes. An interviewer is often testing whether you reach reflexively for a queue and a fleet of consumers when a data tool fits better. Present both and justify the choice.

If it must be event-driven — because the SLA is measured from file arrival and files land unpredictably — then: files land in S3, an event goes to SQS, and a splitter writes partitioned chunks back to S3, keyed by a hash of the matching key so every candidate for a given key lands in the same partition. That is the essential move: it makes each partition independently processable with no cross-partition coordination, which is what makes the parallelism real.

Workers then process one partition each against the internal ledger, writing matches and exceptions to separate stores. Idempotency is a conditional claim on the partition id, so a redelivery is a no-op.

Exceptions go to a queue with a resolution workflow, and the SLA is measured from file arrival to exception published — that framing matters, because the business cares about knowing quickly what did not match, not about the job finishing.

Reconciliation at the end is mandatory: matched plus unmatched plus rejected must equal the declared row count from the file trailer. A mismatch means rows vanished, which is the silent failure this whole system exists to prevent. Alarm on it and do not mark the run complete.

And the operational shape: bad rows go to a rejects file and never fail their partition; the file-level control table tracks progress so a partial failure resumes; and the whole thing scales on queue depth via KEDA with a hard ceiling.

5,500 rows/s is parallel work — and a Glue job may beat all of it
ARITHMETIC FIRST
  20M rows / 1 hour = ~5,500 rows/second sustained
  -> parallel work, NOT extreme throughput.
  -> the problem is PARTITIONING and IDEMPOTENCY, not speed.

OPTION A - the one I would probably choose: it is a batch-analytic join
  S3 (partner files + ledger export, Parquet)
    -> Glue job (Spark) or Athena
       SELECT ... FROM ledger l FULL OUTER JOIN partner p
         ON l.reference = p.reference AND l.amount_minor = p.amount_minor
       WHERE l.reference IS NULL OR p.reference IS NULL     -- exceptions
  -> tens of millions of rows joined in minutes, for a few pounds
  -> an interviewer is often testing whether you reach reflexively for a queue
     and a fleet of consumers when a DATA TOOL fits better.

OPTION B - event-driven, if the SLA is from FILE ARRIVAL and files land
           unpredictably
  S3 ObjectCreated -> SQS control-queue
    -> SPLITTER
         validate header + trailer row count
         INSERT file_control(fileId, declaredRows, checksum, status=SPLITTING)
         partition rows to S3 BY HASH OF THE MATCHING KEY:
            s3://work/{fileId}/part={hash(reference) % 256}/rows.parquet
         <-- THE ESSENTIAL MOVE: every candidate for a key lands in ONE
             partition -> partitions are independently processable, no
             cross-partition coordination. This is what makes the parallelism real.
         enqueue one work item per partition
    -> WORK QUEUE (visibility 600s, maxReceiveCount 4, DLQ + alarm)
       -> WORKERS (KEDA on queue depth, max 64)
            claim: conditional put on workId -> redelivery is a no-op
            load ledger slice for this partition (same hash) -> match in memory
            write MATCHES  -> matches table
            write MISMATCH -> exceptions queue  <-- the SLA output
            bad row        -> rejects file, NEVER fail the partition

RECONCILIATION - mandatory, and the whole point
  sum(matched) + sum(unmatched) + sum(rejected) == file_control.declaredRows
  MISMATCH -> rows vanished -> ALARM, do NOT mark the run complete
# this is the silent failure the entire system exists to prevent

SLA measured FROM FILE ARRIVAL TO EXCEPTION PUBLISHED
  (the business cares about knowing quickly what did NOT match,
   not about the job finishing)

  ingest + split          ~4 min
  partition processing    ~12 min (64 workers, 256 partitions)
  exceptions published    continuously, as each partition completes  <-- key
  reconciliation          ~1 min
  ---------------------------------
  well inside the 1-hour SLA, with the first exceptions visible in minutes
Follow-ups they will ask

Why hash-partition rather than range-partition?

Because matching requires that both sides of a candidate pair land in the same partition, and a hash of the join key guarantees that regardless of data distribution. Range partitioning on a reference number would work only if both files were sorted the same way, and it skews badly when references cluster. The hash also gives you even partition sizes, which matters for worker utilisation.

What if a partner file arrives late or not at all?

Make it explicit rather than implicit: the control table has an expected-arrival time per partner, and a scheduled check raises an alert when a file is overdue — because a missing file produces no event and therefore no failure. Then decide the policy: reconcile against the partners you have and mark the third as pending, or hold the run. Missing-input alerting is the class of monitoring teams most often omit.

How do you handle a file that is re-sent with corrections?

Derive the fileId from content (a hash), not the filename, since partners reuse names. An identical re-send then produces identical work ids and every partition is a safe no-op. A genuinely corrected file is a different file, and it needs an explicit supersede path — reverse the previous run's matches or mark them superseded — because silently processing both double-counts. That path should exist in the design, not be invented during the incident.

510/3

Design round: the migration

A team wants to replace a rules engine with an LLM. Argue the case honestly - when is that right, when is it reckless, and what is the hybrid?

Must coverReckless when the rules are the specification: deterministic, auditable, testable, and cheap. A payments fraud rule that must be explained to a regulator should not become a probability. Right when the input is unstructured and the rules have become an unmaintainable thicket of special cases for text - classification of free-text disputes, extraction, routing. The hybrid is the real answer: the model converts unstructured input into structured features, and the deterministic engine makes the decision. You get the model's flexibility on parsing and the engine's auditability on outcomes. Say clearly what you would need to see - error cost, reversibility, auditability - before agreeing.

StudyAnthropic - when to use Claude →

Migrate twelve services from EC2 with Ansible to EKS, with no big-bang cutover. Give the sequence and the first thing you would do.

Must coverFirst thing: not Kubernetes. Make the services containerisable - externalise config, log to stdout, add health endpoints, remove local disk state, make startup and shutdown clean. Half the migration pain is applications that assume a long-lived host. Then: build the cluster and platform with one low-risk service end to end to prove CI, deploy, observability, secrets and ingress. Then migrate service by service, running both old and new behind a weighted target group or DNS so you can shift traffic gradually and roll back by weight. Migrate the noisiest and most-deployed service second, because it produces the most learning per week. Databases stay on RDS throughout. Decommission only after a full quiet period.
