AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Answer this honestly and in both directions, because the question is testing judgement rather than enthusiasm — and a candidate who says yes, LLMs are better fails it as surely as one who refuses outright.

When it is reckless: when the rules are the specification. A fraud rule that must be explained to a regulator, reproduced identically for the same input, tested exhaustively, and audited — that is a specification written as code, and replacing it with a probability distribution loses every property that made it acceptable. You cannot diff a model against last quarter's behaviour, you cannot prove why a specific decision was made, and you cannot guarantee the same input produces the same output. In a regulated decision path those are not inconveniences; they are the reasons the rules engine exists.

When it is right: when the rules have become an unmaintainable thicket of special cases for text. That is the real tell. A rules engine handling structured fields — amount, country, velocity, merchant category — is doing what it is good at. A rules engine with two hundred regular expressions trying to classify free-text dispute reasons, or to extract an intent from a customer message, is being used far outside its competence, and every new edge case makes it worse. That is where a model is genuinely better.

The hybrid is the actual answer, and it is worth naming as a pattern: the model converts unstructured input into structured features; the deterministic engine makes the decision. The model reads the dispute narrative and produces a typed reason, a confidence and extracted entities. The rules engine takes those alongside the structured data and decides. You get the model's flexibility on parsing and the engine's auditability on outcomes — and the decision remains explainable, testable and reproducible, because the model never made it.

That also gives you a clean fallback: when extraction confidence is low, route to a human rather than to a guess, and the engine's behaviour is unchanged.

Then say what you would need to see before agreeing, because that is the senior move: what is the cost of an error in each direction, is the decision reversible, and does it need to be auditable. High error cost, irreversible, auditable — keep the rules. Low error cost, reversible, internal — a model is fine. And where a team is proposing this mainly because the rules engine is unmaintained, the honest observation is that replacing an unmaintained deterministic system with an unmaintained probabilistic one makes things worse, not better.

Model parses; the engine decides
RECKLESS WHEN THE RULES ARE THE SPECIFICATION
  a fraud rule that must be:
    explained to a regulator      -> a model cannot tell you WHY
    reproduced identically         -> sampling is stochastic
    tested exhaustively            -> you can only sample the input space
    diffed against last quarter    -> no diff exists for a model's behaviour
  -> these are not inconveniences. They are why the rules engine exists.

RIGHT WHEN THE RULES ARE A THICKET OF SPECIAL CASES FOR *TEXT*
  200 regexes classifying free-text dispute reasons
  -> the engine is being used far outside its competence, and every new edge
     case makes it worse. This is where a model is genuinely better.

THE HYBRID - the actual answer
  // MODEL: unstructured in, STRUCTURED out. Makes no decision.
  record DisputeFeatures(
      Reason reason,            // enum, not free text
      BigDecimal claimedAmount,
      LocalDate  claimedDate,
      boolean    goodsReceived,
      double     confidence) {}

  var f = model.extract(disputeNarrative);          // parsing

  if (f.confidence() < 0.85)
      return route(HUMAN_REVIEW);                   // not a guess

  // ENGINE: decides. Deterministic, testable, auditable, unchanged.
  Decision d = rulesEngine.evaluate(
      f,                                            // model-derived features
      txn,                                          // structured facts
      merchant.riskProfile());

  audit.record(disputeId, f, d, MODEL_VERSION, RULES_VERSION);
  // -> the DECISION is explainable and reproducible, because the model
  //    never made it.

WHAT I WOULD NEED TO SEE BEFORE AGREEING
  cost of an error, in each direction?
  is the decision REVERSIBLE?
  must it be AUDITABLE?
    high cost + irreversible + auditable  -> KEEP THE RULES
    low cost + reversible + internal      -> a model is fine
    unstructured INPUT, structured DECISION -> the hybrid above

AND THE HONEST OBSERVATION
  if the real motivation is that the rules engine is unmaintained, replacing an
  unmaintained DETERMINISTIC system with an unmaintained PROBABILISTIC one
  makes things worse. Fix the maintenance problem first.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if the team says the model is more accurate than the rules?

Ask on what measurement, over what sample, and against which failure. Rules engines are usually tuned for a specific error asymmetry — catching fraud at the cost of false positives — and a model with better overall accuracy may be worse on exactly the case the business cares about. Compare on the metric that reflects the business cost, segmented by case type, not on aggregate accuracy. Often the model is better on the text-heavy subset and worse on the structured one, which is precisely the argument for the hybrid.

How do you version the hybrid so a decision remains explainable?

Record both versions on every decision — the model artefact version that produced the features and the rules version that made the decision — plus the extracted features themselves. Then a decision from eight months ago can be re-derived: you can show what the model extracted, what the rules did with it, and re-run the rules against the stored features exactly. That is a stronger audit story than either component alone.

Would you ever let a model make a reversible decision autonomously?

Yes, and the reversibility is the whole justification. Routing a dispute to a queue, prioritising a review backlog, suggesting a category a human confirms — these are cheap to get wrong and easy to correct. The line I would hold is anything that moves money, denies a customer something, or is reported externally. Those need the deterministic path, even when the model would usually be right.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The first thing I would do is not Kubernetes. That is the answer to lead with, because it is the one that distinguishes someone who has run a migration from someone who has read about one.

Make the services containerisable first. Externalise configuration so it comes from the environment rather than a properties file on the host. Log to stdout rather than to a local file. Add real health endpoints with a proper liveness/readiness distinction. Remove local disk state — sessions, uploaded files, caches written to /var — because a container's filesystem is ephemeral. Make startup and shutdown clean: handle SIGTERM, drain in-flight requests, do not assume a long-lived host. Roughly half the pain of a Kubernetes migration is applications that assume a pet server, and none of that work requires a cluster to exist.

Then build the cluster and the platform with one low-risk service end to end. Not twelve. One — ideally something with real traffic but low blast radius — proving CI, image build, deployment, ingress, TLS, secrets, observability and rollback. That first service is where you discover every gap, and discovering them once is much cheaper than discovering them twelve times.

Then migrate service by service, running both old and new in parallel behind a weighted target group or DNS split. That is the mechanism that makes it not a big bang: shift 5% of traffic, watch, shift more, and roll back by changing a weight rather than by redeploying. Keep the EC2 fleet running until the service has been fully on Kubernetes for a quiet period.

Migrate the noisiest, most-deployed service second — after the low-risk proof. It is counter-intuitive and it is right: the service deployed five times a day produces the most learning per week, exercises the pipeline hardest, and its team becomes your internal advocate. Migrating twelve quiet services first teaches you almost nothing.

Databases stay on RDS throughout. Do not compound a compute migration with a data migration; they have different risk profiles and different rollback stories.

Decommission only after a documented quiet period — and actually decommission, because a half-migrated estate with both platforms running indefinitely is the worst outcome: double the cost, double the operational surface, and two places to look during an incident.

Fix the apps first, prove with one, migrate by traffic weight
PHASE 0 - NOT KUBERNETES. ~half the migration pain lives here.
  [ ] config from environment, not /etc/app/app.properties on the host
  [ ] log to STDOUT (structured JSON), not to a file
  [ ] health endpoints, with liveness vs readiness distinguished
  [ ] remove local disk state (sessions -> Redis, uploads -> S3, caches -> ok
      to lose)
  [ ] handle SIGTERM: graceful shutdown, drain in-flight requests
  [ ] no assumptions about hostname, uptime, or a fixed IP
  [ ] build a container image, run it under a memory limit, prove it behaves
  -> none of this needs a cluster to exist. Do it while the cluster is built.

PHASE 1 - ONE service, end to end
  pick: real traffic, LOW blast radius
  prove: CI -> image -> ECR by digest -> Argo -> ingress + TLS -> secrets via
         IRSA -> dashboards + alerts -> ROLLBACK
  -> every gap is discovered here, once, instead of twelve times.

PHASE 2 - migrate by TRAFFIC WEIGHT, not by cutover
  ALB
   +-- target-group-ec2   weight 95   (old ASG, still running)
   +-- target-group-eks   weight  5   (new, ALB controller in IP mode)
  5% -> watch error rate, p99, resource usage -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%
  ROLLBACK = change a weight. Seconds. No redeploy.
  keep the EC2 fleet running until the service has been 100% on EKS for a
  documented quiet period.

  ORDER: low-risk service first (the proof)
         THEN THE NOISIEST, MOST-DEPLOYED SERVICE   <-- counter-intuitive,
              and right: most learning per week, hardest exercise of the
              pipeline, and its team becomes your internal advocate.
         then the rest, easiest-to-hardest

PHASE 3 - DATABASES STAY ON RDS
  do not compound a compute migration with a data migration.
  Different risk profiles, different rollback stories.

PHASE 4 - ACTUALLY DECOMMISSION
  a half-migrated estate running both platforms indefinitely is the WORST
  outcome: double cost, double operational surface, two places to look during
  an incident. Set a date, and hold it.
Follow-ups they will ask

How long should twelve services take?

Realistically two to four months with a small team, and most of it is Phase 0 and Phase 1. Once the platform is proven and the applications are twelve-factor, each subsequent service is days rather than weeks. The estimate people get wrong is the first service — it is not a twelfth of the work, it is closer to a third, because it includes building everything the others will reuse.

What if a service cannot be made stateless?

Then handle it last, and handle it honestly. Some things genuinely need per-instance state, and the options are a StatefulSet with the operational cost that implies, keeping it on EC2 indefinitely (which is a legitimate outcome — not everything must move), or refactoring the state out, which is real product work that needs to be funded. Pretending a stateful application is stateless because the migration plan assumed it is how you get a data-loss incident.

How do you keep the team's confidence during a long migration?

Ship visibly and measure. Publish the count of services migrated, the deploy frequency before and after, and the lead time — because the migration must produce a visible improvement or support evaporates. And make the first migrated team's experience genuinely better than what they had, since their opinion determines whether the next eleven teams cooperate or resist.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Assess before deciding anything, because the biggest choice comes first: Oracle-to-Aurora PostgreSQL (real conversion work, no licence cost, better long-term fit on AWS) or RDS for Oracle (lift and shift, keep the licence cost, far less work). The Schema Conversion Tool produces an assessment report showing what converts automatically and what needs manual work — PL/SQL packages, hierarchical CONNECT BY queries, sequences, DBMS_ package usage, proprietary data types. That report is the input to the decision, not a formality.

Be honest about the trade in an interview: engine conversion is a multi-month application project, because the schema is the easy part and the PL/SQL and the query behaviour are not. Lift-and-shift to RDS for Oracle is weeks and keeps the licence bill. Which is right depends on how much PL/SQL exists and whether the licence cost is material.

The migration mechanism is DMS with full load plus change data capture, and this is what makes an hour of downtime achievable at 4TB. The full load runs for hours or days while the source stays fully live. CDC then reads the source's redo logs and keeps the target continuously current — so at cutover time the target is seconds behind, not days.

The cutover window is therefore only: stop writes at the source, let CDC drain (seconds to minutes), run validation — row counts and checksums per table — repoint the application, and smoke test. That is comfortably under an hour, and the long part of the migration happened while everyone was working normally.

Rehearse the cutover at least twice, timed, with the actual runbook. The first rehearsal always overruns.

Keep reverse replication running — CDC from the new target back to Oracle — for the first days, so rollback is possible after go-live rather than only during the window. That is the difference between a cutover you can undo and one you cannot.

And the item that is most often underestimated: test performance before cutover, not after. Query plans differ between engines. A query that used an Oracle index hint, or relied on Oracle's optimiser behaviour, can be orders of magnitude slower on PostgreSQL — and you will find it under production load if you do not find it in a load test. Replay real production queries against the target and compare timings table by table. That, rather than the data movement, is where migrations actually go wrong.

Full load while live; CDC makes the window small
1. ASSESS - the decision comes before the mechanism
   aws schema-conversion-tool  ->  assessment report
     auto-converted      : tables, indexes, most views, simple procedures
     MANUAL WORK         : PL/SQL packages, CONNECT BY hierarchies, sequences,
                           DBMS_* usage, proprietary types, triggers
   DECISION
     Oracle -> Aurora PostgreSQL   no licence cost, better AWS fit,
                                   MULTI-MONTH application project
                                   (the schema is easy; PL/SQL and query
                                    behaviour are not)
     Oracle -> RDS for Oracle      lift and shift, weeks, KEEP the licence bill
   -> depends on how much PL/SQL exists and whether the licence cost is material.

2. DMS: FULL LOAD + CDC - this is what makes 1 hour achievable at 4 TB
   full load        hours-to-days, SOURCE STAYS FULLY LIVE
   CDC              reads Oracle redo logs; target stays seconds behind
   -> the long part of the migration happens while everyone works normally

   task settings that matter:
     TargetTablePrepMode: DO_NOTHING        (pre-create with converted DDL)
     ParallelLoadThreads / partitioned load for the largest tables
     drop secondary indexes for the full load, rebuild before cutover
     validation: EnableValidation true      (DMS compares row by row)

3. CUTOVER WINDOW - only this part is downtime
   t+0    stop writes at source (put the app in read-only / maintenance)
   t+2    wait for CDCLatencySource -> 0        (seconds to minutes)
   t+5    validate: row counts + checksums per table, sequence values reset
   t+15   repoint the application (connection string / Secrets Manager value)
   t+25   smoke test the critical paths
   t+40   open writes
   -> comfortably under an hour

4. REHEARSE TWICE, TIMED, with the actual runbook. The first one always overruns.

5. REVERSE REPLICATION for the first days after go-live
   CDC from Aurora BACK to Oracle
   -> rollback is possible AFTER go-live, not only during the window.
      This is the difference between a cutover you can undo and one you cannot.

6. THE MOST UNDERESTIMATED ITEM: PERFORMANCE, BEFORE CUTOVER
   query plans DIFFER between engines.
   a query relying on an Oracle hint or optimiser behaviour can be orders of
   magnitude slower on PostgreSQL.
   -> replay REAL production queries against the target, compare timings
      table by table, fix plans and add indexes BEFORE the window.
   This, not the data movement, is where migrations actually go wrong.
Follow-ups they will ask

What are the hardest things to convert from Oracle to PostgreSQL?

PL/SQL packages, because PostgreSQL has no package concept and the state and scoping semantics differ. Hierarchical queries (CONNECT BY) become recursive CTEs, which is mechanical but behaviourally different. Sequences and NEXTVAL semantics, empty-string-versus-NULL handling, and implicit type conversions all differ subtly and produce bugs that pass tests and fail in production. And anything relying on Oracle-specific functions or hints.

How do you validate 4TB actually transferred correctly?

DMS validation compares row by row during and after the load, which is the primary mechanism and worth enabling despite the overhead. Layer on your own checks: row counts per table, checksums or aggregate sums over numeric columns, spot comparisons of the largest and most-referenced tables, and confirmation that sequences were advanced past the maximum existing id — a missed sequence reset produces duplicate key errors on the first write after cutover, which is a memorable way to fail.

What is the rollback plan if you discover a problem three days later?

Reverse replication, which is why it matters. With CDC running from Aurora back to Oracle, you can stop writes, let it drain, and repoint back with the same short window. Without it, three days of writes exist only in the new database and rolling back means either losing them or building a bespoke reverse migration under pressure. Set the duration deliberately — a week is typical — and decommission the reverse path explicitly rather than letting it lapse.

Design round: the hard tradeoff

The business wants AI answers in under 500ms. Your best pipeline takes 4 seconds. Present the options and make a recommendation.

Must coverBe honest about the physics: generation is sequential, so total time scales with output tokens, and no amount of engineering makes a 600-token answer appear in 500ms with a large model. Options - stream, so time to first token is under 500ms and the perceived latency target is met, which is usually the correct answer and should be presented first; shorten the output by design; use a smaller or faster model for this path; precompute answers for the common question set offline and serve from cache; or split the response - an instant deterministic part rendered immediately with the generated part streaming after. Recommend streaming plus output-length discipline, and re-negotiate the metric from total time to time to first token, because that is what users feel.

StudyAnthropic - reduce latency →

Your cluster runs at 25% average utilisation and finance wants it halved. Walk through what you would actually do and what you would refuse.

Must coverMeasure before cutting: split the 75% into headroom for failure (needed), headroom for burst (needed), over-requested pods (waste), and idle node fragmentation (waste). Do: right-size requests from p95 actuals, enable Karpenter consolidation, move batch and dev to spot, scale non-production to zero out of hours, and consolidate small clusters. Refuse: cutting below the capacity to lose one AZ, removing PodDisruptionBudgets to make drains easier, and setting memory limits below observed peak to improve packing - those trade an invisible cost for a visible outage. Present the target as utilisation at a defined reliability level, not utilisation alone, and quantify what each cut costs in risk.

StudyEKS - compute cost optimization →

Single-region with 99.99% or multi-region with 99.995% at three times the cost? Make the argument you would make to a director.

Must coverReframe from availability to failure modes and money. 99.99% is 52 minutes a year; 99.995% is 26. The question is what half an hour of downtime costs against the delta in spend plus the ongoing complexity tax - and complexity has its own failure rate, so a badly run multi-region system is often less available than a well-run single-region one. Push on what actually causes your outages: for most teams it is bad deploys and dependency failures, neither of which multi-region fixes, and both of which canaries and circuit breakers do fix far more cheaply. Recommend: single region multi-AZ, done properly, plus a rehearsed warm standby for regional disaster, and spend the difference on deploy safety. Change the answer if there is a regulatory requirement, because then it is not a cost decision.

AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Lead with the physics, because the honest constraint reframes the whole conversation: generation is sequential in the output length. A 600-token answer requires 600 sequential decode steps, and no amount of engineering makes that appear in 500 milliseconds with a large model. Optimising retrieval from 35ms to 20ms changes nothing a user can feel. Say that first, kindly and clearly, or you will spend the meeting agreeing to something impossible.

Then present the options rather than a refusal.

One — stream, and re-negotiate the metric. This is the answer and it should be presented first. Time to first token can be under 500ms comfortably; the rest arrives at reading speed, which users experience as fast. The business asked for 500ms meaning it should feel instant, and time to first token is the metric that captures that. Changing the measure from total time to TTFT is not moving the goalposts, it is measuring the thing they actually care about.

Two — shorten the output by design. Cap max_tokens, instruct for brevity, remove preambles and restatements. Halving output length halves the sequential work. Often the four-second answer was three sentences of value and a paragraph of throat-clearing.

Three — a smaller or faster model on this path, measured against the eval set rather than assumed to be worse.

Four — precompute. If the question space is narrow and repetitive, generate answers offline and serve from cache. That genuinely achieves sub-500ms because there is no generation at request time. It only works where the answers are not personalised or time-sensitive.

Five — split the response. Render the deterministic part instantly (the table, the figures, the status) and stream the generated narration after it. The user sees something useful in 100ms.

Recommend one, three-plus-two as a package: stream, discipline the output length, and render the deterministic part immediately. And be explicit that the fifth option is often the best product answer anyway, because the table is what the user needs and the prose is the commentary.

Close by naming the anti-pattern: do not hit 500ms by degrading quality silently — truncating mid-sentence, or dropping retrieval so the answer is fast and wrong. A fast wrong answer in a payments context is worse than a slow right one, and that trade should be made explicitly by the business rather than quietly by an engineer.

Change what you measure, not what you promise
THE PHYSICS - say this first
  generation is SEQUENTIAL in output length.
  600 output tokens = 600 sequential decode steps.
  No engineering makes that appear in 500ms with a large model.
  (and optimising retrieval 35ms -> 20ms changes nothing a user can feel)

CURRENT BUDGET
  retrieval + rerank     ~150 ms      4% of the time
  prompt assembly          ~5 ms
  TIME TO FIRST TOKEN    ~400 ms
  generation (620 tok)  ~3,450 ms     <-- 86% of the time. This is the target.
  ------------------------------------
  total                 ~4,000 ms

OPTIONS
1  STREAM + re-negotiate the metric          <-- RECOMMEND FIRST
     TTFT ~400ms; the rest arrives at reading speed
     "500ms" means "it should feel instant". TTFT is the metric that captures
     that. This is not moving the goalposts - it is measuring what they mean.

2  SHORTEN THE OUTPUT
     max_tokens 620 -> 250, instruct for brevity, drop preambles
     -> ~1,400ms total. Often the 4-second answer was 3 sentences of value
        and a paragraph of throat-clearing.

3  SMALLER / FASTER MODEL on this path
     measure against the eval set; do not assume it is worse

4  PRECOMPUTE
     narrow, repetitive, non-personalised question space -> generate offline,
     serve from cache. GENUINELY sub-500ms: there is no generation at request time.

5  SPLIT THE RESPONSE                         <-- often the best PRODUCT answer
     render the deterministic part INSTANTLY (the table, the figures, the status)
     stream the narration after it
     -> user sees something useful in ~100ms

RECOMMENDATION: 1 + 2 + 5 as a package.
  TTFT < 400ms | deterministic content < 100ms | output halved
  and the table is what the user needs anyway; the prose is commentary.

THE ANTI-PATTERN - name it explicitly
  do NOT hit 500ms by degrading quality silently:
    truncating mid-sentence | dropping retrieval so it is fast and wrong
  a fast WRONG answer in payments is worse than a slow right one.
  That trade belongs to the business, made explicitly - not to an engineer,
  made quietly.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if they insist on 500ms total, not TTFT?

Then the answer is option four — precompute — and the conversation becomes about which questions can be precomputed. For a fixed, non-personalised question space that is genuinely achievable. For open-ended personalised questions it is not, and the honest response is to say so with the numbers, offer the alternatives, and let them decide with full information. Agreeing to an impossible target and missing it is worse than disagreeing early.

Does a faster model close the gap?

Partly. Small models generate several times faster per token and can cut total time substantially, so combined with a shorter output they can approach a second. Whether quality holds is an empirical question for your eval set, and for narrow tasks it often does. What no model does is make 600 sequential tokens instantaneous — the per-token time improves, the sequential dependency does not go away.

How do you know 400ms TTFT is achievable?

Measure it, and split it: prompt processing scales with input length, so a 12,000-token context has a noticeably higher TTFT than a 4,000-token one — which is another reason to retrieve fewer, better chunks. Prompt caching on the stable prefix helps here too, since cached input is processed faster. If TTFT is above target, the levers are context length and caching, not the model.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Measure before cutting, and present the 75% as four separate things — because that reframing is what turns an argument into an engineering conversation. Some of it is waste and some of it is the price of surviving a failure, and finance cannot tell them apart without help.

Split it: headroom for AZ loss (needed — roughly 33% across three zones), headroom for rolling-update surge (needed, though smaller than people think), over-requested pods (waste), and node fragmentation from poor bin-packing (waste). Only the last two are recoverable, and typically they are the majority.

What I would do. Right-size requests from observed p95 using VPA in recommendation mode — this is almost always the largest single win, because the scheduler bin-packs on requests and a service reserving ten times what it uses forces the cluster to run several times the nodes it needs. Enable Karpenter consolidation, which actively repacks workloads onto fewer nodes rather than only removing empty ones. Move batch, CI and development to spot. Scale non-production to zero out of hours — a dev cluster running at full size overnight and at weekends is roughly 70% waste and nobody notices. And consolidate small clusters, since each carries fixed overhead in system DaemonSets and control plane charges.

What I would refuse, and why. Cutting capacity below the ability to lose one AZ — that trades an invisible cost for a visible outage. Removing PodDisruptionBudgets to make drains easier — it makes maintenance faster and outages likelier. Setting memory limits below observed peak to improve packing — that is buying utilisation with OOM kills. Each refusal comes with a quantified risk rather than a principle.

Then present the target correctly: utilisation at a defined reliability level. A cluster at 60% may be exactly right; one at 90% is one zone failure from an outage. Offering that framing, with the arithmetic, converts you are wasting 40% into this is what surviving a zone failure costs — and it is a number finance can accept or explicitly decide to reduce.

And offer the honest total: right-sizing plus consolidation plus spot plus non-production scheduling typically recovers most of the gap without touching the reliability headroom. Which usually means you can meet the goal without the argument.

Split the 75% before defending it
SPLIT IT FIRST - finance cannot tell waste from insurance without help
  headroom for AZ loss (n-1 of 3)        ~33%   NEEDED
  headroom for rolling-update surge       ~5%   NEEDED
  over-requested pods                    ~25%   WASTE   <-- usually the biggest
  node fragmentation / poor packing      ~12%   WASTE
  ------------------------------------------------------
  75% "idle"                            ~37% actually recoverable

DO
1  right-size requests from OBSERVED p95        biggest single win
     kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
     spec: { updatePolicy: { updateMode: "Off" } }    # recommend, do not act
     $ kubectl describe vpa api | grep -A6 Recommendation
     # the scheduler bin-packs on REQUESTS. A pod reserving 10x what it uses
     # forces the cluster to run several times the nodes it needs.
2  Karpenter consolidation                       repacks, not just "remove empty"
     disruption: { consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized,
                   consolidateAfter: 1m }
3  spot for batch, CI, development                60-90% on that slice
4  scale NON-PRODUCTION to zero out of hours      dev at full size overnight and
     CronJob: 19:00 -> replicas 0 | 07:00 -> restore     at weekends is ~70% waste
5  consolidate small clusters                     each carries fixed overhead:
                                                  system DaemonSets per node,
                                                  control plane charge

REFUSE - each with a QUANTIFIED risk, not a principle
  x  capacity below n-1 AZ
       -> a zone failure becomes an outage instead of a degradation.
          Trades an invisible cost for a visible incident.
  x  removing PodDisruptionBudgets
       -> makes drains faster and outages likelier. Node upgrades would take
          the whole service down.
  x  memory limits below observed peak
       -> buying utilisation with OOM kills. The pods restart under exactly
          the load that caused the peak.

PRESENT THE TARGET CORRECTLY
  NOT "utilisation"      -> "UTILISATION AT A DEFINED RELIABILITY LEVEL"
  60% may be exactly right. 90% is one zone failure from an outage.
  show the arithmetic:
     3 AZs, must survive losing one  -> 33% reserved, by definition
     rolling updates                 -> 5%
     -> a healthy steady state is ~55-62% utilisation
  This converts "you are wasting 40%" into "this is what surviving a zone
  failure costs" - a number they can accept, or explicitly decide to reduce.

AND THE HONEST TOTAL
  1+2+3+4+5 typically recovers most of the gap WITHOUT touching reliability
  headroom -> you usually meet the goal without needing the argument.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if they still insist after seeing the arithmetic?

Then it is a business decision about risk appetite, and my job is to make it explicit and documented rather than to block it. Write down what is being accepted — we will not survive an AZ failure without degraded service — get the risk owner to acknowledge it, and add monitoring that shows when it bites. Engineers who quietly refuse lose the argument slowly; engineers who quantify the trade and document the decision keep credibility either way.

Is 60% utilisation actually good?

For a cluster that must survive a zone failure and do rolling updates, yes — it is close to the theoretical maximum. Chasing 80% means either accepting a zone failure will cause an outage, or having such fast node provisioning that you can absorb it, which is achievable with Karpenter plus pause pods but is a different design. Quote the arithmetic rather than the number, because the number alone always sounds low.

Which of these gives the fastest result?

Scaling non-production to zero out of hours — it is a CronJob, it takes an afternoon, it carries no production risk, and on a typical estate it removes a meaningful share of total spend immediately. Do that first to buy goodwill and time, then do the right-sizing work, which is more valuable but takes weeks of observation to do properly.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Reframe from availability to failure modes and money, because the two numbers on their own are not decidable. 99.99% is about 52 minutes of downtime a year; 99.995% is about 26. So the question is: is half an hour a year worth twice the infrastructure spend plus the ongoing complexity?

Then make the argument that matters most, and it is uncomfortable: complexity has its own failure rate. A badly-run multi-region system is frequently less available than a well-run single-region one. You have doubled the surface area of deploys, migrations, secrets, IAM and incidents, and every one of those is a source of outages. The additional nines are only real if the operation is mature enough to hold them.

Then push on the actual cause of your outages, which is the strongest move available. For most teams, downtime comes from bad deploys and dependency failures — not from a region disappearing. Multi-region fixes neither. Canary deploys with automatic rollback, circuit breakers, timeout discipline, and expand-contract migrations fix both, and they cost a fraction of a second region. Bring the incident history: in the last two years we had eleven incidents; nine were deploys or dependencies, two were AZ-level, zero were regional. That data ends the argument far more effectively than an opinion.

Recommendation: single region, multi-AZ, done properly — plus a rehearsed warm standby for regional disaster — and spend the difference on deploy safety. That gets you the regional-disaster protection without paying the active-active complexity tax on every change.

Then name what changes the answer, because a recommendation without conditions sounds dogmatic. A regulatory requirement for multi-region — then it is not a cost decision at all, and you build it. A contractual SLA with penalties that exceed the cost. A global user base where multi-region is really about latency and the availability is a side effect. Or genuine evidence that regional failures are your dominant risk.

And close with the discipline point: whatever is chosen, the numbers must be tested. An untested multi-region setup has an unknown real availability, and an unrehearsed failover has an unbounded RTO — so the extra nines exist on a slide rather than in production.

Reframe to failure modes; bring the incident data
THE NUMBERS

  99.995%  ~26 minutes
  DELTA    ~26 minutes/year, for ~3x the cost + a permanent complexity tax

  a badly-run multi-region system is frequently LESS available than a

    + data consistency decisions that are hard to get right
  the extra nines are only real if the operation is mature enough to hold them.

  last 24 months, 11 incidents:

     2  AZ-level                                <-- multi-AZ already covers this
     0  regional

Follow-ups they will ask

How do you make this argument without sounding like you are avoiding work?

By proposing something concrete and more ambitious in a different direction — canary deploys, automated rollback, chaos experiments, a rehearsed warm standby — rather than only pushing back. A director hears no very differently from here is a cheaper plan that addresses more of our actual downtime, and here is what would change my mind. Coming with incident data rather than opinion is what makes it land.

What if the director has already promised the number externally?

Then say what it would genuinely take, honestly and without hedging: the cost, the timeline, the operational maturity required, and the fact that it must be rehearsed to be real. Sometimes the right outcome is building it because a commitment exists — that is a legitimate business reason. What is not acceptable is agreeing to a number nobody has a plan to verify, because the first regional event turns that into a much worse conversation.

Is there a middle option?

Yes, and it is often the right answer: multi-region for the read path and single-region for writes. Static assets, cached content and read-only APIs served from both regions gives you real availability improvement for the majority of traffic and for the majority of failure modes, at a fraction of the cost and none of the write-consistency complexity. It is worth offering explicitly, because it frequently satisfies the underlying concern.

Design round: the incident

Post-incident: your assistant told 400 merchants an incorrect fee amount. Run the review. What went wrong and what changes?

Must coverTimeline first, blame never. Likely chain: a fee schedule document was updated, re-embedding failed silently, retrieval returned the stale chunk, and the model answered confidently because the stale text was internally consistent. Contributing factors: no freshness monitoring on the index, no alert on ingest failure, and fee amounts coming from retrieved text rather than from the fee service. Changes, in order of value: numbers must come from a typed tool call against the system of record, not from a document - that single change makes the class of failure impossible. Then ingest failure alerting, an index freshness SLO, and an eval case for stale content. Also the communication path: how you detected it (a merchant complained) is itself a finding.

StudyAnthropic - reduce hallucinations →

3am: the cluster is up, pods are Running, but 60% of requests return 502. Talk me through it live.

Must cover502 from the ingress means the proxy could not get a valid response from the backend - so the failure is between ingress and pod, not in the client. Check ingress controller logs first for the upstream error: connection refused (endpoints point at pods not listening), timeout (backend slow), or reset. Then check whether Endpoints and EndpointSlices match the pods you expect - Running is not Ready, and a readiness probe passing on a pod whose dependency is broken produces exactly this. 60% suggests a subset: compare the failing endpoints against a deploy, a node, or an AZ. Most likely causes in order: a partial rollout where new pods are Ready but broken, a downstream dependency timing out beyond the proxy timeout, and connection pool exhaustion. Mitigate by rolling back first, diagnose after.

An AWS AZ is impaired - not down, just degraded with elevated latency and packet loss. Why is this harder than a clean failure, and what do you do?

Must coverHarder because nothing is unambiguously dead: health checks flap, some requests succeed slowly, retries amplify load, and automated failover oscillates. Clean failures are easy; gray failures are the ones that cause long incidents. What you do: detect with client-side and cross-zone metrics rather than the impaired zone's own health checks, since a degraded component often reports itself healthy. AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Timeline first, blame never. Open by establishing what happened and when, not who did what — and say that explicitly, because a review that becomes an inquest stops producing information.

The likely chain, reconstructed from the trace: a fee schedule document was updated at source; the re-embedding job failed and failed silently; retrieval continued returning the previous version's chunk; the model answered confidently because the stale text was internally consistent — there was nothing for it to be suspicious about; and 400 merchants received a correct-sounding answer with an obsolete number.

Contributing factors, which is where the real findings are. No monitoring on index freshness, so a stale index was indistinguishable from a current one. No alert on ingest failure, so a job that stopped working produced no signal at all. And — the structural one — fee amounts were coming from retrieved document text rather than from the fee service.

The changes, in order of value. First and by a wide margin: numbers must come from a typed tool call against the system of record, not from a retrieved document. The model narrates figures it was given; it never reads them out of prose. That single change makes this entire class of failure impossible, not less likely — a stale document can no longer produce a wrong number, because no number ever comes from a document.

Then the detection layer: alert on any ingest failure (non-zero is a human's problem), an index freshness SLO — no document more than N hours behind source — monitored rather than assumed, and per-source chunk-count and average-length checks that catch a parser breaking. Then a permanent eval case for stale content.

And the detection finding itself is a finding. How did we learn about this? A merchant complained. That means the system had no way to notice it was wrong, and the mean time to detection was days. That deserves as much attention as the root cause, because the next silent failure will be different but the blindness will be the same.

Close with the follow-through: who was affected, what the correction and communication path is, and — the part reviews often skip — an owner and a date for each action, because a post-incident review whose actions are not tracked produces the same incident again.

The change that makes the class impossible, not less likely
TIMELINE (blame never)
  Aug 12 09:14  fee schedule updated at source (v12 -> v13)
  Aug 12 09:20  re-embedding job failed. Exit non-zero. NO ALERT.
  Aug 12 09:20  retrieval continues serving v12 chunks
  Aug 12 - 20   ~400 merchants ask about fees; each receives a confident,
                internally consistent, OBSOLETE answer
  Aug 20 15:40  a merchant complains        <-- MTTD: 8 DAYS
  Aug 20 16:10  index freshness checked manually; stale index confirmed

ROOT CAUSE + CONTRIBUTING FACTORS
  root        fee amounts were read from RETRIEVED DOCUMENT TEXT
  contributing  no alert on ingest failure
                no index freshness monitoring
                nothing for the model to be suspicious about - stale text is
                internally consistent

ACTIONS, in order of value
1  NUMBERS COME FROM A TOOL CALL, NOT FROM A DOCUMENT       owner: X, by: Sep 5
     var fees = feeService.schedule(merchantId, asOf);   // system of record
     var text = model.narrate(factSheet(fees), policyChunks);
     // the model narrates figures it was GIVEN; it never reads them out of prose
     -> makes this ENTIRE CLASS of failure IMPOSSIBLE, not less likely.
        A stale document can no longer produce a wrong number.

2  alert on ANY ingest failure (non-zero = a human's problem)   owner: Y, by: Sep 1
3  INDEX FRESHNESS SLO: no doc > 6h behind source, monitored    owner: Y, by: Sep 8
4  per-source chunk_count + avg_chunk_length checks             owner: Y, by: Sep 8
     (catches a parser breaking when a partner changes a template)
5  permanent eval case: stale/superseded content                owner: X, by: Sep 5
6  affected-merchant list + correction + comms                  owner: Z, by: Aug 22

THE DETECTION FINDING - as important as the root cause
  "how did we learn about this?"  -> a merchant complained. MTTD 8 days.
  the system had NO WAY to notice it was wrong.
  the next silent failure will be different; the BLINDNESS will be the same.

# a review whose actions have no owner and no date produces the same incident

Follow-ups they will ask

Should the model have caught that the number was stale?

No, and expecting it to is the wrong lesson. The retrieved text was internally consistent and gave no signal of being superseded — a human reading the same chunk would have made the same error. Designing around the model should have noticed produces fragile systems. Designing so the number cannot come from a document produces a robust one.

What if some numbers genuinely only exist in documents?

Then attach an effective-date filter so only the version in force is retrievable, surface the document version and date in the answer so the user can see what it is quoting, and add a freshness assertion — refuse to answer with a document older than a threshold rather than answering confidently from it. It is weaker than a tool call, so treat it as a gap to close by getting that data into a service.

How do you find the 400 affected merchants?

From the audit trace: every interaction records the retrieved chunk ids and versions, so you query for interactions between the two timestamps that cited fees-guide@v12. That is precisely why chunk ids and versions belong in the audit record — without them, the blast radius is unknowable and you either over-communicate to everyone or under-communicate to the people affected.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

502 from the ingress means the proxy could not get a valid response from a backend — so the failure is between the ingress and the pod, not in the client and not (yet) proven to be in the application. Establishing that immediately narrows the search, and stating it first is what makes this sound like someone who has done it.

Check the ingress controller logs first, because they name the upstream error and that distinguishes the three main causes: connection refused means the endpoint points at a pod that is not listening; upstream timed out means the backend is slow rather than dead; connection reset usually means a keep-alive race or the pod dying mid-request.

Then reconcile pods with endpoints, because Running is not Ready, and only Ready pods are in EndpointSlices. The classic shape of this incident is a pod that is Running and passing a shallow readiness probe while its actual dependency is broken — so the ingress routes to it and gets a failure.

60% is the most informative fact in the question. It means a subset, and a subset points at a partial rollout. Six pods, four of them new and broken, and traffic distributed roughly evenly gives you exactly that ratio. So: check whether a rollout is in progress or recently completed, and compare the failing endpoints against the new ReplicaSet. That is usually the whole diagnosis.

Ranked causes: a partial rollout where new pods are Ready but broken — a readiness probe too shallow to catch the failure; a downstream dependency timing out beyond the proxy's read timeout; connection pool or thread pool exhaustion, so some requests are served and some queue past the timeout; and the keep-alive race where the pod's idle timeout is shorter than the proxy's, so reused connections are closed mid-request.

Mitigate first, diagnose after. If a rollout is implicated, kubectl rollout undo — it is fast, safe because the previous ReplicaSet is retained, and it eliminates one variable in about a minute. Capture a describe and the logs of a failing pod before rolling back, because that evidence disappears with the pods.

And say the 3am framing explicitly: restore service, then understand it. The root cause keeps until morning; the users do not.

502 is between ingress and pod — and 60% means a subset
# 1. WHAT KIND of 502? The controller log names the upstream error.
kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deploy/ingress-nginx-controller | grep 502 | tail
  "connect() failed (111: Connection refused)"  -> endpoint points at a pod
                                                   that is NOT listening
  "upstream timed out (110)"                    -> backend SLOW, not dead
  "upstream prematurely closed connection"      -> keep-alive race, or the pod
                                                   died mid-request

# 2. Running != Ready. Only READY pods are in EndpointSlices.
kubectl get pods -n payments -o wide
kubectl get endpointslices -n payments -l kubernetes.io/service-name=payments-api   -o custom-columns=ENDPOINTS:.endpoints[*].addresses,READY:.endpoints[*].conditions.ready

# 3. 60% IS THE MOST INFORMATIVE FACT - it means a SUBSET.
kubectl rollout status deploy/payments-api -n payments
kubectl get rs -n payments --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -3
#   6 pods: 4 new (broken but READY), 2 old (fine)
#   -> traffic spread evenly gives ~60-65% failures. That is the diagnosis.
#   Compare failing endpoint IPs against the NEW ReplicaSet's pods.

# RANKED CAUSES
1  partial rollout, new pods READY BUT BROKEN
     -> readiness probe too shallow to catch the actual failure
2  downstream dependency timing out beyond the proxy read timeout
3  connection/thread pool exhaustion: some served, some queue past the timeout
     kubectl exec <pod> -- curl -s localhost:9090/actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.pending
4  KEEP-ALIVE RACE: pod idle timeout < proxy idle timeout
     -> proxy reuses a connection the pod is closing -> intermittent 502
     FIX: server.tomcat.keep-alive-timeout MUST exceed the proxy's

# 4. CAPTURE EVIDENCE, THEN MITIGATE
kubectl describe pod <failing-new-pod> -n payments > /tmp/incident.txt
kubectl logs <failing-new-pod> -n payments --previous >> /tmp/incident.txt
kubectl rollout undo deploy/payments-api -n payments     # fast, safe, ~1 min
#   the previous ReplicaSet is retained; undo just scales it back up

# 3AM FRAMING - say it out loud
#   RESTORE SERVICE, THEN UNDERSTAND IT.
#   The root cause keeps until morning. The users do not.
#   Rolling back is the cheapest experiment available and removes one variable.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if there was no rollout and it is still 60%?

Then look for another dimension that splits the fleet: a node (one node's pods failing points at a node-level problem — disk pressure, a networking issue, a bad kubelet), an availability zone (a cross-AZ dependency or an impaired zone), or a shard of the data (some requests hit a broken partition or a failing replica). The principle is the same — find the dimension that separates the working 40% from the failing 60%, because that dimension is the cause.

Why not just delete the failing pods?

Because the Deployment recreates them from the same broken spec and you have achieved nothing except losing the evidence. Deleting pods is a reasonable action when the pods are individually bad (a stuck process, a corrupted local state) and the spec is fine. When a rollout is implicated, the fix is at the ReplicaSet level — roll back — not at the pod level.

How would you prevent this specific incident?

A readiness probe deep enough to catch the actual failure, so broken pods never become Ready and the rollout stalls instead of serving errors — that is the mechanism that was supposed to work here. Plus maxUnavailable: 0 with a canary step and automated analysis, so the rollout aborts on error rate rather than proceeding to 60% of the fleet. Both are configuration, and both would have contained this to a handful of requests.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

A gray failure is harder than a clean one because nothing is unambiguously dead — and that ambiguity is the whole problem. Health checks flap rather than fail; some requests succeed slowly; retries amplify load onto the impaired path; and automated failover oscillates because the thing it is checking keeps recovering just enough. Clean failures are easy and automation handles them. Gray failures are what produce the long, confusing incidents.

The specific trap: the impaired component often reports itself healthy. An instance whose network path is degraded still passes a local health check, because the check runs on the instance and does not traverse the impaired path. So the very signal you would use to detect the problem is generated inside the failure domain. That is the core insight and it drives the detection strategy.

So detect from outside. Use client-side and cross-zone metrics: success rate and latency measured by callers, broken down by target availability zone. If callers in zone A see 8% errors talking to zone B while zone B's own health checks are green, that comparison is your detection. AWS also surfaces this as zonal impairment signals, and the ALB's per-AZ metrics plus access logs grouped by target AZ will show it directly.

Then evacuate deliberately rather than waiting for convergence. Route 53 Application Recovery Controller zonal shift is the purpose-built mechanism — one API call moves traffic away from an availability zone at the load balancer, and it is reversible with an expiry so it cannot be forgotten. Failing that, remove the subnet from the target group or scale that zone's capacity to zero. The point is that a human makes a deliberate decision, because automation based on flapping health checks will not converge.

Two things must be true for that to be safe. First, retries must have jitter and a budget, or the impairment triggers a retry storm that amplifies load and turns partial degradation into total failure. Second, the remaining zones must have capacity — which is the n-1 sizing question made concrete: if you are sized for exactly three zones' worth of traffic across three zones, evacuating one means the other two are immediately overloaded and you have converted a gray failure into a clean outage of your own making.

And the general principle worth stating: design for evacuation as a routine operation. If shifting away from a zone is a rehearsed, one-command action, gray failures become manageable. If it is an improvisation, they become multi-hour incidents.

Detect from outside; evacuate deliberately
WHY GRAY IS HARDER THAN DEAD
  health checks FLAP        -> automated failover oscillates
  some requests succeed     -> "is it even broken?" costs 40 minutes
  retries amplify load      -> partial degradation becomes total failure
  THE TRAP: the impaired component reports ITSELF healthy, because the check
            runs inside the failure domain and never traverses the bad path.

DETECT FROM OUTSIDE - the only reliable signal
# ALB access logs in Athena, grouped by TARGET AZ
SELECT target_az,
       approx_percentile(target_processing_time, 0.99) AS p99,
       sum(CASE WHEN elb_status_code >= '500' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0
         / count(*) AS error_rate,
       count(*) AS reqs
FROM alb_logs WHERE day = '2026/08/29' AND hour >= 14
GROUP BY target_az;
--  eu-west-1a  p99 0.09  err 0.001   412,000
--  eu-west-1b  p99 2.80  err 0.081    98,000   <-- impaired, and its OWN
--  eu-west-1c  p99 0.11  err 0.001   408,000       health checks are GREEN

# plus: client-side success rate by target AZ, emitted by CALLERS
#       (a caller in 1a seeing 8% errors to 1b IS the detection)

EVACUATE DELIBERATELY - do not wait for automation to converge
aws arc-zonal-shift start-zonal-shift   --resource-identifier <alb-arn>   --away-from euw1-az2   --expires-in 3h   --comment "gray failure: elevated latency + packet loss"
# reversible, and it EXPIRES so it cannot be forgotten

# fallbacks if ARC is unavailable:
#   detach the subnet from the target group
#   set that AZ's ASG desired capacity to 0

TWO THINGS MUST BE TRUE FOR THIS TO BE SAFE
1  retries have JITTER and a BUDGET
     without: the impairment triggers a retry storm that amplifies load and
              turns partial degradation into total failure
     RetryPolicy.maxAttempts(2).backoff(exponentialWithFullJitter(...))
2  the REMAINING ZONES HAVE CAPACITY  <-- n-1 sizing, made concrete
     sized for exactly 3 zones' traffic across 3 zones?
     -> evacuating one overloads the other two
     -> you converted a gray failure into a clean outage of your own making

PRINCIPLE
  design for EVACUATION AS A ROUTINE OPERATION.
  rehearsed and one command -> gray failures are manageable.
  improvised -> they are multi-hour incidents.
Follow-ups they will ask

How do you distinguish a gray failure from your own bug?

By the dimension that separates working from failing. If failures correlate with a target availability zone and nothing else — same code, same version, same tenants, same routes — it is infrastructure. If they correlate with a deploy, a tenant, or a route, it is yours. That is why grouping ALB logs by target AZ is the first query: it answers the infrastructure-versus-application question in one step, and getting that fork right saves the most time.

Should zonal shift be automated?

AWS offers zonal autoshift, where AWS itself shifts traffic away from a zone it detects as impaired, and for well-architected multi-AZ workloads it is worth enabling — AWS often sees the impairment before you do. The prerequisite is honest: you must genuinely be able to serve from n-1 zones, and you must have practised it. Enabling autoshift on a fleet sized for exactly three zones converts an AWS-detected impairment into your outage.

What if the impaired zone holds your database primary?

Then evacuating compute does not help — the writes still cross into the impaired zone, and you may be better failing the database over deliberately than leaving it degraded. That is a judgement call with a real cost: an RDS failover is 60–120 seconds of full unavailability against continued degradation of unknown duration. Decide the threshold in advance and put it in the runbook, because it is not a decision to reason about for the first time at 3am.

45 minutes, one question: design a fraud-review copilot for internal analysts. Do the whole round properly - and narrate how you are allocating the time.

Say the tradeoffs out loud and write the numbers down; a silent design round scores badly regardless of the design.

StudyAnthropic - building effective agents →

Same 45 minutes: design the deployment and runtime platform for it on Kubernetes, assuming a Software Engineer audience who will ask why at every step.

Must coverNamespace with quota and default-deny NetworkPolicy; Deployment with requests equal to limits for the API tier; readiness probe on a shallow endpoint plus a startup probe for the JVM; HPA on in-flight requests via a custom metric, not CPU; topology spread across three AZs plus a PDB of maxUnavailable 1; IRSA for AWS access with no static credentials; secrets via the CSI driver; ingress with TLS from cert-manager; Argo Rollouts canary with automated analysis on error rate and latency; OTel agent injected by the platform. For each, be ready with the concrete failure it prevents - that is what why at every step is testing.

StudyKubernetes - production best practices →

Same 45 minutes: the AWS bill for this system. Estimate it from first principles and identify the top three line items before you look at a price list.

Must coverReason in units first: requests per day, tokens per request, gigabytes stored, gigabytes transferred, instance-hours. For an internal copilot with 200 analysts and 100 cases a day each, the model spend dominates and is computed directly from tokens. Second is compute, which for 20k requests a day is small - single-digit instances, so the interesting question is whether the baseline is right-sized rather than the peak. Third is usually data transfer and logging, not storage. Say the top three before pricing: model tokens, compute baseline, observability. Then sanity-check the total against a per-user-per-month figure, because that is the number a director will actually ask for, and being able to produce it is the point of the exercise.
