AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Narrate the time allocation out loud at the start. That is itself a scored behaviour — it tells the interviewer you have run these rounds and it gives them a chance to redirect you before you spend ten minutes in the wrong place.

0–5 requirements. Who uses it — fraud analysts reviewing flagged cases, not customers. How many cases a day. What decision it supports — approve, decline, escalate. And explicitly what it must never do: it recommends, it never blocks a transaction alone. Stating the non-goal unprompted is one of the strongest signals available in a design round, because it shows you understand where the risk sits.

5–10 numbers. 40 analysts, 60 cases each a day is 2,400 cases — trivial QPS, so this is not a throughput problem. It is a quality, latency-per-case and trust problem. Say that conclusion; deriving numbers and not using them is a common miss.

10–20 architecture. Case context assembly from transaction, device, velocity and history services — plain code, parallelised. Retrieval over prior similar cases and fraud policy. A generation step producing a structured recommendation with evidence links, not prose. The analyst's action captured as a label. And a rendering layer that shows the evidence alongside the recommendation.

20–35 deep dive, wherever they push — usually evidence grounding or the feedback loop. For grounding: every claim in the recommendation cites a specific signal with a value and a source, and figures come from tool calls rather than generated text, so an analyst can verify in seconds. For the feedback loop: the analyst's decision plus their agreement or disagreement with the recommendation is the highest-quality training and eval data you will ever get, and capturing it is nearly free at the point of decision.

35–45 failure, cost, evaluation, rollout. Fallback to the existing case view. Cost trivial at this volume. Evaluation split into recommendation accuracy against analyst decisions, and — the more important one — whether analysts are faster and no less accurate, because the product goal is throughput per analyst at constant quality.

And the two behavioural points that decide the round: say the tradeoffs out loud, and write the numbers down where the interviewer can see them. A silent design round scores badly regardless of the design.

45 minutes, narrated, with the non-goal stated first
0-5    REQUIREMENTS
  users      fraud analysts reviewing flagged cases (NOT customers)
  decision   approve | decline | escalate
  MUST NEVER it RECOMMENDS. It never blocks a transaction alone.
             <-- state the non-goal UNPROMPTED. Strongest signal available.
  success    analyst throughput UP, decision quality NOT DOWN

5-10   NUMBERS
  40 analysts x 60 cases/day = 2,400 cases/day = ~0.05 QPS
  -> NOT a throughput problem. It is QUALITY, LATENCY PER CASE, and TRUST.
  latency budget: analyst opens a case -> recommendation visible < 3s
                  (longer and they start working without it)

10-20  ARCHITECTURE
  case opened
    -> CONTEXT ASSEMBLY (plain code, parallel calls)
         transaction | device fingerprint | velocity counters | customer history
         | prior cases for this merchant
    -> RETRIEVAL: similar prior cases (with their OUTCOMES) + fraud policy
    -> GENERATION: STRUCTURED recommendation, not prose
         record Recommendation(
             Action suggested,           // APPROVE | DECLINE | ESCALATE
             double confidence,
             List<Evidence> supporting,  // each: signal, VALUE, SOURCE, link
             List<Evidence> contradicting) {}   // <-- both sides. Trust.
    -> RENDER: evidence beside the recommendation, every value clickable
    -> CAPTURE: analyst's action + agree/disagree with the recommendation

20-35  DEEP DIVE (have both ready)
  GROUNDING   every claim cites a signal with a VALUE and a SOURCE
              figures come from TOOL CALLS, never generated
              -> an analyst verifies in seconds, which is what earns trust
  FEEDBACK    analyst decision + agreement flag = the highest-quality eval and
              training data you will ever get, captured free at the point of
              decision. This is the flywheel.

35-45  FAILURE / COST / EVAL / ROLLOUT
  fallback    model unavailable -> the existing case view, unchanged
  cost        2,400 cases/day: trivial. Do not over-engineer it.
  eval        (a) recommendation vs analyst decision - agreement rate
              (b) THE ONE THAT MATTERS: are analysts FASTER at EQUAL accuracy?
                  measure cases/hour and post-hoc decision quality, A/B
  rollout     shadow (recommendation computed, NOT shown) -> compare against
              analyst decisions for 2 weeks -> then show to 5 analysts -> all

# TWO BEHAVIOURS THAT DECIDE THE ROUND
#   say the TRADEOFFS out loud
#   WRITE THE NUMBERS DOWN where the interviewer can see them
# A silent design round scores badly regardless of the design.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why show contradicting evidence?

Because a recommendation that only argues one side trains analysts to either rubber-stamp it or ignore it, and both destroy the value. Showing what points the other way keeps the analyst engaged in the decision, makes the recommendation feel like a colleague's opinion rather than an oracle, and is honest about uncertainty. It also gives you a much better signal when they disagree, because you can see which evidence they weighted differently.

What is the risk of automation bias here?

That analysts stop genuinely reviewing and defer to the recommendation, so the system's errors become the organisation's errors at scale. Mitigations: show contradicting evidence, do not show a confidence number so precise it implies false authority, randomly withhold the recommendation on a small percentage of cases and compare decision quality, and monitor agreement rate — an agreement rate approaching 100% means analysts have stopped thinking, not that the model is perfect.

How would you know it is actually working?

Not by recommendation accuracy alone. The product metric is cases resolved per analyst-hour at constant or better decision quality, measured against a control group. If analysts are faster but their decisions are worse, the feature is harmful and the accuracy metric would have hidden that. Design the A/B before building, because retrofitting a control group after full rollout is impossible.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The audience matters: they will ask why at every step, so every field needs the concrete failure it prevents attached to it. Reciting a manifest without those reasons is exactly what this round is testing for.

Namespace with a ResourceQuota, RBAC bound to the team's group, and a default-deny NetworkPolicy plus an explicit DNS allow — because Kubernetes networking is flat by default and a namespace is not a network boundary until you make it one.

Deployment with requests equal to limits on memory for the API tier — memory is incompressible, so exceeding the limit is an instant OOM kill and there is no benefit to bursting; equal values also give Guaranteed QoS so the pod is evicted last. CPU request from observed p95, and a deliberate choice on the CPU limit: omitted for this latency-sensitive path, because CFS throttling produces latency spikes with no errors and nothing in the logs.

Readiness probe on a shallow endpoint plus a startup probe. Readiness gates traffic and gates the rollout — without it a rolling update replaces every healthy pod with a broken one at full speed. The startup probe gives the JVM time to boot so liveness can then run with a tight threshold, rather than choosing between slow-start tolerance and fast failure detection.

Liveness shallow and local, on a separate management port. A liveness probe that checks the database means one database blip restarts the entire fleet simultaneously — turning a degraded dependency into a total outage.

HPA on in-flight requests, not CPU, because this service is IO-bound: under overload it is blocked on the database while CPU sits at 25%, so a CPU-based policy never fires and the service degrades without scaling.

Topology spread across three zones plus a PodDisruptionBudget of maxUnavailable: 1 — spread so a zone loss costs a third of capacity, and the PDB so a node drain during a cluster upgrade cannot take the service down.

IRSA so there is no static AWS credential anywhere, and secrets via the CSI driver so rotation happens outside the cluster. Ingress with TLS from cert-manager. Argo Rollouts canary with automated analysis against Prometheus, so a bad deploy aborts on error rate without a human watching. OTel agent injected by the platform, so tracing needs no code change.

And the two that get skipped: a preStop sleep, because endpoint removal and SIGTERM race and traffic hits a closing listener otherwise; and securityContext with non-root, read-only root filesystem and all capabilities dropped.

Every field, with the failure it prevents
FIELD                        PREVENTS
namespace + quota + RBAC     one team exhausting the cluster; over-broad access
default-deny NetworkPolicy   flat networking: any pod can reach any pod
  + allow DNS                (forgetting DNS breaks everything - the classic)
memory request == limit      OOM kill with no benefit to bursting; Guaranteed
                             QoS -> evicted LAST
CPU request from p95,        CFS throttling: latency spikes, NO errors,
  NO CPU limit (deliberate)  NOTHING in the logs
startupProbe                 JVM boot time vs fast failure detection - without
                             it you must choose one
readinessProbe (shallow)     GATES THE ROLLOUT. Without it a rolling update
                             replaces every healthy pod with a broken one at
                             full speed
livenessProbe SHALLOW+LOCAL  a DB-checking liveness probe restarts the ENTIRE
  on port 9090               FLEET during one database blip -> degraded
                             dependency becomes total outage
topologySpread 3 zones       a zone loss costs 1/3 of capacity, not all of it
PodDisruptionBudget          a node drain during a cluster upgrade taking the
  maxUnavailable: 1          service down
HPA on in-flight requests    IO-bound service: CPU sits at 25% under overload,
  NOT CPU                    so a CPU policy never fires
preStop: sleep 10            endpoint removal races SIGTERM -> traffic hits a
                             closing listener -> 502s on every deploy
terminationGrace 45s         SIGKILL mid-drain
securityContext              container escape lands as root; attacker drops a
  nonRoot/readOnly/drop ALL  binary and persists
ServiceAccount + IRSA        a static AWS credential existing anywhere
secrets via CSI driver       rotation inside the cluster; secrets in git
Ingress + cert-manager       manual certificate rotation, expiry outages
Argo Rollouts + analysis     a bad deploy reaching 100% because no human was
                             watching the dashboard
OTel agent (platform-injected) twelve codebases each instrumenting differently

# The two most often skipped, and both cause visible user impact:
#   preStop sleep       -> a burst of 502s on EVERY deploy that nobody explains
#   readiness probe     -> converts a failed deploy into an outage

# Say each REASON, not each FIELD. The manifest is not the answer;
# the failure each line prevents is the answer.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why omit the CPU limit — is that not irresponsible?

It is a deliberate, current position rather than an omission, and I would say so. CPU is compressible, so the request already guarantees your share under contention; the limit only adds throttling, which for a latency-sensitive service costs p99 with no reliability gain. I would still set a generous limit for batch and untrusted workloads, where a runaway process monopolising spare capacity is a real risk. The key is that it is a choice with a reason, not a missing field.

What would you add for a payments service specifically?

An idempotency mechanism before anything writes money — that sits above Kubernetes but belongs in the answer. Then admission policies enforcing image provenance and digest pinning, an audit log of Secret access shipped off-cluster, and a NetworkPolicy that explicitly denies egress except to the endpoints the service needs. In a regulated context, the ability to evidence those controls continuously matters as much as having them.

How do you make sure twelve services actually have all of this?

Not by review. Put it in a Kustomize base or Helm chart that every service inherits, and enforce the non-negotiable parts at admission with Kyverno — no resource requests, no securityContext, no digest, rejected. Then a manifest missing a probe is a build failure rather than something a reviewer might notice on a Friday afternoon.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Reason in units first, before touching a price list — that is the discipline the question is testing, and it also produces a number that survives price changes.

The units: requests per day, tokens per request, gigabytes stored, gigabytes transferred, instance-hours. For an internal copilot with 200 analysts and 100 cases a day each, that is 20,000 requests a day — trivial QPS — with roughly 6,000 input and 400 output tokens per request.

Now name the top three before pricing anything, because that prediction is the skill: model tokens, compute baseline, observability. Not storage — the data is small. Not data transfer — it is internal.

Model tokens dominate and are computed directly: 20,000 × 6,400 tokens is 128 million tokens a day, and output is priced several times higher per token than input, so the 8 million output tokens carry disproportionate weight. This is the line to optimise: prompt caching on the stable prefix, a small model for classification and retrieval query rewriting, and a capped output length.

Compute for 20,000 requests a day is small — single-digit instances or a handful of Fargate tasks. So the interesting question is not can it handle peak but is the baseline right-sized, since you are paying for idle capacity most of the day. That is a different optimisation from a high-throughput service and worth calling out.

Observability is third and it surprises people: full prompt-and-response traces at 20,000 a day is roughly 500MB a day before tool calls, and CloudWatch Logs with no retention set accrues indefinitely. Tiered retention and sampling handle it.

Then sanity-check the total against a per-user-per-month figure, because that is the number a director will actually ask for and it is the one that makes the estimate legible. Being able to say about £X per analyst per month, against a fully-loaded cost of £Y is what turns a technical estimate into a business conversation — and it is the point of the exercise.

Finally, close the loop: state the largest uncertainty. Here it is tokens per request, since retrieval size drives it and a design change that retrieves twenty chunks instead of five triples the dominant line item. Name the sensitivity rather than presenting a single confident number.

Units first, top three predicted, then a per-user figure
UNITS FIRST - before any price list
  200 analysts x 100 cases/day       = 20,000 requests/day
  tokens per request                 ~6,000 in / 400 out
  storage (cases + index)            ~50 GB
  data transfer                       internal, negligible
  compute                             ~0.25 QPS  -> tiny

PREDICT THE TOP THREE BEFORE PRICING  <-- this is the skill being tested
  1. MODEL TOKENS      dominant, and computed directly
  2. COMPUTE BASELINE  small, but you pay for idle most of the day
  3. OBSERVABILITY     surprises people
  NOT storage (small). NOT data transfer (internal).

1. MODEL TOKENS
   20,000 x 6,000 in  = 120 M input tokens/day
   20,000 x   400 out =   8 M output tokens/day
   output is priced SEVERAL TIMES higher per token -> it carries
   disproportionate weight despite being 6% of the volume
   LEVERS: prompt caching on the stable prefix (system + tools + policy)
           small model for classification and query rewriting
           cap max_tokens

2. COMPUTE
   0.25 QPS average, business-hours peak maybe 2 QPS
   -> 2-4 Fargate tasks, or a small ECS service
   THE QUESTION IS NOT "can it handle peak" - it is "is the BASELINE
   right-sized", because you pay for idle most of the day.
   (a different optimisation from a high-throughput service)

3. OBSERVABILITY
   full traces: ~25 KB x 20,000 = ~500 MB/day, before tool calls
   CloudWatch Logs default retention = NEVER EXPIRE
   -> tier it: 100% of failures 90d | 5% of successes 30d | minimal record forever

SANITY CHECK - the number a director will actually ask for
  total / 200 analysts / month  = cost per analyst per month
  compare against a fully-loaded analyst cost
  -> "about GBP X per analyst per month, against a fully-loaded cost of GBP Y"
  THIS is what turns a technical estimate into a business conversation,
  and it is the point of the exercise.

STATE THE LARGEST UNCERTAINTY - do not present one confident number
  TOKENS PER REQUEST. Retrieval size drives it.
  retrieve 20 chunks instead of 5 -> the dominant line item TRIPLES.
  -> quote a range, and name the design decision that moves it.
Follow-ups they will ask

Why estimate in units rather than looking up prices?

Because the units are stable and the prices are not, and because the units tell you which lever matters. Knowing that output tokens are 6% of volume but a large share of cost immediately tells you to cap output length rather than trim retrieval. An estimate built from a price list gives you a number; an estimate built from units gives you a plan.

What if the estimate comes out higher than expected?

Go back to the units and find which one is large, then attack that specifically — usually tokens per request, driven by retrieval size or an oversized system prompt. Present the optimised estimate alongside the naive one so the saving is visible, and be honest about what it costs in quality. What you should not do is quietly change the design to hit a number and not say so.

How do you account for growth?

Model it as a multiplier on the driving unit, not on the total — if adoption doubles, requests double and model cost doubles, but compute may not because you were paying for idle. Show two or three scenarios rather than a single figure, and identify the point at which a different architecture becomes worthwhile (batching, caching, a fine-tuned small model). That forward-looking sensitivity is usually what the question is really probing.

Rapid-fire definitions, your own experience told well, two full mocks, the pushback round, and the questions you ask them.

The last six days are rehearsal, not study. If something here is still shaky, that is your signal - go back to the specific day rather than re-reading everything.

AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The skill here is compression, not knowledge. You know all of these; the test is whether you can deliver each in one clean definition plus one sentence of why it matters, and then stop. A screen that spends four minutes on the first definition never reaches the interesting questions, and the interviewer forms a view about your communication rather than your depth.

The shape for every answer: definition, then consequence, then silence. The silence is the hard part — resist the urge to add the caveat you know. If they want depth they will ask, and being asked is a better signal than volunteering.

Token — a subword unit of text, typically about four characters in English. It is the unit of billing, of the context limit and of generation time, so every cost and latency decision is denominated in tokens.

Embedding — a fixed-length vector where distance approximates semantic similarity. It lets you search by meaning rather than by keyword, which is what makes retrieval over paraphrased questions work.

RAG — retrieve relevant text and put it in the prompt. It fixes knowledge the model does not have, keeps it fresh, and gives you citations, all without retraining.

Context window — the maximum sequence the model can attend over, shared between the prompt and the output. It is a budget, so retrieved context competes with room to answer.

Temperature — reshapes the probability distribution before sampling. Low sharpens toward the most likely token; use near zero for anything with a correct answer.

Tool call — the model emits a structured request to run a function; your code executes it and returns the result. That boundary is where every security control lives.

Agent — a model in a loop with tools, deciding its own next step. Use one only when the sequence genuinely cannot be known in advance; otherwise a workflow is testable and cheaper.

Grounding — every claim in the output is supported by supplied context or a tool result. It is the property you measure to detect hallucination.

Practise these out loud until they are automatic. Not read — spoken, timed. The gap between knowing a definition and delivering it crisply under pressure is real, and it is closed by rehearsal, not by more reading.

Definition, consequence, stop
RULE: one sentence defining it. One sentence on why it matters. STOP.
      Resist the caveat you know. If they want depth, they will ask -
      and being asked is a better signal than volunteering.

  so every cost and latency decision is denominated in tokens.

EMBEDDING

  It lets you search by meaning, which is why retrieval works on paraphrases
  that keyword search misses entirely.

RAG
  Retrieve relevant text and put it in the prompt.
  It fixes knowledge the model lacks, keeps it fresh, and gives you citations -
  without retraining anything.

  It is a budget: retrieved context competes with room to answer.

TEMPERATURE
  Reshapes the probability distribution before sampling; low sharpens toward
  the most likely token.
  Use near zero for anything with a correct answer - extraction, classification,
  structured output.

  and returns the result.

  the system decides.

Follow-ups they will ask

What if I genuinely need two sentences?

Then take two. The rule is not brevity for its own sake — it is finish the thought and stop. What loses points is trailing off into related material, hedging, or answering a follow-up nobody asked. A crisp two-sentence answer beats a rambling one-sentence answer that never quite lands.

What if I am asked one I only half know?

Say what you do know, mark the boundary explicitly, and stop. An embedding is a vector where distance means similarity; I have used them for retrieval but I have not worked with the training side. That is a strong answer. Bluffing past the boundary is the one thing that reliably damages a screen, because interviewers probe and the collapse is memorable.

Does this apply to the design round too?

The compression does, but the silence does not. In a rapid-fire screen you answer and stop; in a design round you are expected to narrate your reasoning, state tradeoffs, and think out loud. Reading which mode you are in matters — being terse in a design round reads as having no depth, and being expansive in a screen reads as being unable to prioritise.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Same discipline: one sentence of definition, one of consequence, then stop. These are the questions that gate a phone screen, and they are scored on crispness rather than depth.

Pod — the smallest schedulable unit: one or more containers sharing a network namespace and lifecycle. It exists because some processes must be co-located and share an IP; the default is one container per pod.

Deployment — declarative management of a ReplicaSet, giving rolling updates and rollback. It never touches pods directly; it creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts replicas between them.

Service — a stable virtual IP and DNS name load-balancing across a changing set of Ready pods. It decouples callers from pod churn, and only Ready pods receive traffic.

Ingress — HTTP routing into the cluster by host and path. It does nothing on its own; a controller watches it and programs a real proxy.

ConfigMap — non-sensitive configuration as key-value data. As env vars it is read once at start; as a mounted volume it updates in place.

Probe — readiness gates traffic, liveness gates restarts. That contrast is the whole answer, and it is the one they are listening for.

Request versus limit — the request is what the scheduler reserves, the limit is what the runtime enforces. Exceed memory and you are killed; exceed CPU and you are throttled.

PDB — a cap on voluntary disruption. It stops a node drain taking down your whole service, and it does not protect against a node crashing.

Taint — a property on a node that repels pods unless they tolerate it. It reserves nodes for specific workloads; a toleration only permits, it does not attract.

StatefulSet — stable ordinal identity, stable per-replica storage, ordered updates. It is for workloads where each replica has its own data and peers must find each other by name.

Then stop talking. The interviewer will ask for depth exactly where they want it, and letting them choose is both faster and a better signal than pre-empting.

Ten definitions, sixty seconds each

              Default is ONE container per pod.

DEPLOYMENT    declarative management of a ReplicaSet - rolling updates, rollback.
              Never touches pods directly: it creates a NEW ReplicaSet and
              shifts replicas between them.

SERVICE       stable virtual IP + DNS name, load-balancing across a changing
              set of READY pods.
              Only Ready pods receive traffic - that is the whole traffic
              management mechanism.

INGRESS       HTTP routing into the cluster, by host and path.
              Does NOTHING on its own - a controller watches it and programs
              a real proxy.

CONFIGMAP     non-sensitive configuration as key-value data.
              As env vars: read ONCE at start. As a volume: updates in place.

PROBE         READINESS GATES TRAFFIC. LIVENESS GATES RESTARTS.
              <-- that contrast IS the answer. It is what they are listening for.

REQUEST/LIMIT request = what the SCHEDULER reserves.
              limit   = what the RUNTIME enforces.
              Exceed memory -> KILLED. Exceed CPU -> THROTTLED.

PDB           a cap on VOLUNTARY disruption.
              Stops a node drain taking your whole service down.
              Does NOT protect against a node crashing.

TAINT         a property on a NODE that repels pods unless they tolerate it.
              Reserves nodes for specific workloads.
              A toleration only PERMITS - it does not ATTRACT. (You also need
              a nodeSelector.)

              For workloads where each replica has its OWN data and peers must

# The interviewer asks for depth exactly where they want it.
# Letting them choose is faster AND a better signal than pre-empting.
Follow-ups they will ask

Which of these do people most often get wrong?

The probe distinction, and requests versus limits. Both are frequently answered as vague synonyms — probes check health, requests and limits control resources — which reads as textbook familiarity without operational experience. The crisp contrasts (traffic versus restarts; scheduler versus runtime; killed versus throttled) immediately signal someone who has debugged these.

Should I mention the failure mode alongside each definition?

One, if it is short and it lands — liveness gates restarts, which is why a liveness probe that checks the database restarts your whole fleet during a database blip. That single clause demonstrates real experience in eight words. Do not do it for all ten; it turns a rapid-fire round into a monologue and you lose the crispness that was being tested.

What if I am asked to compare two of them?

Answer with the axis first, then the two positions. Deployment versus StatefulSet: the axis is identity. A Deployment's pods are interchangeable; a StatefulSet's have stable names and their own volumes. Leading with the axis makes the comparison legible in one sentence, where listing properties of each takes four and lands less clearly.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

These are fast-screen filter questions and they are effectively pass or fail on crispness. The pattern that scores: one contrast sentence, then the decision rule. The decision rule is the part that shows you have actually chosen between them in real work rather than read about both.

Region versus AZ — a region is a geographic area; an AZ is an independent failure domain inside it with its own power and cooling. Inter-AZ latency is about a millisecond, so synchronous replication across AZs is normal and across regions is not. Rule: multi-AZ always; multi-region only with a stated RTO and RPO or a residency requirement.

Role versus user — a user has permanent credentials; a role has none and is assumed, yielding short-lived tokens. Rule: applications and humans use roles; a long-lived access key is an exception that needs justification.

Security group versus NACL — security groups are stateful, attach to an ENI, allow-only, and can reference other security groups. NACLs are stateless, attach to a subnet, and support deny. Rule: default to security groups for everything; NACLs for a coarse subnet-level block.

SQS, SNS, EventBridge — SQS is a queue with per-message retry and a DLQ; SNS is fan-out filtered on attributes; EventBridge routes on the event body with archive and replay. Rule: EventBridge for domain events, with each consumer's rule targeting their own SQS queue.

ALB versus NLB — ALB is layer 7 with host and path routing and WAF; NLB is layer 4, preserves the source IP, and supports static IPs. Rule: ALB for HTTP; NLB when a partner must allowlist a fixed IP or the protocol is not HTTP.

S3 storage classes — they trade storage price against retrieval price and latency, with minimum durations. Rule: Intelligent-Tiering when the access pattern is unknown; lifecycle rules with a minimum object size, because transitions are billed per object.

Multi-AZ versus read replica — Multi-AZ is a synchronous, non-readable standby for failover; read replicas are asynchronous and readable for scale. Rule: Multi-AZ for availability, replicas for read scale, and expect lag to break read-your-own-writes.

Practise saying the decision rule, not just the contrast. Anyone can recite two definitions; the rule is what separates a candidate who has made the choice from one who has read the comparison table.

Contrast, then the decision rule
REGION vs AZ
  region = geographic area. AZ = independent failure domain inside it.
  Inter-AZ ~1ms -> sync replication is fine. Cross-region is not.
  RULE: multi-AZ ALWAYS. Multi-region only with a stated RTO/RPO or residency
        requirement.

IAM ROLE vs USER
  user = permanent credentials. role = no credentials, assumed, short-lived tokens.
  RULE: applications and humans use ROLES. A long-lived access key is an
        exception that needs justification.

SECURITY GROUP vs NACL
  SG  = stateful, on an ENI, allow-only, can REFERENCE other SGs.
  NACL= stateless, on a subnet, supports deny, numbered rules.
  RULE: default to security groups for everything. NACLs for a coarse
        subnet-level block during an incident.

SQS vs SNS vs EVENTBRIDGE
  SQS  = queue: one logical consumer, per-message retry, DLQ.
  SNS  = fan-out, filtered on message ATTRIBUTES, no retention.
  EB   = bus: routes on the event BODY, schema registry, archive + REPLAY.
  RULE: EventBridge for domain events, each consumer's rule targeting THEIR
        OWN SQS queue (that queue is the failure-isolation boundary).

ALB vs NLB
  ALB = L7: host/path routing, header rules, WAF, TLS termination.
  NLB = L4: preserves SOURCE IP, static/Elastic IPs, huge connection counts.
  RULE: ALB for HTTP. NLB when a partner must allowlist a fixed IP, or the
        protocol is not HTTP.

S3 STORAGE CLASSES
  trade storage price against RETRIEVAL price + latency, with minimum durations.
  RULE: Intelligent-Tiering when the access pattern is unknown. Lifecycle rules
        with a MINIMUM OBJECT SIZE filter - transitions are billed PER OBJECT.

RDS MULTI-AZ vs READ REPLICA
  Multi-AZ = SYNCHRONOUS standby, NOT READABLE, exists for failover (60-120s).
  replica  = ASYNCHRONOUS, readable, scales reads, LAGS.
  RULE: Multi-AZ for availability, replicas for read scale. Expect lag to break
        read-your-own-writes - route post-write reads to the writer.

# PRACTISE SAYING THE RULE, not just the contrast.
# Anyone can recite two definitions. The rule is what separates someone who
# has MADE the choice from someone who has read the comparison table.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if they push back on one of my rules?

Good — that is the interesting part of the conversation. Name the condition under which their position is right, then say why it does not apply here. You are right that NACLs give defence in depth, and I would use one on an isolated data subnet; for the app tier, security group references are self-maintaining under scaling and NACLs are not. Holding a position with a stated condition beats both caving and digging in.

Is it a problem if I do not know one of them?

Only if you bluff. I have not used Gateway Load Balancer in anger — my understanding is it transparently inserts third-party appliances into the traffic path, but I would not want to design with it without reading properly. That is a completely acceptable answer at Software Engineer and it costs nothing. Confidently wrong is what costs you the screen.

How much depth should the follow-up get?

Match their question. If they ask why, give the mechanism in two or three sentences. If they ask when have you used it, give a specific instance with the decision and the outcome. The failure mode is escalating a one-line follow-up into a five-minute answer — the screen has a fixed length, and time you spend over-answering is time not spent on questions you would score better on.

Most teams hiring a Software Engineer for a payments backend want someone who will make good decisions about where this technology fits, not someone who has already built three chatbots. Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Use situation, complication, investigation, resolution, and what changed afterwards — and spend most of the time on the investigation, because that is the part being assessed. Candidates routinely spend thirty seconds on how they found it and three minutes on the fix, which is backwards: the fix is usually obvious once you know the cause, and the interviewer is trying to learn how you think.

Situation — brief. What the system does and what the observable symptom was, in the words a user or an alert would have used.

Complication — why it was not obvious. Intermittent, only some users, nothing in the logs, healthy dashboards. This is what makes it worth telling.

Investigation — the substance. Name the hypotheses you formed, how you eliminated each, and the piece of evidence that changed the picture. Say what you measured, what you ruled out, and why that observation ruled it out. That reasoning is legible to an interviewer in a way that then I found the bug is not.

Include the wrong turn. An investigation with no dead end sounds rehearsed and slightly dishonest — real debugging has one. Saying I spent an hour convinced it was the database, because latency correlated, and it was actually connection pool exhaustion caused by a thread leak makes the whole story credible and shows you update on evidence.

Resolution — the immediate mitigation and then the actual fix, distinguished. Mitigating and fixing are different acts and knowing that matters.

What changed afterwards — the systemic fix and, crucially, the detection you added. Ending on and we added an alert on connection pool saturation, because we had no way to see it is what separates an engineer who fixes bugs from one who improves systems.

From your background, strong material: a Kafka consumer lag incident, connection pool exhaustion, a rolling deploy that dropped in-flight requests, or a memory leak found from a heap dump. The technology matters far less than whether your reasoning is legible — a well-told JDBC pool story beats a badly-told distributed systems story every time.

And keep it to five or six minutes. If they want more they will ask.

Most of the time on the investigation, and include the dead end
STRUCTURE - and the time allocation is the point

SITUATION (30s)
  "Settlement service, ~2,000 req/min. Support reported that some merchants
   saw timeouts, intermittently, mostly mid-morning."

COMPLICATION (30s)  - why it was not obvious
  "No errors in the application logs. CPU and memory flat. The database looked
   healthy. It affected maybe 5% of requests and it self-resolved within a
   few minutes each time."

INVESTIGATION (3 min)  <-- MOST OF THE TIME. This is what is being assessed.
  "First hypothesis: the database. Latency correlated with slow queries, so I
   looked at Performance Insights - top queries were unchanged and well under
   their normal timings. That ruled it out, but it cost me an hour.  <-- DEAD END

   Second: I looked at what was DIFFERENT about the failing requests. They
   were not a particular endpoint or merchant, but they clustered in TIME -
   bursts of 30-60 seconds.

   Third: I checked the connection pool metrics, which we were collecting but
   not alerting on. hikaricp.connections.pending spiked to 40+ during exactly
   those windows while active connections sat at the max of 20.

   So requests were queueing for a connection, not waiting on the database.
   Then: WHY was the pool exhausted at 2,000 req/min when it had been fine?
   A recent change added a call inside a transaction that made an outbound
   HTTP request to a partner. When the partner was slow, transactions held
   connections for seconds instead of milliseconds."

RESOLUTION (45s)  - distinguish MITIGATION from FIX
  "Mitigation: raised the pool size and added a timeout on the partner call,
   which stopped the bleeding within the hour.
   Fix: moved the partner call OUT of the transaction entirely - it did not
   need to be inside it - and made it asynchronous via the outbox."

WHAT CHANGED (45s)  <-- ends on systems, not on the bug
  "Two things. An alert on connection pool pending count, because we had the
   metric and no way to see it. And a review rule: no network call inside a
   database transaction. That second one has caught two more since."

# TOTAL: 5-6 minutes. If they want more, they will ask.
# INCLUDE THE DEAD END. An investigation with no wrong turn sounds rehearsed.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if my hardest bug was quite simple in the end?

That is fine and often better — the assessment is on the investigation, not on the exoticism of the cause. A simple root cause found through disciplined elimination tells a stronger story than an exotic one found by luck. What you should avoid is a story where the resolution was someone else fixed it or we restarted it and it went away, because neither demonstrates your reasoning.

Should I name the technology or keep it generic?

Name it. Specifics make the story credible — HikariCP, Kafka consumer groups, a particular metric name — and they give the interviewer somewhere to probe, which is good: a follow-up you can answer well is worth more than a story with no handholds. Keep proprietary details out, but the technical specifics are the point.

How do I handle it if they interrupt with a question mid-story?

Answer it fully and then return to where you were, explicitly: so, back to the investigation. Interruptions are a good sign — it means they are engaged and probing. What loses points is either brushing the question off to finish your narrative, or losing the thread entirely and never reaching the systemic fix, which is the part that lands best.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

There are two reliable ways to lose this question: criticising your current employer, and giving an answer with no direction. The first makes the interviewer wonder what you will say about them; the second suggests you have not thought about your own career, which at Software Engineer is itself a signal.

The shape that works is scope-based. Describe the kind of problem you want more of, rather than complaining about what you have. I want to own a service end to end — the design, the on-call, the cost, the roadmap — rather than being handed well-defined tickets against someone else's design. That is a statement about growth, not a grievance, and it happens to be exactly the difference between Junior Engineer and Software Engineer work.

Tie it to something you have already done that points that way, because a direction with no evidence is an aspiration. I did the settlement reconciliation work end to end, including the on-call, and that was the part of the last two years I learned most from — I want more of that shape of problem. Evidence converts the answer from a wish into a trajectory.

Then connect it to what this team actually does. That requires having read about them, and the connection should be specific: their scale, their domain, the fact that they run their own platform, the fact that they are building something you would learn from. A generic answer that would fit any company is a wasted question.

Then ask a real question back. How does this team make technical decisions — who decides, and how do disagreements get resolved? That is a genuinely useful question for you and it signals seniority, because it is the question of someone who intends to participate in those decisions.

The framing to keep in mind: at Software Engineer they are hiring someone who will still be growing in two years. So a concrete direction beats enthusiasm, and honesty about what you want beats telling them what you think they want to hear — partly because the latter is transparent, and partly because taking a job that does not match what you actually want is a bad outcome for both sides.

And keep it to two minutes. This is not the question to spend five on.

Follow-ups they will ask

What if the honest reason is money or a bad manager?

Both are legitimate and neither is the answer you give. Translate to what you are moving toward: compensation becomes I am looking for a role at the scope and level this one is pitched at; a difficult manager becomes I want to work somewhere technical decisions are made transparently — which is also why the question you ask back is a good one, since the answer tells you whether this place is different. Say nothing negative and nothing false.

What if I do not have a clear two-year plan?

Almost nobody does, and claiming one sounds rehearsed. A direction is enough: the kind of problems, the kind of scope, the kind of team. Enough to make one specific connection — their engineering blog, their scale, their stack, something a recruiter told you. It does not need to be deep, but it needs to be real, because a specific reference immediately distinguishes you from candidates giving the same answer to five companies. Fifteen minutes of preparation buys you that.

StudyAnthropic - batch processing →

Full mock: you are on call. I will give you three symptoms in sequence and you talk through each. One - all pods in one namespace stuck Pending.

Must coverPending means the scheduler cannot place them, so it is never an application problem. Describe the pod and read the scheduler event verbatim - it usually tells you exactly which predicate failed. Ranked causes: insufficient CPU or memory across all nodes, and check whether the node autoscaler is failing to add nodes (quota, no capacity in the instance type, subnet IP exhaustion); a ResourceQuota on the namespace already exhausted, which is namespace-scoped and matches the symptom well; unsatisfiable affinity, topology spread with a hard maxSkew, or a taint with no toleration; and a PVC that cannot bind because the StorageClass is missing or the volume is in the wrong AZ. Ask what changed - a quota edit or a new node taint is the usual trigger.

StudyKubernetes - scheduler →

Full mock: same on-call, AWS symptoms. One - intermittent 5xx from an ALB with all targets healthy.

Must coverHealthy targets plus 5xx means the failure is in the connection, not the process. Split by ALB error code: 502 is a malformed or dropped response from the target, 503 is no healthy targets at that instant, 504 is a target timeout. The classic 502 cause is a keep-alive race - the target's idle timeout is shorter than the ALB's, so the ALB reuses a connection the target is closing; the fix is to set the application idle timeout above the ALB's, which for Spring Boot and most servers is a one-line configuration and is a genuinely common production bug. Others: a target dying mid-request, response headers exceeding limits, and a security group or NACL dropping return traffic. Confirm from ALB access logs, which record the exact elb_status_code and target_status_code.

StudyALB - troubleshooting →
AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Clarify before designing — four questions, thirty seconds, and one of them changes the entire architecture. Who reads it. How often is it generated. Does it need to be identical if regenerated. And is it advisory, or does anything downstream depend on it.

That third question is the key one, and the answer to how often is what unlocks the design: a monthly summary is a batch workload, not an interactive one. Generate it on a schedule when the month closes, store the result, and serve it statically thereafter.

That single decision changes everything else. Latency stops mattering — nobody is waiting, so a summary taking thirty seconds is fine. Cost becomes bounded and predictable: 5,000 merchants once a month is 5,000 generations, not 5,000 times however many times they open the page. You can use a larger model because the per-item cost is amortised over a month of views. You can use the Batch API at roughly half price. And — the one that matters most in a payments context — you can review a sample before publishing, because generation and delivery are separated in time.

It also answers the determinism question cleanly: store the output rather than re-deriving it. Regenerating on every page load would produce different text each time for the same month, which looks broken to a merchant and is impossible to support. Generate once, store, serve.

Numbers come from tool calls or a precomputed structured input, never from the model's arithmetic. The pipeline computes the month's totals, comparisons and outliers in code, hands the model a fact sheet, and the model writes prose about figures it was given. Every number is traceable, which is what makes this acceptable at all.

Evaluation is a sampled human review before publication in the first months, plus automated checks that every figure in the text matches the source fact sheet — which is deterministic and free, not a judge model. Track the review pass rate and reduce the sample as it holds.

And expect the interruptions to probe: what if a merchant disputes a number (the audit record has the fact sheet and the version), what about new merchants with one month of data (comparisons need a fallback), and what if the model says something embarrassing (which is precisely why the review gate exists and why this being batch is such an advantage).

The key call: this is batch, not interactive
CLARIFY FIRST (30 seconds, and one answer changes everything)
  who reads it?            merchant owners, monthly
  how often generated?     ONCE per merchant per month     <-- the unlock
  identical if regenerated? YES - merchants screenshot these  <-- store, do not
                                                                 re-derive
  advisory or depended on? advisory. Nothing downstream consumes it.

THE KEY CALL: THIS IS A BATCH WORKLOAD, NOT AN INTERACTIVE ONE
  generate on a schedule when the month closes -> STORE -> serve statically

WHAT THAT CHANGES
  latency        stops mattering. 30s per summary is fine. Nobody is waiting.
  cost           BOUNDED: 5,000 merchants x 1/month = 5,000 generations
                 (not 5,000 x however many times they open the page)
  model choice   can use a LARGER model - per-item cost amortised over a
                 month of views
  pricing        Batch API, ~50% cheaper, latency explicitly irrelevant
  QUALITY GATE   you can REVIEW A SAMPLE BEFORE PUBLISHING, because generation
                 and delivery are separated in time   <-- the biggest win
  determinism    store the output. Re-deriving on every page load gives
                 different text each time for the same month - looks broken,
                 impossible to support.

PIPELINE
  month closes
    -> compute the FACT SHEET in code (no model):
         totals, fees, chargebacks, net settlement,
         month-on-month and year-on-year deltas,
         outliers (largest refund, unusual decline rate)
    -> Batch API: model writes prose about figures it WAS GIVEN
    -> VALIDATE: every number in the text appears in the fact sheet
                 (deterministic string/number comparison - NOT a judge model)
    -> sampled human review (5% initially, reduce as the pass rate holds)
    -> publish; store output + fact sheet + artefact version

EXPECT THESE INTERRUPTIONS
  "merchant disputes a number"     -> audit record holds the fact sheet and
                                      the artefact version; the number came
                                      from the ledger, not the model
  "new merchant, one month"        -> comparisons need a fallback; the schema
                                      must allow null deltas and the prompt
                                      must be told not to invent them
  "model says something embarrassing" -> EXACTLY why the review gate exists,
                                      and exactly why being batch is such an
                                      advantage over interactive
Follow-ups they will ask

What if they push for it to be interactive and on-demand?

Ask what changes for the user, because usually nothing does — a monthly summary is not more useful for being regenerated. If the real requirement is current month so far, that is a different feature with different properties, and I would design it separately rather than making the monthly one interactive. Conflating them gives you the cost profile of interactive with the value of batch.

How do you handle the first month with no comparison data?

Make it explicit in the schema — nullable delta fields — and instruct the model that null means do not mention a comparison, then test that case specifically. Without an explicit null and a test, the model will produce a plausible comparison to nothing, which is the exact failure this design is otherwise built to avoid. New-merchant edge cases belong in the eval set from day one.

Would you let merchants regenerate a summary?

No, or only with an explicit regenerate action that replaces the stored version and is recorded. A summary that changes when you refresh the page undermines trust in every number on it. If the underlying data is corrected, regenerate deliberately, mark it as revised, and keep the previous version — which is the same discipline you would apply to a restated financial figure.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Pending means the scheduler cannot place the pods, so it is never an application problem — the container has not started, nothing has run, no code is involved. Establishing that immediately is the first move, because it eliminates the entire application surface from the search.

Then read the scheduler's own verdict. kubectl describe pod prints a FailedScheduling event that names each failed predicate and counts how many nodes failed it. That message is usually the whole answer, and skipping past it to guess is the most common time-waster in this scenario.

The fact that it is a whole namespace is the strongest clue in the question. Cluster-wide resource exhaustion would affect other namespaces too; a single namespace stuck points hard at something namespace-scoped. So the first thing I check is the ResourceQuota — an exhausted quota rejects pods regardless of how empty the cluster is, and it produces a message people misread as a resource problem.

Ranked causes. ResourceQuota exhausted — matches the symptom shape best; check kubectl describe quota and look for used equalling hard. Insufficient CPU or memory across all nodes — and here check whether the node autoscaler is failing to add capacity, because that has its own set of causes: an EC2 quota limit, no spot capacity in the requested pools, or subnet IP exhaustion. Unsatisfiable affinity or topology spread with DoNotSchedule. A taint with no matching toleration, which is how pods fail to reach a pool they were meant for. A PVC that cannot bind — missing StorageClass, or a volume in the wrong AZ.

Then ask what changed, because a namespace that was working and is now stuck almost always had something change: a quota edited, a new taint added to a node group, a LimitRange default raised so every pod now requests more, or a deploy that increased resource requests. Correlate the start time with the audit log or the git history.

And the detail worth naming because it catches people: allocatable is not capacity — kubelet and system reservations plus eviction thresholds mean a 16Gi node offers perhaps 14.5Gi to pods, so a pod requesting 15Gi will never schedule on it even though the node looks big enough.

Pending is never the application — read the scheduler's verdict
# 0. FRAME IT: Pending = the SCHEDULER cannot place it.
#    No container started. No code ran. The application is not involved.

# 1. READ THE VERDICT. It usually IS the answer.
kubectl describe pod <any-pending> -n payments | grep -A15 Events
  Warning FailedScheduling  0/14 nodes are available:
    6 Insufficient cpu,
    4 node(s) had untolerated taint {workload: batch},
    4 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict.
# it counts how many nodes failed EACH predicate. Skipping past this to guess
# is the most common time-waster in this scenario.

# 2. THE WHOLE-NAMESPACE CLUE - strongest signal in the question
#    cluster-wide exhaustion would hit OTHER namespaces too.
#    One namespace stuck -> something NAMESPACE-SCOPED. Check quota FIRST.
kubectl describe quota -n payments
  Resource         Used    Hard
  requests.cpu     40      40      <-- EXHAUSTED. Rejects pods regardless of
  requests.memory  78Gi    80Gi        how empty the cluster is.
  pods             118     120

# RANKED CAUSES
1  ResourceQuota exhausted        matches the symptom shape best
2  insufficient CPU/memory        -> and is the node autoscaler failing?
     kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/cluster-autoscaler | tail -30
     # EC2 service quota | no spot capacity in the requested pools |
     # SUBNET IP EXHAUSTION (VPC CNI: every POD takes a subnet IP)
3  unsatisfiable affinity /       hard anti-affinity with replicas > nodes,
   topology spread                or topology spread with DoNotSchedule
4  taint with no toleration       pods failing to reach the pool they were
                                  meant for (need toleration AND nodeSelector)
5  PVC cannot bind                missing StorageClass, or the volume is in
     kubectl get pvc -n payments  an AZ the pod cannot be scheduled into
     # "volume node affinity conflict"

# 3. WHAT CHANGED? A namespace that worked and is now stuck almost always had
#    something change.
kubectl get events -n payments --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20
#   quota edited | new taint on a node group | LimitRange default raised so
#   EVERY pod now requests more | a deploy that increased requests

# THE DETAIL THAT CATCHES PEOPLE
#   ALLOCATABLE != CAPACITY. kubelet + system reservations + eviction
#   thresholds mean a 16Gi node offers ~14.5Gi to pods.
#   A pod requesting 15Gi NEVER schedules on it, however big the node looks.
kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A6 Allocatable
Follow-ups they will ask

What if the quota looks fine and there is plenty of capacity?

Then it is a constraint rather than a quantity, and the event text will say so — a taint, an affinity rule, a topology spread with DoNotSchedule, or a volume in the wrong zone. Those are all binary: the pod either satisfies them or it never will, so adding nodes does nothing. The distinction between not enough and impossible determines whether you scale or change the manifest.

How do you fix subnet IP exhaustion quickly?

Short term, add a secondary CIDR to the VPC with new subnets and update the CNI configuration to use them. Longer term, enable prefix delegation in the VPC CNI, which allocates /28 prefixes rather than individual IPs and raises pod density dramatically. It is worth knowing this specifically because it is an EKS-only failure that surprises people coming from other Kubernetes environments — every pod consumes a real VPC address.

Should you just raise the quota?

Only after checking whether the consumption is legitimate. A quota exhausted because requests are set far above actual usage should be fixed by right-sizing, not by raising the ceiling — otherwise you have made the waste permanent. If usage is genuine and the team has grown, raise it. Either way, alert on quota utilisation above 80% so this is a warning rather than an outage next time.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Healthy targets plus 5xx means the failure is in the connection, not in the process — the targets are passing their health check and something between the load balancer and the application is going wrong. Saying that first narrows the search immediately.

Split by ALB error code, because they mean different things. 502 — the target returned something the ALB could not parse, or the connection was closed unexpectedly. 503 — no healthy targets at that instant, or the target group was momentarily empty. 504 — the target did not respond within the idle timeout.

The classic 502 cause is the keep-alive race, and it is worth leading with because it is common, confusing, and a one-line fix. The ALB pools connections to targets and reuses them. If the target's idle timeout is shorter than or equal to the ALB's, there is a window in which the ALB sends a request down a connection the target has just decided to close — the target resets it, and the ALB returns 502. It is intermittent, it correlates with low traffic on a given connection rather than with load, and nothing in the application logs shows it, because from the application's point of view nothing happened.

The fix is one line: the application's keep-alive timeout must exceed the ALB's idle timeout — ALB defaults to 60 seconds, so set the server's to 70 or more. This is a genuinely common production bug on AWS and knowing it cold is a strong signal.

Other causes, ranked. A target dying mid-request — check for restarts or deployments correlating in time. Response headers exceeding the ALB's limit, which produces 502 on specific responses only. A security group or NACL asymmetry dropping return traffic. And, for 504 specifically, a downstream dependency slower than your idle timeout.

Confirm from ALB access logs, which are the only source with per-request detail. They record elb_status_code and target_status_code separately, and that pairing usually is the diagnosis: a 502 with target_status_code of - means the ALB never got a valid response, which points at the connection; a 502 with an actual target status code means the target really responded that way.

And group by target — if one instance produces all of them, it is that instance, not the design.

The keep-alive race, and the log field that proves it
FRAME: healthy targets + 5xx -> the failure is in the CONNECTION, not the process.

SPLIT BY CODE
  502  target returned something unparseable, or closed the connection
  503  no healthy targets at that instant / empty target group
  504  target did not respond within the idle timeout

# ---- THE CLASSIC 502: THE KEEP-ALIVE RACE ----
  ALB pools and REUSES connections to targets.
  target idle timeout <= ALB idle timeout
    -> a window exists where the ALB sends a request down a connection the
       target has just decided to close
    -> target resets it -> ALB returns 502

  SYMPTOMS: intermittent | correlates with connection age, NOT with load
            NOTHING in the application logs (from the app's view, nothing
            happened)

  FIX - one line:
    ALB idle_timeout.timeout_seconds = 60      (default)
    server.tomcat.keep-alive-timeout: 70s      <-- MUST EXCEED the ALB's
    # Spring Boot / Tomcat. Netty, Undertow and nginx have equivalents.

# ---- CONFIRM FROM ACCESS LOGS - the only per-request detail ----
SELECT elb_status_code, target_status_code, target, count(*)
FROM alb_logs
WHERE day = '2026/08/29' AND elb_status_code LIKE '5%'
GROUP BY elb_status_code, target_status_code, target
ORDER BY count(*) DESC;

  elb  target  target                    count
  502  -       10.20.19.214:8080         1,204   <-- target_status_code "-" =
  502  -       10.20.32.88:8080          1,187       the ALB NEVER GOT a valid
  502  502     10.20.19.214:8080             3       response -> CONNECTION issue
                                                     (this pairing IS the diagnosis)

  # and if ONE target produces all of them -> it is that instance, not the design

OTHER CAUSES, RANKED
2  target dying mid-request      correlate with restarts / a deployment
3  response headers > ALB limit  502 on SPECIFIC responses only
4  SG / NACL asymmetry           return traffic dropped (NACLs are STATELESS -
                                 they need an explicit ephemeral-port rule)
5  (504) downstream slower than  nest your timeouts: every timeout must be
   your idle timeout             SHORTER than its caller's
Follow-ups they will ask

How would you prove it is the keep-alive race rather than something else?

Two things together: target_status_code is - in the access logs, meaning no valid response was received, and the errors do not correlate with load or with any particular request. Then test the hypothesis directly — raise the application's keep-alive timeout above the ALB's and watch the 502 rate. If it goes to zero, you are done. It is a cheap, reversible experiment, which makes it worth trying early.

What if it is 503 rather than 502?

503 means no healthy targets at that instant, so look at the health check rather than the connection. Usual causes: a deregistration delay shorter than your longest request, so targets leave rotation mid-flight; a health check path that is too deep, so a dependency blip fails all targets at once; or a rolling deploy where the new targets have not passed their health check while the old ones have already been drained. Check HealthyHostCount over time — a dip to zero is definitive.

Does this apply to NLB as well?

The keep-alive race is specific to layer 7 load balancers that pool connections to targets, so it is an ALB phenomenon. An NLB forwards TCP without parsing, so a closed connection surfaces as a reset to the client rather than as a 502 from the load balancer. That difference in symptom is a useful diagnostic — an NLB in the path produces client-side connection errors rather than clean 5xx codes.

AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The skill being tested is whether you can be challenged without either collapsing or digging in, and there is a structure for it.

First, restate their position accurately — better than they did, if you can. The argument for fine-tuning is that it removes the retrieval infrastructure entirely, cuts prompt length and therefore cost, and gives more consistent output because the behaviour is in the weights rather than in an instruction the model may ignore. Doing this properly means they know you understood rather than pattern-matched, and it makes everything after it land better.

Second, name the conditions under which they are right. If the corpus were fixed and never changed, if we did not need to cite sources, and if the task were narrow and high-volume enough that prompt length dominated our cost — fine-tuning would be the better call, and I would advocate for it. This is the move that distinguishes a considered position from a reflex, and it is genuinely honest: fine-tuning is right under those conditions.

Third, give the concrete reason it does not hold here — and make it specific to this system, not generic. The corpus changes weekly, so a tuned model is stale on day one and re-tuning weekly is not viable. We must cite sources, and weights cannot cite. And we must be able to delete a customer's data on request, which weights cannot do — that is the strongest single point, because it is not a preference, it is a capability the architecture either has or does not.

Fourth, offer the test that settles it. Run both against the eval set, compare accuracy, cost per request and latency, and decide on the numbers. That converts a disagreement about opinions into a measurable question, and it is almost always the right ending — it also signals that you would rather be right than win.

And the meta-point worth knowing: changing your mind when given a good argument is a positive signal; changing it under mere pressure is not. If they produce a fact you did not have — the corpus is actually frozen, or citations are not required — update visibly and say why. If they simply repeat the assertion more firmly, hold the position politely. Interviewers use this to see which of the two you do, and the failure modes are symmetric: caving reads as having no conviction, and refusing to engage reads as being difficult to work with.

Restate, concede the conditions, give the specific reason, offer the test
STRUCTURE

1  RESTATE THEIR POSITION - accurately, and generously

    prompts and therefore lower cost per call, and more consistent behaviour
    because it is in the weights rather than in an instruction the model can
    ignore."
   -> they now know you UNDERSTOOD rather than pattern-matched.
      Everything after this lands better.

2  NAME THE CONDITIONS UNDER WHICH THEY ARE RIGHT
   "If the corpus were fixed and never changed, if we did not need to cite
    sources, and if the task were narrow and high-volume enough that prompt
    length dominated our cost - fine-tuning would be the better call and I
    would advocate for it."
   -> this is genuinely honest, and it distinguishes a CONSIDERED position
      from a reflex.

3  THE SPECIFIC REASON IT DOES NOT HOLD HERE - not generic
   "Three things, in increasing order of weight:
      the corpus changes weekly, so a tuned model is stale on day one and
        re-tuning weekly is not viable;
      we must CITE sources, and weights cannot cite;
      and we must be able to DELETE a customer's data on request.
        Weights cannot be unlearned - the only remedy is retraining from a
        cleaned corpus. That one is not a preference, it is a CAPABILITY the
        architecture either has or does not."

4  OFFER THE TEST THAT SETTLES IT
   "The way to settle this is to run both against the eval set and compare
    accuracy, cost per request and latency. If fine-tuning wins on the numbers
    and we can solve the deletion problem, I will change my mind."
   -> converts a disagreement about opinions into a MEASURABLE question,
      and signals you would rather be RIGHT than WIN.

THE META-POINT
  they produce a FACT you did not have (the corpus is frozen; citations are
  not required)          -> UPDATE VISIBLY, and say what changed your mind.
                            That is a positive signal.

Follow-ups they will ask

What if you realise mid-answer that they are actually right?

Say so, immediately and cleanly. You are right — I had assumed the corpus changes, and if it does not, most of my argument disappears. I would want to check the citation requirement, but on what you have described, fine-tuning is the better call. That is a strong moment, not a weak one. Defending a position you have stopped believing is the thing that actually damages you.

How do you disagree with someone more senior without it going badly?

Anchor on the shared goal and on evidence rather than on authority. We both want the lowest-maintenance system that meets the compliance requirement — my concern is specifically the deletion obligation. Can we check what legal actually requires before deciding? That reframes it from a contest into a shared open question, which is how the same conversation goes in real work.

Is there a version of this where you should just defer?

When the decision is genuinely theirs and the cost of being wrong is low — a naming convention, a library choice, a style preference. Spending capital on those is a poor trade. Save disagreement for decisions that are expensive to reverse or that carry real risk, and be visibly easy about everything else. Knowing which is which is itself part of what is being assessed.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Concede the strong version of the argument first, because it is often right. For a small team with a handful of services, EKS is a platform team you do not have — control plane upgrades on a roughly annual cadence with deprecated-API breakage, add-on lifecycle for the CNI, CoreDNS, CSI drivers and the autoscaler, admission policy, and an observability stack. ECS on Fargate delivers the same outcome with a fraction of that surface, and a backend engineer is productive in a day rather than a fortnight.

Saying that without hedging is what earns the right to disagree afterwards — a candidate who defends Kubernetes reflexively has told the interviewer they choose technology by fashion.

Then draw the line where Kubernetes actually wins. Many teams needing self-service, where the platform's declarative model and namespace isolation let teams move independently. A genuine need for the ecosystem — operators for stateful workloads, Argo Rollouts for progressive delivery with automated analysis, KEDA for event-driven scaling, Kyverno for policy as code. Multi-cloud or on-prem portability as a real requirement rather than a slide. And workloads with placement requirements ECS cannot express — GPU pools, node affinity, topology spread, DaemonSets.

Finish with the decision rule rather than a preference, because a preference sounds like taste and a rule sounds like judgement: choose the least infrastructure that meets the requirement, and be explicit that adopting Kubernetes is a staffing decision as much as a technical one. If nobody owns the platform, you have not chosen Kubernetes — you have chosen an unmaintained cluster, which is worse than ECS by every measure.

And offer the honest current caveat: EKS Auto Mode has moved this line. AWS managing node provisioning, scaling and core add-ons removes a real slice of the burden — it does not remove control plane upgrades, deprecated-API breakage, or the need to understand Kubernetes when something breaks at 3am. Acknowledging that the answer is closer than it was two years ago demonstrates current knowledge rather than a memorised position.

Follow-ups they will ask

What if you actually prefer Kubernetes and they are pushing ECS?

Then your preference is not the argument — the requirement is. Ask what the team looks like in eighteen months and how many services they expect, because that is what decides it. If the answer is five engineers, twelve services, no platform team, ECS is right and I would say so even though I would personally rather work with Kubernetes. Being able to recommend against your own preference is a strong signal.

How do you argue for Kubernetes when it genuinely is right?

With the specific capability you need and cannot get otherwise, not with generalities. We need Argo Rollouts' automated canary analysis and KEDA's scale-to-zero on queue depth, and neither exists on ECS — that is worth the operational cost given we already have two engineers who have run clusters. A named capability plus an honest staffing statement is far more persuasive than a list of Kubernetes' virtues.

What is the strongest argument against your own position here?

That migrating from ECS to EKS later is real, funded work, so choosing ECS to save six months can cost you eighteen later. It is a fair point, and the counter is that the container images and twelve-factor discipline transfer unchanged — you rewrite the orchestration layer, which is bounded and mechanical. So starting on ECS is not a trap, provided application code stays free of platform-specific assumptions.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Agree readily and specifically first, because the position is substantially right for a large class of workloads. For event-driven, spiky and low-volume work, Lambda plus managed services is less code, less operational surface, and frequently cheaper — you write a handler instead of a service, and there is no fleet, no patching, no autoscaling to tune. For glue work, S3 event processing, scheduled jobs and API backends with modest traffic, it is clearly correct.

Then push back on specifics, not on principle, because serverless is bad is not an argument and will not land.

Sustained high throughput — per-request pricing overtakes an always-on instance somewhere in the low millions of requests per month, so a service doing 50 requests a second continuously is meaningfully cheaper on a container. Do that arithmetic out loud; it is the most persuasive single point.

Long-running and streaming — the 15-minute timeout and the payload limits are hard walls, and a streaming LLM response held for thirty seconds is an awkward fit.

JVM cold starts — a Spring Boot context is seconds, and while SnapStart and provisioned concurrency mitigate it, provisioned concurrency is paying for idle capacity, which is precisely what serverless was supposed to avoid.

Connection-pool exhaustion against a relational database — this is the sharpest one. Unbounded Lambda concurrency means unbounded database connections, and three hundred concurrent invocations against an RDS instance with a two-hundred-connection limit is an instant outage for every other service on that database. RDS Proxy exists for exactly this, and needing it is itself evidence of an impedance mismatch.

And local development and testing — a distributed set of functions is harder to run and reason about than a service you can start on your laptop, and that cost is paid by every engineer every day.

Land on the honest position: serverless for the async and bursty edges, containers for the sustained synchronous core, and let the workload shape decide each time rather than the architecture having a house style. That last clause is the real answer — the failure mode being argued against is not serverless, it is uniformity imposed by preference rather than by fit.

Follow-ups they will ask

What about Fargate as the middle ground?

It is a genuinely good answer and worth offering: containers with no node management, so you get the serverless operational model with the container execution model — no cold starts, no timeout, normal connection pooling, and a service you can run locally. It costs a premium per vCPU over EC2, which is far cheaper than the engineering time it saves for most teams. For a sustained synchronous service that someone wants to be serverless, Fargate usually satisfies both concerns.

How do you decide the boundary in practice?

Three questions: is the work bursty or sustained, is it shorter or longer than a few seconds, and does it hold a connection to a relational database. Bursty, short and stateless goes to Lambda. Sustained, long or connection-heavy goes to a container. Anything ambiguous, start with Lambda because it is cheaper to abandon than to adopt — moving a handler into a service is easier than the reverse.

Is there a cost to mixing both?

Yes, and it is worth naming: two deployment models, two observability setups, two sets of IAM patterns, and engineers needing to be fluent in both. That is a real tax and it argues for keeping the split simple — one clear rule about which workloads go where, rather than a case-by-case decision that produces a scattered estate nobody can reason about.

AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Ask about the operational reality, not the technology — because that is where you learn whether the AI work is real or a demo, and because those questions signal that you understand an AI feature is a maintained system rather than a project.

How do you evaluate changes before they ship? The single most revealing question. A team with an eval suite in CI and a critical set that blocks merges is doing this seriously. A team that says we try it and see if it looks better is where you will spend your first six months building the thing they should already have — which may be a great opportunity, but you should know which one you are joining.

Who owns the eval set, and how does it grow? The answer tells you whether failures feed back into it or whether it was written once and forgotten.

What happens when a model version is deprecated? Reveals whether they pin versions, whether they have done a migration, and whether they understand it as recurring work.

How do you handle customer data in prompts? In a payments context this tells you both their compliance maturity and whether they have had the conversation with legal at all.

And: what has gone wrong so far? A team that answers honestly and specifically is a good team. A team that says nothing has gone wrong either has not shipped it or does not have the observability to know.

Avoid asking which model they use. It tells you almost nothing, it dates instantly, and it signals that you think the model is the interesting part.

Then one honest scope question: what would the person in this role own end to end? This is the one that determines whether the job matches the description, and the specificity of the answer is itself the signal — a vague answer usually means the role is not well defined, which is worth knowing before you accept it.

The principle underneath all of these: ask the questions of someone who intends to do the work, not someone evaluating a technology. That is what reads as senior, and it also happens to get you the information you actually need.
