4  "How do you handle customer data in prompts?"
     -> compliance maturity, AND whether they have had the conversation with
        legal at all. In payments, this one matters.

5  "What has gone wrong so far?"
     -> an honest, specific answer is a GOOD sign.
        "nothing has gone wrong" means they have not shipped it, or they do
        not have the observability to know.

DO NOT ASK
  x  "which model do you use?"
     tells you almost nothing, dates instantly, and signals that you think
     the MODEL is the interesting part.

THEN ONE HONEST SCOPE QUESTION
  "What would the person in this role own end to end?"
  -> determines whether the job matches the description.
     The SPECIFICITY of the answer is itself the signal: a vague answer
     usually means the role is not well defined, which is worth knowing
     BEFORE you accept it.

THE PRINCIPLE
  ask the questions of someone who intends to DO THE WORK,
  not someone evaluating a technology.
  That reads as senior - and it gets you the information you actually need.
Follow-ups they will ask

What if their answers reveal the AI work is immature?

That is information, not a disqualifier — and it may be the more interesting job. What matters is whether they know it is immature. A team that says we do not have evals yet and we know that is our biggest gap is a team you can help. A team that thinks eyeballing outputs is sufficient is one where you will spend your energy on persuasion rather than engineering. Ask a follow-up to find out which.

How many questions should you actually ask?

Two or three, well chosen, with follow-ups. A list of eight reads as an interrogation and you will not get depth on any of them. Pick the evaluation question, one about ownership or scope, and one about what has gone wrong — then follow the answers wherever they go, because the follow-up is where the real information is.

Is it risky to ask about failures?

No, if you frame it as curiosity rather than as a test — what has been surprising or gone wrong so far? is an invitation to talk about interesting problems, which most engineers enjoy. It only lands badly if you sound like you are auditing them. The way you ask matters more than what you ask.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Ask for specifics with numbers, not philosophy — because we value quality tells you nothing and we deploy four times a day and a deploy takes eleven minutes tells you a great deal.

How many times a day do you deploy, and how long does a deploy take? The single best proxy for engineering health. Frequent, fast deploys mean the pipeline works, the tests are trusted, and rollback is cheap. Weekly deploys with a change-advisory board mean something upstream is broken and your work will move at that speed.

How do you roll back, and when did you last do it? The second half is the important half. A rollback mechanism nobody has used is an untested code path — and the honest answer, last Tuesday, it took four minutes, tells you rollback is routine rather than frightening.

Who is on call, and how many pages a week? This tells you about both the system and the culture. Engineers on call for their own services is healthy. A separate operations team paging developers is a sign of a handoff culture. And more than two or three pages a week per person is either an unreliable system or a noisy alerting setup, both of which will consume you.

How long does it take a new engineer to get a change into production? Measures onboarding, tooling and trust in one number. Days is good; weeks means there is a lot of undocumented ceremony.

Then the health question: what is the biggest piece of technical debt, and what is the plan for it? A team that answers honestly and specifically is a good sign — everyone has debt, and the ones who can name theirs are the ones who are managing it. A team that says there is none is not being honest with you or with themselves.

These also read as senior, because they are the questions of someone who has carried a pager. An interviewer notices the difference between what technologies do you use and how many pages a week.

And listen for hesitation as much as content: if two interviewers give materially different answers about deploy frequency or on-call load, that discrepancy is itself the finding.

Numbers, not philosophy
ASK - and listen for NUMBERS

1  "How many times a day do you deploy? How long does a deploy take?"
     <-- best single proxy for engineering health
     several times a day, minutes    -> pipeline works, tests trusted,
                                        rollback cheap
     weekly, with a change board     -> something upstream is broken, and
                                        your work will move at that speed

2  "How do you roll back? When did you last do it?"
     the SECOND HALF is the important half.
     "last Tuesday, took four minutes"  -> routine, not frightening
     "we have never needed to"          -> an UNTESTED code path

3  "Who is on call? How many pages a week?"
     engineers on call for their own services      -> healthy
     a separate ops team paging developers         -> handoff culture
     > 2-3 pages/week/person -> unreliable system OR noisy alerting.
                                Both will consume you.

4  "How long before a new engineer gets a change into production?"
     measures onboarding, tooling and TRUST in one number.
     days   -> good
     weeks  -> a lot of undocumented ceremony

5  "What is the biggest piece of technical debt, and what is the plan for it?"
     honest and specific    -> GOOD SIGN. Everyone has debt; the teams who can
                              NAME theirs are the ones managing it.
     "there isn't any"      -> not being honest with you, or with themselves.

WHY THESE READ AS SENIOR
  they are the questions of someone who has CARRIED A PAGER.
  an interviewer notices the difference between
     "what technologies do you use?"     and     "how many pages a week?"

AND LISTEN FOR DISCREPANCIES
  if two interviewers give materially different answers about deploy frequency
  or on-call load, THAT DISCREPANCY IS THE FINDING.
  Ask the second one about it directly - politely - and watch how they handle it.
Follow-ups they will ask

What is a red flag in the answers?

Vagueness where a number should exist. We deploy pretty regularly from someone who deploys is a strange answer — people who deploy know roughly how often. Also: nobody being on call for their own code, a rollback procedure nobody can describe, and any version of we do not really have technical debt. Individually each is survivable; together they describe a team that has not looked closely at itself.

Should you ask about work-life balance directly?

Ask about on-call load and deploy frequency instead — they give you the same information with better answers, because people answer factual questions honestly and normative ones defensively. How many pages a week and do people deploy on Fridays tell you more about the actual rhythm than any direct question about hours will.

What if they cannot answer because they are not on that team?

Ask who you could ask, and treat the offer to connect you as part of the signal — a team confident in its answers will happily put you in touch with an engineer who has the numbers. If nobody in the process can tell you how often they deploy or who carries the pager, that itself is worth weighing.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Ask how the estate is actually run, not how they would describe it in an architecture document — because the gap between those two is where you will be working.

How are the accounts structured? A single account for everything, or an Organization with separate accounts per environment. The answer tells you about blast radius, IAM clarity and cost attribution in one question, and it is the thing that is hardest to change later.

How are infrastructure changes made — console, IaC, or a mix? Expect a mix, and treat that as the honest answer rather than a bad one; almost everyone has a mix. What matters is whether they know where the console-managed parts are and whether that boundary is shrinking.

Who can deploy to production, and how? Reveals whether access is federated and least-privilege, and whether the deployment path is automated or someone with admin credentials running commands.

How is cost attributed to teams? Tells you whether anyone owns spend. Teams that see their own cost behave differently from teams where finance raises it quarterly in aggregate.

And: what was your last significant incident, and what changed afterwards? The best question on the list, because the answer reveals their observability, their review culture and their honesty simultaneously.

What would worry me. A single account for everything — it means IAM is a mess and blast radius is unbounded. Console-driven changes with no infrastructure as code and no plan to get there. Nobody knowing what anything costs. And an inability to describe a recent incident, which usually means they either lack observability or do not do reviews — either way, incidents happen and nothing is learned from them.

Then close with the forward-looking question: what would you want me to change in my first ninety days? The specificity of the answer tells you whether they have thought about the role or are hiring for a vague gap. A concrete answer — we need someone to own the settlement service and get its deploy story fixed — is a good sign. Just get up to speed and see what needs doing usually means nobody has decided what the role is.

How it is run, not how it is described
ASK

1  "How are the accounts structured?"
     Organization with separate accounts per environment  -> blast radius,
       IAM clarity and cost attribution all handled
     one account for everything                           -> WORRYING (below)
     -> also the thing that is HARDEST TO CHANGE LATER

2  "How are infrastructure changes made - console, IaC, or a mix?"
     expect "a mix". That is the HONEST answer, not a bad one.
     what matters: do they know WHERE the console-managed parts are,
                   and is that boundary SHRINKING?

3  "Who can deploy to production, and how?"
     -> federated, least-privilege, automated pipeline
        vs someone with admin credentials running commands

4  "How is cost attributed to teams?"
     -> teams that SEE their own cost behave differently from teams where
        finance raises it quarterly in aggregate

5  "What was your last significant incident, and what changed afterwards?"
     <-- BEST question on the list. Reveals observability, review culture and
         honesty, all at once.

WHAT WOULD WORRY ME
  x  a single account for everything
       -> IAM is a mess, blast radius is unbounded, cost is unattributable
  x  console-driven changes with no IaC AND no plan to get there
  x  nobody knowing what anything costs
  x  inability to describe a recent incident
       -> either no observability, or no reviews.
          Incidents happen; nothing is being learned from them.

CLOSE WITH THE FORWARD-LOOKING ONE
  "What would you want me to change in my first ninety days?"
     "own the settlement service and fix its deploy story"
        -> concrete. They have thought about the role. GOOD.
     "just get up to speed and see what needs doing"
        -> usually means nobody has decided what the role IS.

# The gap between how an estate is DESCRIBED and how it is RUN is exactly
# where you will be working. Ask about the second.
Follow-ups they will ask

Is a single account always a red flag?

Not for a small startup where it is a deliberate, temporary simplification and they know the migration is coming. It is a flag for a payments company at any real scale, because it means production and development share an IAM boundary and a quota pool, and cost cannot be attributed. Ask whether they consider it a problem — the answer tells you more than the fact does.

How do you ask about incidents without sounding like you are auditing them?

Frame it as interest in the systems rather than in their competence: what is the most interesting thing that has broken recently? Engineers generally enjoy that conversation, and you get the same information — how they found it, how they fixed it, what changed — without it feeling like a review. The framing does most of the work.

What if the answers are bad but the role is still interesting?

Then go in with clear eyes and make the scope explicit before accepting: if the estate needs IaC, account separation and cost attribution, that is a substantial piece of work and it should be part of the role's remit rather than something you take on informally. A team that agrees it is needed and funds it is a good opportunity. A team that agrees it is needed and expects it alongside full feature delivery is not.

600/3

Last day: the summary you can give in two minutes

Summarise, in two minutes, what you now know about building with LLMs and what you would still want to learn. This is the closing question.

Must coverStructure: what the technology is good and bad at (excellent at unstructured input, format and language; unreliable for arithmetic, freshness and anything needing an audit trail), the architecture pattern you would default to (retrieval for knowledge, tools for facts and actions, deterministic code for decisions, the model for language), the operational reality (evaluation in CI, versioning everything, cost modelled per request, guardrails outside the model), and then honestly what you have not done at production scale and want to. Naming the gap deliberately is a senior move - it is what separates someone who has thought about it from someone reciting.

AI Engineering · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Structure it in four parts and keep to two minutes, because this is a closing question and rambling here undoes a good round.

What the technology is good and bad at. It is excellent at unstructured input, at format, and at language — turning messy text into structure, classifying, summarising, drafting. It is unreliable for arithmetic, for anything that must be current, and for anything requiring an audit trail, because it produces a correct answer and a confidently wrong one by exactly the same mechanism. Leading with that symmetry is the clearest way to show you understand the technology rather than the marketing.

The architecture pattern I would default to. Retrieval for knowledge, tools for facts and actions, deterministic code for decisions, and the model for language. That one sentence is the most useful thing I have learned — it assigns each responsibility to the component that can actually be held accountable for it, and almost every design question resolves into applying it.

The operational reality. An LLM feature is a system with moving parts you do not own: the model changes, the corpus changes, and user behaviour changes, all without you doing anything. So it needs evaluation in CI with a regression gate, every version pinned and recorded, cost modelled per request, and guardrails enforced outside the model. It needs an owner and a maintenance budget the way a database does.

Then name the gap deliberately. What I have not done is run one at production scale over a long period — I have prototyped, evaluated and reasoned about the architecture, and the thing I want next is ownership of one in production through a model migration and a real incident.

That final move is the senior one. It is specific about what you have and have not done, it shows you know what the hard part is (the operating, not the building), and it converts a limitation into a direction. Claiming completeness at this point in a conversation is transparent and it invites a probe you cannot survive; naming the gap is credible and it ends the round on your terms.

Two minutes. Then stop.

Good at, bad at, the pattern, the gap
TWO MINUTES. FOUR PARTS. THEN STOP.

1  WHAT IT IS GOOD AND BAD AT  (~30s)
   EXCELLENT   unstructured input | format | language
               messy text -> structure, classification, summarisation, drafting
   UNRELIABLE  arithmetic | anything that must be CURRENT | anything needing
               an AUDIT TRAIL
   WHY: a correct answer and a confidently wrong one are produced by EXACTLY
        the same mechanism. There is no internal signal distinguishing recall
        from fabrication.
   -> leading with that symmetry shows you understand the technology rather
      than the marketing.

2  THE PATTERN I WOULD DEFAULT TO  (~25s)
   RETRIEVAL for knowledge.
   TOOLS for facts and actions.
   DETERMINISTIC CODE for decisions.
   THE MODEL for language.
   -> the single most useful thing I have learned. It assigns each
      responsibility to the component that can actually be held ACCOUNTABLE
      for it, and almost every design question resolves into applying it.

3  THE OPERATIONAL REALITY  (~40s)
   an LLM feature is a system with moving parts you DO NOT OWN:
     the model changes | the corpus changes | user behaviour changes
     - all without you doing anything.
   therefore:
     evaluation in CI with a regression gate and a critical set
     every version pinned and RECORDED on the response
     cost modelled per request, with caching and small-model routing
     guardrails enforced OUTSIDE the model - authorisation, validation, audit
   it needs an OWNER and a MAINTENANCE BUDGET, the way a database does.

4  NAME THE GAP  (~25s)
   "What I have not done is run one at production scale over a long period.
    I have prototyped, evaluated, and reasoned carefully about the
    architecture. What I want next is ownership of one in production -
    through a model migration and a real incident, because that is where
    the learning is."

# WHY PART 4 IS THE SENIOR MOVE
#   specific about what you have and have not done
#   shows you know the hard part is the OPERATING, not the building
#   converts a limitation into a DIRECTION
#   claiming completeness here is transparent, and invites a probe you
#   cannot survive. Naming the gap is credible, and ends the round on
#   YOUR terms.
Follow-ups they will ask

Is it risky to admit a gap in a closing question?

Less risky than the alternative. Everyone has gaps, the interviewer knows roughly what yours are from the preceding hour, and claiming otherwise damages everything you said before it. A specific, deliberately-chosen gap — paired with what you have done and what you want next — reads as self-awareness. A vague or defensive answer reads as either overclaiming or not having thought about it.

What if you have more than two minutes?

Do not use them. A tight two-minute close is more memorable than a five-minute one, and the interviewer usually has a hard stop. If they want more they will ask a follow-up, and answering a follow-up well is worth more than filling silence. Ending slightly early with something crisp is a deliberate choice, not a failure to fill time.

How do you practise this?

Out loud, timed, several times, until the four parts are automatic and you are not reconstructing them under pressure. Record yourself once — most people are surprised by how much longer their spoken answer runs than their mental one. The four-part skeleton is what lets you stay on time while sounding unrehearsed, because you are only recalling the structure, not the words.

Docker & K8s · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

Give the mental model, not the object list — because a colleague starting from zero does not need to memorise fields, they need the idea that makes the fields predictable.

A container is a process with a restricted view of the machine, packaged with its own filesystem. Namespaces restrict what it can see; cgroups restrict what it can consume. It shares the host kernel, which is why it starts in milliseconds and why the isolation is weaker than a VM's.

Kubernetes is a control loop. That is the whole idea. You declare desired state as objects; controllers continuously compare reality against that declaration and act to close the gap. Nothing is imperative — you do not tell it to start three pods, you record that three pods should exist, and something notices they do not.

Everything else follows from that one idea. A Deployment reconciles ReplicaSets; a ReplicaSet reconciles pods; the scheduler places them; the kubelet runs them; the endpoint controller keeps Services pointing at whatever is currently Ready. Custom resources and operators are the same pattern extended to your own objects. Once someone has the loop, the object model stops being arbitrary.

Then the three practical consequences, which is what makes the model useful rather than just elegant.

Nothing happens instantly. Everything converges, so I applied it and nothing happened usually means wait a moment, then read the events. Debugging is reading the gap between declared and actual.

Health is defined by your probes, so the cluster is exactly as smart as your probes are. A readiness probe that only checks the port means Kubernetes will confidently route traffic to a broken pod, and a liveness probe that checks the database means it will restart your entire fleet during a database blip. Almost every self-inflicted Kubernetes outage traces back to a probe.

Requests and limits are how you talk to the scheduler. Requests are a reservation and drive placement; limits are enforcement. Memory overrun kills, CPU overrun throttles.

That model answers most questions without memorising object fields — which is the point. Someone who has it can reason about a new controller they have never seen; someone who has memorised YAML cannot.

One idea, three consequences
A CONTAINER
  a process with a RESTRICTED VIEW of the machine, packaged with its filesystem.
    namespaces -> what it can SEE
    cgroups    -> what it can CONSUME
  shares the host kernel -> starts in milliseconds, isolates less than a VM.

KUBERNETES IS A CONTROL LOOP
  you DECLARE desired state as objects.
  controllers continuously compare REALITY against that declaration and act
  to close the gap.
  nothing is imperative. You do not say "start three pods" - you record that
  three pods SHOULD exist, and something notices they do not.

EVERYTHING ELSE FOLLOWS FROM THAT ONE IDEA
  Deployment  reconciles -> ReplicaSets
  ReplicaSet  reconciles -> Pods
  scheduler   places them
  kubelet     runs them
  endpoint controller  keeps Services pointing at whatever is currently READY
  CRDs + operators     the SAME pattern, extended to your own objects
  -> once you have the loop, the object model stops being arbitrary.

THREE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES - what makes the model useful

1  NOTHING HAPPENS INSTANTLY
     everything CONVERGES.
     "I applied it and nothing happened" usually means "wait, then read the
     events". Debugging is reading the GAP between declared and actual.
       kubectl describe <obj>     # events = the controller telling you why

2  HEALTH IS DEFINED BY YOUR PROBES
     the cluster is EXACTLY as smart as your probes are.
       readiness checks only the port -> Kubernetes confidently routes traffic
                                         to a broken pod
       liveness checks the database   -> one DB blip restarts your ENTIRE FLEET
     almost every self-inflicted Kubernetes outage traces back to a probe.

3  REQUESTS AND LIMITS ARE HOW YOU TALK TO THE SCHEDULER
     request = a RESERVATION, drives placement and bin-packing
     limit   = ENFORCEMENT at runtime
     memory overrun -> KILLED (incompressible)
     CPU overrun    -> THROTTLED (compressible, silent, latency only)

# THAT MODEL ANSWERS MOST QUESTIONS WITHOUT MEMORISING OBJECT FIELDS.
# Someone who has it can reason about a controller they have never seen.
# Someone who has memorised YAML cannot.
Follow-ups they will ask

What is the one thing you would tell them to learn first?

Probes, and specifically the readiness/liveness distinction. It is a small amount of material, it is where most self-inflicted outages come from, and understanding it forces you to understand Services, endpoints and rolling updates — because readiness is what connects all three. Everything else can be looked up; getting probes wrong causes incidents that are hard to diagnose.

How do you explain why Kubernetes is worth the complexity?

By naming what it replaces: the scripts and runbooks that would otherwise reschedule failed workloads, roll out changes safely, keep load balancers pointing at healthy instances, and bin-pack machines. If you only run three services, you do not need it and you should say so. Its value appears when many teams need those behaviours consistently, which is a scale and organisation argument rather than a technical one.

What is the most common misconception for someone starting out?

That a pod is a container, and that Running means working. The first makes the object model confusing; the second causes real incidents, because 1/1 Running with a failing readiness probe means the pod is alive and receiving no traffic — which looks like a networking problem and is not. Correcting both early saves people a lot of confusion.

AWS · model answerSay it out loud first. Reading this before answering teaches you nothing.

The mental model: AWS is a set of primitives with an identity system in front of everything, deployed into failure domains you choose. Almost every service is a managed version of something you could run yourself; the two things that are genuinely AWS-shaped are IAM, which gates every single API call, and the region/AZ structure, which is how you choose what you can survive losing.

That framing gives you the four decisions that matter most — and the organising principle is which decisions are irreversible, because that is what should get the most thought.

One: the account and identity boundary. An account is the only hard blast-radius, quota and IAM boundary AWS provides. Getting this wrong — one account for everything — is nearly impossible to unwind later, because every resource, every policy and every cost report is built on it.

Two: the network layout. CIDR ranges and subnet topology are similarly hard to change. You cannot shrink a CIDR, overlapping ranges cannot be peered, and on EKS the subnet sizing determines how many pods you can run. Decisions made in an afternoon constrain you for years.

Three: the data store per workload. It decides your consistency model, your scaling characteristics, your cost curve and — most importantly — which questions you will be able to answer later. Migrating a datastore is a project; choosing it is a meeting.

Four: the failure domain strategy, stated as RTO and RPO numbers rather than as we are multi-AZ. How many zones, whether multi-region, and what you are willing to lose.

Then the crucial second half: almost everything else is reversible in a quarter. Compute choice — EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda — deployment tooling, observability vendor, CI system, even most of the managed services. Those feel like big decisions and they are not, because the application code and the data survive them.

Leading with what is irreversible is what makes this sound senior. It reframes architecture from which services do we use to which decisions do we have to get right first time, and it tells you where to spend the design effort. Most teams spend their architecture debate on the reversible choices and their afternoon on the irreversible ones.

Two minutes, then stop.

Four irreversible decisions; everything else is a quarter
THE MODEL
  AWS is a set of PRIMITIVES with an IDENTITY SYSTEM in front of everything,
  deployed into FAILURE DOMAINS you choose.
  almost every service is a managed version of something you could run yourself.
  the two genuinely AWS-shaped things:
    IAM       - gates every single API call
    region/AZ - how you choose what you can survive losing

THE FOUR DECISIONS THAT MATTER MOST
(organising principle: WHICH ARE IRREVERSIBLE)

1  ACCOUNT AND IDENTITY BOUNDARY                    nearly impossible to unwind
     the ONLY hard blast-radius, quota and IAM boundary AWS provides.
     one account for everything -> every resource, policy and cost report is
     built on it. Unwinding means moving everything.

2  NETWORK LAYOUT                                   very hard to change
     you cannot shrink a CIDR. Overlapping ranges cannot be peered.
     On EKS, subnet size determines POD capacity.
     Decisions made in an afternoon constrain you for years.

3  DATA STORE PER WORKLOAD                          a project to change
     decides consistency, scaling, cost curve - and MOST IMPORTANTLY,
     WHICH QUESTIONS YOU CAN ANSWER LATER.
     choosing it is a meeting; migrating it is a quarter.

4  FAILURE DOMAIN STRATEGY                          expensive to retrofit
     stated as RTO and RPO NUMBERS, not as "we are multi-AZ".
     how many zones | multi-region or not | what you are willing to lose

THE CRUCIAL SECOND HALF
  ALMOST EVERYTHING ELSE IS REVERSIBLE IN A QUARTER:
    compute choice (EC2 / ECS / EKS / Lambda)
    deployment tooling
    observability vendor
    CI system
    most managed services
  they FEEL like big decisions and they are not - the application code and the
  DATA survive them.

# WHY LEADING WITH IRREVERSIBILITY SOUNDS SENIOR
#   it reframes architecture from "which services do we use"
#                              to "which decisions must we get right first time"
#   and it tells you WHERE TO SPEND THE DESIGN EFFORT.
#   most teams spend their architecture debate on the REVERSIBLE choices,
#   and an afternoon on the IRREVERSIBLE ones.

TWO MINUTES. THEN STOP.
Follow-ups they will ask

Is compute choice really reversible?

More than it feels. Moving from EC2 to ECS or EKS is real work — weeks per service — but it is bounded, mechanical, and the application code and data are untouched. Compare that with changing your account structure or your primary datastore, which touch everything and take quarters. The point is relative, not absolute: compute is a decision you can revisit, and the account boundary is not.

What would you add as a fifth decision?

The identity model for humans — federated single sign-on with permission sets versus IAM users — because it is hard to retrofit once people have credentials and habits, and it determines how joiners and leavers are handled forever. I keep it inside the first decision because it is part of the identity boundary, but it is worth naming separately if the interviewer wants more.

How do you apply this when joining an existing estate?

Audit the four first, because they tell you what you can and cannot change. If the account structure is wrong, that is a multi-quarter programme and everything else is downstream of it. If the CIDRs overlap with on-prem, you know peering is off the table before someone proposes it. Knowing which constraints are permanent is what stops you proposing work that cannot be done.

Model answers are written to be spoken in about two minutes each. If yours runs to four, you are narrating instead of answering — lead with the conclusion, then support it.
